life.more: I keep a scrapbook of every poem a boy’s ever written me. There are eleven. Most are terrible. The Megan and vegan one is the worst and my favorite. He’s an accountant now and doesn’t write poems. I think he peaked.

life.news: A patient ground his teeth so hard he cracked a crown. He’s hiding something. They always are.
life.more: Grinding is the most honest thing about a person. He sat there telling me he sleeps like a baby. His molars said otherwise. Can’t say names. I could write a book. I won’t.

life.news: My mom lent me a romance she’s read nine times. She’s underlined the kissing.
life.more: We read the same romances. She marks the good bits in pencil and I can see where she sighed. I’ve been in love eleven times and engaged three, which she says is very efficient. She married my dad after two dates. She says when you know, you know. I believe her. Every time.

gossip.says: Anna Voss does the front desk at our practice three mornings a week. She calms every nervous patient by talking about her terrible bath novels. Nobody’s ever cried in the waiting room on her shift.
gossip.note: Megan O'Keefe says Anna Voss works on the dental practice’s front desk.
gossip.ask: Megan says you calm every nervous patient by talking about your terrible novels.
gossip.answer: Darling, a man about to have a filling doesn’t want calm. He wants a story about a duke falling in love with a lighthouse keeper. At the club I’m basically furniture, but at the dentist I’m the entertainment. It’s a promotion.

gossip.says: Ruth Calder from the Bluebirds curtsied to the mayor at her appointment. He’s our dentist. I had to leave the room to laugh.
gossip.note: Megan O'Keefe says Ruth Calder curtsied to the mayor at a dental appointment.
gossip.ask: Megan says you curtsied to the mayor at your dental appointment.
gossip.answer: He is the mayor. My mother said always curtsy to authority. She did not specify the setting. I was wearing a paper bib. It was, I admit, the least dignified curtsey of my career. I’d do it again.

gossip.says: The other Megan, Megan Torres, works in menswear and our manager mixes us up. She measures men for suits. She says you can tell a man’s character from his shoulders. I say teeth. We should open a shop.
gossip.note: Megan O'Keefe says Megan Torres reads a man’s character from his shoulders.
gossip.ask: Megan O'Keefe says you can tell a man’s character from his shoulders.
gossip.answer: Shoulders, and whether he looks in the mirror before or after he asks the price. I’d never say that out loud. Only in writing. She’d do teeth and I’d do jackets. We’d know everything about everyone. That’s frightening. Let’s do it.

own.label: Ask what she studies
own.player: What are you studying?
own.reply: History. I like the dead. They don’t text back, but they don’t ghost you either.

own.label: Ask about campus life
own.player: Is campus as tense as everyone says?
own.reply: You can’t say anything in seminars. I write what I actually think in my notebook and say something safe out loud.

own.label: Ask what she’s scared of
own.player: What scares you about leaving college?
own.reply: That I’ll get a job I hate, an apartment I can’t afford, and nobody to come home to. Everyone says you have time. Do I?

own.label: Ask what she’ll do after college
own.player: What happens after college?
own.reply: Everyone keeps asking. I have a degree in a subject I picked at eighteen and a debt I can’t picture. I’ll probably be fine. Probably.

own.label: Ask how she’s a senior at eighteen
own.player: How are you in your final year at eighteen?
own.reply: I started at sixteen on the early-entry scheme and I’ve been overlooked ever since. Being young in a seminar is like being furniture with opinions.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Who are your family?
own.reply: Dad’s a librarian at the university. Mom left for the coast when I was twelve and writes, sometimes. I learned to be quiet in libraries and it stuck everywhere else.

calls.label: Ask about her dissertation
calls.player: What’s your dissertation about?
calls.reply: The thirtieth year. The year the parish moved the founding families’ weddings from the Old Mission to St. Brigid’s, the year the bell cracked, and the year the sewing circle became a charity. Three changes in one year. Nobody writes about why.
calls.note: Emma Frost says the founding families stopped marrying at the Old Mission in the same year its bell cracked and the sewing circle became the charity.

life.news: Found a letter in the archive from a girl my age, a hundred years ago, complaining about her tutor. Same complaints.
life.more: History. I like the dead. They don’t text back, but they don’t ghost you either. She wrote to her sister that her tutor talked over everyone and wore the same vest for a whole term. I laughed out loud in the reading room. Then I copied it into my notebook.

life.news: Said the true thing in a seminar instead of the safe thing. The room went quiet. Then someone agreed.
life.more: You can’t say anything in seminars, so I write what I actually think in my notebook and say something safe out loud. Today I read from the notebook by accident. I said the sonnet was lying. The lecturer gave me a cookie. I’m still shaking.

life.news: Worked out how long it’ll take to pay back my student loan. I’ll be forty.
life.more: A degree I picked at eighteen, a debt, and a fear of a job I hate, an apartment I can’t afford and nobody to come home to. Everyone says you have time. They say it like it’s free. I’m going to make a cup of tea and not think about it until tomorrow.

life.news: Bought a kettle with my housemate. Our first big purchase. We named it.
life.more: Chloe and I boiled water in a saucepan for a week like pioneers. Today we went halves on a kettle. It’s called Margaret. We said a few words when we plugged her in. Chloe painted a little sunset on her side. She’s the best thing in the house.

gossip.says: Chloe Farrow, my housemate, paints landscapes while everyone else makes installations about their feelings. Her tutor gave her a C. She stuck it on her sketchbook like a medal.
gossip.note: Emma Frost says her housemate Chloe Farrow wears a bad grade like a medal.
gossip.ask: Emma says you stuck your C on your sketchbook like a medal.
gossip.answer: It is a medal. Beauty isn’t old-fashioned, it’s just hard. Emma says the safe thing in seminars and writes the brave thing at home. I’ve told her she should stick her notebook on the fridge. She went white.

gossip.says: Rosalie Kemp at St. Brigid’s let me read the old registers for my dissertation. She brought me tea and said nothing for three hours. Best library in Sunfall, and it’s a vestry.
gossip.note: Emma Frost says Rosalie Kemp let her research in the chapel registers.
gossip.ask: Emma says you brought her tea and said nothing for three hours.
gossip.answer: She read without speaking and turned every page by the corner. People who handle registers like that can come back whenever they like. Every name in this town is in my books somewhere. She’s looking for a year, not a name. That’s rarer.

own.label: Ask about the movie theater
own.player: What’s it like working at the movie theater?
own.reply: Free popcorn and watching the ends of films I’ve never seen the start of. I know how everything ends and nothing about how it began.

own.label: Ask about films now
own.player: Are films worse now?
own.reply: Everything is a sequel, a remake or a superhero. Nobody takes a risk any more. I miss films that trusted you to be sad.

own.label: Ask about a regular customer
own.player: Any strange regulars?
own.reply: A man buys a ticket to the late showing every night and never watches the film. He sits in the lobby facing the parking lot.

own.label: Ask which film ending she’d change
own.player: Which film ending would you change?
own.reply: None. Sad endings are the honest ones. Real life doesn’t do credits.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Brown Avenue. Dad runs a garage, my brother’s a mechanic, my sister’s still at school. Our kitchen smells of engine oil and toast.

own.label: Ask why her dad lost the Foundation
own.player: Did your dad ever lose a big customer?
own.reply: The Foundation took its cars to a garage on the ridge road instead. Dad said once that their cars came back with things in the boot he didn’t want to see. Then he changed the subject to carburettors.

calls.label: Ask what the man in the lobby is doing
calls.player: What’s the man in the lobby doing every night?
calls.reply: His name’s Ken Yamada. He built the lodge’s cellar. He sits facing the parking lot because the lodge’s van parks there for the all-night pharmacy, and he counts the men. He told me on the third coffee.
calls.note: Paige Dalton says Ken Yamada, who built the lodge’s cellar, sits in the movie theater lobby counting the men from the lodge’s van.

life.news: Watched the last ten minutes of a film I’ve never seen the start of. Cried. No idea who anyone was.
life.more: Free popcorn and the ends of films. I know how everything ends and nothing about how it began. Tonight an old man ran through an airport and I was in bits behind the counter. My manager asked if I was all right. I said, he made it! He said, who? I don’t know. But he made it.

life.news: Everything’s a sequel now. Today we showed the fourth one of something. Nobody I asked had seen the first three.
life.more: Sequels, remakes, superheroes. Somebody’s grandad came out and said, I don’t know who the blue man was but he seemed upset. Best review the movie theater’s had all year. It’s on the staff whiteboard.

life.news: My brother fixed my bike, my sister did my hair, my mom made my lunch. Brown Avenue family day.
life.more: Dad runs a garage, my brother’s a mechanic, and my sister’s at the hill school and does everyone’s hair whether they want it or not. I’m homesick for a place I’ve never left. Today I didn’t need to be. I was already in it.

life.news: Showed a film today where nobody made it. Everyone came out angry. I loved it.
life.more: Sad endings are the honest ones. Real life doesn’t wrap up. People came out saying it was depressing and I gave them extra popcorn. A woman stayed in her seat after the credits, just sitting. I sat with her. She said thank you. I don’t know what for.

gossip.says: Jessica Rivera works at the all-night pharmacy next door to the movie theater. She rehearses phone calls in the shower and says you too to waiters. I love her.
gossip.note: Paige Dalton says Jessica Rivera at the pharmacy next door rehearses phone calls.
gossip.ask: Paige says you say you too to waiters.
gossip.answer: Only once! Okay, often. He said enjoy your meal and I panicked. Paige brings me leftover popcorn at the end of her shift and I bring her bandages for her popcorn burns. It’s a very good arrangement. Please don’t tell her about the shower.

gossip.says: Khadija Rahman borrows our old film reels for her slapstick nights. She brings them back with popcorn in the canisters. Every time. I think it’s on purpose.
gossip.note: Paige Dalton says Khadija Rahman borrows the movie theater’s old reels.
gossip.ask: Paige says you always bring the reels back with popcorn in the canisters.
gossip.answer: It’s a tip. Old comedies, popcorn, a full hall. The reels deserve a little treat after a night like that. Paige knows the end of every film and the start of none. I’ve offered to show her a whole one, beginning to end. She’s nervous.

own.label: Ask about planning events
own.player: What’s the worst event you’ve planned?
own.reply: A gender reveal where the cannon set fire to a hedge. The baby’s fine. The hedge is not.

own.label: Ask about the wedding industry
own.player: Are weddings out of control?
own.reply: Couples spend a year’s salary on one day and then can’t afford the marriage. I tell them: spend less on the flowers, more on the counseling.

own.label: Ask about the gala set-up
own.player: Did you work on the gala?
own.reply: I set up the tables. Table 9 was moved twice on the day, closer to the kitchen. Nobody would tell me why.
own.note: Nicole Ashbury says Table 9 was moved closer to the kitchen twice on gala day.

own.label: Ask what her own wedding would be like
own.player: What would your own wedding be like?
own.reply: Small. A church, a dress that fits, and nobody filming. I’ve planned two hundred weddings for other people and every one of them was for the camera.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you married?
own.reply: To a sound engineer at the Vestry. Two children who think the benefit is where Mommy goes to shout at florists. They’re not wrong.

own.label: Ask how she got into events
own.player: How did you get into events?
own.reply: Mom ran the late-service crew at the club for years. I grew up stacking chairs with the volunteers at midnight. Mom still knows every waitress in Sunfall by name.

calls.label: Ask about the day’s seating plan
calls.player: Do you still have the real seating plan?
calls.reply: Not the published one. The day’s, with the two moves of Table 9 in my handwriting and the times, and the man who told me to do it: Dorian Kell. The volunteer who asked me why was wearing a badge that said Elena.
calls.note: Nicole Ashbury’s seating plan shows Dorian Kell ordered Table 9 moved, and the volunteer who asked why wore a badge saying Elena.

calls.label: Ask if her mother knows the catering crew
calls.player: Does your mom know the late-service crew?
calls.reply: Every one. She knows who R.M. is: Ruth Marchetti. And she knows where Ruth went. She says she’ll tell nobody. She told me.
calls.note: Nicole Ashbury says R.M. is Ruth Marchetti of the late-service crew, and her mother knows where Ruth went.

life.news: Gender reveal today. The cannon set fire to a hedge. The baby’s fine. The hedge is not.
life.more: Every event goes slightly wrong and turns out fine. This one went very wrong and turned out on fire. The fire brigade came and the grandad asked if they could do the reveal instead. They did. It’s a girl. The hedge is a memory.

life.news: A couple spent a year’s wages on one day. They argued at the cake. I gave them a counselor’s card.
life.more: Couples who spend a year’s salary on one day and can’t afford the marriage. Spend more on counseling. I mean it. I’ve started tucking a card into the order of service. Two have rung. One canceled the wedding. That’s a success.

life.news: A bride’s dress split at the back and I sewed her into it in the parking lot with dental floss. She danced all night.
life.more: You learn to carry a kit: safety pins, bandages, dental floss and a tiny bottle of brandy. The floss held through the conga. She sent me a thank-you card with a drawing of dental floss on it. Framed.

life.news: Two hundred weddings for other people. Today I let myself plan my own, in my head, for five minutes.
life.more: Small. A church, a dress that fits, and nobody filming. That’s all I want. After two hundred, that’s what I’ve learned. The quiet ones last. The ones with a string quartet and a drone are lovely, and then they’re in my office asking about counselors.

gossip.says: Julia Mercer makes all my wedding cakes and predicts who’ll last by how they use their forks. She’s never been wrong. I’ve started booking her for the tastings just to know.
gossip.note: Nicole Ashbury says Julia Mercer predicts marriages from the cake tasting.
gossip.ask: Nicole says you’ve never been wrong about which couples will last.
gossip.answer: Never! Well, once. A couple used two forks and they’ve been married forty years. But they were both left-handed, so it doesn’t count. Nicole books me early now. She says it saves her a lot of seating plans.

gossip.says: Tiffany Nash does the after-parties at my weddings. She makes everyone feel like the main character for an hour, then disappears with the leftover champagne.
gossip.note: Nicole Ashbury says Tiffany Nash runs the after-parties at her weddings.
gossip.ask: Nicole says you disappear with the leftover champagne.
gossip.answer: Babe, it’s a fee. Unspoken. Nicole knows. I make the third hour the best hour of the wedding, and the champagne makes the fourth hour mine. Everybody’s happy. Everybody’s slightly drunk. That’s a wedding.

gossip.says: Phoebe Sutton and I grew up stacking chairs at the club. Her family were staff who were allowed to call themselves members. Mine were caterers. We still stack chairs together. Neither of us has ever said it’s funny.
gossip.note: Nicole Ashbury says she and Phoebe Sutton grew up stacking chairs at the club.
gossip.ask: Nicole says you two grew up stacking chairs at the club.
gossip.answer: It’s always the same five women stacking the chairs. When we were kids, it was us. Now it’s me and the nuns. Nicole still comes and helps after her own events. She doesn’t have to. She does. That’s the whole story of the club, really.

own.label: Ask about the rodeo
own.player: What’s the rodeo like?
own.reply: Dust, beer and men who think they can ride a bull. Some of them can. Most of them are brave in a way that’s mostly stupid.

own.label: Ask if she rides
own.player: Do you ride?
own.reply: Since I was four. Horses are honest. They know if you’re scared before you do.

own.label: Ask about real cowboys
own.player: Are there real cowboys left?
own.reply: A few. They don’t own phones and they hold doors. My grandpa was one. I’m still waiting for one my age.

own.label: Ask about her worst fall
own.player: What was your worst fall?
own.reply: Broke my wrist at sixteen. Got back on the next season. My dad said the horse doesn’t care about your feelings, and he was right.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A room at the Whitlock ranch. I work the horses with Isabel and ride the canyon road. I tell the collision lady which days the gray car is on it.

own.label: Ask about her grandfather
own.player: Who’s the old cowboy?
own.reply: My grandpa Buck. Real cowboy, no teeth, laughs like a door. He rode with Diana Moore’s first husband and was in the arena the day the bull killed him.

calls.label: Ask what her grandfather says about the bull
calls.player: What does your grandpa say about that day?
calls.reply: That the bull wasn’t the bull Tommy drew. It was swapped in the chute by the stock contractor, whose business the casino bought the next year. And Tommy’s widow was taken to lunch at the funeral by a lady from the club.
calls.note: Audrey King’s grandfather says the bull that killed Tommy Moore was swapped in the chute.

life.news: Sold four hundred rodeo tickets today. Dust, beer and men who think they can ride a bull.
life.more: Some of them can. Most of them are brave in a way that’s mostly stupid. A man in brand-new boots told me he’d ride anything. Then he saw the bull. He bought a beer and a program and watched from the top row. Smart man. Bad boots.

life.news: A horse knew I was scared before I did today. Horses are honest. I’m not, apparently.
life.more: I got on a new mare at the ranch and she stood very still and looked back at me like, really? I hadn’t even felt it yet. Then I did. I got off, had a cup of tea, got back on. She let me. Horses don’t care about your feelings, Dad says. They notice them, though.

life.news: Grandpa told the Tommy Moore story again. He tells it better every year.
life.more: He rode with Tommy Moore, the bravest stupid man he ever knew. Tonight Tommy rode a bull backwards and kissed a judge, which last year was a horse forwards and a wave. I don’t correct him. Real cowboys are mostly stories now. I like the stories.

life.news: My wrist ached today. The one I broke at sixteen. It always knows when the weather’s turning.
life.more: Got back on the next season. Dad said the horse doesn’t care about your feelings, so get back on before you have too many. It’s good advice for most things. The wrist is my weather forecast now. Rain in two days. I’m never wrong.

gossip.says: Isabel Morales and I work the horses at the ranch together. She’s so patient she makes me feel like a firework. She says you can’t force trust. I say you can bribe it with apples.
gossip.note: Audrey King says she and Isabel Morales work the ranch’s horses together.
gossip.ask: Audrey says you can’t force trust, but she thinks you can bribe it with apples.
gossip.answer: Apples get you to the gate. Being the same every day gets you through it. Audrey’s brave in a way that’s mostly loud. The horses love her anyway. She keeps apples in her pockets and forgets, and they find them. That’s trust, I suppose.

gossip.says: My grandpa rings a girl from the Daily on her birthday every year. Celina Rojas. Her boss took his picture once. He says she’s the only one who listens to the whole story.
gossip.note: Audrey King says her grandfather rings Celina Rojas every birthday.
gossip.ask: Audrey says her grandpa calls you every birthday.
gossip.answer: Buck! No relation to Catalina, I always have to say. He rang last week for no reason at all and told me about a horse he loved. Forty minutes. I didn’t want it to stop. Tell Audrey her grandpa is the best phone call I get all year.

gossip.says: Caroline Prescott from the Bluebirds lost to me at arm-wrestling at a charity fair. She comes to my ticket booth every season and asks for a rematch. She’d win. That’s why I say no.
gossip.note: Audrey King says Caroline Prescott keeps asking her for an arm-wrestling rematch.
gossip.ask: Audrey says you’d win a rematch, which is why she won’t give you one.
gossip.answer: At last, an honest woman. Taking part is what losers call it. I lost fairly, which I’m told builds character. I’d like to build it back down. She sells me a ticket every season with a smirk. I’ll get her one day.

own.label: Ask about the library
own.player: What’s the library like?
own.reply: Quiet, cool, and full of the only people in Sunfall who still read for pleasure. We’re a secret society with late fees.

own.label: Ask about banned books
own.player: Do people try to ban books?
own.reply: From both sides! One group wants to ban the old novels, another wants to ban the new ones. I keep both and hide the complaints in the returns box.

own.label: Ask what’s been borrowed
own.player: Has anyone borrowed anything strange?
own.reply: Someone’s taken out every book we have on moon cycles and old Latin rites. Always the same library card. It belongs to a man who died last year.
own.note: Someone is borrowing every library book on moon cycles and Latin rites on a dead man’s card.

own.label: Ask why libraries matter
own.player: Why do libraries still matter?
own.reply: Because they’re the last place in town where you can sit for free and nobody tries to sell you anything. That’s rarer than gold now.

own.label: Ask about her sisters
own.player: Are you close to your sisters?
own.reply: Odette does the radio, Samantha sells houses, I keep the library. Once a week we meet here and argue. I run the quietest room in Sunfall and I’m the loudest person in it.

own.label: Ask what the library is really for
own.player: What is a library really for?
own.reply: A secret society with late fees. The last place in town you can sit for free and nobody sells you anything. Both sides have tried to ban things. I lend them all.

views.dispute: Priya at the parish reading room and I swap the books we’re not allowed to stock. The council wants her room closed and the diocese wants her land reviewed, in the same month. I’m a librarian. I notice when two letters have the same handwriting.

calls.label: Ask about the books on the dead man’s card
calls.player: Who borrows the books on moon cycles?
calls.reply: Every one, on the same card. Harold Oakley’s. He died last year. His grandson Ethan uses it. Moon cycles, Latin rites, the old mission. I lend them, because I lend everything. But I’ve started writing the dates down.
calls.note: Bethany Price says Ethan Oakley borrows books on moon cycles and Latin rites on his late grandfather’s library card.

life.news: A boy returned a book forty years overdue. His grandad’s. He paid the fine in coins from a jar. I nearly cried.
life.more: We’re a secret society with late fees. The fine came to more than the book’s worth. I took one coin, gave him the rest back, and gave him a library card of his own. He asked if he could take out the same book. Reader, he could.

life.news: One side wants a book banned and the other side wants it promoted. Both are cross with me. Good week.
life.more: The library is the last place in Sunfall where you can sit for free and nobody sells you anything. I’ve put the book on the display table between a cookbook and a book about owls. Let them fight the owls.

life.news: Argued with my sisters for two hours about whether toast is a meal. Toast is a meal.
life.more: Odette from the radio says it isn’t. Samantha from the houses says it depends on the toppings. I say if you sit down to it, it’s a meal. We meet once a week to argue about everything. We’ll be arguing about toast at ninety.

life.news: The council cut the library’s hours again. One less evening. The old men will have nowhere to go.
life.more: Students, old men, and a woman who comes in every day just to sit by the radiator and read the paper. I’ve written a letter. I’ve written a stronger letter. Next I’m writing a poem, which is the nuclear option.

gossip.says: My sister Odette Price works at Sunfall FM and plays our grandad’s old shipping forecast tapes when she can’t sleep. She says it’s the best lullaby there is. It’s about the North Sea. We live in a desert.
gossip.note: Bethany Price says her sister Odette Price falls asleep to their grandfather’s shipping forecast tapes.
gossip.ask: Bethany says you fall asleep to shipping forecasts in a desert.
gossip.answer: Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. He read it every night for thirty years and nobody in the desert needed it. That’s what makes it beautiful. Bethany falls asleep to audiobooks about murder. Which of us is the strange one?

gossip.says: Priya Nair at the parish reading room and I swap the books we’re not allowed to stock. We meet at the Lucky Cactus with tote bags and look shifty. Very nearly smuggling.
gossip.note: Bethany Price says she and Priya Nair swap books between their libraries.
gossip.ask: Bethany says you two meet at the Lucky Cactus with tote bags and look shifty.
gossip.answer: We do look shifty. Bethany wears sunglasses. It’s very obvious. I catalog everything, including the smuggled ones, under a heading I won’t tell you. The radiator in the reading room sang the whole time she was there once. It likes her.

gossip.says: Keiko Nakamura from the police sits in my top window after closing. She eats the ginger nuts first. Always the ginger nuts.
gossip.note: Bethany Price says Keiko Nakamura reads in her library window after closing.
gossip.ask: Bethany says you always eat the ginger nuts first.
gossip.answer: Ginger nuts are the most efficient cookie. They don’t crumble on the paperwork. I didn’t know she’d noticed. I find the pattern in the noise. She found the pattern in my cookies. That’s fair.

own.label: Ask about lifeguarding
own.player: Is lifeguarding as easy as it looks?
own.reply: It’s eight hours of watching people almost drown and then not. I’ve saved four children and one very proud businessman.

own.label: Ask about influencers at the pool
own.player: Do influencers come to the pool?
own.reply: Every day. They film themselves living their best life for forty minutes and never touch the water.

own.label: Ask about night swimmers
own.player: Does anyone swim at night?
own.reply: The club pool. On the gala night someone threw a phone in the deep end. I fished it out the next morning. It’s in the lost property box. Nobody’s claimed it.
own.note: Erin Doyle found a phone thrown in the club pool on gala night; it’s unclaimed in lost property.

own.label: Ask about the one she saved
own.player: Have you ever actually saved someone?
own.reply: A little boy, my first summer. His mom was filming a video for her followers. She never thanked me. She posted the video.

own.label: Ask if she’s a member of the club
own.player: Are you a member at the club?
own.reply: Staff, not a member. I say it before anyone else can. Mom cleans there, which is how I got the pool. It’s the only thing at the club I have that she cleans.

own.label: Ask who she lives with
own.player: Do you live alone?
own.reply: With Georgina, who coaches swimming. We swam county together. I beat her on the shout and she’s never let it go. We get on brilliantly.

calls.label: Ask what was on the phone from the pool
calls.player: Did you ever turn that phone on?
calls.reply: I did. The lock screen is a blue dress on a hanger, next to a notebook. It’s Elena Cross’s, or it was. It’s locked, and it’s in the lost-property box in the plant room. Someone else has the key.
calls.note: Erin Doyle says the phone fished out of the club pool is Elena Cross’s, kept in the plant room’s lost property.

calls.label: Ask about the boy she saved
calls.player: Who was the little boy you saved?
calls.reply: Celeste Van Doren’s grandson. His mom’s the influencer who filmed it. The video has a hundred thousand views and my face in it, and since then the club has asked me to be discreet about the pool.

life.news: Pulled a very proud businessman out of the deep end again. He said he was swimming. He was not swimming.
life.more: Eight hours of watching people almost drown and then not. He did a dive to impress someone and forgot the part where you come back up. I got him to the side. He said, thank you, I had it. He didn’t have it. Nobody ever has it.

life.news: An influencer did a whole photo shoot at the pool and never touched the water. Four hours. Not one toe.
life.more: She had a lilo, sunglasses and a ring light. Her friend took two thousand photos. When they left, I swam a length just to make the water feel useful. Influencers who never swim. I’m counting them. Eleven this summer.

life.news: The first boy I ever saved is eleven now. His mom filmed it and never thanked me. I saw the video again today.
life.more: My first summer. Thousands of views and my face in it, and she never once said thank you. I don’t need thanks. But I’d like the boy to know a person pulled him out, not a phone. He’s fine. That’s what matters. Mostly.

life.news: Swam at dawn before the pool opened. Catherine Bell was there too. We nodded. Perfect conversation.
life.more: She plays tennis like she’s angry at it and swims like she’s thinking. We’ve been nodding at each other at dawn for a year and never spoken. If we ever speak, it’ll ruin it. Best friendship I’ve got.

gossip.says: Catherine Bell swims at dawn at the club pool. We nod at each other every morning. A year of nodding. If she ever speaks to me, I’ll have to change pools.
gossip.note: Erin Doyle says Catherine Bell swims at dawn and the two of them have only ever nodded.
gossip.ask: Erin says you two have nodded every morning for a year and never spoken.
gossip.answer: It’s the best relationship I have. She’s the only person at the club who doesn’t want anything from me at dawn. If she spoke I’d have to answer. Tell her I nodded at you. That counts.

gossip.says: Tiffany Nash throws pool parties and hires me to stop her guests drowning. She pays well and on time, which in this town makes her a saint in a sequinned bikini.
gossip.note: Erin Doyle says Tiffany Nash hires her to lifeguard pool parties.
gossip.ask: Erin says you’re a saint in a sequinned bikini because you pay on time.
gossip.answer: Finally, someone appreciates my admin. Erin sits up in the high chair all night stone-cold sober and judges everyone, and she’s always right. Last party she blew the whistle at a man’s personality. He went home.

own.label: Ask about office life
own.player: What’s office life like?
own.reply: Endless meetings about meetings. I run the place and nobody knows it. Without me the coffee machine and the printer would both have died years ago.

own.label: Ask what she does to escape
own.player: What do you do to escape?
own.reply: Motorcycle, desert roads, no helmet camera. If I fall off, at least it won’t be online.

own.label: Ask about working from home
own.player: Do you ever wish you worked from home?
own.reply: Never. My friends who work from home talk to their cats more than people. An office is annoying. Loneliness is worse.

own.label: Ask what she’d do if she quit
own.player: What would you do if you quit tomorrow?
own.reply: Drive to the coast and open a bait shop. I’ve never fished. I just want a job where nobody sends me a calendar invite.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you one of the Lucky Cactus Brookses?
own.reply: Dolores’s third girl, Christina’s twin. Four sisters running a diner in shifts and fighting about the booth. I do the weekday accounts. Nobody else can add.

own.label: Ask about her motorcycle
own.player: Where do you ride?
own.reply: Desert roads, no helmet camera. If I fall off, at least it won’t be online. Out past the canyon the road’s so straight you can hear yourself think.

calls.label: Ask about the planning files she copied
calls.player: What’s in the planning files?
calls.reply: Three files. A canal-side variance for the diocese and a consultancy on the ridge. The ridge road leased to a trust. And the weigh station at the junction: the county owns it, the trust rents it. The mayor’s signature is on all three. I copied them on the printer I keep alive.
calls.note: Kimberly Brooks copied planning files showing the mayor signed the trust’s ridge-road lease and its lease of the weigh station.

calls.label: Ask about the circles in the office diary
calls.player: Why do you draw circles in the office diary?
calls.reply: The mayor’s committee only ever meets on nights with no moon. I started drawing a little circle in the margin each time. The next one’s {night}.

life.news: Sat in a meeting about the meeting about the meeting. Nobody noticed I’d already done the thing they were meeting about.
life.more: I run the place and nobody knows it. Without me the coffee machine and the printer would both have died years ago. Today the printer jammed during the big presentation and I fixed it with a paperclip and a look. Nobody clapped. The printer knew.

life.news: Rode the motorcycle out past the canyon at dawn. Nobody filmed it. Nobody will.
life.more: Desert roads and no helmet camera. If I fall off, at least it won’t be online. The road goes straight for twenty miles and the light comes up behind you like it’s chasing. I stopped at a gas station that sells one kind of crisp. Perfect morning.

life.news: Did the diner’s accounts. We’re fine. Mom would’ve done them faster and swearing.
life.more: Four sisters run the Lucky Cactus in shifts since Mom died, and I do the books because I’m the one who can. She ran it forty years on a pencil and a temper. I find her old notes in the margins. One says: Hollis owes us a pie. He still does.

life.news: Looked at a bait shop for sale on the coast. I’ve never fished. I want it anyway.
life.more: Drive to the coast and open a bait shop. That’s the plan, one day. I’ve never fished in my life. I just like the idea of a shop where everyone who comes in is about to be patient for six hours. That’s the opposite of my office.

gossip.says: Madison Pike waits tables at our diner and remembers every order anyone’s ever made. She named the jukebox after my mom. I pretend to mind. I don’t.
gossip.note: Kimberly Brooks says Madison Pike named the diner’s jukebox after her mother.
gossip.ask: Kimberly says you named the jukebox after her mom.
gossip.answer: Dolores! It only works when you kick it and it plays whatever it likes, which is exactly how the regulars describe her. I asked first. Kimberly said absolutely not and then laughed for a whole minute. That’s a yes, in Brooks.

gossip.says: Harper Lin at the paper once hid a serious story about the council next to a headline about a goat eating the mayor’s speech. Everyone read the goat. I read the story. Clever woman.
gossip.note: Kimberly Brooks says Harper Lin hid a council story beside the goat headline.
gossip.ask: Kimberly says you hid a serious story next to the goat headline.
gossip.answer: People only read the crossword and the goats, so I put the serious story next to them. It’s the only way. Kimberly’s one of the nine people who reads the story. I can tell, because she writes in to correct the figures. She’s always right.

gossip.says: Olivia Reid sells houses and files everything through our office. She describes every apartment like a film genre. Her paperwork is immaculate and her descriptions are crimes.
gossip.note: Kimberly Brooks says Olivia Reid’s house sales go through her office.
gossip.ask: Kimberly says your paperwork is immaculate and your descriptions are crimes.
gossip.answer: Fair. Cozy means you can touch both walls. Up-and-coming means bring a dog. Kimberly reads every form I send and leaves little notes in the margins like, liar. She’s the only person in that building who reads anything. I love her for it.

own.label: Ask about the ice-cream van
own.player: What’s it like driving an ice-cream van?
own.reply: Everyone’s happy to see you. It’s the only job where that’s true. Except the dentists. They glare.

own.label: Ask her favorite flavor
own.player: What’s your favorite flavor?
own.reply: Prickly pear sorbet. It tastes like Sunfall: sweet, pink and slightly dangerous.

own.label: Ask what she sees on her route
own.player: Do you see much driving around all day?
own.reply: A gray car follows the same route as me some days, slowly, like it’s looking for someone. It doesn’t buy ice cream. People who don’t buy ice cream are suspicious.
own.note: Grace Wheeler sees a gray car slowly driving her ice-cream route, as if looking for someone.

own.label: Ask what kids teach her
own.player: What do the kids on your route teach you?
own.reply: That joy is cheap. Two dollars and a cone. The grown-ups line with their phones out and never look up.

own.label: Ask who had the van before her
own.player: Did someone run the van before you?
own.reply: My grandma, forty years. She sold ice cream to the club children at the gate and was never once let in. She kept a route book of every stop. I inherited it with the chime.

own.label: Ask what the van is called
own.player: Does the van have a name?
own.reply: Dolores, like the jukebox, because the Brooks girls let me park at the Lucky Cactus. It plays one tune and breaks down on hills. It’s perfect.

calls.label: Ask about her grandmother’s route book
calls.player: What’s in your grandma’s route book?
calls.reply: Forty years of stops, and the names of the club children. By the stop at the Cemetery Chapel she wrote: the ribbon children. Two scoops. Never charged. I don’t understand it. I think she did.
calls.note: Grace Wheeler’s grandmother’s route book calls the children by the Cemetery Chapel the ribbon children, never charged.

calls.label: Ask about the gray car
calls.player: Did you ever get the gray car’s number?
calls.reply: I wrote the plate on a cone wrapper and gave it to a policewoman from the archive. Kelsey. She thanked me and put it in her pocket. I haven’t heard anything since.
calls.note: Grace Wheeler gave the gray car’s license plate to Kelsey Donovan, and heard nothing more.

life.news: Sold the last prickly pear sorbet of the day to a little boy who’d saved coins all week. Gave him two scoops.
life.more: Everyone’s happy to see you. It’s the only job where that’s true. Except the dentists. They glare. He counted his coins out on the counter one by one, very seriously. It was exactly enough for one. Joy is two dollars and a cone. Sometimes it’s two cones.

life.news: The van’s chimes got stuck on one note for the whole route. Children followed me like I was the pied piper.
life.more: I’ve named the van Dolores, like the jukebox at the diner, because they both only work properly when you hit them. Today she just sang one long note for three streets. A dog howled along. I sold more ice cream than ever. I’m keeping it broken.

life.news: Ran out of cones halfway through the route. Had to serve sorbet in teacups. My grandmother would be horrified.
life.more: She ran this van for forty years before me and never ran out of anything. She sold to the club children at the gate and was never once let in. I found her route book in the glovebox. Every stop, every child’s name. I think about her at every corner.

life.news: Invented a new flavor. Lemon and cactus flower. A man cried. Good cried.
life.more: Prickly pear tastes like Sunfall: sweet, pink and slightly dangerous. This one tastes like Sunfall after rain. The man said it reminded him of his wedding. I didn’t ask how. I gave him a second one free. That’s the job.

gossip.says: Eliza Montoya lives two doors down from me on Brown Avenue. She runs the food pantry and never makes anyone feel small. I give her the broken cones for the kids who come in.
gossip.note: Grace Wheeler says she gives Eliza Montoya’s food pantry her broken ice-cream cones.
gossip.ask: Grace says she gives you the broken cones for the pantry children.
gossip.answer: Every week. The children think broken cones are a special kind, so we call them pantry cones and they’re the most popular thing we have. Grace never says it’s charity. She says, I’ve got too many, help me out. That’s the right way to give.

gossip.says: Madison Pike won’t let me park the van outside the Lucky Cactus because she says the chimes make the regulars order dessert. Bad for business. Good for dessert.
gossip.note: Grace Wheeler says Madison Pike won’t let her park the van outside the diner.
gossip.ask: Grace says you won’t let her park outside the Lucky Cactus.
gossip.answer: Because everyone runs out to her van and nobody orders pie! I’ve got pie quotas! She parks around the corner now and I bring her a coffee and she brings me a sorbet, and that’s our treaty. It’s holding. Mostly.

own.label: Ask about training horses
own.player: How do you train a horse?
own.reply: Patience. You can’t force trust, only earn it. People could learn a lot from horses.

own.label: Ask about the ranch
own.player: Where do you work?
own.reply: A ranch out past the canyon, owned by a family that’s been here five generations. The developers keep offering. The old man keeps saying no.

own.label: Ask about family
own.player: Do you want a family?
own.reply: A big one. Kids, horses, a long table, too much noise. My friends think that’s quaint. I think it’s the whole point.

own.label: Ask how a horse learns to trust
own.player: How does a horse learn to trust you?
own.reply: Slowly, and only if you’re the same every day. Horses can’t be flattered. Neither can I.

own.label: Ask about the ranch house
own.player: What’s it like living at the ranch?
own.reply: A long table with too much noise. The old man, his grandson Jesse, Audrey from the rodeo and me. Every dinner is an argument about horses and land and who left the gate open.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mom like?
own.reply: She died when I was seventeen, of a thing they caught late. Inez got her politics from that. I got my patience. Same grief, different directions.

calls.label: Ask if anyone at the ranch is in trouble
calls.player: Is anyone at the ranch in trouble?
calls.reply: Jesse, the old man’s grandson. He was in love with Alice Beaumont and wasn’t approved. Now he rides the fastest horse up the ridge road at night, alone, and comes back before dawn. I haven’t told his grandfather.
calls.note: Isabel Morales says Jesse Whitlock rides up the ridge road alone at night since the club refused him.

life.news: The gray mare let me put a saddle on her for the first time. Three months of patience. Three months.
life.more: Patience. You can’t force trust, only earn it. Every morning, same time, same voice, same apple. Today she stood still and let me. I didn’t even ride her. I just stood there with my hand on her neck. That was the whole point.

life.news: Another man in a suit drove up to the ranch today. The old man said no before he got out of the car.
life.more: Five generations on this land and the developers keep offering. Old man Whitlock keeps a tally on the kitchen door. He didn’t even let this one open his door. He just stood on the porch shaking his head. The man reversed all the way down the track.

life.news: Long table at the ranch tonight. Too much noise, too much food. My favorite kind of evening.
life.more: Everyone shouting over everyone, Audrey telling a rodeo story that gets bigger every time, Naomi correcting her figures, the old man pretending to be asleep. I grew up in a big loud family and I found another one. I’m lucky.

life.news: My dad’s back is bad again. He won’t stop shoeing horses. Inez and I argued about it for an hour.
life.more: He’s a farrier, the stubbornest man in the canyon. Inez says make him rest. I say you can’t make a horse do anything and he’s basically a horse. We argue every night on the phone. It’s how we say we love each other.

gossip.says: My sister Inez Morales runs a student co-op and organizes everyone. She says she organizes people and I train horses, and it’s the same job. She’s not wrong. Don’t tell her.
gossip.note: Isabel Morales says her sister Inez Morales runs a student co-op.
gossip.ask: Isabel says you organize people and she trains horses, and it’s the same job.
gossip.answer: It IS the same job. You can’t force anyone, you just turn up every day and don’t flinch. She says it about horses, I say it about landlords. We ring every night and fight about our dad. Tell her I said she’s right. Then run.

gossip.says: Audrey King works the horses with me and keeps apples in her pockets and forgets them. The horses find them. She thinks they love her. They love the apples. Same thing, really.
gossip.note: Isabel Morales says Audrey King keeps forgetting apples in her pockets for the horses.
gossip.ask: Isabel says the horses love your apples more than they love you.
gossip.answer: Rude. True, probably. Horses are honest. They know if you’re scared before you do, and they know where the apples are before you do too. Isabel’s so patient it’s frightening. I’m the firework. She’s the fence post. We work.

gossip.says: Rachel Lowe from the vet’s comes out to the ranch and talks to the horses like they’re her friends. Her dad was the county vet for thirty years. The old horses remember him in her.
gossip.note: Isabel Morales says Rachel Lowe the vet’s assistant reminds the old horses of her father.
gossip.ask: Isabel says the old horses remember your dad in you.
gossip.answer: That’s the nicest thing anyone’s said to me this year. Dad did the ranch for thirty years. The old bay still puts his head down for me the way he did for Dad. Animals bite you honestly. They also remember honestly. Tell Isabel thank you.

own.label: Ask about the flower shop
own.player: What’s it like running a flower shop?
own.reply: Quiet, mostly. People only buy flowers when something big happens: love, death, apology. I see the whole town’s heart.

own.label: Ask about the meaning of flowers
own.player: Do flowers still mean things?
own.reply: They used to. Red roses for love, yellow for friendship. Now people just want whatever photographs well.

own.label: Ask about a strange order
own.player: Have you had any strange orders?
own.reply: White lilies, every few days, delivered to the old interstate junction. No card. Paid in cash. Lilies are for funerals.
own.note: Elena Vargas delivers white lilies to the old interstate junction every few days, paid in cash, no card.

own.label: Ask which flower lasts longest
own.player: Which flower lasts the longest?
own.reply: Chrysanthemums. People think they’re funeral flowers. They are. They’re also the ones still standing when the roses have gone.

own.label: Ask about her flower dictionaries
own.player: Do flowers really mean things?
own.reply: I’ve a shelf of flower dictionaries. Red for love, yellow for friendship. Now people just want whatever photographs well. The flowers still mean it, even if nobody reads them.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Did your family grow flowers?
own.reply: Dad kept the Bluebird Club’s grounds for twenty years, until the lodge’s men took over the planting. He said once they planted lilies at the Cemetery Chapel on the club’s instructions. He doesn’t garden any more.

calls.label: Ask who sends the lilies
calls.player: Who sends the lilies to the junction?
calls.reply: The cash comes through my door in an envelope with no name. Twice I’ve seen the woman who posts it: tall, a creased white linen suit, sleepy eyes. She waits until it’s through, then walks to the reservoir side. A widow, I think. I don’t know whose.
calls.note: Elena Vargas says the lilies for the old junction are paid for by a tall widow in a white linen suit from the reservoir side.

life.news: A man came in to buy flowers for a first date and asked me what each one meant. We were there an hour.
life.more: People only buy flowers when something big happens: love, death, apology. I see the whole town’s heart. He wanted to say I’m nervous but I mean it. I gave him sweet peas and one yellow tulip. He went out holding them like they might go off.

life.news: Made three funeral wreaths today and one wedding bouquet. The wedding was the hardest. The bride was crying, and not the good kind.
life.more: I’m quiet, mostly. People think I don’t notice. I notice everything about flowers and the hands holding them. Her hands were shaking. I put a sprig of rosemary in the bouquet, for remembrance, without telling her. I hope she remembers who she is.

life.news: The same order came again today. Lilies, cash, no card. Delivered to the same lonely place.
life.more: White lilies, every few days, for years. Lilies are for funerals. The envelope comes through the door with the money and an address and nothing else. I always choose the best ones. Whoever they’re for, somebody still loves them very much.

life.news: My chrysanthemums outlasted every rose in the shop. Again. Nobody believes me about chrysanthemums.
life.more: People think they’re funeral flowers. They’re the ones still standing when the roses have gone. I put a jar of them on the counter with a sign saying, still here. A woman bought the whole jar. She said she needed the sign more than the flowers.

gossip.says: Brittany Hale has the other flower shop and we share a wholesaler and a van. She says she sells more sorry than love. Men come in on the way home after doing something stupid. She can tell what they did from what they buy.
gossip.note: Elena Vargas says Brittany Hale can tell what a man did from the flowers he buys.
gossip.ask: Elena says you can tell what a man did from the flowers he buys.
gossip.answer: Roses, he forgot something. Lilies, he’s in real trouble. A mixed bunch from the bucket by the door, he hasn’t even noticed there’s a problem. I sell more sorry than love. Elena does the opposite. She’s gentler than me. Her flowers are too.

gossip.says: Agnes Castillo grows the roses for the chapel altar and asks my advice, then ignores it, then her roses are better than mine. I don’t know how she does it. She says prayer. I think it’s stubbornness.
gossip.note: Elena Vargas says Agnes Castillo grows the chapel’s altar roses.
gossip.ask: Elena says your altar roses are better than hers and you ignore her advice.
gossip.answer: Roses if you’re stubborn. Prickly pear if you’re sensible. Elena gives very good advice and I listen to every word and then do what my grandmother did. Things that wait grow best. Her lilies are better than anything I grow. Tell her that.

gossip.says: Natalie Cross and I both get asked if we’re related to someone with our name. Everyone asks her about her surname and me about my first name. We had a coffee once and laughed about it. Mostly.
gossip.note: Elena Vargas says she and Natalie Cross both get asked about their names.
gossip.ask: Elena says you two both get asked whether you’re related to somebody.
gossip.answer: Same surname for me, same first name for her, different towns, different people. We sat in a café and listed everyone who’d asked. Forty-one between us. Then we stopped laughing, because it’s not really funny, is it. But it was a good coffee.

own.label: Ask about cosmetology
own.player: What’s cosmetology school like?
own.reply: Doing eyebrows on mannequins called Brenda. I’ve made Brenda beautiful forty times. She never thanks me.

own.label: Ask about everyone looking the same
own.player: Why does everyone online have the same face?
own.reply: Same filters, same fillers, same three tutorials. I want to teach women to look like themselves, just more.

own.label: Ask about her love life
own.player: Are you a romantic?
own.reply: Completely. I want flowers, a slow dance and someone who looks at me like I’m the only person in the room. Apparently that’s a lot.

own.label: Ask what she thinks is beautiful
own.player: What do you think is actually beautiful?
own.reply: Faces that look like someone. Everyone at school wants the same face from the same filter. My nana’s face had eighty years in it. That was beautiful.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have a twin?
own.reply: Imogen. She’s loud where I’m soft. She works at the radio and paints Brown Avenue. Our big sister Catalina is the brave one, at the club. We all three look the same and nothing alike.

own.label: Ask about the photo above her mirror
own.player: Whose photo is above your mirror?
own.reply: My nana. She raised us. Her face had eighty years in it. When I do someone’s make-up I think: let them look like that, one day.

own.label: Ask about her nan’s pew
own.player: Did your nana have a pew at St. Brigid’s?
own.reply: Third from the front on the left, under the window with the cloak. Eighty years in it. The parish office rang to say the chancery wants a list of who sits where at the first-light Mass. Mom said over her dead body, and then said sorry, because nana only just died. The pew is still ours. I sit in it so it isn’t empty when the bishop’s man counts.

calls.label: Ask if she’s seen anything odd on Hinge
calls.player: Seen anything odd on the app?
calls.reply: A profile with your name under it and your pictures. Except one, where the eyes are wrong. I know those eyes. I did that face for a student show at seventeen. A boy called Theon. Someone’s wearing you.
calls.note: Camila Reyes recognized Theon’s eyes in a Hinge profile that uses your name and pictures.

calls.label: Ask about her sister’s photograph
calls.player: What happened with your sister’s photograph?
calls.reply: I did Catalina’s face for the club’s picture. Now that photo is on an invitation to a private dinner, sent to a girl on Brown Avenue in Catalina’s name. My work, on a thing that frightens me.
calls.note: Camila Reyes says her sister Catalina’s club photograph is being used on private dinner invitations sent in Catalina’s name.

life.news: Made Brenda the mannequin beautiful for the forty-second time. She still hasn’t thanked me.
life.more: Doing eyebrows on mannequins called Brenda. She’s got the best brows in the college and the worst attitude. My tutor says I’m the only student who talks to her. Someone has to. She’s been through a lot. Forty-two makeovers.

life.news: A girl asked me to make her look like someone off her phone. Same filters, same fillers. I talked her out of it.
life.more: I want to teach women to look like themselves, just more. She had freckles she hated. I did her make-up so you could see every one. She looked in the mirror for ages and then took a photo of herself, not a filter. I nearly cried in the salon.

life.news: My twin and I did our nana’s birthday tea without her. Same cake, same table, same songs. She’d have loved it.
life.more: Nana raised us, three sisters, on Brown Avenue. Her face had eighty years in it and it was beautiful. Imogen is the loud twin and I’m the soft one. Today we were both soft. We put her photo at the head of the table and sang to it.

life.news: Watched a couple slow dance in the street outside the salon. No music. He just held her hand and swayed.
life.more: Flowers, a slow dance and someone who looks at you like you’re the only person in the room. That’s all I want. They didn’t even notice me watching through the window. I put down my brush and just watched. That’s the most romantic thing I’ve ever seen.

gossip.says: I did Nia Walker’s make-up for the founding musical. She plays a pioneer woman who dies of fever in act one. She asked me to make her look tragic but gorgeous. She dies beautifully.
gossip.note: Camila Reyes says she does Nia Walker’s make-up for the founding musical.
gossip.ask: Camila says she makes you look tragic but gorgeous for your death in act one.
gossip.answer: She does! The fever blush is all Camila. I die of fever in act one and I die beautifully, and half of it is her. She did my eyelashes so well a man in the front row gasped when I collapsed. That’s the review I live for.

gossip.says: Mei Chen teaches at my college one day a week. She’s the quietest teacher and everyone tells her everything. Even the teachers. She just keeps cutting.
gossip.note: Camila Reyes says Mei Chen teaches at the beauty college once a week.
gossip.ask: Camila says everyone at the college tells you everything, even the teachers.
gossip.answer: I think it’s the scissors. People relax when someone’s concentrating on them. Camila is my best student. She talks to the mannequin like it’s a friend going through a hard time. That’s the right instinct. Everyone in the chair is going through something.

own.label: Ask about being a ranger
own.player: What’s a park ranger’s day like?
own.reply: Telling tourists not to touch cacti, and then pulling cactus out of tourists.

own.label: Ask about the bear
own.player: What’s the real story with the bear?
own.reply: He’s a young male, pushed out by an older one. He’s lost, hungry and too curious. Honestly? Relatable.

own.label: Ask about the bear’s collar
own.player: Is it true the bear has a collar?
own.reply: It does. It isn’t ours. Someone tagged him without telling the park service, and the signal goes to a private receiver.
own.note: Marisol Fuentes says the bear wears a tracking collar that isn’t the park’s, sending to a private receiver.

own.label: Ask about the night sky out there
own.player: What’s the night sky like out in the desert?
own.reply: Like being told how small you are, kindly. Everyone should get told that once a week.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A ranger’s cabin at the end of the canyon, with a telescope I never use and a dog I always do. My parents were rangers too. Mom was the county’s first woman ranger.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: Where are your parents now?
own.reply: Retired to a house halfway up the ridge road. Mom sits on the porch and watches the vans go up to the lodge. She says it’s better than television.

calls.label: Ask where the collar’s signal goes
calls.player: Where does the bear’s collar signal go?
calls.reply: I tracked it on my own time with the service’s receiver. It’s strongest at the lodge gate. My director, who dines at the lodge, told me to leave it. I haven’t.
calls.note: Marisol Fuentes tracked the bear’s collar signal to the lodge gate.

calls.label: Ask about the illegal trap
calls.player: Who set the trap the rangers didn’t?
calls.reply: I have the trap’s manufacturer plate. It was bought on the Foundation’s conservation grant. Somebody is using conservation money to catch a bear for a lodge.
calls.note: Marisol Fuentes says the illegal bear trap was bought with the Foundation’s conservation grant.

life.news: Told a tourist not to touch a cactus. He touched the cactus. I spent forty minutes pulling cactus out of a tourist.
life.more: Every day. Every single day. He said it looked soft. It’s a cactus. It has never once in history looked soft. He took a selfie with the tweezers. I’m in the back of it, mid eye-roll. I hope it goes everywhere.

life.news: Saw the bear on the far ridge at dusk. Just walking. Not causing trouble for once.
life.more: He’s a young male, pushed out by an older one. Lost, hungry and too curious. Honestly? Relatable. Tonight he just walked along the ridge with the sun going down behind him like he was in a film. I didn’t radio it in for ten minutes. I just watched.

life.news: Clear night at the cabin. The sky was so full I lay on the hood of the truck for an hour.
life.more: The night sky tells you how small you are, but kindly. My mom was the county’s first woman ranger and she taught me the constellations before I could read. I still say their names out loud like a register. They’re all present.

life.news: Had to tell a family their dog wasn’t coming back from the canyon. Worst part of the job.
life.more: He went after a rabbit and the canyon’s big. We searched until dark. The little girl gave me his lead to keep in the truck in case I found him. I’ve got it on the dashboard. I’ll keep looking on my rounds. You don’t stop looking.

gossip.says: Rachel Lowe from the vet’s and I drink together on a terrible bar trivia team. We’ve never won. She knows every animal answer and nothing else. I know every star and nothing else.
gossip.note: Marisol Fuentes says she and Rachel Lowe are on a hopeless bar trivia team.
gossip.ask: Marisol says you two have never won a bar trivia.
gossip.answer: We came fourth once! Out of four, but still. She does the stars, I do the animals, and between us we know nothing about soccer, money or the royal family. Animals bite you honestly. Bar quizzes don’t. I’ve made peace with it.

gossip.says: Tessa Larkin at the wildlife rescue takes everything I bring her. A hawk, a fox, a tortoise. She never says no. Then she cries when they go back to the wild. Every time.
gossip.note: Marisol Fuentes says Tessa Larkin cries every time an animal goes back to the wild.
gossip.ask: Marisol says you cry every time an animal goes back to the wild.
gossip.answer: Every single time. You feed it, you heal it, and you open the box and it doesn’t look back. That’s how you know you did it right. You can’t love something into staying. Marisol pretends she doesn’t cry. She does. In the truck.

own.label: Ask about her boutique
own.player: What do you sell?
own.reply: Dresses for women who want to feel like the main character for one evening. Then they go home and take their shoes off in the car.

own.label: Ask about fast fashion
own.player: Can a boutique survive fast fashion?
own.reply: Barely. People buy ten dresses that fall apart instead of one that lasts. I sell the one that lasts.

own.label: Ask about a dress she sold
own.player: Do you remember a dress you sold?
own.reply: I sold Elena Cross her blue gala dress. She asked for one with pockets deep enough for a phone and a notebook. Who takes a notebook to a party?
own.note: Daniela Cruz sold Elena Cross a blue gala dress with pockets deep enough for a phone and a notebook.

own.label: Ask what makes something well made
own.player: What makes something well made?
own.reply: Seams you never notice, and a fabric that gets better with age. Like people, honestly. The ones worth keeping improve.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Is Hector your dad?
own.reply: Hector and his taco van, yes. Mom died when Paola and I were twelve and he bought a van and fed the town. I have lunch with him every day. Free tacos are the best inheritance.

own.label: Ask about her neighbor
own.player: Who’s next door to the boutique?
own.reply: The jeweler. I can see straight into her window from my sewing room. She sells to the club. She also sells to people who arrive after dark.

calls.label: Ask about the gowns for private dinners
calls.player: What do the club girls order from you?
calls.reply: Gowns for private dinners. The juniors order them without knowing what for, and they’re all the same dress: pale, a sheath, like a slip. The one Valerie Huxley wears in her portrait. Every time.
calls.note: Daniela Cruz says every gown ordered for the club’s private dinners is the same pale dress.

life.news: A woman tried on a dress in my shop and stood up straighter. That’s the whole job. That moment.
life.more: Dresses for women who want to feel like the main character for one evening. Then they go home and take their shoes off in the car. She was a nurse buying something for her daughter’s wedding. She did a little turn in the mirror and laughed at herself. Sold.

life.news: Lunch at Dad’s van again. He gave me extra salsa because I looked tired. I wasn’t tired. I was sad.
life.more: My dad runs Hector’s van on the Sunfall Road. He feeds the whole town and he still feeds me like I’m twelve. He knows the difference between tired and sad. He put two extra tortillas on the plate and didn’t ask. That’s my dad.

life.news: Someone brought back a dress I made ten years ago to be altered. It still looks new. I’m so proud I could burst.
life.more: One dress that lasts beats ten that fall apart. Well-made things get better with time. The seams I never let anyone see were still perfect. She’s wearing it to her fortieth birthday. I took it in a tiny bit and didn’t charge her.

life.news: A big shop opened on the corner selling dresses that fall apart in a month. They’re very cheap. People love them.
life.more: Seams you never notice, that’s what you pay for. They sell a dress a minute and I sell four a week. My twin says don’t look at their window. I looked. A mannequin’s hem was already coming down. I felt better, and then worse.

gossip.says: Sophia Moretti from the Sisters asked me to make a dress for the parish picnic that could survive shortbread warfare. Pockets for napkins. A hem for kneeling. It’s the best brief I’ve ever had.
gossip.note: Daniela Cruz says she made Sophia Moretti a dress built for the parish picnic.
gossip.ask: Daniela says you asked her for a dress that could survive shortbread warfare.
gossip.answer: It had to! Pockets for napkins, room for kneeling, and a color that hides crumbs. She made it so beautifully I won the shortbread prize in it. I said a prayer for her hands. And made her shortbread, because prayers go better with shortbread.

gossip.says: Elise Harrow from the Bluebirds borrows dresses from photo shoots and wears them better than the models. I’ve offered to make her one. She says she can’t afford it. I’ve said she can pay me in compliments.
gossip.note: Daniela Cruz says Elise Harrow wears borrowed dresses better than the models.
gossip.ask: Daniela says you wear borrowed dresses better than the models.
gossip.answer: Daniela is very generous and very dangerous. If she makes me a dress I’ll have to go somewhere worthy of it. I was charming at the right party once, in a borrowed dress. Imagine what I could do in one that fits properly.

own.label: Ask about design work
own.player: What do you design?
own.reply: Logos for companies that don’t exist yet and won’t exist next year. Currently: a disruptive sandwich app.

own.label: Ask why everything looks the same
own.player: Why do all brands look the same now?
own.reply: Everyone copied the same three tech companies: flat, beige, rounded, friendly. It’s the visual equivalent of saying nothing politely.

own.label: Ask about a strange commission
own.player: Have you had a strange commission?
own.reply: Someone paid me to design a crescent symbol for an exclusive social club. No name, cash. I recognized it later on a gig poster.
own.note: Hana Park designed a crescent symbol for an anonymous exclusive social club, later seen on a gig poster.

own.label: Ask what she’d make if nobody paid her
own.player: What would you make if nobody was paying you?
own.reply: Something ugly and alive. Every client wants clean and minimal. Clean and minimal is what a hospital looks like.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What did your family do?
own.reply: We had a dry cleaner’s that closed when I was thirteen. Dad went to the city. Mom went quiet. I became the artist and my sister became the earner.

own.label: Ask where she works
own.player: Where do you work?
own.reply: An apartment above the dance studio. I can hear ballroom lessons through the floor. My logos all have a waltz in them now, very faintly.

calls.label: Ask about the crescent commission
calls.player: Who commissioned the crescent?
calls.reply: Three lines and a sketch, in a hand I now know from the club’s Christmas cards, and the cash came in an envelope with the Foundation’s watermark on the flap. I’ve hidden the brief in the back of a picture frame, because my sister visits.
calls.note: Hana Park says the crescent commission came in the club’s Christmas-card handwriting, paid in a Foundation envelope.

life.news: Designed a logo for a sandwich app that wants to disrupt sandwiches. The sandwiches seemed fine as they were.
life.more: Logos for companies that don’t exist yet and won’t exist next year. They wanted it flat, beige, rounded and friendly, the visual equivalent of saying nothing politely. I did them a beige circle. They loved it. I died a little.

life.news: Printed a hundred stickers that say UGLY AND ALIVE. Gave them all away in a day.
life.more: Every client wants clean and minimal. I want ugly and alive. The stickers are on lampposts, a bus shelter and a very surprised mailman’s van. An art student put one on her easel. I’ve never been prouder of a sticker.

life.news: A client said my design was too much. Then asked for it to pop more. I’m lying on the floor.
life.more: Too much and not enough, in the same meeting, from the same man. I made it pop. He said it was too much. I made it beige. He said it needed to pop. Tomorrow I’m sending him both and going for a walk.

life.news: Watched the ballroom class through the floor of my apartment. Someone was counting the waltz out loud. Very loudly.
life.more: I live above the dance studio. Every week the same girl counts one, two, three like she’s doing sums, and her partner apologizes to the floor in Spanish. I’ve started counting along. My upstairs neighbor thinks I’m doing a workout.

gossip.says: Zara Brooks drew most of her own flash, but I did the lettering on some of it when she was too tired to hold a pencil. She paid me in a tiny tattoo. Don’t ask where.
gossip.note: Hana Park says she did some lettering for Zara Brooks’s tattoo designs.
gossip.ask: Hana says you paid her for some lettering with a tiny tattoo.
gossip.answer: A very small comma. She thinks in punctuation, so it seemed right. Hana’s lettering is better than mine. I said that once out loud and she asked for it in writing. She’s not getting it in writing. She’s getting it in ink, if she wants another.

gossip.says: Brittany Hale sells flowers in the Quarter and collects the worst souvenirs in Arizona: a snow globe of a cactus, a spoon from a burned motel, a fridge magnet of the bear. I designed her shop sign for free. She paid me in peonies.
gossip.note: Hana Park says Brittany Hale collects terrible souvenirs and paid her in peonies.
gossip.ask: Hana says you collect the worst souvenirs in Arizona, and you paid her in peonies for your shop sign.
gossip.answer: The bear magnet is a collector’s item now. People don’t understand that. Hana’s sign is beige and rounded and friendly, like everything she makes, and I love it. I told her to make it weirder. She said weird doesn’t sell flowers. She’s wrong, but it’s a lovely sign.

own.label: Ask about the salon
own.player: What’s it like doing hair?
own.reply: People tell their hairdresser everything. I’m quieter than most, so they tell me even more.

own.label: Ask what people confess
own.player: What do people confess in the chair?
own.reply: Affairs, debts, crushes. A woman once told me she’d never loved her husband. Then she tipped me forty dollars and went home to him.

own.label: Ask about a client
own.player: Has a client said anything worrying?
own.reply: A woman from the foundation had me dye her hair dark the morning after the gala. Very dark. She said she needed to look different for a while.
own.note: Mei Chen dyed a foundation woman’s hair very dark the morning after the gala because she needed to look different.

own.label: Ask what people say in the chair
own.player: What do people tell you in the chair?
own.reply: Everything they can’t tell their husbands. I’ve heard three affairs and one confession of murder. The murder was a cat. Still.

own.label: Ask how she became a hairdresser
own.player: How did you get into hair?
own.reply: A course at sixteen, the only one we could afford. I turned out to be good at the listening part. The cutting came later.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Who lives upstairs?
own.reply: My sister Daisy. I hear everything and say nothing. She makes art and says nothing. The street thinks we’re a comedy double act.

calls.label: Ask about the murder confession
calls.player: Who confessed to the cat?
calls.reply: A grand lady from the club. Honoria Blackwood. The cat was the mother of her daughter’s cat, and she said it was the last time she’d clean up after her daughter. Then she tipped me very well.
calls.note: Mei Chen says Honoria Blackwood confessed to killing her estranged daughter’s cat’s mother.

life.news: A woman cried in my chair today and then laughed and then tipped me forty. Hair is very emotional.
life.more: People tell their hairdresser everything. I’m quieter than most, so they tell me even more. She came in to cut off the hair her ex liked. When I finished, she looked in the mirror and said, there you are. I don’t think she meant the hair.

life.news: A man told me a secret in the chair and then asked me to forget it. I said I already had. I hadn’t.
life.more: I never repeat anything. But I don’t forget either. That’s the hard part of being quiet. Everything goes in and nothing comes out. Sometimes I go upstairs and sit with my sister and we don’t talk about anything. It helps.

life.news: Taught a student to cut a straight fringe today. It took her nine tries. The ninth was perfect.
life.more: I teach at the beauty college one day a week. She kept apologizing to the mannequin. I told her the mannequin’s had worse. On the ninth go she held her breath and it came out straight as a ruler. She clapped. The mannequin didn’t.

life.news: Dad’s old restaurant has been a phone shop for a year now. I walked past and didn’t look.
life.more: He ran it until he died in it, at the stove. Mom sold it and went to the coast. Daisy and I stayed. Sometimes I can still smell the ginger when I walk past. Then I go and cut someone’s hair and listen to their troubles instead of mine.

gossip.says: Hana Park sits in my chair every six weeks, asks for something completely different, and leaves with exactly the same haircut. She designs logos for companies that don’t exist yet. I think she just likes being told she looks nice.
gossip.note: Mei Chen says Hana Park asks for a new haircut every six weeks and leaves with the same one.
gossip.ask: Mei says you ask for something different every six weeks and leave with exactly the same haircut.
gossip.answer: That’s branding. You don’t change the logo every six weeks, you freshen it. Mei knows exactly what I mean. She cuts her own hair in a mirror with kitchen scissors, and it looks better than anything she’s ever done on me. Don’t tell her I said that.

gossip.says: Camila Reyes is my best student at the college. She talks to the mannequin like it’s going through a hard time. That’s the right instinct. Everyone in the chair is going through something.
gossip.note: Mei Chen says Camila Reyes is her best student at the beauty college.
gossip.ask: Mei says you talk to the mannequin like it’s going through a hard time.
gossip.answer: Brenda IS going through a hard time! Forty-two makeovers and no thanks. Mei is the best teacher I’ve ever had. She never raises her voice. She just stands next to you very quietly until your hands stop shaking. Then you cut a straight line.

own.label: Ask about community theater
own.player: What are you rehearsing?
own.reply: A musical about the founding of Sunfall. I play a pioneer woman who dies of fever in act one. I die beautifully.

own.label: Ask why she acts
own.player: Why do you love acting?
own.reply: Because for two hours, everyone in the room agrees to feel the same thing. That hardly ever happens any more.

own.label: Ask about the director
own.player: What’s your director like?
own.reply: He cast me for diversity and said so out loud. I wanted the part because I’m good. Both of those things can be true, and only one was his business.

own.label: Ask which role she’d die to play
own.player: Which role would you give anything to play?
own.reply: Lady Macbeth. Everyone wants to play the nice girl. The nice girl never gets the speech.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do your family come to your shows?
own.reply: Every one. Dad drives buses and Mom nurses nights. They sit in the front row and Mom cries when I die in act one, every time, even though she knows.

own.label: Ask what she wants from acting
own.player: What do you want from acting?
own.reply: Somewhere to belong. A company that’s mine. The Players are lovely, but they’re a Foundation production, and it shows in the songs.

calls.label: Ask about the boy who spoke in verse
calls.player: Who was the boy who spoke in verse?
calls.reply: Theon. We did a student play together, three years ago, before they sent him down. I was the only one who was kind to him. He still sends me a line on my birthday.
calls.note: Nia Walker was in a student play with Theon before he was sent down.

calls.label: Ask when the musical opens
calls.player: When does the founding musical open?
calls.reply: {night}, the night with no moon, which is a strange choice for a show about pioneers. Act two has nine women singing a round at the Old Mission. Somebody copied the music from the club’s archive.

life.news: Died of fever in act one again tonight. A woman in the front row wept. I die beautifully.
life.more: A musical about the founding of Sunfall. I play a pioneer woman who dies in act one, and then I sit backstage eating chips for two hours in my death make-up. Tonight the death got a round of applause. I’m going to milk it until closing night.

life.news: Practiced Lady Macbeth in my bedroom mirror. My mom knocked to ask who I was shouting at.
life.more: Everyone wants to play the nice girl. The nice girl never gets the speech. I want the speech. I was halfway through out, damned spot when Mom came in with a cup of tea and asked if it was about the washing up. It wasn’t. It is now.

life.news: The director said in rehearsal, in front of everyone, that he cast me for diversity. I wanted the part because I’m good.
life.more: Both of those things can be true, and only one of them was his business. I said, thank you, and then I did the scene so well he had to look at his shoes. My mom says I’ve got a face for theater. Tonight I had a face for revenge.

life.news: A little girl came to the stage door with a drawing of me dying. It was very accurate. Lots of red crayon.
life.more: She said, you were my favorite dead lady. I signed it and she gave it back to me. It’s on my mirror now. I’ve had reviews. That’s the only one I’ll keep.

gossip.says: Jennifer Tate comes to the musical and heckles my death scene. Lovingly. She shouts, not like this! every night. The audience has started joining in.
gossip.note: Nia Walker says Jennifer Tate heckles her death scene in the founding musical.
gossip.ask: Nia says you heckle her death scene every night.
