gossip.answer: Not like this! It’s a tribute! She beat me at a poetry slam and then bought me a drink, so I go to every performance and refuse to let her die quietly. Loud isn’t dangerous. It’s supportive. The cast have started waiting for my line.

gossip.says: Camila Reyes does my make-up for the show. She gives me a fever blush so good that a man in the front row gasped when I collapsed. I owe her my whole career.
gossip.note: Nia Walker says Camila Reyes does her make-up for the musical.
gossip.ask: Nia says she owes you her whole career for that fever blush.
gossip.answer: She owes her career to her own face! I just make it look tragic but gorgeous. My nana used to say a good face tells the truth. Nia’s tells the whole story before she opens her mouth. I only did the eyelashes.

gossip.says: The show wanted Raven Solis to sing in act two. She has the best voice in the Old Quarter. She didn’t say yes or no. She just didn’t answer. Very her.
gossip.note: Nia Walker says the musical asked Raven Solis to sing and she never answered.
gossip.ask: Nia says the show asked you to sing and you never answered.
gossip.answer: I’m not mysterious. I just didn’t know what to say, so I said nothing, and people decided it meant something. I don’t really like singing in front of people who are watching. I like singing in front of people who are praying. That’s different.

own.label: Ask about planning the gala
own.player: How’s the gala planning going?
own.reply: Three hundred guests, one string quartet and a seating plan that would make a general weep. I adore it.

own.label: Ask about Professor Vale
own.player: You’re friends with Professor Vale?
own.reply: Adrian is the most delightful man in Sunfall. He says the unsayable over dessert. We need more men brave enough to be disliked.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun, away from the galas?
own.reply: I ride. Horses don’t care who your father was, which is refreshing.

own.label: Ask what she really wants
own.player: What do you really want, Alice?
own.reply: To run the Foundation one day, and to run it honestly. That second part is harder than people think.

own.label: Ask about the portrait in her hall
own.player: Who’s in the big portrait in your hall?
own.reply: Ada Beaumont, my great-grandmother. Founding family. Look closely at her brooch next time anyone lets you in: there’s a crescent in it. I asked my father why once. He changed the subject so fast he nearly fell over it.

own.label: Ask how she spends money
own.player: Do you think about money much?
own.reply: Not at all, which is the luxury. I spend it like weather. But I know to the penny what everybody else at the club spends, and on whom. That’s not money. That’s maps.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you get on with your sister?
own.reply: Audra was meant to be the heir and stepped aside for me. She wears dead women’s dresses to dinners to make a point. I love her. I have never understood the point.

views.campus: If you can’t bear to hear an idea, you haven’t got an education, you’ve got a fan club.
views.speakers: Paglia was a triumph and Houellebecq was a delight. The Progressives call them dangerous. Ideas are only dangerous to people who haven’t got any.
views.thunderbirds: We fund half the good in this town and get blamed for the other half.

calls.label: Ask who she trusts at the club
calls.player: Who do you actually trust at the club?
calls.reply: I keep two lists in my head. Everyone who’ll be loyal to me when Honoria is gone. And a much shorter one: the women who sit at the treasurer’s table. I haven’t decided yet whether to burn that table or inherit it.
calls.note: Alice Beaumont says there is an inner circle at the treasurer’s table, and she hasn’t decided whether to break it or take it over.

calls.label: Ask what the founders were really like
calls.player: What were the founding women really like?
calls.reply: Before the charity, before the club, they used to sit up at the Old Mission on nights with no moon. Ada’s letters say so. Grandmother called it their little religion. Nobody at the club says the word mission without looking at the floor.
calls.note: Alice Beaumont says the founding Bluebird women once met at the Old Mission on moonless nights.

life.news: Rode at dawn before anyone was awake. Horses don’t care who your father is. Bliss.
life.more: I ride every morning before the house wakes up. The canyon’s pink, the horse is cross, and nobody needs a seating plan. It’s the only hour of the day when I’m not running something. Then I come home and run everything.

life.news: Seated a lunch for forty so that three divorced couples never made eye contact. Nobody noticed. That’s the art.
life.more: Forty is a warm-up. The trick with exes is a pillar and a flower arrangement. The trick with mothers-in-law is the window seat. They feel chosen. They are, in a way.

life.news: My sister and I had a row across the hall. We don’t shout. We close doors very precisely.
life.more: Audra was meant to be the heir. Then she wasn’t, and I was. We’ve never said it out loud in that house. Today she said something about my shoes that was really about the inheritance, and I said something about her garden that was really about Father.

life.news: Said something honest at a committee meeting and the room went silent. I enjoyed it enormously.
life.more: I intend to run the Foundation one day, and to run it honestly. The second part is where the fun is. Today I asked where some money had gone, very sweetly, with a cookie in my hand. Nobody knew. I made a note of who didn’t know first.

gossip.says: Caroline Prescott wants the chair as much as I do. She’s better at winning and I’m better at being liked. Between us we’d run the club perfectly. Neither of us will ever suggest it.
gossip.note: Alice Beaumont says Caroline Prescott is her rival for the Foundation’s chair.
gossip.ask: Alice says you two would run the club perfectly together, and neither of you will suggest it.
gossip.answer: She’s right, which is irritating. She’s better at being liked. I’m better at being right. The club needs both and will get one. Taking part is what losers call it. I don’t intend to take part.

gossip.says: Sofia Delgado has made three marriages at the club and one messy divorce, and she takes credit for all four. She says outreach to the rich and rent to the poor and means exactly the same thing both times.
gossip.note: Alice Beaumont says Sofia Delgado has made three marriages at the club and one messy divorce.
gossip.ask: Alice says you’ve made three marriages at the club and one messy divorce, and you take credit for all four.
gossip.answer: All four, yes. The divorce was my best work. Two people who should never have met, apart in under a year with the silver split fairly. Alice should be grateful I haven’t started on her. I have a list. She’s on it.

own.label: Ask what drives her
own.player: What gets you out of bed in the morning?
own.reply: Winning. Targets, tennis, auctions. I don’t do taking part. Taking part is what losers call it.

own.label: Ask about women in charge
own.player: Is it hard being a woman running things here?
own.reply: Not really. The men are scared of me and the women want my diary. The real problem is everyone younger wants a title before they’ve done the work.

own.label: Ask about Dorian Kell
own.player: What do you make of Dorian Kell?
own.reply: Charming, connected, and he never once looks you in the eye when he talks about money. I keep my purse closed around Dorian.
own.note: Caroline Prescott doesn’t trust Dorian Kell around money.

own.label: Ask if ambition is lonely
own.player: Is ambition lonely?
own.reply: Very. Men tell me I’m intimidating like it’s a diagnosis. I’d trade three board seats for one man who wasn’t threatened by them.

own.label: Ask where she keeps her trophies
own.player: Where do you keep all the trophies?
own.reply: In the downstairs bathroom. People have to sit and look at them. It’s the only time anyone at the club stays still long enough to be impressed.

own.label: Ask who she plays tennis with
own.player: Who do you play tennis with?
own.reply: I have a court in my garden and nobody to play on it. The good ones are scared of losing and the bad ones are scared of me. I hit against the wall. The wall is a gentleman.

own.label: Ask about the Prescotts
own.player: Your family built something here, didn’t they?
own.reply: The dam’s second wall. We lost a son on it, my great-uncle, nineteen. There’s a plaque. Everyone reads the plaque and nobody reads the name.

own.label: Ask about the man who left
own.player: Has anyone ever left you?
own.reply: Daniel. He left the month after a man from the club bought him lunch. I thought he’d stopped loving me. I’ve since worked out he hadn’t. He left so they couldn’t use him. That’s worse.

calls.label: Ask what she’s working on in secret
calls.player: You sound like someone working on something in secret.
calls.reply: Nine years of donor records, the dates a certain events director signed anything, and every payment to a trust on the ridge. I could end something with it. The trouble is, the real work dies with the fraud, and my own mother is in one of the photographs.
calls.note: Caroline Prescott keeps a private file on nine years of payments to the trust on the ridge.

calls.label: Ask about her mother
calls.player: Is your mother still at the club?
calls.reply: She’s at the lodge on Halcyon Ridge more than she’s at home. I have a photograph of her up there with a man who never appears on any guest list. Lyle Marchbanks. Remember the name and then forget I said it.
calls.note: Caroline Prescott says a man called Lyle Marchbanks is often at the lodge and never on any guest list.

life.news: Won an auction for a painting I didn’t want, just to beat a man who did. Worth every penny.
life.more: Winning drives me. Targets, tennis, auctions. He wanted it for his office. I outbid him by a hundred and watched his face. It’s a terrible painting of a horse. It’s going in the downstairs bathroom with the trophies.

life.news: Played tennis against the wall on my own court. Nobody to play. Again.
life.more: A tall house with a court in the garden and no one to play against. Men are scared of me and women want my diary. I’d trade three board seats for one man who wasn’t threatened by them. I’ve checked. The exchange rate is terrible.

life.news: My mother was out all night again. She says it’s bridge. Nobody plays bridge until dawn.
life.more: She has a lot of friends up on the ridge, and I’ve noticed. I notice everything. She came home with her shoes in her hand and said, wonderful evening. I made her tea and didn’t ask. I’ll ask one day.

life.news: Got my first parking ticket in a year. The officer recognized me and apologized. I paid it double.
life.more: I drive fast and park badly. Today a young officer wrote the ticket, looked up, went pale and said sorry. I said don’t you dare be sorry, you’re doing your job. I paid it twice so he’d remember the lesson. He looked very confused.

gossip.says: Catherine Bell plays tennis like she’s angry at the ball. She’s what I was at twenty-two. I won’t warn her about anything, because nobody warned me.
gossip.note: Caroline Prescott says Catherine Bell reminds her of herself at twenty-two.
gossip.ask: Caroline says you’re what she was at twenty-two.
gossip.answer: She said that? That’s either the best or the worst compliment I’ve ever had. Caroline beat me twice and then bought me lunch. I’m going to beat her a third time and buy her lunch. That’s how we say things at the club.

gossip.says: Audrey King at the rodeo beat me at arm-wrestling at a charity fair. First person to beat me at anything in years. I’ve been back four times. She won’t give me a rematch.
gossip.note: Caroline Prescott says Audrey King beat her at arm-wrestling at a charity fair.
gossip.ask: Caroline says you beat her at arm-wrestling and won’t give her a rematch.
gossip.answer: Why would I? I’m undefeated against her. She comes to the ticket booth every season in her tennis whites and asks politely. I sell her a ticket and say no. Horses are honest and so am I. She’d win the rematch. That’s why.

own.label: Ask about the volunteers
own.player: Who actually volunteers at these things?
own.reply: Retirees, students who need it for their CV, and the Sisters, who do the real work and never post about it.

own.label: Ask what keeps her sane
own.player: How do you stay sane doing that job?
own.reply: I run the canyon trail before sunrise. No phone. It’s the only hour of the day nobody needs anything from me.

own.label: Ask about the gala roster
own.player: Were you working the night of the gala?
own.reply: I did the roster. Two volunteers were swapped off Table 9 at the last minute and replaced by people I’d never met. The order came from upstairs.
own.note: Phoebe Sutton says two volunteers were swapped off Table 9 at the last minute on orders from upstairs.

own.label: Ask what nobody notices about her work
own.player: What does nobody notice about your work?
own.reply: The chairs. Somebody has to put out four hundred chairs and stack them again at midnight. It’s always the same five women.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you live alone?
own.reply: With my little sister, Molly, who talks enough for both of us. I cook, pay the bills and am asleep by ten. She answers the phone at the Foundation and names cacti.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: How did your family end up at the club?
own.reply: We had the boat yard on the reservoir until the club bought it for the sailing annex. That’s how a working family gets two daughters in: as staff who are allowed to call themselves members. Dad drinks on the boats he used to own.

own.label: Ask who stacks the chairs
own.player: Who actually does the work at those nights?
own.reply: The same five women stack four hundred chairs at midnight. I’m one. Three are Sisters of Mercy. They never post about it. The board posts about it.

own.label: Ask what her volunteers found
own.player: Did your volunteers find anything when they cleared up?
own.reply: One of my five found a torn ticket under the treasurer’s table and handed it to the Sisters’ lost property, because she trusts nuns more than the committee. So do I. I’ll ask her to send you a photograph of it.

calls.label: Ask about the original roster
calls.player: Do you still have the roster from before it was changed?
calls.reply: I kept it. The order to swap two of my volunteers off Table 9 came from upstairs, meaning the events director’s office. The men who replaced them wore our lanyards and didn’t stack a single chair. My sister answers the phone in that office. That’s why I’ve said nothing.
calls.note: Phoebe Sutton kept the original roster; the order to swap Table 9’s volunteers came from the events director’s office.

life.news: Ran the canyon before sunrise with no phone. Saw a coyote. We both pretended we hadn’t.
life.more: It’s the only hour nobody can need anything from me. You can’t be asked to roster anything if you can’t hear them. The coyote looked at me like it knew the feeling. Then it went one way and I went the other. Professional courtesy.

life.news: Stacked four hundred chairs after a lunch. The same five women again. Me and the nuns.
life.more: Volunteers are retirees, students who want it on their CV, and the Sisters, who do the real work. Four hundred chairs, always the same five women. One of the nuns does it faster than me. She says it’s prayer. I think it’s her shoulders.

life.news: My dad was drinking on the boats again. The boats he used to own.
life.more: The club bought our boat yard for the sailing annex. That’s how a working family got two daughters into the Bluebirds: as staff who’re allowed to call themselves members. He sits on the boats and drinks. I bring him a sandwich. He says thank you, sweetheart, and I go.

life.news: Molly talked for an hour straight at dinner. I said four words. Perfect evening.
life.more: My little sister says good morning three hundred times a day at the front desk. She talks enough for both of us. I cook, I pay the bills, I’m asleep early. She tells me everything that happened to everyone. I don’t need a life. I have Molly’s.

gossip.says: My little sister Molly Sutton says good morning about three hundred times a day at the front desk, and means it every time. It scares people. She has forty-one cacti and talks to all of them.
gossip.note: Phoebe Sutton says her sister Molly Sutton says good morning three hundred times a day.
gossip.ask: Phoebe says you say good morning three hundred times a day and mean every one.
gossip.answer: Three hundred and twelve yesterday! I counted. People look so surprised when you mean it. Also, it’s forty-two cacti now, Phoebe’s out of date. The new one’s called Gerald the Second, after Gerald, who had an incident. Long story. Do you want the long story?

gossip.says: Margaret Holloway brings the Sisters to every event and they stack chairs faster than anyone at the club. She makes rosters for her rosters. I’ve stolen three of them.
gossip.note: Phoebe Sutton says Margaret Holloway’s Sisters stack chairs faster than anyone.
gossip.ask: Phoebe says she’s stolen three of your rosters.
gossip.answer: Four. I counted. Chaos is a choice, and she chooses not to have it, which I respect. The Sisters stack chairs because nobody else will. Phoebe stacks them because she’s a Sister in all but name. I’d never tell her that.

gossip.says: Emily Fairchild found me once on the third bend of the canyon trail, crying. She sat down next to me, didn’t say anything, and then ran on. I’ve never forgotten it.
gossip.note: Phoebe Sutton says Emily Fairchild once sat with her on the canyon trail without a word.
gossip.ask: Phoebe says you once sat with her on the canyon trail and didn’t say a word.
gossip.answer: I remember. Twelve hours holding strangers’ hands teaches you when not to say anything. She looked like she needed somebody to sit, not somebody to talk. So I sat. Then I ran, because I’m terrible at sitting. Tell her she can find me on the third bend any morning.

own.label: Ask what a community liaison does
own.player: What does a community liaison do?
own.reply: I translate. Rich people say outreach and poor people say rent. I stand in the middle and make sure nobody gets slapped.

own.label: Ask if she sets people up
own.player: Do you ever set people up?
own.reply: Constantly. Three marriages and a very messy divorce. I’ve already decided which of my friends you’d suit. Don’t ask. Fine, ask.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: My abuela crossed a desert to get here and now I organize canapés for people whose grandfathers owned the desert. She thinks it’s hilarious. So do I, most days.

own.label: Ask who she’d set you up with
own.player: Who would you set me up with, if not you?
own.reply: Nobody, now. I’m keeping you. That’s the risk of being a matchmaker: sometimes you meet the good one first.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother
own.player: Tell me about your abuela.
own.reply: She crossed a desert to get here. Now I serve canapés to the grandsons of the men who owned it. We both think it’s hilarious. Most days.

own.label: Ask about the shortbread war
own.player: Is it true about your mom’s shortbread?
own.reply: Better than Sophia Moretti’s, whatever the parish says. The Sisters judge it every bake sale and it’s always a draw, which is how nuns say no.

own.label: Ask what her job really is
own.player: What do you actually spend your days doing?
own.reply: The food program, the scholarship interviews, the parish partnerships. Three jobs, one salary. I stand between people who say outreach and people who say rent, and nobody gets slapped.

views.dispute: I run the food program with Margaret Holloway and I translate between her and the treasurer. The treasurer says review. Margaret says land. My abuela says both of them should eat something. I refuse to take a side and I bring the trays.

calls.label: Ask about her father
calls.player: What happened to your dad?
calls.reply: He drove deliveries for the Foundation. After he died I found his last sheet in his jacket. One drop at the old junction, for the Halcyon Ridge Trust. Crates, not food. I’ve kept it nine years. I matchmake instead of opening that drawer.
calls.note: Sofia Delgado kept her late father’s delivery sheet: crates for the Halcyon Ridge Trust, dropped at the old junction.

calls.label: Ask what the Sisters are up to
calls.player: Anything odd going on at the chapel?
calls.reply: My mom bakes for the Sisters. She counts plates the way other people count money. There’s one more plate going up the back stairs of the charity shop than there are Sisters. Every day. I didn’t say that.
calls.note: Sofia Delgado says an extra plate of food goes up the back stairs of the Sisters’ charity shop every day.

life.news: Matched two people at a funeral. They’re getting married. My abuela says I’ve gone too far.
life.more: They were the only two at the wake who didn’t cry at the right moments. I introduced them over the sandwiches. Six months later, engaged. Three marriages and one very messy divorce. I’ve already decided who you’d suit, by the way. Fine, ask.

life.news: My abuela laughed for ten minutes at the canapés I served today.
life.more: She crossed a desert to get here. I serve canapés to the grandsons of the men who owned it. We both think it’s funny. Today it was tiny tacos on silver trays, and she said, mija, they’ve made our food small so it fits their mouths. She’s not wrong.

life.news: It’s nine years today since my dad’s accident. Mom lit a candle. We didn’t talk about it.
life.more: He drove for the food program and the canyon road took him. Single vehicle, they said. Mom lights a candle on the windowsill every year and we eat his favorite soup and don’t say his name until bedtime. Then we say it all night.

life.news: Mom’s shortbread lost to Sophia Moretti’s at the parish picnic. She’s been in mourning since.
life.more: The great shortbread war. Sophia’s my friend and her shortbread is better, but my mother is my mother. She wore black to breakfast. She’s sent Sophia’s nonna a tin with a note that just says: next year. War is war.

gossip.says: Isabel Morales has been my best friend since school and I’ve set her up four times. Four disasters. She says horses can’t be flattered and neither can she. I’m on attempt five.
gossip.note: Sofia Delgado says she’s set up her best friend Isabel Morales four times.
gossip.ask: Sofia says she’s set you up four times, and she’s on attempt five.
gossip.answer: Four disasters! A vet who was scared of horses, a man who called my mare it, a nice boy who cried at a calf, and one who talked about crypto for an hour. Horses can’t be flattered and neither can I. Tell her number five had better ride.

gossip.says: Sophia Moretti is a Sister of Mercy and my mom’s mortal enemy in the shortbread war. We’re best friends. If our families found out, we’d both be disowned.
gossip.note: Sofia Delgado says she and Sophia Moretti are secret friends despite the shortbread war.
gossip.ask: Sofia says you two are secret best friends despite the shortbread war.
gossip.answer: God bless her, she loves a drama. Our grandmothers would never forgive us. We have lunch every week and talk about everything except shortbread. Hers is very good, you know. Don’t tell her I said so. Mine is better.

gossip.says: Brenda Velasco was the young officer at my dad’s accident. She drives slower than anyone in Sunfall now. I think it’s because of nights like his.
gossip.note: Sofia Delgado says Brenda Velasco was the officer at her father’s accident.
gossip.ask: Sofia says you were the officer at her father’s accident.
gossip.answer: I was. I sat with her in the cab of my dad’s breakdown truck with a blanket. I’ve never closed it in my head. Nothing comes out of nowhere. Tell her I think about him. Tell her I’d like that coffee.

own.label: Ask about keeping the books
own.player: Is accounting for a charity as dull as it sounds?
own.reply: Duller. Except when it isn’t. Charity accounts are where the most interesting lies in town are written down in very neat columns.

own.label: Ask about her style
own.player: You always look immaculate. Is that on purpose?
own.reply: Everything is on purpose. If you look perfect, people assume you’re perfect, and they stop checking your work. Useful, for an accountant.

own.label: Ask what she’s noticed
own.player: Have you noticed anything odd in the accounts?
own.reply: Someone pays a catering firm that doesn’t cater. Same amount, every quarter. I’ve flagged it twice. The flags keep disappearing.
own.note: Yumi Tanaka says the foundation pays a catering firm that doesn’t cater, and her flags keep disappearing.

own.label: Ask what numbers tell her about people
own.player: What do the numbers tell you about people?
own.reply: Everything they won’t say. A man can tell you he’s generous. His expense report tells me the truth.

own.label: Ask how she learned accounts
own.player: How did you get into accounts?
own.reply: My father taught me double entry at ten with a box of buttons. Red buttons in, blue buttons out. I still see buttons when a column doesn’t balance.

own.label: Ask how long her face takes
own.player: How long does looking like that take you?
own.reply: Eleven minutes. If you look perfect, people assume you are and stop checking your work. It’s the single most useful thing I know.

own.label: Ask about her parents’ practice
own.player: Do your parents still work?
own.reply: They do the taxes for half the ranchers in the county, including the Whitlocks. My mother can tell a man is lying about his cattle from the way he holds his pen.

calls.label: Ask about the firm that doesn’t cater
calls.player: Tell me about the catering firm you flagged.
calls.reply: Late Service Catering. Paid the same every quarter, registered at the boarded-up weigh station at the old junction. I flagged it twice. Both flags vanished, removed with the treasurer’s login. So I keep a third copy, on paper, in a shoebox under my second-best heels.
calls.note: Yumi Tanaka says Late Service Catering is registered at the boarded weigh station at the old junction, and her warnings were deleted with the treasurer’s login.

calls.label: Ask if she’d share her third copy
calls.player: Would you let me see the third copy?
calls.reply: Only a page. The page with the trust’s payments on it. I’ll put it somewhere only you’ll look. If anyone asks, you found it in a shoe.

life.news: Did my face in eleven minutes this morning. Nobody checked my work all day.
life.more: If you look perfect, people assume you are perfect and stop checking your work. It’s the single most useful thing I know. Today my eyeliner was so sharp the treasurer apologized for a typo he hadn’t made yet.

life.news: My dad taught a little girl from a ranch double-entry with a box of buttons. The same box he used on me.
life.more: My parents do half the ranchers’ taxes in the county. Today a farmer’s daughter sat at their table and Dad brought out the buttons. Red for debit, blue for credit. She got it in ten minutes. I was slower. He says I was more careful.

life.news: Someone at work called me an ice queen. To my face. In a lift.
life.more: I was the quiet girl at school who came first and was mocked for it, and I learned that nobody mocks a woman who looks expensive. It mostly works. Today it didn’t. I said, thank you, the elevator’s very warm. Then I sat in my car for ten minutes.

life.news: Reorganized my wardrobe by color again. Spring is a very confusing season.
life.more: Everything I own is chosen. Nothing in my apartment is an accident. The wardrobe goes from white to black like a gradient, and spring ruins it every year with pastels. Today I put a mint sweater between sage and pistachio and felt completely at peace.

gossip.says: Sarah Whitcomb took over my old desk. She says a budget is a list of what someone loves. She cried catering a wedding once. She’ll be a wonderful accountant and a terrible poker player.
gossip.note: Yumi Tanaka says Sarah Whitcomb took over her old desk.
gossip.ask: Yumi says you’ll be a wonderful accountant and a terrible poker player.
gossip.answer: She’s not wrong about the poker. My face does everything my heart does. People think numbers are cold. They’re not. A budget is just a list of what someone loves. Yumi left me a note in the drawer that said, check everything twice. I do.

gossip.says: Cecilia Prado brings her old rescue dog to the office at the end of the week, and nobody has the heart to tell her it isn’t allowed. The dog sleeps under my desk. I keep treats in my drawer for her now.
gossip.note: Yumi Tanaka says Cecilia Prado brings her old rescue dog to the office at the end of the week.
gossip.ask: Yumi says your dog sleeps under her desk at the end of every week, and she keeps treats in her drawer for her.
gossip.answer: She’s fourteen and she doesn’t like being alone anymore. Neither do I, if I’m honest. Yumi pretends the treats are for her own lunch. They’re liver flavored. I’ve seen the packet. That woman keeps a whole heart in a drawer.

own.label: Ask about homicide work
own.player: What’s homicide work really like?
own.reply: Mostly sad families and bad coffee. The television version has better lighting and fewer forms.

own.label: Ask about the gala photo
own.player: I saw you in the gala photo in the paper.
own.reply: I was on duty, in a dress, because the board wanted security that blended in. The caption makes it look like I was a guest. I wasn’t. I was watching the door.
own.note: Officer Porter was on duty at the gala, watching the door, not attending as a guest.

own.label: Ask what she saw at the door
own.player: Did you see anything at the gala door?
own.reply: A man in a charity lanyard left by the kitchen, not the front. People who belong use the front.
own.note: Abigail Porter saw a man in a charity lanyard leave the gala through the kitchen.

own.label: Ask about the case she can’t forget
own.player: Is there a case you can’t forget?
own.reply: A girl the same age as my sister. We got the man. It didn’t help. Getting the man never helps the way you think it will.

own.label: Ask what she does to unwind
own.player: What do you do when you’re not working?
own.reply: I fix things. A toaster, a lamp, the station’s coffee machine twice. Something broken that wants to be fixed is very restful after people.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are the Porters a big Sunfall family?
own.reply: Gallery district money. Dad’s an architect who designed the club’s sailing annex and drank the fee. Mom is on the flower committee. I’d rather be in my workshop than at any of their tables.

own.label: Ask if it’s like television
own.player: Is homicide like it is on TV?
own.reply: The television version has better lighting and fewer forms. And on television the coffee is never this bad.

calls.label: Ask about the nine minutes
calls.player: Did you ever leave the door that night?
calls.reply: Nine minutes. My sergeant rang and told me to check the parking lot. In those nine minutes the kitchen door was unwatched and a gray car left. The sergeant was Vic Lowry. My log says I never moved. I wrote it that way, and I’ve been sick about it since.
calls.note: Abigail Porter left the door for nine minutes on gala night because Sergeant Vic Lowry called her; a gray car left by the kitchen meanwhile.

calls.label: Ask about the note about her
calls.player: Someone’s trying to blame you, aren’t they?
calls.reply: An unsigned note, asking where Officer Porter drove E.C. after the benefit. I didn’t drive anyone. Somebody inside wants me to be the story.
calls.note: An unsigned note is trying to frame Abigail Porter for driving Elena Cross away.

life.news: Fixed the station coffee machine for the third time. They’ve put my name on it.
life.more: A label on the front: property of Porter, ask before kicking. The coffee’s still bad, but now it’s bad on time. The television version has better lighting and fewer forms. It never shows you who fixes the coffee machine.

life.news: My mother invited me to her flower committee lunch. In a dress. I said I had a murder.
life.more: I didn’t have a murder. I had a toaster with a loose element and a quiet evening. My family’s lovely and their tables go on for ever. I love them better from the workshop.

life.news: Hard day. A case that looked like a girl my sister’s age.
life.more: Homicide is sad families and bad coffee. Most days I can keep them apart from my own. Today I rang my sister at the hospital just to hear her complain about a doctor. She did, for twenty minutes. Best twenty minutes of my week.

life.news: Restored an old lamp I found in a dumpster. Brass, a hundred years old, works perfectly now.
life.more: Someone threw it out because the switch went. A switch! Twenty minutes and a screwdriver. It’s on my bedside table, glowing like it’s grateful. Things want to work. You just have to listen to what’s wrong with them.

gossip.says: Eleanor Graves and her dog Major both check every room before they lie down. I’ve watched them do it at a crime scene. Same pace. Same head tilt.
gossip.note: Abigail Porter says Eleanor Graves and her dog Major check every room the same way.
gossip.ask: Abigail says you and Major check rooms with the same head tilt.
gossip.answer: We do not have the same head tilt. Fine. We might. He was a police dog for eight years. He checks every room before he lies down, and so do I. We’re a good match. Don’t tell Abigail she’s right. She’ll fix something to celebrate.

gossip.says: Maya Serrano works emergency at the hospital with my sister. She once got a key out of a man who’d swallowed it, then ate cookies in the parking lot like nothing had happened.
gossip.note: Abigail Porter says Maya Serrano, an emergency nurse, works with her sister.
gossip.ask: Abigail says you once got a key out of a man who’d swallowed it.
gossip.answer: Standard shift! He swallowed his own house key so his wife couldn’t lock him out. Genius, honestly. Cookies in the parking lot are how I survive. Beth brings the good ones. Tell Abigail her sister is the best nurse on the ward.

own.label: Ask what a sergeant does
own.player: What does a sergeant actually do?
own.reply: I stop clever young detectives from doing clever things that end up in court. It’s babysitting with handcuffs.

own.label: Ask how the job has changed
own.player: Has the job changed much?
own.reply: We used to know the town. Now we know its phones. Fewer people talk to us and more people film us. I can’t decide if that’s progress.

own.label: Ask what her gut says
own.player: What does your gut say about Sunfall right now?
own.reply: That three separate things are happening and someone wants us to think they’re one. Or one thing wants us to think it’s three. I haven’t decided which.

own.label: Ask what the job did to her
own.player: What has the job done to you?
own.reply: It made me sit with my back to the wall in every restaurant. My ex said it was romantic at first. It isn’t, after a while.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you from Sunfall?
own.reply: Born and bred. Dad drove the Moretti bakery’s bread van. Mom did the books for Ortega Repair. I knew every shop in this town by smell before I was ten.

own.label: Ask why she sits facing the door
own.player: Why do you always face the door?
own.reply: Back to the wall in every restaurant. My ex said it was romantic at first. It isn’t, after a while. It’s just tired.

own.label: Ask if she has a dog
own.player: Have you got pets?
own.reply: A dog I inherited from a dead colleague. He still waits by the door at six. So do I, some nights.

calls.label: Ask what’s in her drawer
calls.player: What do you keep in your desk drawer?
calls.reply: Eleven accident reports. Fourteen years. Every one a man who married a Bluebird and died inside three years: the dam, the junction, the reservoir, a heart attack at a dinner. I pulled them one at a time so nobody would notice. I’m waiting for a twelfth.
calls.note: Helen Markham keeps eleven accident reports: men who married Bluebirds and died within three years.

calls.label: Ask why she wants to see Diana Moore
calls.player: Why do you keep asking Diana Moore to lunch?
calls.reply: Because her second husband is report number nine, and she knows it, and one day she’ll be brave enough to eat a sandwich with a policewoman. I’ll keep asking.
calls.note: Helen Markham believes Diana Moore knows something about her husband Walter’s death.

life.news: The dog I inherited ate a whole cake off the counter. It wasn’t my birthday. It wasn’t my cake.
life.more: He belonged to a colleague who died, so he came to me, and he’s never once done as he’s told. The cake was for the station. I bought another on the way in and said nothing. The job is babysitting with handcuffs. The dog is babysitting without them.

life.news: My daughter rang to say she’s top of her class. Then she asked for money. In that order. Clever girl.
life.more: Rosie’s at the university in the city. She rings when she needs something and pretends she’s ringing to chat. I pretend I believe her. We’ve done this for three years. It’s the best conversation I have all week.

life.news: Sat with my back to the wall at a wedding today. Someone asked if I was expecting trouble.
life.more: I always am. Twenty years of it. My ex said it was romantic at first. Then it was a problem. I watched the door through the speeches and ate a very good piece of salmon. Nobody came through it. That’s the best kind of day.

life.news: Planted something in the garden. First time in five years. It hasn’t died yet.
life.more: A rosemary bush. I’m told you can’t kill rosemary. I’ve killed everything else that garden’s ever had. I water it before work and talk to it after. If you tell anyone at the station I talk to a plant, I’ll arrest you for something.

gossip.says: Diana Moore, the Bluebird donor with the big house, eats dinner alone at the end of a twelve-seat table. I’ve asked her to lunch twice. She said yes twice and canceled twice.
gossip.note: Helen Markham says Diana Moore eats alone at a twelve-seat table and has canceled lunch with her twice.
gossip.ask: Helen says you’ve canceled lunch with her twice.
gossip.answer: Darling, I cancel everything twice. It’s how I find out who really wants to see me. Has she asked a third time? No, she hasn’t. Tell her to ask a third time. I’ll come. I’ll even wear something she’ll find hard to arrest.

gossip.says: Brenda Velasco measures skid marks for a living and drives like a grandmother. She holds her breath at every junction. Best collision investigator I’ve ever worked with.
gossip.note: Helen Markham says Brenda Velasco is the best collision investigator she’s worked with.
gossip.ask: Helen says you hold your breath at every junction.
gossip.answer: Every single one. I’ve seen what a second does. Everyone says the other car came out of nowhere. Nothing comes out of nowhere. Helen’s kind about my driving. Everyone else at the station overtakes me and waves.

gossip.says: Kira Henson and I drink whiskey once a month in my kitchen and barely talk. It’s the most restful hour I have.
gossip.note: Helen Markham says she and Kira Henson drink whiskey together once a month.
gossip.ask: Helen says you two drink whiskey once a month and barely talk.
gossip.answer: Barely talking is the point. I write down every word in court all day. In Helen’s kitchen nobody’s taking notes. She pours, I sit, the dog snores. We once went forty minutes without a word. Best evening of the year.

own.label: Ask what undercover is like
own.player: What’s undercover work like?
own.reply: Exhausting. You spend your days being someone else and your nights remembering who you are. Dating is… complicated.

own.label: Ask if she lies on Hinge
own.player: Are you lying to me right now?
own.reply: Only about my job, sometimes. Never about whether I like someone. That’s the one thing I can’t fake.

own.label: Ask where she’s been working
own.player: Where have you been working lately?
own.reply: The motel strip. A room there was paid for in cash on the night of the gala by a man who used a fake name. I can’t say more. I’ve said too much.
own.note: Maria Vega says a motel room was paid for in cash under a fake name on the night of the gala.

own.label: Ask who she is when she isn’t undercover
own.player: Who are you when you’re not undercover?
own.reply: I’m still working that out. I’ve been other people so long that my own laugh sounds fake to me.

own.label: Ask where she sleeps
own.player: Where do you actually live?
own.reply: Two places. Lena’s apartment above the bar, with a photo of a boyfriend who doesn’t exist. And my dad’s spare room, two nights a week, where he makes me eggs and doesn’t ask.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mom like?
own.reply: Founding-family girl who married a police sergeant against the committee. They never forgave her. She died when I was fourteen. She used to give fake names at restaurants as a joke. Mrs. Swallow was her favorite.

own.label: Ask what undercover does to her
own.player: Does it change you, being someone else?
own.reply: My own laugh sounds fake to me now. Lena’s sounds real. That should worry someone. It worries my dad.

calls.label: Ask about the men on the strip
calls.player: Who are the men you’re watching?
calls.reply: Money lenders. Two days a week they work for the lodge up on the ridge. One’s called Brad Keller, and he has a key to the back door of the old Rialto. I don’t know why. I hate not knowing why.
calls.note: Maria Vega says the strip’s money lenders work for the lodge, and one, Brad Keller, has a key to the Rialto’s back door.

calls.label: Ask about room twelve
calls.player: Who paid for room twelve?
calls.reply: A woman, not a man. Cash. She signed the book Mrs. Swallow, which was my mom’s joke name. I reported a man with a fake name, because a woman would send the station looking for Elena, and the station includes people I wouldn’t send looking for my cat.
calls.note: Maria Vega says room twelve was paid for in cash on gala night by a woman calling herself Mrs. Swallow.

life.news: Bumped into an old schoolfriend while I was being someone else. I had to pretend I didn’t know her.
life.more: I can’t tell you much about work. I spend my days being someone with a different name, and she walked up and said mine. I said, sorry, you’ve got me confused. She looked hurt. I’ll find her later and explain. Or I won’t, and that’s the job.

life.news: My dad made me eggs and didn’t ask a single question. That’s love, in my family.
life.more: I sleep at his two nights a week, in the room I grew up in. He was a sergeant for thirty years. He knows not to ask. He just makes the eggs too runny and puts the radio on. I’d do anything for that man and his runny eggs.

life.news: Scored the winner at five-on-five. Top corner. My teammates lifted me up.
life.more: We play on the rec whenever we can get a field. It’s the one place I’m completely myself. My own name, my own laugh. Today I laughed and it sounded real. That’s worth more than the goal. The goal was also very good.

life.news: Long day. My own laugh sounded fake to me again.
life.more: When you’re someone else all day, it takes a while to come back. I sat in the car for half an hour before I went into Dad’s. I’ll lie about my job. Never about whether I like someone. That’s the one thing I can’t fake. So, I like you. There.

gossip.says: There’s a girl on the ridge road, Lavinia Gravesend, who paints the desert purple and makes lockets. She comes into a bar I know with bruises she explains too quickly. If you’re her friend, be a good one.
gossip.note: Maria Vega says Lavinia Gravesend, a jeweler on the ridge road, has bruises she explains too quickly.
gossip.ask: Maria asked me to be a good friend to you.
gossip.answer: Did she? That’s kind. I don’t think I know her. People say things about the ridge. I’m fine. Really. Tell me something boring about your day. I like boring.

gossip.says: Linh Tran sold a picture of the bear to a magazine in the city and it paid her rent for two months. She’s the only freelancer in Sunfall who eats properly. At Hector’s van, but properly.
gossip.note: Maria Vega says Linh Tran’s bear photo paid two months of rent.
gossip.ask: Maria says your bear photo paid two months of rent.
gossip.answer: Two months and a pair of boots. The bear didn’t get a cut, which I feel bad about. Maria comes to Hector’s sometimes in a terrible wig. I’ve never asked. She’s in my novel as a woman with a terrible wig.

own.label: Ask what a police analyst does
own.player: What does a police analyst do?
own.reply: I find the pattern in the noise. Most crime is boring and repetitive. That’s what makes the strange ones stand out.

own.label: Ask if she likes quiet
own.player: You seem like someone who likes quiet.
own.reply: I do. Everyone else in the station talks. I listen to the numbers. They don’t interrupt.

own.label: Ask what pattern she sees
own.player: What’s the pattern you can’t stop thinking about?
own.reply: The bear calls spike on nights with no moon. So do the calls about lights at the old chapel. I don’t think the bear cares about the moon.
own.note: Keiko Nakamura says calls about lights at the old chapel spike on moonless nights.

own.label: Ask what pattern she’s noticed in Sunfall
own.player: What pattern have you noticed in Sunfall?
own.reply: Crime rises when the casino pays out and falls when the churches run their summer fairs. Make of that what you will.

own.label: Ask where she goes to think
own.player: Where do you go to think?
own.reply: The top floor of the library. The window faces the desert. Bethany lets me in after hours. It’s the quietest place in Sunfall, and I’ve measured.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family local?
own.reply: My grandparents came to farm, and in the war they were put in a camp an hour from here. The town never mentions it. My grandmother mentions it every time she rings.

own.label: Ask what she reads
own.player: What do you read?
own.reply: Japanese crime novels my grandmother posts me. In those, the detective is usually right and usually lonely. I find that very relaxing.

calls.label: Ask when the next dark night is
calls.player: When’s the next night with no moon?
calls.reply: {night}. That’s when the calls about lights at the old chapel spike, every time, on my map. Bears don’t care about the moon. People do.

calls.label: Ask what else her map shows
calls.player: What else is on your map?
calls.reply: Eleven men dead within three years of one particular kind of wedding. And a gray car on the same streets the week after every benefit night. Nobody upstairs reads my reports.
calls.note: Keiko Nakamura’s map shows eleven men who died within three years of marrying into the Bluebirds.

life.news: My grandmother sent another box of crime novels from Japan. Twelve. I’m happy for a month.
life.more: She sends them every season with a note telling me to eat more. Old ones, the kind where the detective has a pipe and a terrible marriage. I read them in the library window after hours. Bethany lets me. It’s the quietest place in town.

life.news: Plotted a month of calls against the weather. Cold nights, more burglaries. Hot nights, more fights.
life.more: Most crime is boring, and boring things repeat. That’s what makes the strange ones stand out. Nobody upstairs reads my reports. I write them anyway, very carefully, and put the interesting part on page three. Someone will read page three one day.

life.news: My grandmother rang. She talked about the camp again.
life.more: Her family were interned an hour from here during the war. The town doesn’t mention it. She mentions it every time she rings, because somebody should. I listen. I always listen. Then I run the dry river path until I can’t think.

life.news: Went to Sasha’s book club and said one sentence. A record.
life.more: Officially it’s a serious novel about grief. Actually it’s wine and exes. Tonight someone asked what I thought, and I said the dog in chapter two is the only honest character. They all agreed. I’ll be quiet for another six months now.

gossip.says: Bethany Price at the library lets me sit at the top-floor window after closing. Quietest place in Sunfall. She leaves a cookie on the sill and never asks what I’m working on.
gossip.note: Keiko Nakamura says Bethany Price lets her use the library’s top window after hours.
gossip.ask: Keiko says you leave her a cookie on the windowsill after closing.
gossip.answer: One cookie, every time, a different kind, so she has something to look forward to. She thinks I don’t notice which ones she eats first. Ginger nuts. Always the ginger nuts. A secret society with late fees, and she’s our quietest member.

gossip.says: Sasha Mahoney knows the odds of everything and ignores every one. She’s afraid of nothing except her toaster, which statistically makes sense.
gossip.note: Keiko Nakamura says Sasha Mahoney, a statistician, ignores every odd she knows.
gossip.ask: Keiko says the only thing you’re scared of is your toaster.
gossip.answer: Statistically your toaster is a bigger threat than any stranger. Sleep well. Keiko comes to my book club and says one sentence every six months, and it’s always the best sentence of the night. I’d frame them if I could.

gossip.says: Eleanor Graves is the only detective who reads page three of my reports. That’s where I put the interesting part.
gossip.note: Keiko Nakamura says Eleanor Graves is the only detective who reads her reports properly.
gossip.ask: Keiko says you’re the only one who reads page three of her reports.
gossip.answer: Page three is where she hides the good bits, because she knows nobody upstairs gets past page one. Two isn’t a pattern. Three would be. Keiko finds the threes. Tell her I’m still reading.

own.label: Ask about her megaphone
own.player: Is it true you own three megaphones?
own.reply: Four. One is for emergencies. One is decorative. One makes a duck noise by accident. I love them all equally.

own.label: Ask if people blame her
own.player: Do people blame you for the trouble with Vale?
own.reply: Everyone looks at me first because I’m loud. Loud isn’t dangerous. Quiet is. Look at the quiet ones.
own.note: Jennifer says the dangerous people at the protests are the quiet ones, not the loud ones.

own.label: Ask about poetry slams
own.player: Do you do anything besides protests?
own.reply: Poetry slams. I came second last time to a man who just read his tax return angrily. Robbed.

own.label: Ask why she organizes
own.player: Why do you organize?
own.reply: Because nobody else would book the hall. Leadership is mostly booking the hall.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A room in the housing co-op. Megaphones on a shelf, banners under the bed. Inez runs the place with a glare and I respect the glare.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where are your family from?
own.reply: The hills. Logging people, came down with nothing and an opinion. Dad drives a timber truck. Mom teaches drama at the hill school, which explains the megaphones.

views.speakers: I protest Vale’s speakers because they make kids on our campus feel small. Say what you like, but don’t pretend it doesn’t land on real people.
views.campus: Best protest yet! We had a drum. Nobody could play the drum. It was beautiful.
views.police: They know my name, my face and my megaphone. We’re practically pen pals.

calls.label: Ask about the drum nobody can play
calls.player: Where did that drum at the protests come from?
calls.reply: A man in a charity lanyard donated it. Said he admired the cause. Nobody can play it and the case is weirdly heavy at the bottom. I keep meaning to look. I never have. Loud people don’t look at things, apparently.
calls.note: Jennifer Tate says the protest drum was donated by a man in a charity lanyard, and its case is oddly heavy at the bottom.

life.news: Poetry slam tonight. Came first! Beat a man who reads his tax return angrily. Justice.
life.more: He beat me last time with that tax return and I’ve never recovered. Tonight I did a poem about megaphones and the whole room shouted the last line back at me. He came second. He was very gracious. I wasn’t.

life.news: The duck megaphone went off by accident during a minute’s silence. Nobody’s speaking to me.
life.more: It’s the emergency one. It quacks when you press the wrong button. In a silence. In a hall. Forty people turned around. I said sorry into the megaphone, which quacked again. I’m going to live in a cave now.

life.news: Got told to be quieter at a meeting. By someone who said nothing for an hour.
life.more: Everyone looks at me first because I’m loud. Loud isn’t dangerous. Quiet is. Look at the quiet ones. I went home and wrote a poem so angry the pen went through the paper. It’s my best one.

life.news: My mom came to see me perform. She teaches drama at the hill school. She cried and then gave me notes.
life.more: She taught me to project, then spent eighteen years telling me to stop projecting at dinner. Tonight she said, your diaphragm was lazy in the second verse, and I love you. In that order. I’ll take both.

gossip.says: Nia Walker beat me at a poetry slam once and then bought me a drink. She dies beautifully in the town musical every night. We’re rivals and friends. Mostly friends.
gossip.note: Jennifer Tate says Nia Walker is her poetry slam rival and friend.
gossip.ask: Jennifer says you two are poetry rivals, and mostly friends.
gossip.answer: Mostly friends! She lost gracefully, which for Jennifer means she only shouted a little. I play a pioneer woman who dies of fever in act one of the founding musical. She comes and heckles my death. It’s the nicest thing anyone does for me.

gossip.says: Eleanor Graves, the detective, and I are pen pals. Real letters. She writes like a police report and signs off with a drawing of her dog.
gossip.note: Jennifer Tate says she and detective Eleanor Graves write each other letters.
gossip.ask: Jennifer says you two write real letters, and you sign off with a drawing of your dog.
gossip.answer: Major insists. Jennifer wrote to the station after a protest to complain about a parking ticket, very politely and very loudly, and I wrote back. Now we write every month. Loud isn’t dangerous. She’s right about that. Don’t tell her I said it.

own.label: Ask about her books
own.player: Is it true your apartment is full of books?
own.reply: Floor to ceiling. Most of them are about how ordinary people finally said no. History is a list of people who stopped asking nicely.

own.label: Ask why she’s an activist
own.player: Why did you get into activism?
own.reply: Because I watched polite people lose, again and again, to powerful people who don’t care about polite.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever scared
own.player: Do you ever scare yourself?
own.reply: Anger is a tool. You only get scared of a tool when you don’t know how to hold it.

own.label: Ask about the Back Row
own.player: People mention something called the Back Row.
own.reply: People say a lot of things at meetings. The back row is where you sit when you’re done talking. That’s all it is. Isn’t it?

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where are you from?
own.reply: The gallery district, which I don’t say on campus. Mom’s on the museum board. Dad drafts wills for rich people. I grew up reading the endings of other people’s lives on his desk.

own.label: Ask what she does for money
own.player: What do you actually do for money?
own.reply: A campaigns job for a non-profit in the city, done from my sofa. It pays the rent. The real work happens in the evenings.

views.speakers: Vale invites men who say cruelty is honesty. Every lecture tells a room full of nineteen-year-olds who matters and who doesn’t. At some point, talking about it stops being enough.
views.campus: Protest is the polite version. The university has had its polite version.
views.police: They protect property. Ask them what they protect people from.

calls.label: Ask about the will she read
calls.player: You said you read a will once?
calls.reply: Walter Hallam’s. My father drafted it. I know exactly what the Foundation is and what it does to the men who marry into it. But the Bluebirds are old and slow, and a movement needs a target it can reach. They can wait.
calls.note: Vanessa Greer read Walter Hallam’s will, drafted by her father, and knows what the Foundation does to the men who marry in.

life.news: Read a whole history of a strike in one sitting. Two hundred pages. I haven’t eaten.
life.more: History is a list of people who stopped asking nicely. These ones were laundry women, a hundred years ago, and they won. Nobody remembers their names. I wrote three of them on a card and stuck it on my fridge. Somebody should.

life.news: Lit every candle in the apartment and read until the light came up. Best night in weeks.
life.more: Two glasses out, always, in case someone interesting knocks. Nobody did, so I had both glasses. Polite people lose to powerful people. Tonight I was neither. I was just a woman with a book and a lot of candles.

life.news: My mother asked me to a museum dinner. I said I had a meeting. I had a meeting.
life.more: She’s on the museum’s board. My father drafts wills for people with very old money. They don’t know what I do on campus. They think I’m a student who reads too much. That’s true. It’s just not the whole truth.

life.news: Someone left a book on my doorstep with no note. About a woman who said no. I love an anonymous book.
life.more: It’s the first thing I’ve been given in months that I didn’t ask for. Either I have an admirer or I have an enemy with very good taste. Both are fine. I’ve started reading it. I’ll know which by chapter four.

gossip.says: Allison Kent keeps a professor’s diary, and her own in a code she invented when she was fourteen. I’ve tried to crack it. I can’t.
gossip.note: Vanessa Greer says Allison Kent keeps a diary in a code she invented at fourteen.
gossip.ask: Vanessa says you write your diary in a code she can’t crack.
gossip.answer: Funny you’d ask me that. It’s not a code, it’s shorthand. Very personal shorthand. I invented it at fourteen to keep my mother out. Vanessa’s cleverer than my mother, so I improved it. I read the whole book before I burn it. That includes hers.

gossip.says: Rebecca Shaw has seventeen spreadsheets, eleven rabbits and the most patience on campus. She’ll ask why you think something and actually wait for the answer. It’s unsettling.
gossip.note: Vanessa Greer says Rebecca Shaw actually waits for people’s answers.
gossip.ask: Vanessa says you actually wait for people’s answers, and it’s unsettling.
gossip.answer: Respectfully, it’s called a conversation. Vanessa talks to everyone like she’s the only person who’s ever listened to them. I just listen. We’re very different kinds of dangerous. Mine’s the spreadsheet kind.

gossip.says: Lucy Bennett taught me English and says her seminars are hostage videos. She’s the cleverest woman on campus and she pretends to be lazy so nobody asks her to do anything.
gossip.note: Vanessa Greer says Lucy Bennett pretends to be lazy so nobody asks anything of her.
gossip.ask: Vanessa says you pretend to be lazy so nobody asks you to do anything.
gossip.answer: Pretend? Darling, I’ve worked very hard at it. It’s a full-time job looking that relaxed. Vanessa was my most frightening student. She read everything and agreed with none of it. I gave her the highest mark in the year and slept with the light on.

own.label: Ask what it’s like working for Vale
own.player: What’s it like working for Professor Vale?
own.reply: He’s brilliant, vain and exhausting. I keep his diary, so I know where he’ll be before he does. That’s more power than people think.

own.label: Ask which side she’s on
own.player: So which side are you on, the protesters or Vale?
own.reply: I’m on the side of people who read the whole book before they burn it. Which, in this town, makes me lonely.

own.label: Ask about the people at the back of the room
own.player: Who are the people who sit at the back of the campus meetings?
own.reply: Funny you’d ask me that. They’re just students. Very serious students. I wouldn’t worry about them, if I were you.
own.note: Allison Kent got oddly defensive when asked about the people at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask what she’d write in her own diary
own.player: If you kept your own diary, what would be in it?
own.reply: Mostly other people’s appointments, sadly. I’ve organized a famous man’s life so long I forgot to schedule mine.

own.label: Ask about her own diary
own.player: Do you keep a diary of your own?
own.reply: In a code I invented at fourteen. Nobody has cracked it. Nobody has tried, which is the same thing and also sadder.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your dad do?
own.reply: He ran a stationery shop that printed the Foundation’s programs until they went elsewhere. He died of the loss, slowly, over six years. I spent them being brilliant at a man who didn’t see me.

calls.label: Ask who else drives Vale’s car
calls.player: Does anyone else drive Professor Vale’s car?
calls.reply: Dr. Pemberton borrows it on the days after public events. I arrange the loan myself. I haven’t told anyone that. I’m not sure I mind what that means.
calls.note: Allison Kent says Dr. Hal Pemberton borrows Professor Vale’s car on the days after public events, and she arranges it.

life.news: I knew where my boss would be today before he did. Again. Three times.
life.more: I keep a professor’s diary, so I know where he’ll be before he does. That’s more power than people think. Today he asked me where his lunch was. I told him. Then where his keys were. Then where his afternoon had gone. I said, to you, mostly.

life.news: Finished a book I’d been meaning to burn. Didn’t burn it. Annoyingly good.
life.more: I’m on the side of people who read the whole book before they burn it. In this town that makes me lonely. This one I was sure I’d hate. I didn’t. I’ve lent it to a friend so she can hate it for me.

life.news: My dad’s old stationery shop is a vape shop now. I walked past and didn’t go in.
life.more: He printed programs and invitations for thirty years, until his biggest customer went elsewhere. It took him six years to die of it, slowly. I spent them at university being brilliant at a man who didn’t notice. Sorry. That’s a lot. Ask me something easy.

life.news: Sat in on a psychology seminar for fun. The girl next to me diagnosed me in ten minutes.
life.more: Clara Weiss. She looked at how I hold my pen and told me my attachment style. She was right, which was upsetting. Then she showed me forty photos of her dogs. I’ve never been so thoroughly read by someone so cheerful.

gossip.says: Clara Weiss in my psychology seminar has six dogs and diagnoses everyone she meets. She diagnosed me in ten minutes. She was right. I’m still annoyed.
gossip.note: Allison Kent says Clara Weiss diagnoses everyone she meets.
gossip.ask: Allison says you diagnosed her in ten minutes and you were right.
gossip.answer: ok WAIT she said that?? I only said she holds her pen like someone who doesn’t trust the pen. that’s not a diagnosis that’s an observation!! she leaves the seminar early every week looking really pale though. is she ok? you’d tell me if she wasn’t ok right

gossip.says: Alice Beaumont books every speaker the Bluebirds have and plans seating for three hundred like a general. I’ve seen her move a table with one look.
gossip.note: Allison Kent says Alice Beaumont plans Bluebird seating like a general.
gossip.ask: Allison says you can move a table with one look.
gossip.answer: Three hundred guests and one seating plan. I could run a country with less. A look is cheaper than an argument, and much harder to complain about afterwards. Tell Allison she’s welcome at any of my tables. I’ll seat her somewhere interesting.

gossip.says: Rosa Gutierrez checks her lock twice and doesn’t sleep. She says it’s deadlines. I’d keep an eye on her, if I were you. Gently.
gossip.note: Allison Kent says Rosa Gutierrez isn’t sleeping.
gossip.ask: Allison says I should keep an eye on you, gently.
gossip.answer: Allison said that? That’s strangely kind of her. I’m fine. It’s deadlines. Probably. I check the lock twice. Everyone checks the lock twice. Do you check the lock twice? Say yes.

own.label: Ask about her thesis
own.player: What’s your thesis on?
own.reply: Water rights in the desert. Who owns the rain. It sounds boring until you realize the answer is whoever got there first with a lawyer.

own.label: Ask how she’s doing
own.player: How are you doing, really?
own.reply: I don’t sleep much. I check the lock twice. It’s probably just deadlines. Probably.

own.label: Ask about her friends at the meetings
own.player: What are the people at your meetings like?
own.reply: Most of them are lovely. A few of them sit at the back and never vote, and when they look at me I feel like I’ve already said too much.
own.note: Rosa is frightened of a few people who sit at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family nearby?
own.reply: My mom’s an hour south. She thinks I’m studying. I am studying. Mostly.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Water people, an hour south. Grandad lost a well to a lawyer in a suit, which is why I study water. Dad fixes pumps. Mom cleans for a judge. They think I’m studying. I am, mostly.

own.label: Ask why her lights are always off
own.player: Why are your lights always off at night?
own.reply: I sit in the dark and check the lock. Twice. It’s probably deadlines. Probably.

own.label: Ask what her supervisor wants
own.player: What does your supervisor think of the thesis?
own.reply: He’s asked me to soften the part where I name who owns the rain. It was the Shawcrosses. Whoever got there first with a lawyer.

views.campus: I agree with the protests. I just don’t agree with everyone in them.
views.speakers: I think Vale’s guests are wrong. I also think some of the people who hate them have stopped seeing the professor as a person. That scares me more than any speech.

calls.label: Ask about the man with the poems
calls.player: Who’s leaving poems outside your seminar?
calls.reply: He was on our course before they asked him to leave. He speaks to the porters in verse. His name’s Theon. He signs the poems Orsino, and he’s using someone else’s photographs. Campus security says there’s nothing to be done.
calls.note: Rosa Gutierrez says the man leaving poems was on her course: his name is Theon.

life.news: Found a water case from eighty years ago where the judge ruled the rain belonged to whoever owned the cloud. Owned the cloud.
life.more: Who owns the rain. It sounds boring until you realize the answer is whoever got there first with a lawyer. That judge actually wrote it down. Somebody owned a cloud. I’ve pinned it over my desk to remind me what I’m up against.

life.news: Didn’t sleep. Checked the lock twice. Then again.
life.more: It’s probably just deadlines. Probably. Some nights the apartment feels like it’s listening. I sat in the dark with tea until it got light. My neighbor waved from her window. I waved back. That helped more than it should have.

life.news: My mom sent a parcel from an hour south. Tamales and a note saying eat something green. The tamales are not green.
life.more: She thinks I’m studying. I am studying. Mostly. The note says eat something green, and underneath, in my dad’s writing: ignore her, eat the tamales. My whole family on one piece of paper.

life.news: Met a woman at a water meeting who knows the ranch country better than anyone. Isabel. I liked her straight away.
life.more: Isabel Morales. She trains horses past the canyon and talks about wells like they’re people. Her grandfather never sold a drop. Mine lost his well to a man in a suit. We talked for two hours. I slept that night. Properly.

gossip.says: Isabel Morales trains horses past the canyon and talks about wells like they’re people. Her family has never sold a drop of water. In this county that makes them saints.
gossip.note: Rosa Gutierrez says Isabel Morales’s family has never sold their water.
gossip.ask: Rosa says your family has never sold a drop of water.
gossip.answer: Five generations and never a drop. My great-grandfather said water you sell is water your grandchildren can’t drink. My father says no to every man in a suit who drives up. He’s very good at no. Rosa should come out to the ranch. The horses would like her.

gossip.says: Rebecca Shaw vouched for me when nobody else would. She asks why you think something and genuinely waits for the answer. I’d follow her into any hall she booked.
gossip.note: Rosa Gutierrez says Rebecca Shaw vouched for her.
gossip.ask: Rosa says she’d follow you into any hall you booked.
gossip.answer: Rosa’s the cleverest person at our meetings and she sits at the edge like she’s not allowed in. She is. I’d vouch for her again tomorrow. Tell her to come back to the office. We miss her. The rabbits miss her.

gossip.says: Leila Sayeed, the nurse at the police station, sat with me one night when I couldn’t speak. She brought tea in a paper cup and didn’t ask anything. I haven’t thanked her.
gossip.note: Rosa Gutierrez says custody nurse Leila Sayeed sat with her on a bad night.
gossip.ask: Rosa says you sat with her one night and never asked anything.
gossip.answer: The quiet ones. The ones who say they’re fine and look at the wall. I sit with them longer. Rosa doesn’t need to thank me. Tell her the tea’s on me any time. And tell her I meant what I said, whatever she decides.

own.label: Ask how she runs the parish
own.player: How do you keep the whole parish running?
own.reply: Lists. Lists of lists. A roster for the flowers, a roster for the food pantry, and a roster for the rosters. Chaos is a choice.

own.label: Ask about the guitar dispute
own.player: What’s really going on with the bishop and the guitars?
own.reply: The bishop wants to modernise us. We have sung the same Mass in that chapel since before he was born. I have written him four letters. He has replied to none.

own.label: Ask why she isn’t married
own.player: Can I ask why you’re not married?
own.reply: Because nobody has yet passed my questions. I don’t mean to sound proud. I mean that marriage is forever, and I take forever seriously.

own.label: Ask about the old vigils
own.player: Do the Sisters still hold vigils?
own.reply: When there’s need. A vigil needs a leader, keys, someone on the door and enough voices. I’ve organized harder things. Never a more frightening one.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: Is your mother still in the parish?
own.reply: Alive, sharp, and at every Mass in a hat that has opinions. My great-grandparents gave St. Brigid’s its organ. My mother behaves as if she’s still paying for it.

own.label: Ask about her morning walk
own.player: What do you do first thing?
own.reply: I walk the parish. I know which lights are on and which should be. A coordinator who doesn’t walk is just a woman with a clipboard.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever silly
own.player: Are you ever not stern?
own.reply: Ask Teresa or Sophia. Nobody else has seen it and I intend to keep it that way. I do a very good impression of the bishop’s secretary.

own.label: Ask about the bishop’s review
own.player: What’s this review of the Sisters about?
own.reply: The chancellor’s letter came the week after our caretaker stopped coming to Mass. The guitars are an excuse. Somebody wants our land, and our papers. I have put the papers where the review won’t find them, and I don’t have the key. Truthfully.
own.note: Margaret Holloway says the bishop’s review of the Sisters is about their land and papers, which she has hidden.

own.label: Ask what she wrote to the bishop
own.player: What did you write to the bishop?
own.reply: The first letter was about the music. The second asked whether he knew what that round of his was. The third asked whether he had read the second. The fourth asked where his chancellor’s informant had gone. The fifth is in the post. None has been answered, and I have kept copies, which is the only part of this I enjoy.
own.note: Margaret Holloway has written the bishop five letters: the music, the founding round, the unread letters, the missing caretaker, and one more in the post. None answered.

views.believe: In order. God made an orderly world and people keep untidying it.
views.campus: Young people shouting is not new. Young people refusing to listen at all is.
views.sisters: We are not a museum. We are a household. We just happen to have very old furniture.
views.dispute: Five letters. No replies. A reply is a reply. The guitars are an excuse and the review is the thing, and I have put the papers where the review won’t find them. Ask me anything else about it and I’ll tell you I don’t have the key, which is true.

life.news: Made a roster for the rosters. It works. Nobody believes me.
life.more: Lists. Lists of lists. A roster for the flowers, a roster for the pantry, and now a roster for the rosters. Chaos is a choice. Teresa laughed at it. Then she asked to borrow the template. I’m not saying I won. I’m saying I’m right.

life.news: Wrote to the bishop again. Fifth letter. No reply.
life.more: About the guitars at the evening Mass. I’ve written to him five times. He has replied to none. That is a reply. My mother says to stop writing. My mother sits at every Mass in a hat that disagrees with the guitars too.

life.news: Walked the parish at dawn and every light was where it should be. Best feeling I know.
life.more: I walk it every morning. I know which lights are on and why. Mrs. Ortiz’s kitchen light means she’s baking. The Morettis’ oven light means the bread’s in. When they’re all where they should be, the town’s all right.

life.news: Laughed so hard at something Teresa said that I had to leave the parish office. Nobody saw. Please keep it that way.
life.more: I’m stern. It’s very important that I’m stern. Only Teresa and Sophia know I’m funny, and I’d like it to stay that way. She did an impression of the bishop reading my letters. I had to go and stand in the garden for five minutes.

gossip.says: Evelyn Rosales keeps every account in the parish and checks every sum twice. She’s the bravest woman I know, and she’d rather die than say anything in front of people.
gossip.note: Margaret Holloway says Evelyn Rosales checks every parish account twice.
gossip.ask: Margaret says you’re the bravest woman she knows.
gossip.answer: Margaret said that? Oh. I just keep the books. Nobody notices me unless something’s missing, which is how I like it. I’ll do anything, so long as I don’t have to do it in front of people. Please don’t tell anyone she said brave.

gossip.says: Cassandra Finch sits at the back of our vigil and says she doesn’t believe. She hasn’t missed one in a year. I’ll take a woman who comes without believing over one who believes and stays at home.
gossip.note: Margaret Holloway says Cassandra Finch never misses the Sisters’ vigil though she doesn’t believe.
gossip.ask: Margaret says you haven’t missed a vigil in a year, believing or not.
gossip.answer: It’s the quietest room in Sunfall and everyone in it means what they’re saying. I sit at the back and think about the people I’m worried about. Margaret says that’s praying. I say it’s sitting. We’ve agreed to disagree, with cake.

gossip.says: Sofia Delgado runs the food program with us and has already decided who every Sister should marry. She’s usually right. It’s alarming.
gossip.note: Margaret Holloway says Sofia Delgado has decided who every Sister should marry.
gossip.ask: Margaret says you’ve already decided who every Sister should marry.
gossip.answer: Not every Sister! Seven out of nine. Margaret is the hardest. She needs a man who can keep up with a roster of rosters. I have a list. Of course I have a list. I learned from her.

own.label: Ask about teaching
own.player: What’s it like teaching at the parish school?
own.reply: Twenty-two eight-year-olds and one class hamster who is, theologically speaking, a menace.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother’s shop
own.player: Your grandmother has a shop?
own.reply: Bellamy & Daughters Antiques. She’s sold rings to half the parish. She says every ring has a story and she knows most of them.

own.label: Ask about the old chapel
own.player: What’s the story of the old chapel outside town?
own.reply: The old mission chapel lost its bell in a storm, long ago. The old women say it was the night the bell forgot its voice. Children dare each other to go there.
own.note: Teresa says the old mission chapel is the one whose bell forgot its voice.

own.label: Ask about her favorite saint
own.player: Do you have a favorite saint?
own.reply: Saint Brigid, of course. Patroness of our chapel, and she once turned bathwater into beer for visitors. Hospitality is holy.

own.label: Ask about living above the shop
own.player: What’s it like living above an antiques shop?
own.reply: Granny’s cuckoo clocks go off at different times, so phone calls are a lottery. If you hear a bird, that’s not me, that’s eighteen-forties Bavaria.

own.label: Ask about her grandparents’ wedding
own.player: How did your grandparents meet?
own.reply: Granddad Walter dropped the ring in the font at their wedding, fifty-one years ago, and Father fished it out with the aspergillum. Granny still says it was the most blessed ring in the county.

own.label: Ask about her exams
own.player: Are you a strict teacher?
own.reply: Ruthless. Twenty-two eight-year-olds know the seven sacraments in order or they don’t get the hamster for the weekend. It works on adults too, I find.

own.label: Ask who asked her about the bell tower
own.player: Did anyone ever ask you about the old bell tower?
own.reply: A girl in black at a parish open day, two years ago, with a notebook. Victoria, she said. I told her which chapel’s bell forgot its voice, and why the Sisters keep vigil on the new moon, because I answer questions. She thanked me and wrote it all down. I think I gave somebody a calendar.
own.note: Teresa Bellamy told Victoria Blackwood which chapel’s bell went silent and why the Sisters keep vigil on the new moon.

own.label: Ask when the next vigil is
own.player: When is the Sisters’ next vigil?
own.reply: On the new moon: {night}. We keep the vigil because once, long ago, other women kept something else on those nights. Come and stand at the back if you like. Bring a coat.

own.label: Ask about the bishop’s visit to the school
own.player: Did the bishop really visit your school?
own.reply: Twice. The hamster bit him both times. The second time he asked my children which of their parents went to the first-light Mass, and I said that was not a question for children, and he smiled the way men smile when they have decided to remember you. I am on a list now. I’ve put a gold star next to it.
own.note: Teresa Bellamy says the bishop asked her class which parents go to the first-light Latin Mass, and she refused him.

views.believe: That small kindnesses are how the world gets mended, one stitch at a time.
views.goths: One of them asked me about the old bell tower once. She wasn’t curious. She was taking notes.
