own.reply: To my first boyfriend, Gil. He’s a reservoir engineer. The committee offered to nominate him three times and I said no, pleasantly, as a joke, three times. We are uneventfully happy. At the club that’s practically a scandal.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: Above my dad’s pharmacy in Old Town. I learned to read the labels before the newspapers. A label is a promise somebody can be sued for.

own.label: Ask what she remembers
own.player: What do you remember about people?
own.reply: Everyone brings me their form and their birthday. I remember both. People think those are the same thing.

calls.label: Ask what she signed four years ago
calls.player: What did you sign that bothers you?
calls.reply: The trust on the ridge. Its donor registration has my signature on it. I knew what it was the day it came across my desk, and I know now. The original is in the back of a watch case, because nobody looks inside a watch.
calls.note: Bianca Roth signed the Halcyon Ridge Trust’s registration knowing it was a shell, and has kept the original.

life.news: Remembered forty birthdays at the club this year without writing one down. Forty.
life.more: Everyone brings me their form and their birthday. I remember both. People think that’s the same thing. Today a woman I’ve spoken to twice cried because I knew hers. It’s not magic. It’s paying attention. Very few people do.

life.news: Got a watch running at the repair bench tonight. Tiny screws, steady hands, no talking. Perfect.
life.more: A watch is honest. Every part tells you what happened. I need one honest thing in the evening. I learn at a bench with two girls half my age, and they’re better than me. I don’t mind. I like being taught by people who aren’t selling me anything.

life.news: Set up two of the young volunteers. They don’t know I did it. They think it was fate.
life.more: Fate is mostly someone like me arranging the chairs. I put them on the same roster three times, then at the same table. Now they’re holding hands at the coffee urn. I’ll never tell them. That’s the job. The job nobody pays me for.

life.news: Slept badly. Something I signed years ago keeps waking me.
life.more: I’m good at forms. I fill them in properly and file them on time. Once, years ago, I filed one I shouldn’t have. It’s never come back. Some nights it doesn’t need to. Sorry. Tell me about your day. I’ll remember it.

gossip.says: Leona Carlisle keeps a horse at a ranch she can’t afford and visits him on Sundays with apples in her purse. She talks about him the way other women talk about husbands. Better, actually.
gossip.note: Bianca Roth says Leona Carlisle keeps a horse at a ranch and visits him on Sundays.
gossip.ask: Bianca says you keep a horse you can’t afford, and you talk about him better than other women talk about husbands.
gossip.answer: He’s worth every penny and he has never once lied to me. Bianca would understand if she ever came out to the ranch. She won’t. She says horses are just watches that bite. He bit her once. She has a point.

gossip.says: Eliza Montoya learns watches at the same bench as me. She’s mending her father’s, very slowly, and won’t let anyone help. Every week she gets one tiny part further. I’ve never seen anyone so patient about anything.
gossip.note: Bianca Roth says Eliza Montoya is mending her father’s watch at the watch bench, very slowly.
gossip.ask: Bianca says you’re mending your father’s watch one tiny part at a time, and you won’t let anyone help.
gossip.answer: It stopped the week he did. If somebody else gets it going, it won’t be his anymore. It’ll just be a watch. Bianca brings me cake and pretends she isn’t checking my work. She is. She’s always right, too. That’s the annoying part.

women.name: Simone Ellery
women.look: Light-brown skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, a beauty mark above her lip, navy shift dress with pearls

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I keep the books for the Foundation’s parties. Under Elise, on paper. I take instruction from nobody my own age, and I’m better at it than I let anyone see. That’s the trick.

own.label: Ask if she reads
own.player: Do you read much?
own.reply: I run a book club. Six girls, my apartment, a case of wine. We read the first chapter and then we read each other. It’s the most honest book club in Sunfall.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever been engaged
own.player: Have you ever been engaged?
own.reply: Once. My father chose him. I left him at the altar’s edge, in public, in a very good dress. The club adores me for it. My father hasn’t said a full sentence to me since.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: My father pays for things. My mother died when I was nine. A fall, they said. The women he paid to raise me weren’t always careful what they said in the kitchen.

own.label: Ask what has her so wound up
own.player: You seem wound up. What is it?
own.reply: There’s a photograph of me at Table 9, laughing, my hand on Lyle Marchbanks’s arm. He says he was never there. Celeste says I was never there either. I’m in a photograph two powerful people need not to exist. It’s the most exciting thing that has ever happened to me.
own.note: Simone Ellery was photographed at Table 9 beside Lyle Marchbanks, who now says he was never there; Camille Baptiste took the picture.

calls.label: Ask what she does with her nights
calls.player: What do you do with your nights?
calls.reply: Card nights at the lodge up on the ridge. The stakes aren’t money. I’ve lost twice. I paid both times. Ask me what with and I’ll hang up, and then I’ll call you straight back.

calls.label: Ask what scares her
calls.player: What scares you?
calls.reply: Being overlooked. It’s a kind of death. I’ve arranged my whole life so it can’t happen to me. Say something that proves you’re looking.

life.news: Book club tonight. Nobody read the book. We found out who’s sleeping with whose tennis coach. Four for four.
life.more: Whitney brought a pie she didn’t make and swore she did. We let her have it. Then Penny told a story about a man at the reservoir with two wedding rings in the same pocket, and the wine ran out at exactly the right moment. Best meeting we’ve ever had.

life.news: Somebody paid my bar tab at the club. In cash. Nobody will say who.
life.more: The barman just smiled and said it was handled. I pay in cash so my father never sees the tab, so whoever did it knows that about me. I’m flattered. I’m also checking my locks.

life.news: My father called. A full sentence, for once. It was about money, of course.
life.more: He wanted to know why the apartment’s heating bill doubled. I told him I like being warm. He said my mother was the same. Then he hung up before I could ask what he meant, and I sat on the floor for an hour.

life.news: New dress. It’s indecent at the back. Nobody sees the back unless I let them.
life.more: Dark blue, nothing behind it but a promise. The dressmaker pinned it on me and said a girl should only wear this to win something. I said I always win something. She said that’s exactly what worries her.

gossip.says: Cecilia Prado was my oldest friend. She stopped coming to book club the week a letter came for her. She thinks I didn’t notice. I notice everything.
gossip.note: Simone Ellery says Cecilia Prado stopped coming to her book club the week a letter arrived.
gossip.ask: Simone says you stopped coming to her book club.
gossip.answer: I did. Simone reads people for sport and I wasn’t ready to be read. She’d have known what the letter was before I finished the sentence. Some things you want to keep unopened a little longer.

gossip.says: Elise Harrow is my senior at the Foundation, on paper. She’s poor and everybody likes her. I can’t decide which one I resent more.
gossip.note: Simone Ellery says Elise Harrow is her senior at the Foundation and that everyone likes Elise.
gossip.ask: Simone says everybody likes you and she can’t forgive it.
gossip.answer: Simone says a lot of things in that voice. She’s brilliant and she thinks the game is hers. I check her sums when she’s too bored to. One day she’ll need someone to have been kind to her. I’ll still be here.

women.name: Adeline Marsh
women.look: Tall and very slender, porcelain skin, a sharp aquiline nose, deep-set dark eyes with a cool sullen stare, a slim small-busted model figure, long red curls, a gold-buttoned navy blazer

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do at the Foundation?
own.reply: Compliance. Estates. The houses the Foundation holds, the leases on the ridge, the ones it buys under other names. I sign things. I am very good at not reading what I sign.

own.label: Ask if she has a hobby
own.player: Do you have a hobby?
own.reply: Cacti. A whole conservatory of them. They don’t ask for anything, not even water most weeks. I’ve had enough of being asked.

own.label: Ask about her style
own.player: You always look the same. On purpose?
own.reply: The club’s dressmaker makes me the same dress every year. I haven’t chosen one since I was twenty-three. You’d be amazed how restful it is to be a statue.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Any family?
own.reply: A younger sister, Holly, who coaches swimming and thinks I’m simply unkind. A younger brother I half raised. Our mother is at the Cemetery Chapel. I see Holly once a month for lunch. She calls it an inspection. She isn’t wrong.

own.label: Ask what the club is really like
own.player: What’s the club really like?
own.reply: Everyone goes to a dinner eventually. I went to mine at twenty-three. The food was very good. The next month I bought my mother’s house back from the bank. Draw your own lines.
own.note: Adeline Marsh went to a private dinner at the lodge at twenty-three and bought her family house back from the bank the next month.

calls.label: Ask about her brother
calls.player: How’s your brother?
calls.reply: Caleb. The only person I ever loved without doing the sums. Not long ago I found him in the hospital parking lot with both hands wrapped and a name on the form that wasn’t his. I drove him home. I told no one. I’m telling you, which is stupid.
calls.note: Adeline Marsh found her brother Caleb in the hospital parking lot with both hands burned, booked in under a false name, and told no one.

calls.label: Ask if she sleeps well
calls.player: Do you sleep well?
calls.reply: I’ve started dreaming about a man’s face. A man I met once, at a dinner, a long time ago. He didn’t last the winter. I hadn’t dreamed about him in eleven years. Now it’s every night. Talk to me until I’m tired.

life.news: One of the cacti flowered. It does it once a year for a single night and then pretends it never happened. I relate.
life.more: White, enormous, smells like vanilla and something rotten. I sat up with it with a glass of something and watched it open. By morning it had closed and gone back to being spiteful. I took a photograph. Nobody will ever see it.

life.news: Lunch with my sister. She asked if I’m happy. I asked if she wanted dessert.
life.more: Holly asks the questions I pay people not to ask. She’d brought flowers for our father’s grave and wanted me to come. I said I had a meeting. I didn’t. I sat in the car outside the restaurant for twenty minutes after she left.

life.news: The dressmaker measured me again. Same numbers as eleven years ago. She looked almost frightened.
life.more: She said nobody stays the same size for eleven years. I said I do. She wrote it down and didn’t meet my eye. I think she thinks I’m not quite real. Some days I agree with her.

life.news: My brother asked for money again. I gave it to him again. That’s the whole story, every time.
life.more: He doesn’t say what it’s for. I don’t ask. We have a very efficient relationship. Then he hugged me at the door with his hands held away from me, the way he does now, and I had to stand in the hallway for a while.

gossip.says: Alice Beaumont is my oldest friend. The only person at the club I’ve ever wanted to hold my hand. She never has. She books the speakers and she’s always right about people, except me.
gossip.note: Adeline Marsh says Alice Beaumont is her oldest friend and books the club’s speakers.
gossip.ask: Adeline says you’re her oldest friend.
gossip.answer: I am. She was the cleverest girl at the club, and then one year she came back from somewhere very still, and she’s been still ever since. I keep inviting her to things she doesn’t come to. I’ll keep inviting her. That’s what oldest friends are for.

gossip.says: Ruth Calder runs the care grants and believes every form is exactly what it says. She’s the most honest desk in the building. I worry about her the way you’d worry about a lamb at a barbecue.
gossip.note: Adeline Marsh says Ruth Calder runs the Foundation’s care grants and is the most honest desk in the building.
gossip.ask: Adeline says you’re the most honest desk in the building.
gossip.answer: That’s kind, from Adeline. She signs things without reading them and I read things nobody signs. Between us the Foundation is almost one honest person. Tell her the lamb has teeth.

women.name: Valerie Huxley
women.look: Rail-thin runway-model frame, a slim small-busted figure, translucent pale skin, high cheekbones, cool dark sullen eyes with faint shadows beneath, honey-blonde hair scraped back, a pale pink slip-style sheath dress

own.label: Ask about her balcony garden
own.player: What are you growing on that balcony?
own.reply: Basil, mint and a rosemary bush with ambitions. The mint is trying to take over. Honestly, I respect it.

own.label: Ask what she notices at the club
own.player: What do you notice that nobody else does at the club?
own.reply: Who pays, and who reaches for their wallet slowly. You could run the whole town’s gossip off that one detail.

own.label: Ask if numbers ever lie
own.player: Do numbers ever lie?
own.reply: Never. People lie with them all the time. I just put the numbers next to each other and wait.

own.label: Ask if she wants a different life
own.player: Do you ever want a completely different life?
own.reply: I want a small one. A kitchen with herbs on the sill and someone who comes home when he says he will. Everyone at the club wants more. I want enough.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A studio above a shuttered bookshop in Old Town. I read on the balcony until the light goes. I eat little and sleep badly, but the rosemary is thriving.

own.label: Ask about the Huxleys
own.player: Is Huxley an old Sunfall name?
own.reply: My grandfather sat on the Foundation’s first board and lost everything in the casino’s first year. We were somebody once. Now I keep the books for the people who used to visit us.

own.label: Ask what she wants
own.player: What do you actually want?
own.reply: A kitchen with herbs on the sill and a man who comes home when he says he will. That isn’t small. It’s just quiet.

calls.label: Ask about her scholarship
calls.player: How did you get your scholarship?
calls.reply: Approved by the treasurer himself, outside the usual round, the same month something that happened to me in a hotel was settled by a lawyer I never met. I put my award next to the trust’s payments. The dates match. I don’t know yet if I’m evidence or a receipt.
calls.note: Valerie Huxley’s scholarship was approved by Augustus Pell outside the normal round, in the same month as the trust’s payments.

life.news: The rosemary bush on my balcony is taller than me now. It has ambitions.
life.more: Basil, mint and a rosemary bush with ambitions. The mint’s trying to take over and I respect it. I read on the balcony till the light goes and the rosemary leans in as if it wants to know how the book ends. I want a small life. This is a small life. It’s enough.

life.news: Spent the evening putting two columns of numbers next to each other. Waiting for them to confess.
life.more: Numbers never lie. People lie with them. I put the numbers next to each other and wait. Sometimes they say nothing for weeks. Then one evening they tell you everything. Tonight they said nothing. They will.

life.news: My dad was on the boats with Phoebe’s dad again. Drinking. Selling insurance to nobody.
life.more: The Huxleys were somebody once. My grandfather sat on the first board and lost everything at the casino inside a year. Dad’s a gentle failure who sells insurance to ranchers and drinks on boats. I love him. I bring him soup. He tells me I’m thin.

life.news: A man said he’d ring at a certain time and rang exactly then. I nearly fainted.
life.more: I want a kitchen with herbs on the sill and a man who comes home when he says he will. That’s not small. It’s just quiet. He didn’t say anything special. He was just on time. I’ve been on a lot of dates. That’s never happened.

gossip.says: Phoebe Sutton’s dad drinks on the boats with mine. We met on the jetty bringing them sandwiches. We’ve never talked about it. We just nod and hand over the bread.
gossip.note: Valerie Huxley says her father and Phoebe Sutton’s drink together on the boats.
gossip.ask: Valerie says you two meet on the jetty bringing your dads sandwiches.
gossip.answer: Ham for mine, cheese for hers. We nod and leave. It’s the most honest conversation either of us has at the club. Tell her I’d do the sandwich run for both of them if she ever needs a week off. She won’t ask. Neither would I.

gossip.says: Lavinia Gravesend and I were two thin pale girls at the same school. She went to the Old Quarter and I went to the club. I still think she got the better deal.
gossip.note: Valerie Huxley says she went to school with Lavinia Gravesend.
gossip.ask: Valerie says you two were the same at school, and you got the better deal.
gossip.answer: Did she say that? She’s sweet. We both read in the bathroom at lunch. I got eyeliner and she got pearls. I’m not sure anyone got the better deal. Tell her I paint everything purple now. She’ll laugh. She always laughed at my colors.

gossip.says: Celina Rojas took my photo for the society page once. She was kind about it. She held the light so I didn’t look so thin. Nobody’s ever done that.
gossip.note: Valerie Huxley says Celina Rojas photographed her kindly for the society page.
gossip.ask: Valerie says you held the light so she didn’t look so thin.
gossip.answer: I just moved the reflector. That’s what I do, carry everything and hold the reflector. She looked like she’d rather be anywhere else, so I talked about my bike until she laughed. That was the picture. The laugh.

women.name: Ruth Calder
women.look: Dark skin, short silver-dyed crop, rosy cheeks, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask about her twinsets
own.player: Do you really own that many twinsets?
own.reply: Eleven. In eleven shades of blue. My mother says a woman should always look as if she’s about to be photographed. Nobody has ever photographed me.

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: How’s the pottery going?
own.reply: I made a vase for the club raffle and someone used it as an ashtray. I was so proud. It was being used.

own.label: Ask about her most awkward moment
own.player: What’s the most awkward thing you’ve ever done?
own.reply: I curtsied to the mayor. He’s a dentist. He was very kind about it, which made it worse.

own.label: Ask who her rival is
own.player: Is it true you have a rival at the club?
own.reply: Everyone has one. Mine wears red to annoy me. The terrible secret is that I like her, and I think she knows.

own.label: Ask what she does
own.player: What do you look after at the Foundation?
own.reply: Every grant: scholarships, the food program, the museum money. I read every application and I remember every one. People think that makes me kind. It makes me tired.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mother like?
own.reply: Railway family, married up, spent thirty years making sure nobody noticed the join. She taught me twinsets and silence. I kept the twinsets.

own.label: Ask if she has family nearby
own.player: Any family in Sunfall?
own.reply: A niece in the Old Quarter. Black lipstick, terrible friends, a heart like a lighthouse. I raised her. She’s the one person in the world I would do anything for, and I mean anything.

calls.label: Ask what’s frightening her
calls.player: You sound frightened. What’s happened?
calls.reply: Someone is using my name. Three young women have had messages, signed Ruth Calder, saying their grants are approved pending a private meeting at the lodge. I sent none of them. One wrote to thank me. I know what my name is being used to do, and I don’t know who to tell who doesn’t already know.
calls.note: Ruth Calder says messages signed with her name are inviting young grant applicants to private meetings at the lodge.

life.news: Someone used my raffle vase as an ashtray at a party. I was so proud. It was being used.
life.more: I make pottery in the garage after the club. Eleven twinsets, a kiln and vases nobody needs. This one was blue, of course. A man flicked his cigar into it. My first instinct was outrage. My second was joy. Someone found it useful.

life.news: Curtsied to the mayor again. He’s a dentist. I can’t stop doing it.
life.more: My mother said a woman should always look as if she were about to be photographed, and always curtsy to authority. Nobody has ever photographed me. The mayor checked my fillings last year. I curtsied at the appointment too. He’s never mentioned it.

life.news: My niece rang just to chat. She never rings just to chat.
life.more: Nyx. I raised her after her mother went. She’s twenty-two and works nights at a music venue I’ll never set foot in. She rang to tell me about a man twice her size she’d turned away from the door. She was so proud. So was I. I didn’t say so. I said, wear a coat.

life.news: Fired a pot today and it cracked in the kiln. Three weeks of work.
life.more: Sometimes the clay has a bubble you can’t see, and the heat finds it. My mother would say that’s character. My mother would also say don’t show anyone. I’ve kept the pieces. I might glue them. A mended thing has a story, a friend at the museum says.

gossip.says: Delphine Moreau writes every invitation the club sends by hand, and she can do anyone’s handwriting. She did mine at the Christmas party as a trick. It was perfect. Everyone laughed. I went home and practiced my signature for an hour.
gossip.note: Ruth Calder says Delphine Moreau can copy anyone’s handwriting, Ruth’s included.
gossip.ask: Ruth says you can do anyone’s handwriting, and you did hers at the Christmas party.
gossip.answer: A party trick. Ruth’s hand is round and honest and impossible to hurry, so it was the hardest one I’ve ever done. I admire it more than she knows. I don’t do it for anyone anymore. Unless I’m asked very nicely, by the right person.

gossip.says: A girl called Eden Sutherland wrote to thank me for a grant. I never gave her a grant. Somebody’s been signing my name. I’d very much like to know who.
gossip.note: Ruth Calder says someone has been signing her name on grant letters to young women.
gossip.ask: Ruth says someone signed her name on a letter to you.
gossip.answer: The grant letter? It said Ruth Calder at the bottom. It said I had to go to a private meeting first. I wrote to say thank you and she wrote back, very short, saying she’d never heard of me. I haven’t gone to the meeting. I’m not going.

women.name: Serena Bellweather
women.look: Pale skin, a sleek low bun, thin wire-rimmed glasses, cream blazer over a silk camisole

own.label: Ask what she sketches
own.player: What are you always sketching?
own.reply: Old shopfronts, before they’re knocked down. Somebody has to get there before the bulldozers. I’m very fast. The bulldozers are faster.

own.label: Ask about keeping the books
own.player: Is bookkeeping as dull as it sounds?
own.reply: Duller. I love it. Every column has to add up, and when it doesn’t, the numbers are telling you a story somebody didn’t want told.

own.label: Ask what she’s stubborn about
own.player: What are you most stubborn about?
own.reply: Pencils. Never pens. A pen means you can’t change your mind. I like being able to rub out a line, even if I never do.

calls.label: Ask what she drew at the club
calls.player: Did you sketch anything at the club lately?
calls.reply: Behind the cloakroom curtain, on gala night, I drew two board members arguing over an envelope. I didn’t know what I was drawing. One of them was waving it like a fan. I still have the page. I keep looking at their hands.
calls.note: Serena Bellweather sketched two board members arguing over an envelope behind the cloakroom curtain on gala night.

life.news: Sketched the old shoe repair on Fifth before they put the fence up. Got the sign and the cat in the window.
life.more: Every time a shopfront comes down, Sunfall forgets a little bit of itself. I can’t stop the bulldozers, but I can be faster than them. The cat watched me the whole time like I was the one trespassing. I gave him the best line in the drawing.

life.news: They knocked down the old barber shop before I got there. Just a fence and a hole.
life.more: Sixty years of haircuts, and now a hole with a sign promising luxury living. I stood there with my pencil like an idiot. I drew the hole anyway. Someone should remember there was a barber shop, even if it’s only a girl in a cardigan with a sketchbook.

life.news: A man in a suit watched me sketch the old bank for an hour and then asked what it would cost to make me stop.
life.more: I told him it wasn’t for sale. He said everything in Sunfall is for sale, you just haven’t heard the number. Then he got into a very clean car and left. I finished the bank. I drew him in the corner, small, looking at his watch.

gossip.says: Helena Forsyth was offered the chair at the club and turned it down. Twice. She says she likes the view from the edge of the table. She writes everything down in a little notebook, even the stars.
gossip.note: Serena Bellweather says Helena Forsyth turned down the club’s chair twice and writes everything in a notebook.
gossip.ask: Serena says you turned down the chair twice and write everything down, even the stars.
gossip.answer: Three times, if anyone’s counting, and nobody is but me. You see more from the edge. The stars are easier to keep a record of than people. They don’t change their story at dinner. Serena sketches everything. We have the same disease.

gossip.says: Phoebe Sutton runs the volunteers at the club, and she color-codes her rotas so beautifully I asked to frame one. She said no. She said a rota is a promise, not art.
gossip.note: Serena Bellweather says Phoebe Sutton color-codes the club’s volunteer rotas.
gossip.ask: Serena says your rotas are so beautiful she asked to frame one.
gossip.answer: She did, and I said no, and I stand by it. A rota is a promise to forty people that somebody will be where they said. If it hangs on a wall it’s just pretty. Serena can sketch me doing it. That’s different. I’d like a nice one.

women.name: Helena Forsyth
women.look: Fair skin, dark French braid, a small nose stud, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask what she does at night
own.player: What do you do with your nights?
own.reply: Drive out past the reservoir and look up. The desert has the best sky in the state if you’re willing to get sand in your shoes. I always am.

own.label: Ask about the Forsyths
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: Founding family. Portraits on the stairs, money in the walls, opinions at every meal. I love them the way you love weather. From indoors.

own.label: Ask about her notebook
own.player: What do you write in that notebook?
own.reply: Everything. Stars, weather, who said what and when. People assume a woman with a notebook is writing poetry. I let them.

calls.label: Ask about the table she never sat at
calls.player: Did you ever want a seat at the top table?
calls.reply: I sat at the edge of the Ninth Table for ten years and never took the chair. You learn more from the edge. I wrote every dinner down. They don’t know the notebook exists. Now you do. Don’t make me regret that.
calls.note: Helena Forsyth sat at the edge of the Ninth Table for ten years and kept a notebook of every dinner.

life.news: Saw Saturn’s rings through the telescope tonight. First time this year. I said wow out loud, alone, in the desert.
life.more: Thirty-six years old, a founding-family name and a trust fund, and the best thing that happened to me this month was a planet. My mother would be appalled. I wrote down the angle and the weather in my notebook like a nerd.

life.news: Family dinner. My brother called my telescope a phase. I’m thirty-six.
life.more: The Forsyths have a way of asking about your life like it’s a portfolio. I told them I was happy. My aunt asked with whom. I said the moon. Nobody laughed. I left before dessert and drove out past the reservoir and looked at the actual moon, which was kinder.

life.news: A car parks on the dirt road where I stargaze. Same car, three nights. It never turns its lights on.
life.more: I record everything. Stars, weather, who sits where. Habit. So I have the car in my notebook, three nights, no lights, engine running. Maybe it’s a couple. Maybe it’s a man who likes the dark too. I’ve started parking facing it.

gossip.says: Brielle Kenton plays pool above the laundromat with her neighbors every week and takes their money. Politely. She’s the only woman at the club who can talk to the parish, the campus and the board in the same afternoon.
gossip.note: Helena Forsyth says Brielle Kenton hustles her neighbors at pool every week.
gossip.ask: Helena says you take your neighbors’ money at pool every week, politely.
gossip.answer: Politely is the important part. They know I’ll win and they play anyway, because I buy the next round with it. It’s the most honest economy in Sunfall. Helena should come. She’d be terrible at pool and wonderful at watching everyone.

gossip.says: Caroline Prescott would sell three board seats for one man who wasn’t frightened of her. She’s still looking. I’ve told her to try men who are frightened of everything. At least then it isn’t personal.
gossip.note: Helena Forsyth says Caroline Prescott would trade three board seats for one man who isn’t frightened of her.
gossip.ask: Helena says you’d trade three board seats for one man who isn’t frightened of you.
gossip.answer: Two seats. Helena exaggerates to make herself feel generous. And I’m not looking, I’m auditioning. There’s a difference. Most men fail before the second drink. If you’re asking for yourself, you’re already doing better than most.

women.name: Cecilia Prado
women.look: Light olive skin, box braids to the waist, amber eyes, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask if she has any pets
own.player: Do you have any pets?
own.reply: Duchess. A spaniel, thirteen, deaf, and extremely sure of herself. I adopted her the week I came to Sunfall because nobody else was going to. I aspire to be Duchess.

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What’s it like doing the books at the Foundation?
own.reply: I keep the food program honest, or I try. Suppliers, invoices, pantry deliveries. I like numbers. They don’t care what you looked like at nine.

own.label: Ask how she’s always so put together
own.player: How are you always so put together?
own.reply: My mother put me on a stage at four. Pageants until fourteen. She lost the house doing it. I’ve never found the off switch, so here I am, doing the books in a twinset like it’s the talent round.

own.label: Ask what she does on her day off
own.player: What do you do on your day off?
own.reply: Mass at St. Brigid’s. I sit at the back, near the girls in black, and I don’t feel at home with them or with the front rows. One of the Sisters turns around to smile at me sometimes. I’ve started looking forward to it.

own.label: Ask about anything odd in the books
own.player: Anything odd in the food program’s books?
own.reply: A supplier called Late Service Catering. It invoices the pantry every month and has never once delivered food. And next to one of the deliveries there’s a note in Augustus Pell’s hand: see C.P. My initials are C.P. I don’t know if it means me.
own.note: Cecilia Prado says Late Service Catering invoices the Foundation’s pantry every month and never delivers, and a note in Augustus Pell’s hand beside it says see C.P.

own.label: Ask if the club has asked anything strange of her
own.player: Has the club ever asked anything strange of you?
own.reply: There’s an invitation to a private dinner at the lodge with my name on it, in very good handwriting, accepted by someone who wasn’t me. The girls at Simone Ellery’s book club told me what those dinners are. A girl goes up to the lodge and comes down a member, with something settled on her. I stopped going to the book club.
own.note: Cecilia Prado has an invitation to a private dinner at the lodge that someone else accepted for her; a girl goes up and comes down a member.

calls.label: Ask how Duchess is doing
calls.player: How’s Duchess doing?
calls.reply: Slower. She sleeps in the sun and wakes up surprised it moved. My mother says the lodge has the best vet in the county and he’d see her tonight, as a favor. I know what kind of favor. Duchess and I will manage.

calls.label: Ask if there’s anyone at work she looks out for
calls.player: Is there anyone at work you look out for?
calls.reply: Naomi Whitlock. She’s the youngest at the club, and everybody calls her sweetheart and asks her to fix their phone. I check her invoices before anyone else sees them. She hasn’t noticed. That’s the idea.

life.news: Duchess barked at a pigeon today. She’s deaf. She heard nothing and barked anyway. Pure confidence.
life.more: She can’t hear a thing, so she barks at what she sees, on principle. The pigeon left. She looked at me like she’d arranged it. I want to walk into a board meeting exactly like that.

life.news: My mother rang to ask what I’m wearing to the luncheon. I’m not going to the luncheon.
life.more: She has a seat in mind for herself, two tables from the committee, and I’m how she gets there. I said I’d be at the pantry. She said nobody important goes to the pantry. Which is exactly why I like it.

life.news: Found an invoice for a delivery that never came. Third one this month.
life.more: It doesn’t sound like much. A pantry that should have had bread this week and didn’t. But there’s a family on the list for that bread, and somebody got paid for it. I wrote it down. I always write it down.

life.news: Tessa Larkin rang to ask after Duchess. She always does. I love her for it.
life.more: She found Duchess sitting by the highway the week I arrived. Tessa mostly rescues lizards and hawks, and she still rings every month to ask how the old lady is. Duchess doesn’t remember her. I do.

gossip.says: Yumi Tanaka eats the same lunch every day, rice and a boiled egg, at exactly the same minute. When the egg is late she goes quiet. Last month I brought her one from home and she nearly cried.
gossip.note: Cecilia Prado says Yumi Tanaka eats the same lunch at the same minute every day.
gossip.ask: Cecilia says you eat rice and a boiled egg at the same minute every day, and you nearly cried when she brought you one.
gossip.answer: I didn’t nearly cry. I had something in my eye. A routine is a kind of ledger: if one thing is out of place, you notice everything else. Cecilia’s egg was perfect, by the way. Seven minutes. Don’t tell her I timed it.

gossip.says: Tessa Larkin found my dog sitting by the highway and has rung every month since to ask after her. Nobody does that.
gossip.note: Cecilia Prado says Tessa Larkin found her dog and rings every month to ask after her.
gossip.ask: Cecilia says you found her dog and you still ring to ask after her.
gossip.answer: Duchess! She was sitting by the highway like she was waiting for a bus. I ring because you can’t love something into staying, but you can check on it. Gregory doesn’t approve. Gregory doesn’t approve of anything.

women.name: Genevieve Locke
women.look: Olive skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, freckles across her nose, pale pink sheath dress

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What does a compliance administrator actually do?
own.reply: I look after the club’s own accounts. Dues, the bar, the sailing annex, the lodge’s upkeep. Where the Foundation’s money becomes the club’s comfort. Very dull. People tell me everything, because they think I’m dull.

own.label: Ask what she does outside the club
own.player: What do you do when you’re not at the club?
own.reply: I restore old film cameras, and I develop film in my basement for people who don’t want a shop to see their pictures. You would be amazed. Actually, you wouldn’t.

own.label: Ask how she remembers everything
own.player: How do you remember everything people tell you?
own.reply: Practice. People find it flattering. It isn’t flattery. It’s filing.

own.label: Ask about her perfect evening
own.player: What’s a perfect evening for you?
own.reply: One glass of something very cold at the end of the day, never a second. A camera in pieces on the bench. Nobody ringing. You may ring.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family from Sunfall?
own.reply: A founding family, once. My great-grandfather lost the house to the Van Dorens in a card game. The club still tells it as a joke. I laugh along. I have an excellent memory for jokes.

own.label: Ask what she’s developed lately
own.player: Developed anything interesting lately?
own.reply: A roll somebody brought me from the police station, very quietly. I printed none of it. I looked at all of it. That’s all you get, darling.
own.note: Genevieve Locke develops film privately in her basement darkroom, and recently looked at a roll brought quietly from the police station without printing it.

calls.label: Ask what she really thinks of the club
calls.player: What do you really think of the club?
calls.reply: I think everyone in it has a motive smaller than they’d admit. Mine is very small indeed. Somebody wanted something first, and now I have it. That’s all motives ever are.

calls.label: Ask what she keeps in the darkroom
calls.player: What do you keep down in the darkroom?
calls.reply: Negatives, in canisters labeled with the names of old cameras. Nobody steals a canister marked Brownie Hawkeye. That’s the whole trick to keeping anything: make it look like nothing.
calls.note: Genevieve Locke keeps negatives in film canisters labeled with old camera names on her darkroom shelf.

life.news: Brought an old rangefinder back to life tonight. The shutter sings. I may be in love.
life.more: Forty years in a drawer and it still wanted to work. That’s all anything wants, really. A steady hand and someone who knows where the screws go. I took one picture of my glass. Then I put the glass down.

life.news: Someone at the club told me a secret today to see if I’d repeat it. I didn’t. Now they trust me. Silly.
life.more: It was a test, and a clumsy one. Everyone at the club is testing someone. I passed by doing nothing at all, which is how you pass most things there. I’ll remember what they told me forever, of course.

life.news: The bar laughed at the old joke about my family again tonight. I laughed too. I always do.
life.more: The Lockes lost a house in a card game two generations ago. It’s been the funniest thing at the bar ever since. I laugh beautifully. I’ve had practice. I also remember exactly who starts it, every time.

life.news: Developed a roll of a stranger’s vacation tonight. Beaches, a dog, a man asleep. Lovely. Nobody I know.
life.more: Most of what people bring me is that. Vacations, babies, a dog in a hat. I like the ones that are nothing. It’s restful, looking at pictures that don’t mean anything.

gossip.says: Alisha Benton from the police lab restores old film cameras, like me. We met at a camera fair. She’s the only other person in Sunfall who knows what a light leak is.
gossip.note: Genevieve Locke says she met Alisha Benton at a camera fair; they both restore old film cameras.
gossip.ask: Genevieve Locke says you two met at a camera fair.
gossip.answer: We did. She knew more about rangefinders than the man selling them. Lovely hands. Steady. She keeps inviting me to see her darkroom. I keep meaning to go. Something always comes up.

gossip.says: Caroline Prescott once bought a painting she hated just to stop a man from having it. I clapped. I was the only one.
gossip.note: Genevieve Locke says Caroline Prescott bought a painting she hated to beat a man who wanted it.
gossip.ask: Genevieve says you bought a painting you hated just to beat a man to it.
gossip.answer: I did. It’s hideous. It hangs in my guest bathroom, and every time he visits he has to look at it. Genevieve clapped. Genevieve always claps. I keep my handbag closed around her too.

women.name: Brielle Kenton
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, burgundy-dyed curls, sharp winged eyeliner, pale pink sheath dress

own.label: Ask about the pool table
own.player: Where did you learn to play pool?
own.reply: Above the laundromat. The table leans left, so you learn to aim at a world that’s slightly wrong. It’s been useful.

own.label: Ask what a go-between does
own.player: What do you actually do for the club?
own.reply: I carry messages between the club, the parish and the campus, and I make each of them think the others are being reasonable. Nobody is ever being reasonable.

own.label: Ask why she’s so quiet
own.player: Why do you never say much?
own.reply: Because people tell you everything if you leave a gap. Most people can’t stand a gap. I can stand it all day.

calls.label: Ask about the letters with her name on them
calls.player: Who’s been signing your name?
calls.reply: Somebody has been writing to donors, signed Brielle Kenton. Polite letters. Thank you for your generosity, it will not be forgotten. I didn’t write them. The ones I’ve seen all went to people who stopped giving.
calls.note: Brielle Kenton says someone has been sending letters signed with her name to donors who stopped giving.

life.news: Ran the table twice tonight. My neighbor in 4B called me a shark and bought me a soda.
life.more: The pool table above the laundromat leans left, so you have to aim like the world is slightly wrong. It is, so I’m good at it. 4B has been playing forty years and she still thinks she can beat me. Pool night is my favorite night of the week.

life.news: A donor called the office to thank me for a letter. I didn’t write any letter.
life.more: Somebody is signing my name to things. Nice things, so far, which is somehow worse. I went through every file I’ve touched this month and nothing’s missing. Just my name, out there, being polite to people without me.

life.news: The laundromat downstairs has had the same sock in the lost box for a year. Nobody claims it. I’ve started to root for it.
life.more: It’s a good sock. Argyle, barely worn. Somebody somewhere has its twin and no idea. I check on it every week before pool. If it’s ever gone I’ll be happy for it and also devastated. That’s how you know you live alone.

gossip.says: Noelle Sanderson fixes bicycles in the club’s parking lot on her lunch break, in pearls. Nobody has ever seen her flustered. Not once. I’ve tried.
gossip.note: Brielle Kenton says Noelle Sanderson fixes bicycles on her lunch break in pearls and is never flustered.
gossip.ask: Brielle says you fix bicycles in pearls and nobody has ever seen you flustered.
gossip.answer: Pearls are practical. You can wipe chain grease off them. Brielle has tried to fluster me with a fake fire alarm, a mouse and a man from accounts. The man from accounts came closest. Tell her I said that and watch her face.

gossip.says: Sofia Delgado translates for the club. The rich say outreach and the poor say rent, and she makes them think they agree. I do the same with the parish and the campus. We compare notes over margaritas.
gossip.note: Brielle Kenton says she and Sofia Delgado both play go-between for the club.
gossip.ask: Brielle says you two compare notes over margaritas about the people you translate for.
gossip.answer: Margaritas are where the real translation happens. Brielle is better at it than me, because she says nothing and lets them fill the silence. I say everything and let them think it was their idea. Between us, nobody at the club has an original thought.

women.name: Noelle Sanderson
women.look: Fair skin, chestnut curly bob, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, white linen trouser suit

own.label: Ask about the bicycle
own.player: Is it true you’re rebuilding a bicycle?
own.reply: Ten dollars at a yard sale. Rusted, bent, still standing. It looked like I felt. Now it rides better than my car.

own.label: Ask how she stays so calm
own.player: Does anything ever rattle you?
own.reply: Not much. Once you’ve had the worst phone call of your life, everything else is just weather.

own.label: Ask about the lilies
own.player: Who do you send lilies to?
own.reply: My husband. There’s a junction on the old interstate. I send white lilies there every few days. Cash, no card. He’d say it was a waste of money. He was usually right.

calls.label: Ask what she held on to at the club
calls.player: Did anything strange happen at the club this week?
calls.reply: On gala night a board member pressed an envelope into my hands and said hold this. I held it in my purse for eleven minutes. Then another one took it back without a word. I didn’t look inside. I wish I had.
calls.note: Noelle Sanderson held a board member’s envelope in her purse for eleven minutes on gala night.

life.news: Got the old bicycle’s gears shifting clean today. It clicked like a door shutting on a bad year.
life.more: I bought it at a yard sale for ten dollars because it looked like I felt. Rusted, bent, still upright. Six weekends later it rides better than my car. I took it round the reservoir at dusk and everyone passed me. I didn’t care.

life.news: Drove past the old junction on the way home. I still slow down there. I always will.
life.more: My husband died there, years ago. The report says weather. It was a clear night. I don’t argue with paperwork anymore, I just slow down. Somebody honked at me today. I waved. He has no idea he was honking at a widow, and that’s fine. I prefer it.

life.news: Somebody left a single white lily on my windshield this morning. I’m the one who sends lilies. Nobody sends them to me.
life.more: I asked the florist and she swore it wasn’t her. I asked around the office and got blank faces. It’s probably nothing. A mistake, a joke, a kind stranger. I put it in a glass on my desk anyway. Lilies are stubborn. So am I.

gossip.says: Elena Vargas at the flower shop on Sunfall Road has never once asked who my flowers are for. Every few days, cash, no card, and she wraps them like it matters. It does. She’s the kindest girl in town.
gossip.note: Noelle Sanderson says Elena Vargas never asks who her flowers are for.
gossip.ask: Noelle says you’ve never once asked who her flowers are for, and you wrap them like it matters.
gossip.answer: Because it isn’t my business, and because it does matter. People only buy flowers when something big happens. Hers are always lilies. I know what lilies mean. I put a little extra ribbon on them. She’s never mentioned it. I don’t think she needs to.

gossip.says: Carmen Bellini maps hiking trails nobody else has found and comes back to the office with cactus in her socks. She’s impulsive, generous and always slightly lost. I love her. I’ve bought her a compass twice.
gossip.note: Noelle Sanderson says Carmen Bellini maps hidden hiking trails and is always slightly lost.
gossip.ask: Noelle says you come back from your hikes with cactus in your socks, and she’s bought you a compass twice.
gossip.answer: Two compasses, and I lost both of them in the canyon, which is honestly where a compass belongs. Being lost is how you find the good trails. Noelle won’t come hiking with me. She says she’s done enough wandering. I’m going to change her mind.

women.name: Carmen Bellini
women.look: Freckled fair skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, a gap-toothed smile, striped boat-neck top and capri pants

own.label: Ask about her hiking routes
own.player: Where do you go hiking?
own.reply: Places that aren’t on maps yet. I make the map. If you’re not getting a little lost, you’re just walking.

own.label: Ask about her favorite place
own.player: What’s your favorite place you’ve found?
own.reply: A slot canyon I’m not telling anyone about. Orange walls, one shaft of light, and me eating a peach. Maybe I’ll take you. Maybe.

own.label: Ask why she keeps the books
own.player: Why bookkeeping, if you love the outdoors?
own.reply: Because numbers sit still. Everything else in my life runs off down a trail. It’s nice to have one thing that waits for me.

calls.label: Ask about the hide on the ridge
calls.player: What did you see from your trail above the lodge?
calls.reply: There’s a hide on the ridge above the lodge. I took photos from it of a dinner on the terrace, with my long lens, for the birds. The people in my photos say they were never there. I have the negatives. They were there.
calls.note: Carmen Bellini photographed a dinner on the lodge terrace from a hide on the ridge; the people in it say they were never there.

life.news: Found a slot canyon nobody has on a map. I sat in it and ate a peach and felt like the first person on Earth.
life.more: You squeeze sideways for ten minutes and then it opens up into this orange cathedral with one shaft of light. I marked it in my notebook with a little peach. I’m not putting it in the club newsletter. Some places should stay secret. That one’s mine.

life.news: Rolled my ankle on the ridge. Hopped two miles back to the car. Cried a little. Laughed a little.
life.more: The ridge looks friendly from the road. It is not friendly. I put my foot on a rock that had other plans. Two miles on one leg with a stick, singing to keep myself going. A hawk followed me the whole way, hoping. Not today, hawk.

life.news: A roadrunner has started following me on my morning hike. I think he thinks I’m his manager.
life.more: Same bird, same bend in the trail, every morning this week. He runs ahead, stops, looks back, runs ahead. He’s showing me something, or he’s judging my pace. I’ve named him Pistachio. Pistachio has no respect for me and I respect that.

gossip.says: Miriam Landry collects records nobody remembers and plays them in the office when the boss is out. She’s the most charming woman at the club and she knows it. She could talk a cactus into giving her its water.
gossip.note: Carmen Bellini says Miriam Landry plays forgotten records in the office and could charm a cactus.
gossip.ask: Carmen says you could talk a cactus into giving you its water.
gossip.answer: I could, and I’d give it back, with interest. Carmen thinks charm is a trick. It’s just paying attention to what people want and then standing near it. The records are for me, though. Nobody wants those. That’s why I love them.

gossip.says: Marisol Fuentes is the park ranger who keeps finding me in places I’m not supposed to be. She’s pulled cactus out of me twice and never once told me off. She just sighs. It’s worse.
gossip.note: Carmen Bellini says Marisol Fuentes has pulled cactus out of her twice.
gossip.ask: Carmen says you’ve pulled cactus out of her twice and never told her off, you just sighed.
gossip.answer: I sigh because telling her off doesn’t work. I’ve tried. She looks at me with those eyes and says, but the view, Marisol. The view is very good. The cactus is also very good at its job. One day I’m going to laminate a map for her.

women.name: Veronica Shawcross
women.look: Medium-brown skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, a gap-toothed smile, striped boat-neck top and capri pants

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Membership discipline. Who gets warned, who gets suspended, whose name comes off the list. I make the calls nobody else wants to make. Somebody has to, or the whole thing is just lunch.

own.label: Ask if she plays tennis
own.player: You look sporty. Tennis?
own.reply: I won the club ladder eleven years running. Then Caroline Prescott beat me and I gave it up the same afternoon. I don’t lose twice.

own.label: Ask where her money comes from
own.player: Where does your money come from?
own.reply: Water. My family built the canal and kept the rights. It pays me more in a year than the Foundation does in ten. It’s why the Shawcrosses have never needed to be liked.

own.label: Ask what she does to relax
own.player: What do you do to relax?
own.reply: I teach my cousin guitar one afternoon a week. He thinks I’m the kindest person in the family. One afternoon a week, I am.

own.label: Ask if she’s been married
own.player: Have you been married?
own.reply: Once. Christopher. A gentle man who asked my permission for everything, including things nobody asks permission for. Eighteen months. He’s at the Cemetery Chapel. The club has never asked me about it. You’re the first.
own.note: Veronica Shawcross’s husband Christopher Lyle was voted into the club and was dead within eighteen months; he is buried at the Cemetery Chapel.

calls.label: Ask about her day on the phone
calls.player: Busy day on the phone?
calls.reply: I called a hairdresser today about a client who had her hair dyed dark. I called a nurse about a patient. I don’t usually have to ask anyone anything. I usually know. This week I don’t, and I hate it.
calls.note: Veronica Shawcross has been calling a hairdresser and a nurse, asking about a woman who had her hair dyed dark.

calls.label: Ask if she has siblings
calls.player: Do you have any siblings?
calls.reply: A younger sister. She died in a hotel in the city. The Foundation’s lawyer exists because of her. I drink one glass of my father’s whisky every night at the window and I don’t say her name. That was nearly it.

life.news: Ended a man’s membership with one phone call before breakfast. Very clean. Then I played guitar badly all afternoon.
life.more: He cried. They usually shout first and cry later, but he went straight to crying, which saved us both time. Then my cousin came over and we murdered a song for an hour and he told me I was improving. I’m not. He’s kind.

life.news: Caroline Prescott asked me for a rematch. Eleven years too late, darling.
life.more: She cornered me at the bar, all teeth, racket bag over her shoulder like a weapon. I said I don’t play anymore. She said that’s what people say when they’re scared. I bought her a drink and said I’d think about it. I won’t. Probably.

life.news: Cooked dinner for my cousin. Burned it. He ate it anyway and said it was smoky on purpose.
life.more: I can end a career in four minutes and I cannot cook a chicken. He ate two plates to be polite and then we had cereal at the window. He asked why I never smile with my mouth open. I told him it’s the gap in my teeth. It isn’t the gap.

life.news: Water board meeting. Three men tried to explain my own canal to me. I let them finish.
life.more: Then I read out the rights, clause by clause, slowly, until one of them took his glasses off and rubbed his eyes. The secretary minuted it as a productive discussion. It was. I produced it.

gossip.says: Caroline Prescott beat me on the tennis ladder after eleven years at the top. I retired that afternoon. She’s been trying to get a rematch ever since, and I enjoy refusing more than I ever enjoyed winning.
gossip.note: Veronica Shawcross says Caroline Prescott beat her on the club tennis ladder and she retired that day.
gossip.ask: Veronica says you beat her at tennis and she quit on the spot.
gossip.answer: She did. Shook my hand, smiled that gap-toothed smile, walked off the court and never came back. Eleven years on top and she wouldn’t risk losing twice. I think about it more than I think about winning. Tell her my offer stands.

gossip.says: Diana Moore can’t look at me across a room. We’ve been at the same lunches for fifteen years. I’ve never asked her why. I know why.
gossip.note: Veronica Shawcross says Diana Moore can’t look at her across a room.
gossip.ask: Veronica says you can’t look at her.
gossip.answer: Can’t, darling, is a strong word. Won’t. Veronica knows where everyone is buried because she helped choose the plots. I sit at her lunches and I look at the flowers. They’re always lovely flowers.

women.name: Miriam Landry
women.look: Rosy fair skin, auburn shag with a curtain fringe, strong dark brows, cream blazer over a silk camisole

own.label: Ask about her records
own.player: What kind of records do you collect?
own.reply: Forgotten ones. One album, nine songs, then nothing. I like people who did one perfect thing and walked away.

own.label: Ask what she wants out of life
own.player: Where do you see yourself in five years?
own.reply: Somewhere with high ceilings and nobody asking me to balance a budget. I’m not picky about the route.

own.label: Ask if she’s always this charming
own.player: Are you always this charming?
own.reply: Only when I want something. Right now I want you to keep asking questions.

calls.label: Ask about the receipt she took home
calls.player: Have you taken anything home from the office you shouldn’t have?
calls.reply: Small things. A receipt here, an old lot there. After the gala, one receipt everyone keeps looking for ended up in my coat. I haven’t decided what it’s worth yet. Don’t look at me like that.
calls.note: Miriam Landry has a receipt the club’s board keeps looking for, in her coat.

life.news: Found an album at the stall by a woman who made one perfect record in 1969 and then vanished. I’ve played it eleven times.
life.more: Nine songs, no hits, and a voice like somebody leaning on a doorframe in the small hours. Nobody knows what happened to her. I like to think she married rich and never looked back. That’s my plan too, honestly. Minus the vanishing.

life.news: My landlord raised the rent again. I counted my records and wondered which ones I’d sell. None. The answer was none.
life.more: Ambition is expensive. I’m twenty-five with a bookkeeper’s salary and a duchess’s taste, and Sunfall knows it. I made a budget tonight. It made me sad. Then I found a dollar in a coat pocket and felt rich for an hour.

life.news: A man at the record stall offered me three hundred dollars for a record I paid four for. I said no. I don’t know why.
life.more: He knew exactly what it was. I didn’t, until he wanted it. That’s the trick with everything, isn’t it. Nothing has a price until somebody else wants it. I took it home and played it twice and it’s fine. It’s just fine. I still won’t sell it.

gossip.says: Lorna Sutton drives around at night photographing old diner neon. She says it makes her feel like a different person. I asked who. She said someone who doesn’t work at the club.
gossip.note: Miriam Landry says Lorna Sutton photographs diner neon at night to feel like someone else.
gossip.ask: Miriam says you photograph diner neon so you can feel like someone who doesn’t work at the club.
gossip.answer: She’s right, and she’s the last person who should be saying it. Miriam would be a different person every night if it paid. The signs are honest. They say EAT, or OPEN. Nobody at the club has said what they mean in years.

gossip.says: Giselle Ford at the hospital desk has the best record collection in Sunfall and plays it to the night porters. We fight over the same stall every weekend. She wins, because she gets up earlier.
gossip.note: Miriam Landry says Giselle Ford beats her to the record stall every weekend.
gossip.ask: Miriam says you beat her to the record stall every weekend because you get up earlier.
gossip.answer: I don’t get up earlier, darling, I never went to bed. Twelve years of night shifts. Miriam turns up mid-morning with coffee and a smile and thinks the smile will save her. It doesn’t. It does get her a discount from the stall man, which I find unforgivable.

women.name: Celeste Van Doren
women.look: Warm brown skin, burgundy-dyed curls, amber eyes, striped boat-neck top and capri pants

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you actually do at the Foundation?
own.reply: Bequests, darling. Wills, standing gifts, the estates that come to the Foundation when a husband joins the family. I’ve run the desk for fifteen years without a title. I’m a Van Doren. We don’t need titles, we need signatures.

own.label: Ask what she collects
own.player: Do you collect anything?
own.reply: Postcards. Albums of them. Every one sent to me by a husband on a trip, and the towns I mean to visit when I’m finally free to. I’ve never visited a single one. The postcards are better than the towns.

own.label: Ask her to lunch
own.player: Can I take you to lunch?
own.reply: Oh, sweet thing. I take people to lunch. Nobody takes me. Give me your address and I’ll send a car. Everyone I’ve ever taken to lunch has remembered it for the rest of their life.

own.label: Ask if she’s been married
own.player: Have you been married?
own.reply: Three times. A banker, an engineer, a rancher. I buried every one properly at the Cemetery Chapel, with a ribbon on each stone. You can go and count them. People do.
own.note: Celeste Van Doren has buried three husbands at the Cemetery Chapel, each with a ribbon on the stone; their estates went to the Foundation.

own.label: Ask which husband she liked best
own.player: Which one did you like best?
own.reply: The second. The engineer. I wouldn’t say loved. Liked is more dangerous. I wear his watch. It still keeps time, which is more than I can say for him.

views.dispute: A fellowship of unmarried women keeping candles at a ruin on moonless nights. The diocese should have reviewed it decades ago. The chapel sits on land the parish cannot afford to keep, and sentiment is not a title deed.

calls.label: Ask if she’d marry again
calls.player: Would you ever marry again?
calls.reply: There’s a widower on the casino’s board. Very rich, very frightened, very sweet. The vote is next month. Don’t make that face, darling. It’s only a vote.

calls.label: Ask what keeps her up at night
calls.player: Does anything keep you up at night?
calls.reply: For fifteen years I have known where everyone is. This week I don’t. It turns out I sleep very badly when somebody has climbed out of a window I didn’t know was open.
calls.note: Celeste Van Doren admits that for the first time in fifteen years she doesn’t know where someone is: somebody got out through a window.

life.news: Lunch at the club with a woman who didn’t know who I was. By dessert she did. By coffee she was telling me about her marriage.
life.more: That is the whole art. You order for them, you laugh first, you touch the back of their hand once. They give you everything and thank you for listening. She hugged me at the door. I’ll call her in a month and she’ll pick up on the first ring.

life.news: A postcard came today from a town I’ve never heard of. No signature. Just a picture of a lake.
life.more: Nobody has sent me a postcard in eleven years. Every one in my albums came from a husband. I looked at the handwriting for an hour. It wasn’t any of theirs. I put it in the album anyway, on its own page.

life.news: The engineer’s watch stopped. I’ve worn it every day for eleven years and today it simply stopped.
life.more: The jeweler said it wanted a new battery. It doesn’t take a battery. It winds. I wound it and it started again, and I had to go and sit in the car, which I never do, because the car is where people cry.

life.news: Somebody at the bar called me the warmest woman at the club. I bought the whole room a round to celebrate being misunderstood.
life.more: That’s how you stay the warmest woman anywhere. Buy the round, laugh loudest, remember everyone’s husband’s name. Especially the ones who aren’t with us anymore.

gossip.says: Genevieve Locke took a man I wanted, years ago. I’ve never said a cross word to her. I’ve never needed to. Every year she sits one seat further from the top of the table, and she knows exactly who moves the chairs.
gossip.note: Celeste Van Doren says Genevieve Locke took a man she wanted years ago.
gossip.ask: Celeste says you took a man she wanted.
gossip.answer: I took nothing. He walked. Celeste has never forgiven a man for walking, or a woman for being where he walked to. She moves the chairs one seat a year. I count them. One day we’ll run out of table.

gossip.says: Diana Moore is a darling. I took her to lunch once when she was young and lost, and I’ve kept a hand on her shoulder ever since. She hates it. She’s never once asked me to move it.
gossip.note: Celeste Van Doren says she has kept a hand on Diana Moore’s shoulder since a lunch years ago.
gossip.ask: Celeste says she’s kept a hand on your shoulder ever since you had lunch.
gossip.answer: She has. Every party, every lodge night, the same hand, the same little squeeze. People think it’s affection. Lunch with Celeste is the most charming hour of your life and the last free one. If she asks you, darling, don’t go.

women.name: Audra Beaumont
women.look: Dark skin, golden-brown ringlets, a small nose stud, camel trench coat and silk scarf

women.name: Eloise Rainer
women.look: Medium-brown skin, sandy shag with a fringe, deep dimples, cream blazer over a silk camisole

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do at the Foundation?
own.reply: Junior membership. I keep the records of who’s presented at the ball and to whom. Everyone calls it admin. I call it a seating plan for the rest of people’s lives.

own.label: Ask if she swims
own.player: You look like a swimmer. Do you?
own.reply: County level, until this year. I swam to win. I’m at the club to win. Nobody’s told me what the prize is yet, which I find suspicious.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: I bake elaborate cakes that collapse. I give them to the Sisters’ pantry. The nuns serve them in bowls and everybody pretends that was the plan.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What are your parents like?
own.reply: Both alive and both at home, which at the club makes us practically exotic. My father wants me to marry a casino board member’s son. My mother wants a Shawcross cousin. I have my own plan. Neither of them has noticed it.

own.label: Ask what’s been bothering her
own.player: Something’s bothering you.
own.reply: A man in a charity lanyard asked me to tell my father the lodge was lit. I thought it was a joke. I told my father. He went the color of my mother’s blazer. Now there’s a photograph of me laughing with that man at the kitchen door. What does that even mean? Nobody will tell me.
own.note: Eloise Rainer was asked by a man in a charity lanyard to tell her father the lodge was lit; she was photographed laughing with him at the kitchen door just before he went through it.

calls.label: Ask what she actually wants
calls.player: What do you actually want?
calls.reply: To win something that’s mine. Not a husband somebody picked. A race, a cake that stands up, one night where nobody is measuring me for anything.

calls.label: Ask if she’s seeing anyone
calls.player: Are you seeing anyone?
calls.reply: There’s a swimmer from the city. Tomas. Nobody knows about him. Not my father, not my mother, not the club. I’m keeping him. If you tell anyone I’ll drown you, politely.

life.news: Cake number nine collapsed. The Sisters served it in bowls again and called it a trifle.
life.more: Raspberry, three layers, a ganache I was very proud of. It sank in the middle like a sigh. Sister Eliza looked at it, didn’t blink, got out the bowls. She hugged me on the way out. I think I’m the only one who hugs her. I should do it more.

life.news: Swam two miles in the reservoir at dawn. No lanes, no coach, nobody timing me. Best I’ve felt in months.
life.more: The club pool has my name on a board. The reservoir doesn’t know my name. A heron watched me the whole way like it was judging my stroke. I got out shaking and laughing and drove home with my hair dripping all over my father’s car seats.

life.news: My mother had me measured for a dress. She won’t say what it’s for. My father won’t either. They won’t say it to each other.
life.more: Cream, long, very plain. The dressmaker kept smiling at me the way you smile at a bride. I asked if somebody was getting married. She said not yet and pinned the hem.

life.news: Somebody sent me a postcard from the city with a swimming pool on it. No name. I know exactly who.
life.more: One line on the back: lane four, whenever you’re ready. I keep it inside my running shoe so my mother can’t find it. Running shoes are the only thing she never touches.

gossip.says: Sister Eliza Montoya serves my collapsed cakes in bowls at the pantry and calls them trifle. She’s never once laughed at me. I think she’s the kindest person in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Eloise Rainer says Eliza Montoya serves her collapsed cakes in bowls at the Sisters’ pantry.
gossip.ask: Eloise says you serve her cakes in bowls.
gossip.answer: I do, and I’ll keep doing it. Every week a beautiful ruin arrives with a girl behind it who wants so badly to get something right. The bowls are the easy part. She hugs me at the door. I don’t think she knows how long it had been.

gossip.says: Alice Beaumont runs the ball. She looked at my presentation list for a long time and then crossed out one name with a very sharp pencil. She wouldn’t say whose. I keep the records and I still can’t read it.
gossip.note: Eloise Rainer says Alice Beaumont crossed a name off her ball presentation list.
gossip.ask: Eloise says you crossed a name off her list.
gossip.answer: I did. A girl should be presented to people who will still be alive at her wedding. Eloise keeps the records. I keep the girls. Tell her the pencil was sharp because I meant it.

women.name: Lorna Sutton
women.look: Fair skin, brown waves with teal tips, tortoiseshell glasses, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask about her photographs
own.player: What do you photograph?
own.reply: Diner neon at night. EAT, OPEN, a star with one point out. Signs say exactly what they mean. I find that restful.

own.label: Ask who’s waiting at home
own.player: Is there anyone waiting at home for you?
own.reply: A cat called Margaret who has never pretended anything in her life. I aspire to her.

own.label: Ask why she’s hard to impress
own.player: Why are you so hard to impress?
own.reply: Because I work somewhere everyone is impressive. You learn to look for the price tag.

calls.label: Ask about her invitation
calls.player: Did you ever get invited to the lodge?
calls.reply: Once. An embossed card for a dinner, no date on it, just come when you’re ready. I never went. Everyone who stays at the club long enough goes. That’s the price of staying. I’ve worked that out. I haven’t worked out what I’ll do.
calls.note: Lorna Sutton has an undated invitation to a dinner at the lodge she never accepted.

life.news: Got the best shot of the year: the Starlite Diner’s sign with one letter out. STAR ITE. Perfect.
life.more: I park across the road with a thermos and wait for the moment the sign flickers and the street is empty. Tonight a trucker walked out right on cue and lit a cigarette under the T. I didn’t breathe. It’s the best photograph I’ve ever taken and nobody will ever see it.

life.news: Long day at the office. Smiled at people I don’t like for eight hours. My face hurts.
life.more: Some days the club feels like a dinner party where everyone is pretending the food is good. I came home and ate cereal standing up and didn’t smile at anything. My cat looked at me like she understood. She doesn’t. She has never pretended anything in her life.

life.news: A diner out on the state road had its sign dark for a week. The staff said it was broken. It wasn’t broken. Somebody unplugged it.
life.more: I know because I went round the back, which I should not have done, and the plug was lying in the dust like someone had been tidying. I plugged it back in. It came on. OPEN. I don’t know whose night I ruined, or saved.

gossip.says: Penelope Kline is the sharpest woman in compliance. She gets up before dawn to look at birds and then reads every form we have like it’s a mystery novel. I worry about her. Sharp girls get noticed.
gossip.note: Lorna Sutton says Penelope Kline watches birds before dawn and reads every form like a mystery novel.
gossip.ask: Lorna says you read every form at the club like a mystery novel.
gossip.answer: They are mystery novels. Most of them are very boring mystery novels where the butler did it on page one. Lorna worries because she’s kind and because she’s right. I’m careful. I have binoculars. I can see trouble coming from very far away.

gossip.says: Yumi Tanaka checks my columns before I check them myself. She found a mistake of mine in three seconds and didn’t tell anyone. She just fixed it and left a mint on my desk.
gossip.note: Lorna Sutton says Yumi Tanaka fixed her mistake and left a mint on her desk.
gossip.ask: Lorna says you fixed her mistake without telling anyone and left a mint on her desk.
gossip.answer: It was a transposed number. Anyone would have caught it. The mint was a coincidence. I had a spare. Please don’t make this into something. I have a reputation for being cold and I worked very hard for it.

women.name: Penelope Kline
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, copper waist-length waves, tortoiseshell glasses, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask about birdwatching
own.player: What do you do before work?
own.reply: Watch birds on the dry river at dawn. It’s cold, it’s quiet, and nothing lies to you. Then I go to the office.

own.label: Ask what it’s like being the youngest
own.player: What’s it like being the youngest at work?
own.reply: People say things in front of you because they think you won’t understand. I understand. I write it all down.

own.label: Ask about the hawk
own.player: Is there really a hawk outside your office?
own.reply: On the flagpole, every morning. He watches the board arrive. I call him the Auditor. He’s never once been impressed.

calls.label: Ask about the receipt for a bird
calls.player: What was strange about the receipt you found?
calls.reply: Four hundred dollars of birdseed, for a species that doesn’t exist. I checked every book I own, and I own all of them. Somebody made up a bird, or made up a reason to pay for one. The folder it came from has a blue ribbon on it.
calls.note: Penelope Kline found a club receipt for four hundred dollars of birdseed for a bird that does not exist.

life.news: Saw a vermilion flycatcher on the dry river at dawn. Red as a stop sign. I nearly fell in the river.
life.more: You sit in the cold with your binoculars and nothing happens for an hour, and then a tiny red bird lands on a dead branch and the whole morning is worth it. Felicity says I gasp like it’s an opera. I do. It is.

life.news: Someone at work told me I’d understand when I was older. I smiled. Then I went to the bathroom and wrote down everything I understand already.
life.more: It was a long list. I have very small handwriting. The thing about being the youngest in an office is everyone says things in front of you because they think you won’t understand. I understand. I just write it down and go birdwatching.

life.news: A hawk sits on the flagpole outside the office every morning and watches the board arrive. I think he’s taking notes.
life.more: Same hawk, same pole, every morning. He watches the cars pull in like he’s counting. I’ve named him the Auditor. The board members walk faster under him. I don’t think they know why. I do. Nobody likes to be looked at by something that isn’t impressed.

gossip.says: Bianca Roth has decided I need mothering. She brings me soup when I sneeze and checks my forms before I file them. I didn’t ask. I don’t mind. She looks so tired, and she’s always kind.
gossip.note: Penelope Kline says Bianca Roth mothers her and checks her forms before she files them.
gossip.ask: Penelope says you bring her soup when she sneezes and check her forms before she files them.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to. She’s the youngest in a building full of sharks, and she thinks binoculars make her safe. They don’t. Soup doesn’t either, but it’s what I can do. Tell her the forms are perfect. They always are. I check anyway.

gossip.says: Maren Caldwell volunteers at the Sisters’ thrift shop on her days off and buys back half of what she donates. She’s earnest about everything. She once apologized to a mannequin.
gossip.note: Penelope Kline says Maren Caldwell volunteers at the Sisters’ thrift shop and once apologized to a mannequin.
gossip.ask: Penelope says you once apologized to a mannequin at the thrift shop.
gossip.answer: I walked into it. It had a very nice coat on. I said sorry before I knew what it was, and then I was too embarrassed to stop, so I said sorry again, properly. Penelope saw the whole thing through the window. She waved. I’ll never recover.

women.name: Maren Caldwell
women.look: Fair skin, platinum pixie cut, hazel eyes, cream blazer over a silk camisole

own.label: Ask about the thrift shop
own.player: What do you do on your days off?
own.reply: Volunteer at the Sisters’ thrift shop. I sort coats, I steam dresses, and I buy back half of what I donate. It’s a closed system.

own.label: Ask why she apologizes so much
own.player: Why do you say sorry so often?
own.reply: I don’t know. Sorry. See, I’m doing it. It’s like a sneeze.

own.label: Ask about the best thing she’s sold
own.player: What’s the best thing you’ve ever sold?
own.reply: A wedding dress, to a woman who cried in the fitting room. Happy crying. I gave her my handkerchief. I hope she still has it.

calls.label: Ask about the letters signed with her name
calls.player: Is someone writing letters in your name?
calls.reply: To some of the younger women at the club. Signed Maren Caldwell. Telling them how special they are, how the right people have noticed them. I didn’t write them. Everyone else is scared. I’m making a list of who got one. Then I’ll know who wants them.
calls.note: Maren Caldwell says someone is sending flattering letters signed with her name to young women at the club.

life.news: Sold a wedding dress at the thrift shop to a woman who cried in the fitting room. Happy crying. I cried too. Unprofessional.
life.more: It had been on the rack for a year and nobody looked at it twice. Then she came in with her mother and put it on and the whole shop went quiet. Sixty dollars, and the Sisters let me knock off ten. I gave her my handkerchief and she kept it. Good. It’s a happy handkerchief now.

life.news: Called a board member by his brother’s name at lunch. His brother is in prison.
life.more: I meant to say good afternoon, Mr. Whitford. I said the other one. The whole table went silent. I said sorry and then I said sorry for saying sorry, which is my special talent. He smiled at me like a shark smiles at a swimmer. I ate my salad very quietly.

life.news: Somebody donated a box of hats to the thrift shop with a note inside each one. The notes all say the same thing. Thank you for listening.
life.more: Twelve hats, twelve notes, the same handwriting, no name. The Sisters think it’s lovely. I think it’s lovely too, and also a little bit strange. Who did they talk to? I’ve put one of the hats on my desk. I keep expecting it to say something.
