calls.reply: Shelf nine, bottom row. A box with a case number that doesn’t exist. It was there before Imani started. If anything ever happens to me, I want Imani to open it. Not anyone else. Promise me that.
calls.note: Kelsey Donovan says a box on shelf nine of the evidence archive has a case number that does not exist, and wants Imani Harper to open it if anything happens to her.

life.news: Found a record at the market by a singer who made one album and vanished. Played it in the archive until the lights clicked off.
life.more: A woman with a voice like a cracked bell. Nine songs and then nothing. I like the ones who stopped. You wonder if they were happier after. I hope so. Somebody should be.

life.news: Imani labeled an evidence box today with a little drawing of a cactus on it. Against regulations. I let it go.
life.more: It was a box of stolen garden gnomes, so honestly, it fit. She looked so worried when I noticed. I said it was the best label in the building. It is. I may start drawing on mine.

life.news: Saw my mom today. She didn’t know who I was for a minute. Then she did. That minute.
life.more: Some weeks she’s sharp as anything and folds napkins into swans for the nurses. Today she looked at me like a stranger, and then she said, Kels, you’ve cut your hair. I haven’t. I said yes.

life.news: A detective I’ve known forever said thanks today. Just thanks. I’ve been floating all afternoon.
life.more: Eighteen years and he says thanks maybe twice a year. I filed something for him fast, and he tapped the desk on his way past and said, thanks, Kels. That’s it. That’s the whole story. I’m embarrassed by how good it was.

gossip.says: Imani Harper labels every evidence box like it’s a birthday present and keeps thirty-two cacti at home. I’d fight anyone who was mean to her.
gossip.note: Kelsey Donovan says she is protective of Imani Harper at the evidence archive.
gossip.ask: Kelsey Donovan says she’d fight anyone who was mean to you.
gossip.answer: She would. She nearly did, once, to a detective who called me the new girl for six months. Kelsey plays old records in the archive after hours. Sad ones. I pretend I don’t notice she’s crying. She pretends I’m not there. It works.

gossip.says: Cassidy Boone works in records, in the basement right under my archive, and she reads an old unsolved case every few weeks on her lunch break. Nobody asked her to. She says someone ought to keep looking.
gossip.note: Kelsey Donovan says Cassidy Boone reads old unsolved cases on her lunch break.
gossip.ask: Kelsey says you read old unsolved cases on your lunch break because someone ought to keep looking.
gossip.answer: Every file down there is somebody’s worst week, filed alphabetically. Reading one now and then is the least I can do. Kelsey brings me coffee and pretends she’s just passing. Then she stays and reads over my shoulder. She’s better at it than half the detectives.

women.name: Sheryl Abbott
women.look: Freckled fair skin, a sleek low bun, tortoiseshell glasses, navy polo shirt and khaki pants

own.label: Ask about her postcards
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Postcards of towns I’ve never been to. I write them to myself, from a woman with a different life. She’s happy. She keeps bees.

own.label: Ask about working in custody
own.player: What’s it like nursing in a police cell block?
own.reply: Everyone is having the worst night of their year, on both sides of the handcuffs. I patch them up and write everything down.

own.label: Ask why she writes everything down
own.player: Why do you write everything down?
own.reply: Because the night always looks different in the morning, and somebody should remember what it actually looked like.

calls.label: Ask about the custody suite’s invoices
calls.player: What’s wrong with the custody suite’s invoices?
calls.reply: Our medicine is paid out of the police benevolent fund, on blue paper, with a ribbon on the letterhead. The fund is for widows. Not for the drugs we give the people we lock up. Somebody wanted the custody suite owing a favor.
calls.note: Sheryl Abbott found the custody suite’s pharmacy invoices paid from the police benevolent fund.

life.news: Found a postcard at the stall of a town in Maine with one street and a lighthouse. Wrote on the back as if I lived there.
life.more: I collect postcards of towns I’ve never been to. Then I write them to myself, like a letter from a woman with a different life. This one runs a bookshop and has a dog called Captain. She’s doing well. She says the fog is lovely this time of year.

life.news: Double shift in custody. Patched up a man who spat at me. Patched up the officer he spat at too.
life.more: Everyone who comes through the custody suite is having the worst night of their year, on both sides of the cuffs. I clean the cuts and write everything down. Everything. Even when nobody asks me to. Especially then. My handwriting is very small and very honest.

life.news: The pharmacy invoices for the custody suite are paid by the wrong account. Not ours. Somebody else’s fund.
life.more: I noticed because the paper is a different color. That’s all it took. Our invoices are white. These are blue, with a little ribbon in the corner of the letterhead. I put them back exactly as I found them. Then I wrote down the numbers.

gossip.says: Leila Sayeed is the other custody nurse. She sits longer with the quiet ones and changes her mind about her future every shift. Last week she was going to be a midwife. Now it’s a lighthouse keeper.
gossip.note: Sheryl Abbott says Leila Sayeed changes her mind about her future every shift.
gossip.ask: Sheryl says you change your mind about your future every shift, and now it’s a lighthouse keeper.
gossip.answer: It was a lighthouse keeper for one shift, and it was a quiet one. Sheryl says nothing for eight hours and then says one thing that rearranges your whole week. She keeps better notes than anyone in the building. I don’t know what she does with them. I don’t ask.

gossip.says: Gwen Alder is our junior in custody, and she runs a film night for her street on a bedsheet. She got blamed for a missing key last month. She didn’t take it. I know who didn’t. I don’t know who did.
gossip.note: Sheryl Abbott says Gwen Alder was blamed for a missing key she didn’t take.
gossip.ask: Sheryl says you were blamed for a missing key you didn’t take.
gossip.answer: I didn’t take it. I’ve said it so many times it sounds like a lie now. Sheryl is the only one who never asked me. She just brought me a coffee and said she knew. I don’t know how she knew. I don’t think I want to.

women.name: Amber Colebrook
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, chestnut curly bob, a beauty mark above her lip, plain white shirt and slim black pants

own.label: Ask about the dresses
own.player: What do you do outside work?
own.reply: Restore one ruined old dress a year. Silk, buttons, months of it. My hands need something slow after a shift of fast voices.

own.label: Ask what dispatch is like
own.player: What’s it like taking emergency calls?
own.reply: You sound like a lake while somebody’s house is on fire. Then you hang up and take the next one. Then you sit in your car.

own.label: Ask how she stays unflappable
own.player: Does anything get to you?
own.reply: Plenty. I just let it get to me later, in private, with a bar of chocolate. It’s very efficient.

calls.label: Ask about the dispatch logbook
calls.player: What’s in the dispatch logbook?
calls.reply: Every call for twenty years, by hand. Including the night a woman rang seventeen times. Somebody took the cabinet key, and now pages are missing from one week. The week after the gala, years back. I know because I wrote half of them.
calls.note: Amber Colebrook says pages are missing from the dispatch logbook since its cabinet key went missing.

life.news: Finished restoring this year’s dress. Green silk, nineteen forties, forty tiny buttons. I sewed every one twice.
life.more: Every year I take one ruined old dress and make it whole. It takes months. My hands need something slow after a shift of fast voices. This one belonged to a woman who wore it to dance, you can tell from the hem. I’m going to wear it to nothing. It deserves the rest.

life.news: Rough night on the phones. Took a call I’ll be thinking about for a week.
life.more: You get very good at sounding calm. Calm is the job. You sound like a lake while someone’s house is on fire. Then you hang up and take the next one. Tonight I sat in my car for twenty minutes before I could drive. That’s allowed. Doreen taught me that.

life.news: The dispatch logbook cabinet won’t lock. The key’s gone. Nobody has a spare. Nobody seems bothered.
life.more: That logbook has every call we took for twenty years, written by hand, because Doreen doesn’t trust computers. Now the cabinet sits open in the corner and everyone walks past it like it’s furniture. I’ve started eating my lunch at the desk next to it. Just to be near.

gossip.says: Joanne Kendrick is the trainee on the phones. She sounds like a lake when someone’s house is on fire, and then she hangs up and shakes. She’s going to be the best of us. She makes pottery bowls. None of them are round.
gossip.note: Amber Colebrook says Joanne Kendrick sounds calm on the phones and shakes after.
gossip.ask: Amber says you sound calm on the phones and shake after, and none of your bowls are round.
gossip.answer: They’re round in spirit. Amber taught me to sit in the car after a bad one and not drive until my hands stop. She does it too. Nobody else knows that. She restores old dresses, very slowly, like an apology to somebody. I’ve never asked who.

gossip.says: Sasha Mahoney built a model so no woman would ever have to call seventeen times before anyone came. I took that call, years ago. I bought Sasha a bottle of wine and couldn’t say why.
gossip.note: Amber Colebrook says Sasha Mahoney built a model so no woman would ever call seventeen times before help came.
gossip.ask: Amber says she bought you wine for your model and couldn’t say why.
gossip.answer: I knew why. Everyone in the building knows about that night, and nobody says it. Amber was on the phones. The model is just math. She was a person, holding a phone, while math failed. We drank the wine in the parking lot. It was a very good wine.

women.name: Renee Saunders
women.look: Freckled fair skin, loose spiral curls, a gap-toothed smile, denim shirt with rolled sleeves

own.label: Ask about her baking
own.player: Do you bake?
own.reply: Elaborate cakes, badly. They lean, they slide, they sometimes collapse. Everyone at the station eats them anyway. With spoons.

own.label: Ask about the records room
own.player: What’s it like working in records?
own.reply: It’s a basement full of everybody’s worst week, filed alphabetically. I bring cake. Somebody has to.

own.label: Ask why she’s always in trouble for noise
own.player: Do you get in trouble at work?
own.reply: For volume, mostly. I don’t have an inside voice. I have a voice and a slightly quieter voice I use at funerals.

calls.label: Ask about the uncollected pay
calls.player: Whose pay is sitting on the spike?
calls.reply: Dale Pruett’s. The photographer’s assistant. His pay docket has been on the spike since the week of the gala. Nobody collects it, nobody cancels it, and everyone I ask gets very interested in their shoes.
calls.note: Renee Saunders says Dale Pruett’s pay docket has sat uncollected on the spike since the week of the gala.

life.news: Baked a three-layer cake for the sergeant’s birthday. Two of the layers survived. He said it was the best cake he’s had.
life.more: It slid sideways on the drive in. I put it on the table and announced it was modern art. Everyone ate it with spoons out of the box. The sergeant had three helpings and went pink. Records is the basement, so a cake is a big event down there. I’m the event.

life.news: Got told off for talking too loud in the archive. Again. It’s a basement. Who am I disturbing? The files?
life.more: Cassidy says the files deserve respect. I respect them. I just respect them out loud. I’ve put a sticky note on my desk that says INSIDE VOICE in red. Somebody added a smiley face. I think it was Cassidy. That’s practically a hug from her.

life.news: There’s a pay docket on the spike for a man who hasn’t collected it in weeks. I keep asking. People keep changing the subject.
life.more: It’s just a slip of paper with a name and an amount. Small amount. But nobody leaves pay on a spike. I asked the sergeant, I asked payroll, I asked the man who sweeps the hall. Everyone gets very interested in their shoes. I’m going to ask louder.

gossip.says: Cassidy Boone runs records and reads old unsolved cases at lunch. She’s quiet, she’s kind, and she’s the only person who’s ever eaten one of my cakes and asked for the recipe. I think she was being polite. I’m giving it to her anyway.
gossip.note: Renee Saunders says Cassidy Boone asked for the recipe to one of her cakes.
gossip.ask: Renee says you asked for the recipe to one of her cakes.
gossip.answer: I asked for the recipe so I could find out what went wrong. It was baking soda instead of baking powder. I haven’t told her. She’s so happy down there, making noise and cake in a room full of bad weeks. I don’t want to correct anything about her.

gossip.says: Harriet Boyle in the archive keeps a travel journal of places she’s going to go. She’s been planning the same trip to Scotland for six years. I’m going to buy her the ticket one day and make her go.
gossip.note: Renee Saunders says Harriet Boyle has been planning the same trip to Scotland for six years.
gossip.ask: Renee says you’ve been planning the same trip to Scotland for six years.
gossip.answer: Seven. The planning is the trip, really. I know every bus timetable in the Highlands. If I actually went, the buses would be late and it would ruin everything. Renee doesn’t understand that. Renee does everything immediately and loudly and it nearly always works.

women.name: Lydia Carver
women.look: Porcelain skin, copper waist-length waves, a small nose stud, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask what she does to unwind
own.player: How do you switch off after work?
own.reply: Photograph diner neon on the state road. Ten minutes of pink light and I’m just a woman with a camera.

own.label: Ask about victim liaison work
own.player: What does a victim liaison actually do?
own.reply: Stays. People think it’s talking. It’s not leaving. You answer the same question forty times, the same gentle way.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Was your father in the police too?
own.reply: He was. He died at a junction on the old interstate when I was young. He made me promise not to look into it. I’ve kept the promise. Mostly.

calls.label: Ask what she told the young liaison
calls.player: What did you tell Naoko about the missing photographer?
calls.reply: I told her to let Dale Pruett go. Stop asking, stop calling his mother, stop. I said it the way you say it when you mean the opposite. She understood. I hope she understood. I couldn’t say it any plainer in that building.
calls.note: Lydia Carver told Naoko Watanabe to let Dale Pruett go, meaning the opposite.

life.news: Photographed the diner’s neon at the end of a long shift. The pink was perfect. I sat in the car and felt something.
life.more: My job is sitting with families on the worst day of their lives and being calm. You can’t take that home. So I drive past the diners on the state road and photograph the signs, and for ten minutes I’m just a woman with a camera who likes pink light.

life.news: Sat with a family for six hours today. I didn’t say much. You don’t, in this job. You just stay.
life.more: People think liaison is about talking. It’s about not leaving. They ask the same question forty times and you answer it forty times, gently, the same way. Tonight the mother held my hand when I left and said thank you for not leaving. That’s the job. That’s all of it.

life.news: Drove past the old junction tonight and slowed down without meaning to. I always do. I promised I wouldn’t look. I looked.
life.more: My father was shot there thirty years ago. On his deathbed he made me promise never to look into it. I kept the promise for thirty years. Tonight there was a woman leaving white lilies there. I didn’t stop. I wanted to. I’m still thinking about it.

gossip.says: Naoko Watanabe is the youngest liaison we’ve ever had. She stargazes in the desert to stay sane. She sits with the families of the missing and comes back still kind. I don’t know how. I was never that kind.
gossip.note: Lydia Carver says Naoko Watanabe sits with the families of the missing and comes back still kind.
gossip.ask: Lydia says you come back from the families still kind, and she never was.
gossip.answer: She’s wrong about herself. She just doesn’t show it at the station. I’ve seen her sit on the floor with a grieving kid’s dog for an hour because nobody else noticed the dog was grieving too. Lydia notices everything. She just pretends she doesn’t, so it hurts less.

gossip.says: Lorna Sutton from the club photographs the same diner signs I do. We met in a parking lot at one in the morning pointing cameras at the same pink star. We didn’t say a word. We nodded. Best friendship in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Lydia Carver says she and Lorna Sutton photograph the same diner neon and met in a parking lot at night.
gossip.ask: Lydia says you two met in a parking lot at night pointing cameras at the same pink star.
gossip.answer: We nodded. That was the whole conversation. Now when I see her car at a diner, I park two spaces away and we photograph in silence. She takes better pictures. Hers have people in them. I always wait until the people are gone.

women.name: Opal Franklin
women.look: Freckled fair skin, chestnut high ponytail, deep dimples, maroon fleece and jeans

own.label: Ask about reading skid marks
own.player: What does a collision investigator do?
own.reply: Reads the road. Everyone says the other driver was speeding. The rubber says otherwise. The road never takes sides.

own.label: Ask what she does before work
own.player: What do you do before your shift?
own.reply: Birdwatch. There are owls by the old junction nobody looks at. I look at them. They look back. Nobody wins.

own.label: Ask about her house
own.player: Do you own your place?
own.reply: My grandmother left me a little house beside the Old Mission Chapel. It needs a roof and a miracle. Somebody wants it very badly. I’m not selling.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother and the chapel keys
own.player: Your grandmother kept the Old Mission’s keys?
own.reply: Forty years, for the parish, after the diocese stopped caring. She lent them to the sacristan and, when he died, handed them to the caretaker, and told me the chapel was the parish’s and nobody else’s, and that there was a paper at St. Brigid’s to prove it. She died in the spring. The twin of the crypt key is on a nail in my kitchen. I have never used it.
own.note: Opal Franklin says her grandmother kept the Old Mission’s keys for the parish for forty years, and a twin of the crypt key hangs on a nail in Opal’s kitchen.

calls.label: Ask about the offer for her house
calls.player: Who wants to buy your grandmother’s house?
calls.reply: A company with a name like a perfume, three times the value, on thick paper. Mine is the fourth house beside the Old Mission Chapel. The other three already sold. To the same company. Somebody wants the whole row and the ground under it.
calls.note: Opal Franklin says a company has bought three houses beside the Old Mission Chapel and wants her grandmother’s, the fourth.

life.news: Saw a pair of burrowing owls at the old junction before my shift. They stared at me like I owed them money.
life.more: I birdwatch before work, and the scrub by the old junction is full of owls nobody bothers to look at. Brenda goes quiet whenever I mention that spot. I don’t know why. The owls don’t care. They just stare, and I stare back, and then I go measure skid marks.

life.news: Measured skid marks for four hours in the sun. Turned the color of a fire truck. Worth it, we found out who lied.
life.more: Traffic collisions are physics with tears. Everyone says the other driver was speeding. The road says otherwise. I love the road. It never takes sides. My sunscreen, however, has betrayed me, and I’m going to look like a tomato for the rest of the week.

life.news: A company I’ve never heard of offered three times the value for my grandmother’s house. By letter. On thick paper.
life.more: She left me a little house beside the Old Mission Chapel. It needs a roof and a miracle. Now a company with a name like a perfume wants it for three times what it’s worth. I didn’t answer. They wrote again. Nobody pays three times for a leaky roof unless they want the ground under it.

gossip.says: Brenda Velasco taught me everything about skid marks. She can tell who lied from the rubber on the road. She goes very quiet whenever I mention the old junction. I’ve stopped mentioning it.
gossip.note: Opal Franklin says Brenda Velasco goes very quiet whenever the old junction comes up.
gossip.ask: Opal says you go very quiet whenever she mentions the old junction.
gossip.answer: There were no skid marks there, the night that mattered. I said so. I was moved off the case. Opal is the best junior I’ve had. She birdwatches there before shifts and comes in telling me about owls. I let her. The owls are better than what I remember.

gossip.says: Penelope Kline from the club birdwatches on the dry river before work like I do. She has better binoculars and worse jokes. She gasps at every red bird like it’s an opera.
gossip.note: Opal Franklin says Penelope Kline birdwatches on the dry river and gasps at every red bird.
gossip.ask: Opal says you gasp at every red bird like it’s an opera.
gossip.answer: It is an opera. A tiny red one. Opal sees a hawk and says nice. Nice. I’m trying to teach her wonder. She’s trying to teach me patience. We’re both failing beautifully. She also lent me a pair of socks once, at dawn, without being asked. Good person.

women.name: Taryn Chase
women.look: Fair skin, burgundy-dyed curls, freckles across her nose, charcoal blazer and turtleneck

own.label: Ask about the forensic lab
own.player: What’s it like working in a forensic lab?
own.reply: I’m the trainee, so three people check everything I do. I write it all down twice. It’s the most interesting room in Sunfall.

own.label: Ask if she overthinks things
own.player: Do you overthink things?
own.reply: I’ve thought about how to answer that for the whole time you were typing it. So yes.

own.label: Ask what’s in her pocket
own.player: What do you keep fiddling with?
own.reply: A brass button with an anchor on it, from the lab’s lost and found. Nobody ever claimed it. I carry it around. I’ll give it back. Probably.

calls.label: Ask who paid for the lab’s equipment
calls.player: Who paid for the lab’s new machines?
calls.reply: A grant, from the Halcyon Ridge Trust. It’s on the plaque by the centrifuge. Same trust name that’s on half the Foundation’s paperwork. Our lab tests the evidence, and the evidence people pay for our lab. Nobody else thinks that’s weird.
calls.note: Taryn Chase says the forensic lab’s equipment grant came from the Halcyon Ridge Trust.

life.news: Ran my first real test in the lab without anyone checking it. It worked. I high-fived the centrifuge.
life.more: I’m the trainee, so usually three people check everything I do. Today they were all at lunch and the sample couldn’t wait. I followed the steps, I wrote it all down, and it came out right. The centrifuge didn’t high-five me back. I’ve decided it was proud anyway.

life.news: Overthought a text to my friend for an hour and then sent it with a typo. In her name.
life.more: I spelled her name wrong. Her own name. We’ve been friends since we were small. I wrote nine drafts, deleted all of them, wrote a tenth, and the tenth was the one with the typo. She replied with a laughing face. I lay on the floor for a while. Brains are a lot.

life.news: The lab has a lost-and-found box nobody ever claims from. I took a button from it. A brass one. I don’t know why.
life.more: It’s been there for years: keys, a glove, a hair clip, a brass button with an anchor on it. Nobody ever comes for anything. I put the button in my pocket and now I carry it everywhere. I’ll put it back. I keep meaning to. It feels like it was waiting for somebody.

gossip.says: Alisha Benton is the lab analyst who checks my work. She notices hands before faces. She told me I bite my nails when I’m right and pick them when I’m wrong. Now I can’t do either.
gossip.note: Taryn Chase says Alisha Benton told her she bites her nails when she’s right.
gossip.ask: Taryn says you told her she bites her nails when she’s right and picks them when she’s wrong.
gossip.answer: It’s true and it’s useful. I don’t even have to read her results. I look at her hands. She’s the cleverest person in the building and nobody’s watching her properly. I try to. She deserves someone keeping an eye out.

gossip.says: Maren Caldwell from the club volunteers at the Sisters’ thrift shop with me. She says sorry to coats. She once bought back a scarf she’d donated because she missed it. I love her.
gossip.note: Taryn Chase says Maren Caldwell once bought back a scarf she had donated because she missed it.
gossip.ask: Taryn says you bought back a scarf you’d donated because you missed it.
gossip.answer: I did miss it. It was a good scarf, and somebody was about to buy it, and I panicked. I paid more for it than I did the first time. Taryn laughed so hard she had to sit on the coat rail. It broke. We paid for that too. Best day at the shop.

women.name: Sabrina Wallace
women.look: Sun-kissed fair skin, long red curls, gold hoop earrings, gray hoodie and running shoes

own.label: Ask about the station’s soccer team
own.player: Does the station have a sports team?
own.reply: A five-on-five team, and I captain it with a clipboard. Nobody takes the clipboard seriously until it works.

own.label: Ask how she keeps organized
own.player: Are you an organized person?
own.reply: Everything in my life is on a labeled hook. Keys, coats, feelings. Mostly it works. Lately things keep walking off the hooks.

own.label: Ask what matters most to her
own.player: What matters most to you?
own.reply: The people next to me. Partner, team, neighbors. You stand where you said you’d stand. That’s all loyalty is.

calls.label: Ask about the phone in lost property
calls.player: What was the phone that came into lost property?
calls.reply: Handed in from the club after the gala. Dead battery, no case. Two people asked about it before lunch, very casually. That afternoon the key to my lost-property cabinet walked off its hook. The phone is still in there. I’ve been guarding it with a chair.
calls.note: Sabrina Wallace says a phone from the club turned up in lost property after the gala and her cabinet key vanished that afternoon.

life.news: We beat the fire department at five-on-five. First time in four years. I drew the winning formation on a napkin.
life.more: I captain the station team with a clipboard and nobody takes the clipboard seriously until it works. Tonight it worked. The fire department went very quiet. Their captain asked to see the napkin. I said it was classified. It is now framed in the break room.

life.news: Lost the key to the lost-property cabinet. Of all the keys. The irony is not lost on me. The key is.
life.more: I keep everything in my life on a labeled hook. Everything. And somehow the lost-property key walked off my hook in a locked office. Miranda laughed for ten minutes. I didn’t. I looked everywhere. It’s in the building somewhere, sitting there, being lost on purpose.

life.news: Somebody handed a phone in to lost property this week. No case, no name, a dead battery. Everyone wanted it gone very fast.
life.more: Usually lost property is umbrellas and one sad shoe. This phone came in and two different people asked about it before lunch, very casually, like they weren’t asking. Then my cabinet key went missing. I don’t like coincidences that happen in the same afternoon.

gossip.says: Miranda Sowerby is my partner on community safety. She raised her niece alone and she plays defense like she’s on a home visit. She asks the striker how his week’s going. It works.
gossip.note: Sabrina Wallace says Miranda Sowerby raised her niece alone and plays defense like a home visit.
gossip.ask: Sabrina says you play defense like you’re on a home visit.
gossip.answer: It’s called building rapport. You’d be amazed how many men stop running when you ask about their mother. Sabrina plays like she’s storming a building. Between us we let in very few goals and make a lot of friends. Mostly I make the friends.

gossip.says: Yvette Palmer is the new detective and plays up front for us. She asks why about everything. Why that formation, why that throw-in, why is the sky. I gave her a clipboard of her own. It didn’t help.
gossip.note: Sabrina Wallace says Yvette Palmer asks why about everything, even throw-ins.
gossip.ask: Sabrina says you ask why about everything, even throw-ins.
gossip.answer: Throw-ins are deeply suspicious. Why do you use your hands in a game about feet? Nobody can tell me. Sabrina gave me a clipboard and I wrote my whys on it, and now she’s started answering them at practice. We’re up to thirty. She’s learning.

women.name: Bridget Keogh
women.look: Rosy fair skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, olive field jacket

own.label: Ask what being a detective constable is like
own.player: What’s it like being a detective constable?
own.reply: Four months in. I drive the pool car too fast, I write everything down twice, and I ask one more question than anybody wants. That last part is the job.

own.label: Ask about the drums
own.player: I hear you play the drums.
own.reply: In a lock-up on the railway side. I can’t be loud anywhere else, so I’m loud there. The neighbors have stopped complaining. I think they’ve given up.

own.label: Ask why she’s on Hinge
own.player: Why are you on Hinge?
own.reply: Honestly? Practice. I ask everyone the same four questions and watch who lies. You’re doing well, by the way. Mostly.

calls.label: Ask about her sergeant
calls.player: Who got you onto the force?
calls.reply: Sergeant Lowry. He saw me in the station waiting room years ago, there to collect my dad, and he said he saw something in me. He got me every step after that. Lately he keeps asking when I’ll close my first case, and I keep finding reasons not to. I don’t know why that makes my neck go cold.

life.news: Filed my first report with no corrections. The sergeant signed it without reading it. I’m choosing to take that as a compliment.
life.more: Eleven pages on a stolen pool car that turned out to be parked at the wrong station. I wrote everything down twice, like they taught us. I checked the spelling of every street. The sergeant took it, signed the last page, and handed it back without turning a single one. Either he trusts me or he doesn’t care. I’ve decided it’s trust.

life.news: My first real case file had been signed out twice before it reached my desk. Nobody will tell me by whom.
life.more: A missing-persons file. Old, thin, and supposed to be simple. The records stubs show it went out twice before me, under two different case numbers, and came back both times with nothing added. I asked records. Records looked at me like I’d asked for their bank details. I’ve been told to close it in a week. I’ve taken three.

life.news: Paid my dad’s tab at the Lucky Cactus again before he got there. The barman’s stopped asking why.
life.more: My dad works the track on the railway side, and since my mom died he drinks at the Lucky Cactus most nights. I go in before him and settle the tab so it never gets big enough to be a problem. The barman used to raise an eyebrow. Now he just nods. My dad thinks he has a very generous friend. In a way, he does.

life.news: Drove the pool car back from the ridge under the speed limit the whole way. Nobody at the station believes me.
life.more: I have a reputation. It’s earned. But today there was a family in the back seat, a grandmother and her grandson’s dog, and I drove like a hearse. Sergeant Graves was at the window when I parked. She looked at the clock, looked at me, and said nothing. From her, that’s a medal.

gossip.says: Eleanor Graves is the best detective in Sunfall. I would rather be arrested than tell her that.
gossip.note: Bridget Keogh says Eleanor Graves is the best detective in Sunfall, and would never tell her so.
gossip.ask: Bridget Keogh says you’re the best detective in Sunfall. She’d rather be arrested than tell you.
gossip.answer: She doesn’t have to tell me. She copies how I hold a pen. She’s quick, and she’s more honest than that station deserves, which worries me. I’m keeping an eye on who keeps an eye on her.

gossip.says: Naoko Watanabe sits with the families of the missing. Lately she sits with me too, after my shift, and doesn’t ask anything. I like that more than I can say.
gossip.note: Bridget Keogh says Naoko Watanabe has started sitting with her after her shifts.
gossip.ask: Bridget says you’ve started sitting with her after her shifts.
gossip.answer: She doesn’t talk. She taps her fingers on the table, the same four bars, over and over, like she’s drumming. I’ve started to like the song. She looks like somebody waiting for bad news she hasn’t been given yet.

women.name: Noreen Gallagher
women.look: Rosy fair skin, sandy shag with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, plain white shirt and slim black pants

own.label: Ask what she photographs
own.player: What does a crime scene photographer actually photograph?
own.reply: Whatever’s still there when everyone else has gone. Tire marks, doorways, the things people leave on tables. I make it tidy. Somebody has to.

own.label: Ask about her Italian
own.player: I hear you’re learning Italian.
own.reply: From an old lady’s recipe cards. So I can say flour, patience and too much salt beautifully. Sophia Moretti’s family corrects me at the bakery.

own.label: Ask about the flowers in her photos
own.player: You always have flowers in your pictures.
own.reply: Fresh every week, from Elena Vargas’s shop. If I arrange something every evening, the day stays arranged. That’s the theory.

calls.label: Ask what else she has photographed
calls.player: You said you photograph things nobody asks for. Like what?
calls.reply: A call about something else took me past the drive-in’s back field, late. A van with its lights off, two men, a laptop, and a crate with air holes. I took the pictures out of habit. They’re in my own file, not the station’s. I haven’t decided who should see them.

life.news: Elena threw a sprig of something into my flowers this week. She couldn’t name it. It’s on my kitchen table, being mysterious.
life.more: Elena Vargas does my flowers every week. I arrange them badly and then well, which is the whole point. This one she found growing out of a crack behind the shop. She said it was either a weed or a miracle. I said in my line of work those look alike.

life.news: Italian lesson at the Moretti bakery. I asked for a loaf and accidentally asked for a husband.
life.more: Whitney Ashford lends me recipe cards an old Italian lady wrote, and I learn the words for flour and patience. Sophia’s family corrects me over the counter. Today I mixed up two words and the whole bakery laughed. I got the loaf. Still looking for the husband.

life.news: Elena told me someone orders lilies to the old interstate junction every week. Nobody signs the card.
life.more: She mentioned it over the counter, puzzled, the way you mention a thing you want someone else to carry. Lilies, every week, to a junction where nobody lives. I photograph roads for a living. I know which ones get flowers and why. That one, I don’t know yet.

life.news: A crash on the canyon road went in the file as weather. I photographed the tire marks. There were two sets.
life.more: I took the pictures, the file said weather, and the file was closed. Brenda Velasco measured the second set of tracks with me. Nobody asked for the measurements. I keep them in a drawer next to the money I call my resignation. I haven’t spent either.

gossip.says: Katrina Ford and I share the crime scene rota. She broods, I arrange. Between us the nights are covered.
gossip.note: Noreen Gallagher shares the crime scene rota with Katrina Ford.
gossip.ask: Noreen says she arranges and you brood.
gossip.answer: She’s not wrong. She shows up to a scene with a thermos and a plan. I show up with a feeling. We get the same pictures. Hers are tidier.

gossip.says: Brenda Velasco measured a second set of tire marks on the canyon road with me. Nobody filed them.
gossip.note: Noreen Gallagher says Brenda Velasco measured a second set of tire marks on the canyon road that nobody filed.
gossip.ask: Noreen says you measured a second set of tire marks on the canyon road.
gossip.answer: I did. Nobody wanted the numbers, so I kept them. Two vehicles, one going much faster than the other. The file says weather. Weather doesn’t leave tread.

women.name: Yvonne Barlow
women.look: Fair skin, dark French braid, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, plain white shirt and slim black pants

own.label: Ask what a statistician does at the station
own.player: What does a statistician do at a police station?
own.reply: Counts things nobody wants counted. Where the calls come from, which nights, which streets. Then decides which page to put it on, which is the actual job.

own.label: Ask about her collages
own.player: I hear you make collages.
own.reply: Out of shredded reports. The numbers I’m not allowed to publish, cut up and glued into shapes. Nobody asks what the blue is. You can, if you like.

own.label: Ask about the brooch she wears
own.player: That brooch in your photo. Is it old?
own.reply: It was my mother’s. A blue swallow. A jeweler from the club keeps asking if I’d sell it back. My mother wrote me a letter that says no. So, no.

calls.label: Ask about her mother’s letter
calls.player: What else did your mother’s letter say?
calls.reply: Three pages about loving me. The fourth is about the night before she left the club: a vote, a man, a glass, and her cousin’s hand. She wrote it down because nobody else would. I haven’t shown my dad. I made it into a collage instead. If you know how to read it, it’s all there.

life.news: Got a finding onto page three of a report and the captain read it. Page three. He never reads page three.
life.more: Keiko taught me that page one is for the people who decide what isn’t a finding, so you put the real one on page three, where only the curious go. It’s about where the night calls come from. The captain read it, frowned, and asked who wrote it. Keiko said I did. He said huh. That was the best huh of my life.

life.news: A jeweler from the club asked about my mother’s brooch again. Politely. Twice.
life.more: My mother left me a blue swallow brooch. It was hers before she married my father, back when she was a Van Doren. A jeweler who works for the club has asked me twice now whether I’d consider selling it back. My mother wrote me a letter about exactly this. It says no. So I said no, both times, very politely.

life.news: Read my mother’s letter again tonight. I shouldn’t. It makes the house too quiet.
life.more: She wrote one to each of us, to open when we were older. Mine is four pages. Three are about loving me. The fourth is about something she saw, once, and I haven’t shown it to my dad. He’s downstairs making eggs. He’s always making eggs. I don’t want to be the one who makes him stop.

life.news: Made a collage out of a week of shredded traffic reports. It came out blue. Nobody asks why it’s blue.
life.more: The shredder bags go in the recycling, and I take some home. I cut the numbers up and glue them back into shapes. This one is a map, if you know how to read it. It’s blue because the nights are blue. It hangs next to the others in my room. My dad stood in front of it for a long time and said nothing, which from him is a review.

gossip.says: Keiko Nakamura taught me to put the finding on page three. Page one is for the people who decide what isn’t a finding.
gossip.note: Yvonne Barlow says Keiko Nakamura taught her to put the real finding on page three of a report.
gossip.ask: Yvonne says you taught her to put the real finding on page three.
gossip.answer: She learned it faster than I did. She also takes the shredder bags home and makes art out of them, which is technically evidence. I’ve decided not to know that.

gossip.says: Celeste Van Doren is my mother’s cousin. She has never once said my name.
gossip.note: Yvonne Barlow says Celeste Van Doren is her late mother’s cousin, and has never said her name.
gossip.ask: Yvonne Barlow says you’re her mother’s cousin, and you’ve never said her name.
gossip.answer: Isabel’s girl. She has her mother’s eyebrows and her mother’s stubbornness. Tell her the club remembers her mother very fondly. Tell her exactly that, in those words.

women.name: Harriet Boyle
women.look: Fair skin, rose-gold bob, a beauty mark above her lip, checked flannel shirt

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: Something secret. If I told you, you’d have to solve it. Let’s say I’m very good with words that mean two things.

own.label: Ask about her travel journal
own.player: Where would you travel if you could?
own.reply: Scotland. I’ve planned the same trip for seven years. I know every bus time. I’ve never booked it. The plan is too good to ruin.

own.label: Ask about the archive
own.player: What’s it like in the evidence archive?
own.reply: Quiet, cold, and full of boxes that remember things people would rather forget. I like it. Boxes don’t lie.

calls.label: Ask about the storage contract
calls.player: What’s the storage contract you found?
calls.reply: A unit on the ridge road, paid monthly, run by Halcyon Ridge Storage. Our evidence is supposed to stay in our building. Somebody signed for some of it to go up the ridge instead. The signature is very neat. Nobody remembers it.
calls.note: Harriet Boyle found a contract sending police evidence to a Halcyon Ridge Storage unit on the ridge road.

life.news: Somebody solved my crossword in the paper in under an hour and wrote to complain it was too easy. Wonderful.
life.more: I set the Daily’s cryptic crossword under a made-up name. Nobody at the station knows. When somebody finishes it fast and writes in angry, I feel like I’ve been handed a medal by an enemy. Next week’s is going to be very hard. I’ve been laughing at clue four for days.

life.news: Planned my trip to Scotland again. Got as far as booking the bus from the airport. Closed the laptop.
life.more: Seven years of the same trip in the same journal. Edinburgh, then the Highlands, then a ferry to an island with one shop. I know the bus times by heart. Every year I get close to booking and then I think, what if it isn’t as good as the journal. I’m a coward with excellent planning.

life.news: Found a storage contract in the archive that nobody can explain. A unit on the ridge road, paid every month, no evidence logged in it.
life.more: Our evidence goes in our building. That’s the rule. This contract says some of it goes somewhere else, to a unit run by a company called Halcyon Ridge Storage. Nobody remembers signing it. The signature is very neat. I don’t trust neat signatures.

gossip.says: Imani Harper is the archive’s junior. She labels every evidence box like it’s a birthday present and she keeps saying she’s going home to Atlanta. She’s been saying it for two years. I hope she never goes.
gossip.note: Harriet Boyle says Imani Harper keeps saying she’s going home to Atlanta and never goes.
gossip.ask: Harriet says you keep saying you’re going home to Atlanta and never go.
gossip.answer: I promised my mother. Every month I look at the flights and then somebody brings in a box that needs a proper label, and I stay. Harriet sets crosswords, did she tell you? Under a fake name. She thinks nobody knows. I solved last week’s. I didn’t tell her.

gossip.says: Kelsey Donovan is the senior in the archive. She’s worked there longest and talks least. Lately she’s been buying nice things. She says it’s an inheritance. She’s very happy. I’m happy for her.
gossip.note: Harriet Boyle says Kelsey Donovan has been buying nice things lately and calls it an inheritance.
gossip.ask: Harriet says you’ve been buying nice things lately and call it an inheritance.
gossip.answer: An aunt. In Ohio. She was very old and very generous. Harriet asks a lot of questions for someone who sets crosswords for a living. I told her that. She said that’s exactly what a crossword is. I didn’t have an answer. I don’t like not having an answer.

women.name: Gwen Alder
women.look: Fair skin, dark brown messy bun, a gap-toothed smile, gray hoodie and running shoes

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: What do you do on your nights off?
own.reply: Run a film night on my street off the side of the laundromat. A bedsheet, a projector held together with tape, and forty chairs. Best night of the month.

own.label: Ask about being a custody nurse
own.player: What’s it like nursing in custody?
own.reply: Everyone is scared, even the ones shouting. Especially the ones shouting. I clean the cuts and try to be the nicest thing that happens to them that night.

own.label: Ask about the trouble at work
own.player: Is something wrong at work?
own.reply: A key went missing and I got blamed. I didn’t take it. One person believed me. That’s enough. That’s more than enough.

calls.label: Ask about the man from custody
calls.player: Who’s the man you met in custody?
calls.reply: He was brought in one night after the gala, bruised and polite, no charge on the sheet. I patched him up. In the morning he was gone and the book said released. Now he lives up on the ridge, at the end of the private road. I’ve driven past the gate. Twice.
calls.note: Gwen Alder treated a man in custody after the gala with no charge on the sheet; he now lives at the end of the private ridge road.

life.news: Ran film night on my street on a bedsheet. Forty people, two dogs, one projector held together with tape. Perfect.
life.more: Everyone brings a chair and a snack and we watch something old off the side of the laundromat. Tonight the sheet blew in the wind halfway through and the hero’s face rippled like a ghost. Everybody cheered. I’ve never been so happy holding an extension cord.

life.news: Got blamed at work for something I didn’t do. Again. They looked at me like I was a thief.
life.more: A key went missing from the medicine cabinet and I was the last one who signed the book, so it was me. Except it wasn’t. I’ve said it twenty times. Sheryl believed me straight away. Nobody else did. I went home and watched a cartoon and ate an entire bag of grapes.

life.news: There’s a man I think about who I met at work, once, on the worst night of his life. He lives up on the ridge now.
life.more: He came through custody one night, bruised, polite, and very scared. I patched him up and he thanked me like I’d saved his life. I hadn’t. I just cleaned a cut. Now he lives somewhere up on the ridge and I think about him far too much for a man I met for an hour.

gossip.says: Sheryl Abbott is the other custody nurse. She says almost nothing and writes everything down. She’s the only one who believed me about the key. I’d follow her into a fire. I think she’d prefer I didn’t.
gossip.note: Gwen Alder says Sheryl Abbott was the only one who believed her about the missing key.
gossip.ask: Gwen says you were the only one who believed her about the key, and she’d follow you into a fire.
gossip.answer: Please don’t follow me into a fire. Follow me out of one. Gwen is sunny and stubborn and terrible at hiding what she feels, which in custody is dangerous and everywhere else is lovely. I believed her because she couldn’t lie to save her life. I’ve watched her try.

gossip.says: Amber Colebrook on the phones restores old dresses, very slowly, one a year. She lent me one for my cousin’s wedding and I nearly didn’t give it back. She knew. She let me keep it a week.
gossip.note: Gwen Alder says Amber Colebrook lent her a restored dress for her cousin’s wedding.
gossip.ask: Gwen says you lent her one of your dresses for a wedding and let her keep it a week.
gossip.answer: She looked so happy in it I couldn’t take it back. Dresses should be danced in. Mine mostly hang in a closet waiting. Gwen danced in it for six hours and brought it back with a grass stain and a story. That’s the best thing that dress has had happen to it in eighty years.

women.name: Simone Ashby
women.look: Sun-kissed fair skin, chestnut curly bob, gold hoop earrings, maroon fleece and jeans

own.label: Ask about the night shift
own.player: What’s night dispatch like?
own.reply: Quiet, then not. Lost dogs, loud parties, and the odd call nobody wants written down. I write everything down anyway.

own.label: Ask about the souvenirs on her shelf
own.player: What’s on that shelf in your photo?
own.reply: Roadside junk from the drives home. A snow globe with a gas station in it, a plastic alien from a diner, a spoon from a town of nine. All priceless.

own.label: Ask if she ever did anything else
own.player: Have you always worked dispatch?
own.reply: I sang, for two years, in the city. Then my dad had a stroke and the night line was the only job that let me sit with him in the afternoons. He’s better. I stayed.

calls.label: Ask what she kept from the payphone calls
calls.player: You said you kept the times of those payphone calls somewhere. Where?
calls.reply: In the plastic alien on my shelf. The base is hollow. Three times, three nights, two years apart and then closer. I looked them up against the paper. Each one was the night before a man died out at the junction. They told me to log them as pranks. I don’t think a man rings dispatch from a payphone for a joke.

life.news: Ten years on the night line today. Nobody noticed, which is the job done right.
life.more: Night dispatch is the phones when everyone else is asleep. Lost dogs, loud parties, the odd thing nobody wants to write down. Bravery at night is what you log. That’s all it is. I celebrated with a coffee at the Lucky Cactus at sunrise. Nixie was there. She bought it.

life.news: Found a spoon on the drive home from a town with a population of nine. Best souvenir yet.
life.more: I collect odd roadside things on the long drives home. A snow globe with a gas station inside, a plastic alien from a diner, and now a spoon from a town of nine people. Nixie Adler collects the same junk. We compare at sunrise like it’s a stamp club.

life.news: A line I logged last night is gone from the system this morning. Someone with a sergeant’s login took it out.
life.more: A man rang his wife from the station basement, through my board, and said he had to sign something for the sergeant and would be late. I logged it. This morning it’s not there. I write everything down on paper as well, though. Old habit. It isn’t gone from me.

life.news: The payphone at the weigh station rang again on my shift and cut off. Logged as a prank. Third one in two years.
life.more: A man’s voice, a few words, then nothing. The duty sergeant says log it as a prank, so I log it as a prank. Three times now, in two years. I keep the times somewhere nobody would look. I don’t think they were pranks.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler and I have coffee at the Lucky Cactus at sunrise when my shift ends and her venue closes. We have never once talked about work.
gossip.note: Simone Ashby has coffee with Nixie Adler at the Lucky Cactus at sunrise.
gossip.ask: Simone says you two have coffee at sunrise and never talk about work.
gossip.answer: We talk about souvenirs and diners and who’s been rude to us. It’s the best part of my week. Tell her the alien she found is a fake, and that I’m jealous.

gossip.says: Amber Colebrook takes the paper log home in a dress bag. Every night. Nobody asks why.
gossip.note: Simone Ashby says Amber Colebrook takes the paper dispatch log home every night.
gossip.ask: Simone says you take the paper log home in a dress bag.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to keep the real one. The system forgets things. Paper doesn’t. Simone writes everything down too. We’ve never discussed it. We don’t need to.

women.name: Adriana Ponce
women.look: Golden-tan skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask why she campaigns
own.player: Why climate campaigning?
own.reply: Because my town in Sonora ran out of water when I was twelve. People argue about models. I remember the taps.

own.label: Ask about her soccer
own.player: Five-on-five, I heard?
own.reply: Every week with women half my age. I’m slower and dirtier. They’re learning a lot.

own.label: Ask what she makes of the young activists
own.player: What do you make of the younger activists?
own.reply: They’re brave and they’re online. They mistake a hashtag for a hard week’s work. I tell them: knock on doors, or go home. They hate me. They come back.

own.label: Ask what she got wrong when she was young
own.player: What did you get wrong when you were young?
own.reply: I thought shouting was the same as winning. It isn’t. The people I changed were the ones I had a coffee with.

own.label: Ask about the photographs on her wall
own.player: What are all the photos on your wall?
own.reply: Towns that ran out of water. Mine is the first one, top left. A river sold upstream when I was twelve. My family came north the year the taps stopped.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: What did your parents do here?
own.reply: Dad was a mechanic who became a janitor. Mom cleaned houses and sang while she did it. I learned organizing from watching her get six rich houses to pay on time.

calls.label: Ask about the torn page in the journal
calls.player: What was on the page torn out of the journal?
calls.reply: The night before we voted to join the protest, someone wrote in the shared journal: three names and a parking lot bay number. Vanessa’s hand. The next morning the page was gone. I read it before it went.
calls.note: Adriana Ponce read a torn-out journal page in Vanessa Greer’s hand listing three names and a parking lot bay.

life.news: Scored at five-on-five. Not against Sable, she was off injured, but I’m counting it.
life.more: Soccer with women half my age. I’m slower and dirtier and I’ve got more to prove. They’re learning a lot. I scored with my shin. A goal off the shin counts double when you’re thirty-six.

life.news: My daughter told me I’m embarrassing. In front of her friends. In my soccer uniform.
life.more: Lupe’s sixteen. Everything I do is embarrassing, and the soccer uniform is the worst of it. I said I’ll stop embarrassing you when the reservoir’s full. She rolled her eyes. Later she asked when the next match is. That’s my girl.

life.news: Knocked on forty doors today. Thirty-eight people shut them. Two invited me in for coffee.
life.more: They mistake a hashtag for a hard week’s work. Knock on doors or go home. I thought shouting was winning, once. The people I changed were the ones I had coffee with. Two today. That’s a good day. Most days it’s none.

life.news: Saw a photo of my town in Sonora. The river’s still dry.
life.more: It ran dry when I was twelve. Somebody sold it upstream. People argue about models. I remember the taps. I keep a wall of photos of towns that ran out of water. Today I added one more. I’d like to stop adding them.

gossip.says: Rosa Gutierrez wrote the only honest thing about water anyone in Sunfall has written this year. Her thesis. I’ve tried to take her for coffee twice. She keeps saying she’s busy.
gossip.note: Adriana Ponce says Rosa Gutierrez’s water thesis is the only honest thing written in Sunfall this year.
gossip.ask: Adriana says your thesis is the only honest thing anyone’s written in Sunfall this year.
gossip.answer: She said that? Adriana doesn’t say nice things. She says true things, and they sometimes happen to be nice. I’ll have coffee with her. I keep meaning to. Tell her yes. Tell her I said yes before I could check the lock.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland gives most of her wages away and brings soup to every meeting. She’s blunt because the world’s on fire. I told her to knock on doors. She did. She’s better at it than me.
gossip.note: Adriana Ponce says Eden Sutherland gives away most of her wages and is brilliant at knocking on doors.
gossip.ask: Adriana says you’re better at knocking on doors than she is.
gossip.answer: I’m not better. I’m younger, and nobody slams a door on a girl holding soup. Adriana taught me to say one sentence and then shut up. It works. She’s terrifying and right, which is the worst combination.

gossip.says: Sasha Mahoney plays for the other five-on-five team and she counts my touches. Literally. She knows the odds of me scoring before I take the shot.
gossip.note: Adriana Ponce says Sasha Mahoney calculates the odds at five-on-five.
gossip.ask: Adriana says you work out her odds of scoring before she shoots.
gossip.answer: Eleven percent from outside the box, thirty-two inside. She knows that. She shoots from outside anyway. I know the odds and ignore them. She doesn’t know them and ignores them anyway. We’re very well matched.

women.name: Sienna Navarro
women.look: Olive skin, burgundy-dyed curls, gray-green eyes, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask what she’s organizing
own.player: What are you organizing at the moment?
own.reply: A mural on the underpass. Forty volunteers, three committees and one argument about whether a cactus is problematic. It’s a cactus.

own.label: Ask about the drums
own.player: How are the drums going?
own.reply: Loudly. My neighbor bangs on the wall in time now. I think we’re a band.

own.label: Ask what she overthinks most
own.player: What do you overthink the most?
own.reply: Group chats. If I put a period, am I angry? If I don’t, am I unserious? I once drafted a thumbs-up for ten minutes.

own.label: Ask if she ever tires of causes
own.player: Do you ever get tired of causes?
own.reply: All the time. Some days I just want to paint something pretty that doesn’t mean anything. I’m not allowed to say that at meetings.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: Dad painted houses and Mom sold them. That’s the whole economy in one marriage. I paint walls nobody can sell. I think that’s growth.

own.label: Ask how she got into organizing
own.player: How did you end up organizing?
own.reply: I was a shy art student. Organizing turned out to be a way of being in a room without anyone looking at me. Everyone looks at the clipboard.

calls.label: Ask about the crescent on the mural
calls.player: Why is there a crescent moon on the underpass mural?
calls.reply: A volunteer added it and we voted to keep it, for the desert nights. Then Hana Park told me that crescent is a design somebody paid cash for, and it’s on a flyer for something called the Midnight Rite. The volunteer was a girl called Sorrel, and she paints the night sky like she’s been told where the stars go.
calls.note: Sienna Navarro says the mural’s crescent was added by Sorrel Vane, and the same design is on the Midnight Rite flyer.

life.news: Forty volunteers, three committees and a two-hour argument about whether a cactus is problematic. It’s a cactus.
life.more: The underpass mural. Someone said the cactus was a lazy symbol of the desert. Someone else said it was a symbol of resilience. Someone else said the cactus was a cactus. That was me. We voted. The cactus stays.

life.news: Zadie banged on the wall in time again. We did a whole new song. Neither of us said a word about it after.
life.more: My neighbor. I drum badly when I’m stressed, and she bangs on the wall in time, and over months it’s become a kind of band. We nod in the hallway like strangers. It’s the best band in Sunfall and it has a wall in the middle.

life.news: Drafted a thumbs-up in a group chat for ten minutes. Sent nothing.
life.more: If I put a period, am I angry? If I don’t, am I unserious? Committees have destroyed me. I just wanted to say yes to a paint order. From now on I’m only communicating by mural.

life.news: Painted something pretty that doesn’t mean anything. A cup of tea. Best thing I’ve done all year.
life.more: Some days I just want to paint something that isn’t a cause. A cup of tea on a windowsill, with steam. No message, no committee, no cactus. It’s going in my kitchen, and nobody’s allowed to ask what it represents.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster lives next door and reviews bands for the paper, and she’s in my band without ever having touched a drum. She bangs on the wall. In time.
gossip.note: Sienna Navarro says Zadie Foster plays in her band by banging on the wall.
gossip.ask: Sienna says you’re in her band and you’ve never touched a drum.
gossip.answer: I’m the rhythm section. The wall is my instrument. She thinks I can’t tell her stress drumming from her happy drumming. I can. Stress is faster. Tell her the bridge last night was a four. Possibly a four and a half.

gossip.says: Hana Park designs logos for companies that won’t exist next year. She redid the lettering on our mural for free because she said the original was a crime.
gossip.note: Sienna Navarro says Hana Park redid the mural’s lettering for free.
gossip.ask: Sienna says you redid the mural lettering because the original was a crime.
gossip.answer: It was a crime! Somebody used a font that looked like it was apologizing. I couldn’t sleep. I did it for free so I could walk through that underpass without wincing. Ugly and alive is fine. Ugly and apologetic is not.

gossip.says: Cassandra Finch brings cake to every meeting and votes however she likes. Nobody can argue with her because she’s holding the cake.
gossip.note: Sienna Navarro says Cassandra Finch brings cake to every meeting and votes as she pleases.
gossip.ask: Sienna says nobody can argue with you because you’re holding the cake.
gossip.answer: That’s the strategy. Bring a lemon drizzle and vote how you like. I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down, and cake helps. Sienna once tried bringing a cake too. A cactus-shaped one. Very brave.

women.name: Nora Hadley
women.look: Warm brown skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, a silver ear cuff, vintage windbreaker

own.label: Ask what her heresy is
own.player: What’s an opinion your friends hate?
own.reply: That nuclear power is the best thing for the climate. Say that in our group chat and watch people combust. Ironically.

own.label: Ask about learning Italian
own.player: You’re learning Italian?
own.reply: Badly. I want to read Dante in the original before I die. Ambitious, for someone who still says grazie wrong.

own.label: Ask what’s bothering her
own.player: Something on your mind?
own.reply: A woman from our march saw something on gala night. She told me, then a week later she told the police the exact opposite. Someone got to her.
own.note: Nora Hadley says a witness changed her story about gala night after someone got to her.

own.label: Ask what she believes that her friends don’t
own.player: What do you believe that your friends don’t?
own.reply: That men and women want different things, mostly, and that’s fine. Saying it at a meeting is like admitting you eat meat.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What does your dad do?
own.reply: He’s a surveyor. He surveyed the ridge road once and said it was fine. Mom’s a school nurse. I’m the nobody in particular they made, with opinions.

own.label: Ask what she reads
own.player: What are you reading?
own.reply: Italian grammar, badly, and everything in the library by people who were wrong in public and survived it. I’d like to be wrong in public one day. Properly.

calls.label: Ask about her father’s survey
calls.player: Is something wrong with your dad’s survey?
calls.reply: He said the ridge road was fine. It isn’t fine. Trucks go up it at night that the survey says can’t. I think somebody paid him to say so, and I think he knows I think it.
calls.note: Nora Hadley suspects her father was paid to sign off the ridge road as safe.

life.news: Said nuclear power in the group chat. Three people left. One came back to argue. Progress.
life.more: Nuclear is the best thing for the climate. Say that in our group chat and watch people combust. Ironically. The one who came back wrote me four paragraphs. I wrote five. We’re meeting for coffee. It might be a date. Or a duel.

life.news: Read a canto of Dante in the original. It took four hours. I understood about a third.
life.more: I want to read Dante in the original before I die. Ambitious for someone who still says grazie wrong. I read it with a friend from the library and we argued about one word for forty minutes. She was right. I’ll never admit it.

life.news: Years ago I argued with a teacher until she cried. Today I saw her in the supermarket.
life.more: I was right. I was also fifteen and cruel about it. That’s when I learned that being right is something you have to carry carefully. I said hello. She said hello back and asked what I’m reading. I nearly cried in the cereal aisle.

life.news: My dad took me out surveying for the day. Measuring the desert. Very calming.
life.more: He says the land never lies, only the people who pay for the report. I held the pole while he squinted down the sight. We ate sandwiches on the tailgate. He’s quieter than he used to be. Today he laughed twice.

gossip.says: Adriana Ponce tells us young ones to knock on doors or go home. We hate her. We come back. She’s the only grown-up in the movement who argues with me properly.
gossip.note: Nora Hadley says Adriana Ponce is the only grown-up who argues with her properly.
gossip.ask: Nora says you’re the only grown-up who argues with her properly.
gossip.answer: She argues properly too. She’s wrong about some things and right about nuclear, which I’ll never say in public. Arguing with her is like playing soccer with someone who’s read the rule book. Exhausting. Good for you.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland sings alto in a church choir she doesn’t believe in. She says it’s the only place she feels calm. She’d kill me for telling you.
gossip.note: Nora Hadley says Eden Sutherland sings in a church choir she doesn’t believe in.
gossip.ask: Nora says you sing in a church choir you don’t believe in.
gossip.answer: Of course she told you. Fine. Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell the group. They’d make it a debate. It’s not a debate. It’s just singing.

women.name: Daisy Chen
women.look: Dark skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, tortoiseshell glasses, hand-knitted sweater

women.name: Zoe Whitaker
women.look: Light-brown skin, golden-brown ringlets, freckles across her nose, oversized thrifted cardigan

own.label: Ask what she does in the climate group
own.player: What do you do in the climate group?
own.reply: I write the minutes. I say very little. People think that means I don’t notice anything. It means I’m writing it down.

own.label: Ask about the journal she carries
own.player: What’s that journal you carry?
own.reply: A trip I haven’t taken yet. The coast, a train, a city with a river. I’ve written the whole thing already. I’ll go when the jar is full. The jar is slow.

own.label: Ask what she does in the mornings
own.player: What do you do in the mornings?
own.reply: Three mornings a week at the Lucky Cactus with Madison Pike. She talks enough for both of us, which suits me. I carry plates and listen. You learn a lot about a town from what it orders.

own.label: Ask why she joined the climate group
own.player: Why the climate group?
own.reply: A girl called Nora Hadley argued with me in a seminar, and I’d never been argued with before. I went to a meeting to argue back. I’m still there. So is the argument.

own.label: Ask who’s at home
own.player: Who’s at home?
own.reply: My aunt. She raised me, kindly, with no money. I got to the university on a scholarship that wasn’t the Foundation’s. I’m proud of that in a way I know is small.

own.label: Ask about the evening before the fire
own.player: Were you at the campaign office the evening before the fire?
own.reply: Late, writing up the minutes. Two people left. Since then the two people I trust most have each told me a different reason why. Vanessa Greer says she took Rosa home because Rosa was in a state. Dev Okafor says Vanessa left with Caleb Marsh and a bag from a garden center. One of them is lying. I have to decide which. I don’t want to.
own.note: Zoe Whitaker was at the campaign office the evening before Vale’s fire: Vanessa Greer says she took Rosa home, Dev Okafor says Vanessa left with Caleb Marsh and a garden-center bag.

calls.label: Ask what she saw with her own eyes
calls.player: What did you see with your own eyes?
calls.reply: Only one thing, and I wrote it in my travel journal under the city with a river, where nobody would look. The bag was heavy. Caleb Marsh carried it with both hands.
calls.note: Zoe Whitaker saw Caleb Marsh carry a heavy garden-center bag out of the campaign office with both hands.

calls.label: Ask if she’s okay
calls.player: You sound tired. Are you okay?
calls.reply: I went to the city today. I go once a month. My mom’s in a hospital there, and her mind comes and goes. Today it came. She knew me for an hour. Don’t tell anyone. I don’t.

life.news: Put four dollars in the jar today. Tips from the Lucky Cactus. The jar is getting less slow.
life.more: Madison told a man his pie was her grandma’s recipe, which it isn’t, and he tipped like he believed her. She gave me half. I wrote it in the journal under the train. Four dollars closer to a city with a river.

life.news: Somebody at the meeting asked me to stop writing everything down. I wrote that down.
life.more: He said the minutes should be a summary, not a transcript. I said a summary is just a transcript somebody edited. Nobody laughed except Nora, and Nora never laughs, so I’m counting it.

life.news: Long day. I don’t want to talk about where I was. Tell me something about yours instead.
life.more: I was in the city. It’s family. I’m fine. Mostly I’m tired from pretending I’m fine on the bus home. Tell me something stupid that happened to you. Please.

life.news: Nora argued with me for an hour about trains versus planes. I won. She says I didn’t.
life.more: Trains, obviously. You can write on a train. Nora says the carbon math is closer than I think and pulled up a chart. I said a chart can’t look out of a window. She said that isn’t an argument. It’s the best one I have.

gossip.says: Madison Pike tells customers the pie is her grandma’s recipe. It comes frozen in a box. They tip double.
gossip.note: Zoe Whitaker says Madison Pike tells diner customers the frozen pie is her grandma’s recipe.
gossip.ask: Zoe says you tell customers the pie is your grandma’s recipe.
gossip.answer: It is my grandma’s recipe. My grandma also bought it frozen. That’s the recipe. Zoe won’t lie to a customer, so she carries the plates and I do the talking. Together we’re one great waitress.

gossip.says: Nora Hadley is the only person who has ever argued with me properly. She says nuclear in the group chat just to watch people leave.
gossip.note: Zoe Whitaker says Nora Hadley says nuclear in the group chat to watch people leave.
gossip.ask: Zoe says you say nuclear in the group chat just to watch people leave.
gossip.answer: Not to watch them leave. To see who stays to argue. Zoe stayed. She writes down everything I say and reads it back to me when I contradict myself. It’s the most annoying thing anyone’s ever done for me.

women.name: Khadija Rahman
women.look: Warm brown skin, cornrows into a low bun, strong dark brows, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask about her film nights
own.player: What do you show at the film nights?
own.reply: Old comedies, mostly. I tried a serious documentary once. Twelve people came and one of them was asleep. Now it’s slapstick and popcorn and the hall is full.

own.label: Ask what community meetings are really like
own.player: What are community meetings really like?
own.reply: Two hours, three people talking and a cookie tin nobody opens until the end. The cookies are the only thing everyone agrees on.

own.label: Ask what she disagrees with her friends about
own.player: What do you disagree with your friends about?
own.reply: Quite a lot, quietly. They think everything is a system. I think a lot of things are just people being rude. You can’t fix rude with a workshop.

own.label: Ask what she misses most
own.player: What do you miss most?
own.reply: My grandmother’s kitchen. Everyone shouting and nobody angry. Sunfall is very polite. I miss being shouted at with love.

own.label: Ask how she runs film night
own.player: Where do you get a projector?
own.reply: I share one with Gwen, who runs a yard film night on alternate weeks. It travels between us in a shopping trolley. It has seen things.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What does your family do?
own.reply: Mom runs a pharmacy on the Sunfall Road and has a strong view on everything. Dad died when I was twenty. In our house you were shouted at with love or not at all.

calls.label: Ask what went wrong at film night
calls.player: What happened at the film night you stopped?
calls.reply: Four minutes of film that wasn’t mine came up between reels. A room with candles, a circle of people, and a bell. I said it was a fault. It came in the shared projector from Gwen’s yard night. A man asked her to show it as a favor. Brad Keller. The reel is in my apartment. I don’t want it there.
calls.note: Khadija Rahman has a reel showing a candlelit circle and a bell, passed on by Brad Keller.

life.news: Film night was full again. A man laughed so hard at a pie fight he fell off his chair. Then everyone laughed at him.
life.more: Old comedies, slapstick, popcorn. The documentary nights had twelve people and one asleep. Tonight a man in a cardigan fell off his chair at the pie scene and the whole hall cheered him back up. Better than any film.

life.news: Sat in a committee meeting for two hours. Three people and a cookie tin. Decided nothing.
life.more: They think everything’s a system. I think a lot of things are just people being rude, and you can’t fix rude with a workshop. I said that in the meeting. There was a long silence. Someone ate the last cookie out of spite.

life.news: Missing my grandmother’s kitchen today. Everyone shouting and nobody angry.
life.more: It was in the city, full of aunts and pans and my grandmother shouting with love at everybody. Sunfall is very polite. Nobody shouts here unless they mean it. I rang my aunt just to be shouted at. She obliged.

life.news: Recorded the canal at night on my old reel machine. It sounds like a city breathing.
life.more: I record sounds around town. People think it’s strange. I think in fifty years someone will want to know what Sunfall sounded like when it was quiet. Ducks, a radio from a window, someone laughing two streets away. That’s the reel.

gossip.says: Vanessa Greer comes to our meetings and talks to everyone like they’re the only person who’s ever listened to them. People leave in love with her. I watch the cookie tin.
gossip.note: Khadija Rahman says Vanessa Greer talks to everyone as if they’re the only person who’s ever listened.
gossip.ask: Khadija says people leave your meetings in love with you.
gossip.answer: People leave my meetings thinking, which is rarer. Khadija thinks I’m a cult leader with good books. I think she’s a cynic with a projector. We’re both a little right. She guards the cookie tin like it’s the treasury.

gossip.says: Cleo Rook let me record her old church while it was empty. It hums. A real note. I haven’t worked out where it comes from.
gossip.note: Khadija Rahman says she recorded a hum in Cleo Rook’s old church.
gossip.ask: Khadija says your church hums when it’s empty, and she’s recorded it.
gossip.answer: It does. It’s hummed for twelve years. I leave the light on for it. Khadija sat in the vestry with her machine for an hour, completely still. She’s the only person who’s ever listened to it properly. Whatever it is, it liked her.

women.name: Esther Yu
women.look: Medium-brown skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, oversized thrifted cardigan

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Climate group. I’m the one who opens the office in the morning, puts the kettle on, reads the journal and writes the first line of the day. Somebody has to be the first line.

own.label: Ask what she collects
own.player: Do you collect anything?
own.reply: Roadside souvenirs. A motel snow globe, a spoon from a diner that burned down, a plastic saguaro from a gas station on the state road. The group thinks it’s weird. They’re relics. Somebody should keep them.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: My parents run a laundry on the Sunfall Road. I grew up folding other people’s shirts and learning more about this town from its pockets than from the paper.

own.label: Ask what she looks for in a man
own.player: What do you look for in a man?
own.reply: Respect, before anything. I’ve walked away from two boyfriends because they didn’t have it. I lost no sleep either time. Romance is lovely. It isn’t load-bearing.

own.label: Ask what she does on her days off
own.player: What do you do on your days off?
own.reply: Junk markets, with an older woman from the club I met over a box of spoons. We hunt souvenirs once a week and talk about nothing. The rule is we never talk about her club. It’s the best friendship I have.

calls.label: Ask if anything strange has happened
calls.player: Anything strange going on lately?
calls.reply: A gray car has been parked outside the office every morning for two weeks. Two men in it. They never get out. They leave the minute anyone else arrives. I write the plate down in the journal every day. I write everything down.
calls.note: Esther Yu says two men in a gray sedan wait outside the climate group’s office every morning; she writes the plate in the journal every day.

calls.label: Ask about her market friend
calls.player: Tell me about your market friend.
calls.reply: Marianne. She has a spoon from the same burned diner as mine. Last week I read a license plate out loud as a joke and she went completely still. We don’t talk about her club. I’m starting to think I should.
calls.note: Esther Yu says Marianne Keene went completely still when Esther read the gray sedan’s plate out loud as a joke.

life.news: Opened the office before sunrise and the whole street was pink. I wrote the first line of the journal about the sky instead of the campaign.
life.more: Nobody minded. Jennifer read it when she came in and said it was the best first line we’ve had all year. Then she put the kettle on for me, which has never once happened. I’m framing the page.

life.news: Found a souvenir I’ve hunted for years: a pennant from a drive-in that closed before I was born.
life.more: Faded orange felt, a cartoon car, a phone number with only five digits. The man wanted twenty dollars. Marianne talked him down to six by pretending to be my aunt. We were very pleased with ourselves all the way home.
