life.news: Somebody threw an egg at the office window. I cleaned it off before anyone else got in.
life.more: It was still runny, so it can’t have been long before I arrived. I didn’t write it in the journal. Some things the group doesn’t need first thing in the morning. I wrote it in mine instead.

life.news: Two people in the group stopped arguing long enough to agree with each other. Historic.
life.more: It was about the bike racks. Twenty minutes of shouting and then, suddenly, the same opinion. Everybody looked embarrassed. I made a cake to mark the occasion. It said truce in green icing.

gossip.says: Sienna Navarro is painting the underpass with forty volunteers and one long argument about whether a cactus is problematic. She’s also teaching herself the drums. Badly. Her neighbor bangs on the wall in time.
gossip.note: Esther Yu says Sienna Navarro is teaching herself the drums, badly.
gossip.ask: Esther says you’re teaching yourself the drums badly, and your neighbor bangs on the wall in time.
gossip.answer: In time is a compliment, if you think about it. It means I have a beat. The cactus argument is still going. Esther thinks a cactus stands for resilience. Somebody else thinks it stands for bad landscaping. I think it’s a cactus.

gossip.says: Jennifer Tate lives next door at the co-op and plays the same record every night. I know every word now. I’ve never told her.
gossip.note: Esther Yu says Jennifer Tate, her neighbor at the co-op, plays the same record every night.
gossip.ask: Esther says you play the same record every night and she knows every word.
gossip.answer: She does? Oh no. It was my mother’s favorite and I can’t sleep without it. Tell Esther I’ll buy her earplugs. Actually, tell her to come over and sing it. I’ve always wanted someone to sing the harmony.

women.name: Cassandra Finch
women.look: Bird-like and slight, warm brown skin, cropped bleached hair, enormous dark tired eyes with a sullen look, a small gap between her front teeth, a slim small-busted figure, a linen shirt and a canvas tote

own.label: Ask how she stays so cheerful
own.player: How do you stay so cheerful?
own.reply: Stubbornness. I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down now. Out of spite, mainly.

own.label: Ask what she paints
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: Skies. Sunfall has the best skies in the world and everyone is looking at their phones under them. Sorry. Not you. Well, a bit you.

own.label: Ask if she fits in with her group
own.player: Do you fit in with the others?
own.reply: Not really. I go to the meetings, bring the cake and vote how I like. They keep me for the cake.

own.label: Ask what she’ll never give up on
own.player: What will you never give up on?
own.reply: People. Even the awful ones. Especially the awful ones. Someone gave up on me once, and it took years to undo.

own.label: Ask where she paints
own.player: Where do you paint?
own.reply: On the roof above the Sisters’ charity shop. I rent the room underneath from Lucia. Best sky in Sunfall and nobody up there but me and the pigeons.

own.label: Ask about growing up
own.player: What were you like as a teenager?
own.reply: Ill, mostly. Thin and tired with a thing the doctors were slow to name. Mom left. Dad sold farm machinery and sat with me. I decided to be cheerful out of spite and I’ve never backed down.

own.label: Ask why she goes to the vigil
own.player: Why do you sit at the back of the Sisters’ vigil?
own.reply: Because I don’t believe, and a year ago I was in a home with nothing to believe in, and Margaret Holloway visited me there when nobody else did. The chancery wants the Watch stopped. I don’t pray. I will sit at the back with every candle they give me until somebody carries me out.

views.dispute: I rent a room above the Sisters’ shop and I sit at the back of their vigil and I don’t believe a word of it, and I haven’t missed one in a year. If the bishop wants to know why, he can come and sit at the back too.

calls.label: Ask about her neighbor
calls.player: Who lives next door to you?
calls.reply: Nobody, for two years. Now the light comes on behind the blind at night and goes off before dawn. Lucia takes two lunches up the stairs. Through the wall I heard a woman crying, and once, laughing. I painted the blind with the light behind it. I won’t say more.
calls.note: Cassandra Finch says someone has been living secretly in the apartment next to hers, above the Sisters’ charity shop.

calls.label: Ask what she kept from a meeting
calls.player: Did you keep anything from the group’s meetings?
calls.reply: Vanessa Greer’s cup. She left it, and I don’t give up on anyone. There’s a crescent painted on the bottom. I’m trying to decide if that means anything.
calls.note: Cassandra Finch kept a cup Vanessa Greer left behind, with a crescent on the base.

life.news: Painted the sky from the roof again. Everyone below was looking at their phones. Sorry. A bit you.
life.more: Sunfall has the best skies in the world and everyone looks at their phones under them. Tonight it went orange, then pink, then a purple I don’t have a name for. I painted it fast. I’ll give it to the first person who looks up.

life.news: Brought a lemon drizzle to the meeting and voted against everyone. Delicious and principled.
life.more: I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down. Out of spite, mainly. They wanted to spend the grant on a logo. I wanted to spend it on paint for children. I lost the vote. They ate the cake. I count it as a draw.

life.news: Wrote to an old friend. Fourth letter. No reply yet.
life.more: Someone gave up on me once. It took years to undo. I don’t give up on people now. Even the awful ones. Even the ones who don’t answer. Especially those. I’ll write a fifth. I’ve got plenty of stamps.

life.news: Sat at the back of the Sisters’ vigil again. I don’t believe. I go anyway.
life.more: It’s the quietest room in Sunfall, full of women who mean every word. I sit at the back with my hands in my lap and think about who I’m worried about. I suppose that’s a kind of praying. Don’t tell the Sisters. They’d be too pleased.

gossip.says: Lavinia Gravesend was in a home with me for six months when we were young. I’ve never stopped trying to reach her. If she’s talking to you, keep talking to her.
gossip.note: Cassandra Finch says she has been trying to reach Lavinia Gravesend for years.
gossip.ask: Cassandra asked me to keep talking to you.
gossip.answer: Did she? She draws me, you know. From memory. She always gets the hands right. I don’t call her back because I don’t know what to say. Tell her the purple desert’s coming along. She’ll know what that means.

gossip.says: Margaret Holloway visited me every week when I was in the home. She brought books and lists. She still makes lists. I’ve kept one she wrote me years ago. It says: get better.
gossip.note: Cassandra Finch says Margaret Holloway visited her every week when she was young and ill.
gossip.ask: Cassandra says you visited her every week when she was ill, and wrote her a list.
gossip.answer: She kept it? Of course she did. It was a very short list, for me. Item one: get better. Item two: be difficult about it. She managed both. I’m proud of her. Don’t tell her I said proud. I’ll deny it on parish paper.

gossip.says: Sienna Navarro organizes forty volunteers and then goes home and paints cups of tea. She says she’s tired of causes. She’s not. She’s tired of committees.
gossip.note: Cassandra Finch says Sienna Navarro is tired of committees, not causes.
gossip.ask: Cassandra says you’re not tired of causes, just committees.
gossip.answer: That’s annoyingly accurate. I love the mural. I hate the three committees about the mural. Cassandra brings cake and votes how she likes and somehow gets away with it. I’ve tried bringing cake. I just get asked to take the minutes.

women.name: Eden Sutherland
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, light-brown skin, freckles across her nose, huge dark sleepy eyes with a sullen stare, buzz-cut dark hair, a gap-toothed smile, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask what campaigning is like day to day
own.player: What’s campaigning actually like day to day?
own.reply: Leaflets, rain and men in big cars telling me to get a job. This is my job. It pays less than their car.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell my friends.

own.label: Ask why she’s so blunt
own.player: Why are you so blunt?
own.reply: Because the world’s on fire and I haven’t got time to be nice about it. I’m nice afterwards. I bring soup.

own.label: Ask what she gives away
own.player: What do you give away?
own.reply: Most of my wages, honestly. My roommate calls it a problem. I call it the only bit of my life that makes sense.

own.label: Ask who she lives with
own.player: Do you live with anyone?
own.reply: Jasmin, on the dry river. She calls my giving my wages away a problem. She also eats my soup, so she’s part of the problem.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Grandad was a founding family’s lawyer, struck off. Dad is a kind drunk who teaches piano. Mom is a Bluebird’s lady’s maid, which I don’t say on campus. Don’t you say it either.

calls.label: Ask about the grant letter
calls.player: Did your group ever get a grant?
calls.reply: A letter signed Ruth Calder says it’s approved, pending a private meeting at the lodge. Just me. On a night I worked out has no moon. I wrote to thank her. She didn’t know anything about it. I haven’t told the group, because they’d say no and the water kit is real.
calls.note: Eden Sutherland has a grant letter signed with Ruth Calder’s name inviting her alone to the lodge on a moonless night; Ruth Calder never sent it.

calls.label: Ask who cries in her choir
calls.player: Does anyone in your choir get upset?
calls.reply: There’s a hymn about the deep that makes a girl from the club cry. Elise. I’m blunt, so I asked her why. She’s started telling me. It’s about an invitation.
calls.note: Eden Sutherland says Elise Harrow has started confiding in her about a frightening invitation.

life.news: Leafleted in the rain for four hours. A man in a big car told me to get a job.
life.more: This is my job. It pays less than his car. I gave him a leaflet anyway and he took it, through the window, in the rain. Small wins. The leaflet was soaked, so he got a very wet argument.

life.news: Choir practice. We sang the old hymn with the high bit and nobody’s voice cracked. A miracle, possibly.
life.more: Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell my friends. Raven and Jessica and I stood in a row and nailed the alto line. It felt like flying.

life.news: My roommate found out how much of my wages I give away. She’s calling it a problem. I’m calling it the only honest thing I do.
life.more: Jasmin sat me down with a calculator and a very concerned face. I said I’ve got rent and soup money, what else do I need. She said, shoes. I looked at my shoes. She had a point. I’ve bought shoes.

life.news: My dad played piano at the old people’s home and they all sang. He hasn’t been sober that long in years.
life.more: He teaches piano and drinks, mostly in that order. Today he did a whole hour and the residents sang every word, and he cried at the end, and so did I. I don’t know how long it’ll last. Today it lasted an hour. I’ll take an hour.

gossip.says: Elise Harrow from the Bluebirds sings alto next to me in the choir. Pearls and a cardigan and the filthiest laugh in the church hall. Nobody at the club would believe it.
gossip.note: Eden Sutherland says Elise Harrow, a Bluebird, sings alto in the church choir.
gossip.ask: Eden says you have the filthiest laugh in the church hall.
gossip.answer: Eden exaggerates for effect. It’s a perfectly normal laugh that occasionally frightens a vicar. I was charming at the right party to get my job, and in choir I don’t have to be charming at all. That’s why I go.

gossip.says: Adriana Ponce told me to knock on doors or go home. I knocked. Forty doors. Two cups of coffee. She said that’s a good day. It was.
gossip.note: Eden Sutherland says Adriana Ponce taught her to knock on doors.
gossip.ask: Eden says you taught her to knock on doors instead of shouting.
gossip.answer: I told her what I wish someone had told me. I thought shouting was winning. The people I changed were the ones I had coffee with. Eden learned it in a month. It took me fifteen years. Kids these days. Better than us.

gossip.says: Jessica Rivera sings in the choir too and mouths the high notes because she’s scared. She has the best voice in the room and she’d rather die than do a solo.
gossip.note: Eden Sutherland says Jessica Rivera mouths the high notes in choir because she’s scared.
gossip.ask: Eden says you have the best voice in the choir and mouth the high notes.
gossip.answer: I don’t mouth all of them. Just the ones that might be heard. It’s fine. I’m fine. If I ever did a solo it would be the one about the lighthouse, but I won’t, so it doesn’t matter. Please don’t tell Teresa. She’d put me on the roster.

women.name: Lucille Pembrook
women.look: Fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, rosy cheeks, linen shirt and canvas tote

own.label: Ask about her cookbooks
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Strange old cookbooks. War rations, Victorian puddings, a pamphlet on cooking with cactus. I cook from them for the collective. Nobody has died.

own.label: Ask what she does for the group
own.player: What do you do in the collective?
own.reply: I make the soup. Every movement runs on somebody quietly making soup. History never mentions the soup.

own.label: Ask why she’s slow to trust
own.player: Why are you so careful about people?
own.reply: Because I laugh easily, and people mistake that for agreeing with them. I don’t. I just like the joke.

calls.label: Ask about the evening before the fire
calls.player: Were you at the campaign office the night before the fire?
calls.reply: Eating a pudding from a Victorian book, alone, in the back room, until late. Zoe was told two stories about that evening. Mine is a third. Nobody came in the front. Somebody came in the back with a can, and it wasn’t paint.
calls.note: Lucille Pembrook was in the campaign office the evening before Vale’s fire and saw someone come in the back with a can.

life.news: Cooked the collective dinner from a cookbook printed in 1888. Mutton pudding. Nobody died. Three people asked for seconds.
life.more: I collect strange old cookbooks and cook the collective’s dinners from them, because if we’re going to argue about the future we can at least eat the past. Tonight’s book recommended serving the pudding with a firm hand and a cheerful disposition. I had one of those.

life.news: Someone at the meeting said my cooking was a distraction from the work. I said the work has to eat.
life.more: Every movement runs on somebody quietly making soup, and nobody puts the soup in the history books. I went home and read a cookbook from a war rationing office, which was full of women making something out of nothing and being cheerful about it. I felt better. Slightly.

life.news: Found a recipe in a secondhand cookbook with a note in the margin: Tell nobody about the cellar. Just that.
life.more: The recipe is for a very ordinary apple cake. The handwriting is old and neat. I’ve made the cake twice now, in case it’s a clue. It is not a clue. It’s just a very good cake. I still think about the cellar.

gossip.says: Lara Newsome learns ballroom dancing at a studio in the Quarter, very seriously, in a sequined top over her campaign shirt. She says revolution needs footwork. She might be right.
gossip.note: Lucille Pembrook says Lara Newsome learns ballroom dancing very seriously.
gossip.ask: Lucille says you learn ballroom in a sequined top over your campaign shirt.
gossip.answer: It’s not a sequined top, it’s a practice top with modest sparkle. And revolution does need footwork. Have you seen how people move at a protest? Shuffling. Ballroom teaches you to lead. Lucille just wants a dance partner and won’t admit it.

gossip.says: Zoe Whitaker keeps the campaign journal now and she’s the most trusting person on campus. She believes whoever told her something last. It’s lovely. It’s also terrifying.
gossip.note: Lucille Pembrook says Zoe Whitaker believes whoever told her something last.
gossip.ask: Lucille says you believe whoever told you something last.
gossip.answer: That’s not fair. I believe whoever I trust most, and I trust a lot of people. Lucille thinks being suspicious is clever. I think it’s lonely. She cooks for all of us, though, so I forgive her nearly anything.

women.name: Lara Newsome
women.look: Freckled fair skin, auburn shag with a curtain fringe, a wide bright smile, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask about the dancing
own.player: Is it true you’re learning ballroom?
own.reply: At a studio in the Quarter, from a woman of eighty who says I waltz like I’m marching on city hall. I’m improving. Slowly.

own.label: Ask about her campaigning
own.player: What are you campaigning for right now?
own.reply: Water rates. Four hundred signatures. The council used the petition as a coaster. The next one’s going to be heavier.

own.label: Ask what makes her stop being playful
own.player: What makes you angry?
own.reply: Being handled. Talk to me like a person and I’ll laugh at anything. Manage me and I bite.

calls.label: Ask about the torn page in the journal
calls.player: Who tore the page out of the campaign journal?
calls.reply: My page. Before the big meeting. Everyone says it was Adriana, because she’s old and rude and easy to blame. It wasn’t. I saw the indent on the page underneath. The handwriting that was torn out is mine. The hand that tore it was in the collective. Ask Alma.
calls.note: Lara Newsome says the page torn from the campaign journal was hers, and it was not Adriana who tore it.

life.news: Finally got the turn in the waltz without stepping on my partner. He cried. From relief.
life.more: Six weeks at the studio in the Quarter learning the waltz from a woman of eighty who says I dance like I’m marching on city hall. Tonight I floated. Briefly. Then I marched again. But for one turn I was a lady in a ballroom and not a girl with a clipboard.

life.news: Our petition got four hundred signatures and the council used it as a coaster. I saw the ring mark.
life.more: Four hundred people stood in the sun to sign it. I hand-delivered it. Two weeks later I went in for a meeting and there it was on the councilman’s desk with a coffee ring on the top page. I said nothing. I smiled. I am writing a much longer petition.

life.news: I used to keep the campaign journal. A page I wrote is missing. Torn out, neat, before a big meeting.
life.more: It was my handwriting on that page. I know because I can see the indent of it on the page underneath, like a ghost. Everyone thinks they know who tore it. They’re wrong. I know who. I’m just deciding what to do about it.

gossip.says: Willow Greene repairs watches in the back room of the collective, with a little mirror angled over her bench so she can see the street without turning round. She says it’s for the light. It isn’t for the light.
gossip.note: Lara Newsome says Willow Greene keeps a mirror over her watch bench to watch the street.
gossip.ask: Lara says you keep a mirror over your bench to watch the street, and it isn’t for the light.
gossip.answer: It’s a little for the light. Mostly it’s because I don’t like having my back to a door. Lara dances like she’s storming a council meeting and thinks everybody else should be braver. Some of us are brave sitting down, with a loupe in one eye.

gossip.says: Adriana Ponce is the oldest campaigner on campus and she tells the young ones to knock on doors or go home. They hate her. Then they knock on doors. She’s the only one who ever changed anything.
gossip.note: Lara Newsome says Adriana Ponce tells the young campaigners to knock on doors or go home.
gossip.ask: Lara says you tell the young campaigners to knock on doors or go home, and they hate you.
gossip.answer: They hate me for a week. Then a woman on the east side tells them her rent went up four hundred dollars and they understand what a door is for. Lara knocks on more doors than anyone. She does it in dancing shoes. I don’t ask.

women.name: Willow Greene
women.look: Rosy fair skin, sandy shag with a fringe, amber eyes, band T-shirt under dungarees

own.label: Ask about the watch repair
own.player: Is it true you fix watches?
own.reply: Watches and clocks, for the whole neighborhood, in the back room of the collective. I keep the time. Somebody has to.

own.label: Ask about the mirror over her bench
own.player: Why is there a mirror over your workbench?
own.reply: For the light. Also because I don’t like my back to a door. Both are true.

own.label: Ask what annoys her most
own.player: What drives you up the wall?
own.reply: People who are late to things they started. Everyone wants the revolution. Nobody wants to be on time for it.

calls.label: Ask about the car in her mirror
calls.player: Who’s in the gray car you can see in your mirror?
calls.reply: Two men, a gray sedan, parked across from the campaign office every day for weeks. They take turns sleeping. Once one of them got out and looked straight up at my window. I wrote the plate on a watch tag. I keep it in the drawer with the mainsprings.
calls.note: Willow Greene has watched a gray sedan with two men outside the campaign office for weeks, and kept its plate.

life.news: Got a watch going that’s been stopped since 1962. It ticks like it’s embarrassed it ever stopped.
life.more: I keep the collective’s time, mending clocks and watches in the back room for the whole neighborhood. Tonight a man brought in his father’s watch from the bottom of a drawer. I gave it back running. He held it to his ear like a shell. I pretended I had something in my eye.

life.news: Somebody at the collective said fixing watches isn’t political. I said keeping time is the most political thing there is.
life.more: Everyone wants the revolution and nobody wants to be on time for it. I said that out loud, which was a mistake. Now I’m the woman who’s against the revolution. I’m not. I just want it to start when it says on the flyer.

life.news: There’s a car I can see in my bench mirror that never moves. Two men in it. They take turns sleeping.
life.more: I angled the mirror for the light, and now I can see the street, and on the street there’s a gray sedan, the same one, morning after morning. One of the men got out once and looked straight up at my window. I didn’t look away. I didn’t want him to know I could see him.

gossip.says: Nicolette Parrish grows herbs on a balcony over the campaign office yard and gets very tired of people asking if she’s related to the Parkers. She isn’t. Her basil is better than anybody’s.
gossip.note: Willow Greene says Nicolette Parrish grows herbs on a balcony and is tired of being asked about the Parkers.
gossip.ask: Willow says your basil is better than anybody’s and you’re tired of being asked about the Parkers.
gossip.answer: Parrish. Two Rs. No relation to anyone with a K. Willow sends me a clock-shaped birthday card every year with the right time on it to the minute. She’s strange and very kind. The basil is excellent. I talk to it. Don’t tell anyone.

gossip.says: Esther Yu opens the campaign office every morning and collects roadside souvenirs like they’re holy. She has a spoon from a burned diner. She talks about it like a relic.
gossip.note: Willow Greene says Esther Yu collects roadside souvenirs like holy relics.
gossip.ask: Willow says you talk about your spoon from a burned diner like it’s a relic.
gossip.answer: It is a relic. That diner fed truckers for fifty years and burned down in one night, and the spoon survived. Willow fixes watches that have been stopped for decades and gives them back running. She knows exactly what I mean. She just won’t admit it.

women.name: Jasmin Malik
women.look: Warm beige skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, deep dimples, hand-knitted sweater

own.label: Ask what she does in the climate group
own.player: What do you do in the climate group?
own.reply: I make the leaflets funny. Somebody has to. You can’t save the planet in a font that looks like a tax form. I also make Adriana Ponce laugh, which nobody else can do. That’s my real job.

own.label: Ask what she does in the evenings
own.player: What do you do in the evenings?
own.reply: Book club on the sofa. We drink, we argue, we never finish the book. It’s the most honest reading group in Sunfall.

own.label: Ask if she writes
own.player: Do you write?
own.reply: Plays nobody stages and stories nobody reads. I was the funny girl at school. Now I’m the funny girl with a stack of unstaged plays. It’s a living. It is not a living.

own.label: Ask where her sweater is from
own.player: Where’s that sweater from?
own.reply: My grandmother knits. She’s made me one every winter since I was born. They get bigger every year, like she’s worried I’ll stop growing. I wear them all.

own.label: Ask if she’s always in other people’s drama
own.player: Are you always this busy with other people’s drama?
own.reply: Since I was six. Somebody has to hold the coats. Eden and the group, Nora and everyone, my best friend Tamsin Wilde and the whole world. I’m the coat rack.

own.label: Ask if her friend is okay
own.player: Is your friend okay?
own.reply: Two men came to Tamsin’s kitchen while I was in the next room. One of them said scholarship. The other one said mother. Her mom is in a home the Foundation pays for. The next morning she went to the police and said she saw nothing. I drove her.
own.note: Jasmin Malik heard two men in Tamsin Wilde’s kitchen say scholarship and mother; the next morning Tamsin told the police she saw nothing.

calls.label: Ask if she has any enemies
calls.player: Got any enemies?
calls.reply: One. Zadie Foster, the music reviewer. She gave my brother’s band two stars and called his drumming enthusiastic. Enthusiastic! He sends her a postcard every year that just says no. I helped him pick the first one.

calls.label: Ask what her mom does
calls.player: What does your mom do?
calls.reply: She sews for Rinaldi Bridal. Forty years of hems. She says the owner wears a little swallow brooch every day and never takes it off, and she says it the way you’d say someone keeps a gun in the drawer.

life.news: Book club tonight. Nobody read the book. Eden cried at the blurb. Best meeting yet.
life.more: It was a short novel about a lighthouse keeper. Eden read the back cover out loud and burst into tears before chapter one. Adriana laughed so hard she had to go outside. I wrote it all down for a play. Nobody will stage it.

life.news: Grandma knitted me a sweater with a polar bear on it for the climate group. The ice floe is unraveling. On purpose.
life.more: She said she wanted to support the cause. The bear is standing on a little ice floe and the ice floe is coming apart, stitch by stitch. My grandmother is the most effective activist in the whole group, and she’s never been to a meeting.

life.news: Eden gave away her wages again. I bought the groceries again. I love her. I’m also broke.
life.more: She meets someone who needs it more and that’s it, gone. I can’t even be mad, because she’s right, they did need it more. But somebody in this apartment has to eat, so I made a pot of lentils the size of a bathtub.

life.news: My brother’s band played the Furnace tonight. He drummed like the building owed him money. I screamed myself hoarse.
life.more: Nixie Adler put them on second, which is a huge deal. Twelve people in the crowd and I was three of them. He threw a drumstick into the crowd at the end and I caught it. He wants it back. He’s not getting it back.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland, my roommate, gives most of her wages away and then sings in a church choir she doesn’t believe in. I feed her lentils. Somebody has to.
gossip.note: Jasmin Malik says Eden Sutherland gives most of her wages away.
gossip.ask: Jasmin Malik says you give most of your wages away and she feeds you lentils.
gossip.answer: Most of them. Not all. I kept enough for soup. Jasmin makes lentils in a pot the size of a bathtub and complains the whole time she’s stirring. It’s the nicest thing anyone does for me.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster gave my brother’s band two stars and called his drumming enthusiastic. We are at war. She knows.
gossip.note: Jasmin Malik is feuding with Zadie Foster over a two-star review of her brother’s band.
gossip.ask: Jasmin says you gave her brother’s band two stars, and now it’s war.
gossip.answer: Two stars was generous. He plays like he’s angry at the drums. He sends me a postcard every year that just says no. I’ve kept every one. Tell Jasmin I’d give him three now. Don’t tell her I said that.

women.name: Freya Castillo
women.look: Medium-brown skin, twist-out coils, freckles across her nose, mustard turtleneck

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do for the art collective?
own.reply: I write the grants and tell everyone when the money’s gone. Somebody has to be the kitchen. I keep the film night’s projector running on paperwork alone.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: My grandmother’s house on the Old Mission road. I built a little desert inside it: a glass room full of cacti. Yes, I know there’s a desert outside. Mine has rules.

own.label: Ask if money is hard to find
own.player: Is it hard keeping the collective funded?
own.reply: A trust up on the ridge offered us money for our membership list. Twice. I said no twice. The projector can starve.

own.label: Ask what she does with her weekends
own.player: What do you do with your weekends?
own.reply: Some weekends I have my goddaughter. She’s eight and she names every cactus. There’s one called Mr. Stabs. He is thriving.

own.label: Ask if she has family in town
own.player: Do you have family in town?
own.reply: A sister, Agnes. We haven’t spoken in six years. After our dad died, I said God let him die in that chapel. She said he died happy. It was in a kitchen. It’s always a kitchen.

own.label: Ask who lives next door
own.player: Who lives next door to you?
own.reply: Nobody, for a year. Then, on the last three nights with no moon, candles behind the blinds and cars outside. I count the cars. I’ve heard singing. I’ve heard a bell that can’t ring.
own.note: Freya Castillo says the dark house next to hers on the Old Mission road has candles behind the blinds and cars outside on nights with no moon, and she has heard a bell.

own.label: Ask what she makes of the bishop’s review
own.player: What do you make of this review of the Sisters?
own.reply: I don’t believe in any of it and I still know a land grab when I read one. My sister keeps the garden accounts at that chapel. If the review ends her, it ends the one thing she has that grows. I would have to speak to her about that. I haven’t spoken to her in six years. Don’t tell her I said any of this.

calls.label: Ask if her dad left her anything
calls.player: Did your dad leave you anything?
calls.reply: His sacristan’s diary. It stops the week before his stroke, with one line I didn’t understand until now: they are coming back to the crypt, and the bell knows. I haven’t shown my sister. I’d have to speak to her.
calls.note: Freya Castillo has her father’s sacristan diary; its last line says they are coming back to the crypt, and the bell knows.

calls.label: Ask if she still goes to church
calls.player: Do you still go to church?
calls.reply: No. I drive past St. Brigid’s every day and don’t look. My sister is in there somewhere, pruning roses and praying for me by name. I know she is. That’s worse than if she weren’t.

life.news: A cactus I’d given up on flowered today. Bright pink. Out of nowhere. I said thank you out loud.
life.more: Three years it sat there doing nothing, sulking in the corner of the glass room. I nearly threw it out. Then this morning, a flower the size of my fist. My goddaughter says it was waiting for me to stop looking. She’s usually right.

life.news: Counted six cars on the Old Mission road last night. On a road with four houses.
life.more: I count things. It’s a grant writer’s habit. Six cars, no moon, nobody walking. They were gone by morning. I wrote the plates down, because I don’t know what else to do with a feeling like that.

life.news: Drove past St. Brigid’s and caught myself looking. Six years, and today I looked.
life.more: Just for a second. The roses by the gate were pruned the way our dad taught us. Agnes did those. I know her cuts. I nearly stopped the car. I didn’t. I drove around the block twice instead, like an idiot.

life.news: Got the projector grant renewed. Film night lives. Khadija hugged me so hard my glasses fell off.
life.more: Eleven pages of forms for a machine that shows pie fights. Worth every page. Khadija says the hall would riot without it. She brought cookies to the meeting and opened the tin first, which has never happened. History.

gossip.says: Khadija Rahman runs the film night and guards the cookie tin like it’s the collective’s treasury. I write the grants that keep her projector alive.
gossip.note: Freya Castillo writes the grants that keep Khadija Rahman’s film night projector running.
gossip.ask: Freya Castillo says she writes the grants that keep your projector alive.
gossip.answer: She does, and she reminds me at every meeting. Freya is the only person in the collective who says exactly what she means. No workshop needed. I give her the first cookie. Nobody else gets the first cookie.

gossip.says: My sister Agnes Castillo looks after the gardens at St. Brigid’s. We haven’t spoken in six years. I still know her pruning when I see it.
gossip.note: Freya Castillo says she and her sister Agnes Castillo have not spoken in six years.
gossip.ask: Freya Castillo says you two haven’t spoken in six years.
gossip.answer: Six years. I pray for her every night, by name. She drives past the gate every day and doesn’t look. I always look. One of us has to keep the door open, and God gave me the gate.

women.name: Nicolette Parrish
women.look: Pale skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, gold hoop earrings, oversized thrifted cardigan

own.label: Ask about her balcony garden
own.player: What do you grow?
own.reply: Basil, mint, thyme and a tomato that thinks it’s a tree, all on a balcony the size of a door. Everything grows. It feels like cheating.

own.label: Ask if she’s related to the Parkers
own.player: Are you one of the Parker sisters?
own.reply: Parrish. Two Rs. No relation. I’m going to have cards printed.

own.label: Ask why she campaigns
own.player: What got you into climate campaigning?
own.reply: Growing things in a desert. You learn very quickly what water is worth, and who decides who gets it.

calls.label: Ask about the two stories she heard
calls.player: What did you hear from your balcony about the night before the fire?
calls.reply: From my balcony I can hear the yard behind the campaign office. I heard one person tell Zoe the office was empty that evening. Later I heard another tell her somebody was there till late. I heard the back gate too. Twice. Once going in. Once very fast going out.
calls.note: Nicolette Parrish heard the campaign office’s back gate twice the evening before Vale’s fire.

life.news: The basil on my balcony is taller than the railing. I made pesto for the whole floor. Nobody said no.
life.more: I live on the top floor with a tiny balcony and too many pots. Everything grows, which in this desert feels like a small miracle every morning. I gave jars of pesto to everyone on my landing. My neighbor left a thank-you note with a drawing of a leaf. I stuck it on the fridge.

life.news: Got asked three times today if I was one of the Parker sisters. I’m a Parrish. Two Rs. No relation.
life.more: It’s not even the same name. It just rhymes, in a lazy way. I have explained this to most of Sunfall. I’m going to have a little card printed. NOT A PARKER. Maybe with a basil leaf on it. People respond to basil.

life.news: I heard two different stories about one evening from my balcony. Both were from people I like. They can’t both be true.
life.more: My balcony looks down onto the yard behind the campaign office. Sound carries. I heard two people describe the same night, at different times, completely differently. I haven’t said anything. I keep watering the plants and turning it over, like soil.

gossip.says: Alma Sanders makes pottery after work in the Sisters’ kiln and taught half the campus how to organize. She’s charming, ambitious and slightly terrifying. I’d follow her into anything. I’d check the exits first.
gossip.note: Nicolette Parrish says Alma Sanders taught half the campus how to organize.
gossip.ask: Nicolette says she’d follow you into anything, but she’d check the exits first.
gossip.answer: Good. Always check the exits. I taught her that too. Nicolette thinks I’m terrifying because I say what I want out loud. Most people want things quietly and then resent you for getting them. I just get them. Then I make a bowl.

gossip.says: Cassandra Finch decided to be cheerful out of spite years ago and has never backed down. She paints the sky over the underpass while everyone below looks at their phones. She brings cake to every meeting.
gossip.note: Nicolette Parrish says Cassandra Finch decided to be cheerful out of spite.
gossip.ask: Nicolette says you decided to be cheerful out of spite and never backed down.
gossip.answer: Spite is a very underrated fuel. It burns clean. Somebody gave up on me once and I decided I would be unbearable about being happy for the rest of my life. It’s going well. Nicolette gets cake first. She waters her plants like she’s praying.

women.name: Alma Sanders
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, dark brown messy bun, sharp winged eyeliner, linen shirt and canvas tote

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: What do you do after work?
own.reply: Pottery, in the Sisters’ kiln. I help with their spring fair and they let me fire my bowls. Best deal I ever organized.

own.label: Ask about organizing
own.player: What does a community organizer actually do?
own.reply: Gets people in a room and makes them care about the same thing at the same time. It’s mostly snacks and listening.

own.label: Ask what she wants
own.player: What do you want, really?
own.reply: Everything, on my terms, by next spring. Ask me again in the spring and I’ll have a new list.

calls.label: Ask about the page she burned
calls.player: Why did you tear a page out of the collective’s journal?
calls.reply: A student wrote something in it as a poem. A professor, a parking bay, a day, a device. It rhymed. It was a plan. If anyone had found it, her life was over, and she’s barely started it. I burned the page in the kiln. I’d do it again. I’m not sure I should have.
calls.note: Alma Sanders tore out and burned a journal page where a student wrote the plan against Vale as a poem.

life.news: Pulled a bowl out of the Sisters’ kiln today and it came out the exact blue I wanted. It never does. Today it did.
life.more: The Sisters lend me their kiln if I help with the spring fair, which is the best deal I’ve ever organized. Today the glaze went the color of the sky just before dark. I held it up to the window like a trophy. One of the Sisters said it was very nice. From them, that’s a standing ovation.

life.news: A girl I trained to organize now runs a group I don’t recognize. I taught her everything. I didn’t teach her that.
life.more: You teach someone how to get people in a room and make them care, and then you watch them use it for something that makes you cold. I taught her to knock on doors. She learned to close them. I made a very ugly pot tonight. On purpose.

life.news: I keep the collective’s own journal. It’s missing a page. I know exactly where that page is. I burned it.
life.more: Not the campaign’s journal. Ours. Somebody wrote something in it that would have ruined a very young person’s life, so I tore it out and burned it in the kiln. I don’t regret it. I do think about it every time I light the kiln.

gossip.says: Marlene Coates sketches the old shopfronts for our leaflets, so she’s out on the sidewalk at dawn with a sketchbook while the rest of us are asleep. She overthinks everything. Her drawings are perfect anyway.
gossip.note: Alma Sanders says Marlene Coates is out sketching shopfronts at dawn for the leaflets.
gossip.ask: Alma says you sketch shopfronts at dawn and overthink everything, but your drawings are perfect.
gossip.answer: They’re not perfect, there’s a wobbly awning on the last one. I’ve been thinking about it for days. Alma can say perfect like it’s an order. She asked me to draw the new leaflet and I said yes before I knew what it was for. Everyone does that with her.

gossip.says: Vanessa Greer learned everything she knows about organizing from me. Getting people in a room, making them care. I didn’t teach her what she does with them now. She’s brilliant. I wish she wasn’t.
gossip.note: Alma Sanders says she taught Vanessa Greer to organize, and wishes she hadn’t taught her so well.
gossip.ask: Alma says she taught you to organize and she wishes you weren’t so brilliant at it.
gossip.answer: Alma taught me to knock on doors. Then she stopped knocking. Someone had to keep going after the doors stopped opening. She makes very beautiful bowls now and pretends the world can be fixed one glaze at a time. It can’t. She knows that. She taught me that too.

women.name: Marlene Coates
women.look: Pale skin, glossy black ponytail, gold hoop earrings, mustard turtleneck

own.label: Ask what she draws
own.player: What do you draw?
own.reply: Old shopfronts, for the group’s leaflets. I’m out at dawn when the light is flat and nobody walks in front of me.

own.label: Ask if she overthinks things
own.player: Do you overthink things?
own.reply: I spent an hour on one sentence today. They cut it. I’ve put it on my fridge. So, yes.

own.label: Ask what she believes in
own.player: What do you believe in?
own.reply: Being kind on purpose. It’s harder than being clever and it lasts longer.

calls.label: Ask about the car she keeps drawing
calls.player: Who are the men in the car you keep drawing?
calls.reply: Gray sedan, two men, across from the campaign office. I’ve drawn it eleven mornings running. I can show you the drawings. Same men, same coffee cups. The one in the passenger seat has started to wave. I’ve started to wave back. That’s worse, isn’t it.
calls.note: Marlene Coates has drawn a gray sedan with two men outside the campaign office eleven mornings running.

life.news: Finished the drawing of the old shoe repair for the new leaflet. The awning came out straight for once.
life.more: I’m always on the sidewalk at dawn because that’s when the light is flat and nobody walks in front of you. Today I drew the whole shopfront in one sitting. The man who owns it came out and asked for a copy. I gave him the original. I’m still glowing.

life.news: Spent an hour rewriting one sentence on the leaflet. Then they cut the sentence.
life.more: I overthink everything. A comma can keep me up at night. I wrote it nine ways and chose the kindest one, and then the group decided the leaflet was too long and cut it. It was a good sentence. I’m going to put it on my fridge so it doesn’t feel wasted.

life.news: There’s a car across from the campaign office every morning when I’m sketching. I’ve drawn it eleven times now. One of the men waves.
life.more: It’s become part of the street, like the lamppost. Gray sedan, two men, coffee cups on the dash. I put it in the drawings because it’s there. This morning the one in the passenger seat waved at me. I waved back before I could stop myself. I’ve been nervous all day.

gossip.says: Hollis Bennett is in a book club that never finishes the book. She always votes for the serious novel and always loses. She stargazes from the collective’s roof alone. She’s the most loyal person I know.
gossip.note: Marlene Coates says Hollis Bennett always votes for the serious novel in book club and loses.
gossip.ask: Marlene says you always vote for the serious novel in book club and always lose.
gossip.answer: Every time. They want romance with a duke. I want six hundred pages about a famine. One day they’ll be too tired to argue and I’ll win. Marlene came up to the roof with me once and named every star wrong, very confidently. I didn’t correct her. It was lovely.

gossip.says: Serena Bellweather from the club sketches the same old shopfronts I do. Some mornings we’re on opposite sides of the same street with our sketchbooks. We nod. Her drawings are better. I don’t mind.
gossip.note: Marlene Coates says Serena Bellweather sketches the same old shopfronts she does.
gossip.ask: Marlene says some mornings you’re on opposite sides of the same street with your sketchbooks.
gossip.answer: We are, and her drawings are better, actually. She gets the people in. I only ever get the buildings. I think she’s braver than me about faces. We should trade sketchbooks one day. She’d probably apologize for every line in hers.

women.name: Hollis Bennett
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, strong dark brows, oversized thrifted cardigan

own.label: Ask what she does at night
own.player: What do you do with your nights?
own.reply: Lie on the collective’s roof and look at galaxies. Two-million-year-old light. It makes the week feel very small.

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: Are you in a book club?
own.reply: I am, and I always vote for the serious novel, and I always lose. Six to one. I still go every time. That’s loyalty or madness.

own.label: Ask what she can’t forgive
own.player: What would you never forgive?
own.reply: Somebody abandoning a friend when it got hard. Everything else, I can work with.

calls.label: Ask about the lift she gave
calls.player: Who did you drive to the police station?
calls.reply: A witness, after the gala. She asked me for a lift to the station to tell them what she saw. I waited in the parking lot for two hours. She went in sure and came out saying she’d seen nothing. In the car she said, they already knew what I saw. That’s all she said.
calls.note: Hollis Bennett drove a gala witness to the police station; she came out saying she had seen nothing, and that they already knew.

life.news: Clear night on the collective’s roof. Saw the Andromeda galaxy with my own eyes. Two million years old, that light.
life.more: You lie on the gravel up there and let your eyes adjust and then a smudge appears that is another galaxy, and the light hitting you left it before there were people. I lay there for an hour. Nothing in my week mattered after that. Which was the point.

life.news: Book club voted for another romance with a duke. I lost again. Six to one.
life.more: I proposed a six-hundred-page novel about a famine. They chose a duke who smolders. I read the duke. I hated the duke. Then I went home and read the famine anyway, alone, with a cup of tea. I am the most loyal member of a book club that doesn’t want me.

life.news: Gave someone a lift to an appointment and waited in the car for two hours. When she came out, she’d changed.
life.more: I won’t say who. I sat in the parking lot with the engine off and the radio low, and she went in one person and came out another, quieter, with her eyes on the floor. She thanked me for the lift. She didn’t say anything else. I didn’t ask. I should have asked.

gossip.says: Carla Hadley is the funniest woman in the climate group and the least trusted, because she says the thing everyone’s thinking. She has an old rescue dog called Biscuit. The third Biscuit in Sunfall. She checked.
gossip.note: Hollis Bennett says Carla Hadley is the funniest and least trusted woman in the climate group.
gossip.ask: Hollis says you’re the funniest woman in the group and the least trusted.
gossip.answer: Least trusted because I’m funny. People think jokes are a weapon. Mine are mostly a coping mechanism with timing. Hollis is the opposite: she never jokes and everyone tells her everything. Biscuit likes her best. Biscuit has excellent judgment.

gossip.says: Sasha Mahoney runs the book club I’m in. She builds statistical models at the station and picks the books by mood. She’s the only person who has ever outvoted me with a spreadsheet.
gossip.note: Hollis Bennett says Sasha Mahoney once outvoted her in book club with a spreadsheet.
gossip.ask: Hollis says you once outvoted her in book club with a spreadsheet.
gossip.answer: It was a very good spreadsheet. It showed that the group finishes romance novels at three times the rate of famine novels. Hollis wants to read things that are good for us. I want us to actually read things. Data wins. Data is very boring and always wins.

women.name: Carla Hadley
women.look: Porcelain skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, a wide bright smile, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask about her dog
own.player: Do you have any pets?
own.reply: Biscuit. Fourteen, three good legs and one opinionated one. The third Biscuit in Sunfall. I checked the vet’s records.

own.label: Ask why people don’t trust her
own.player: Why don’t people trust you?
own.reply: Because I’m funny, and the jokes are usually true. People find that more alarming than lying.

own.label: Ask if she’s good at small talk
own.player: Are you good at small talk?
own.reply: Terrible. Big talk, I’m great at. Crisis, perfect. Weather, I panic and say something about tectonic plates.

calls.label: Ask about the apartment across her landing
calls.player: Who uses the apartment across your landing?
calls.reply: Nobody lives there. People meet there. Students, I think, by the shoes. They go in and the lights never come on. Biscuit growls at the door. The night before Vale’s car was found, they were in there for hours, very quiet, and somebody was crying.
calls.note: Carla Hadley says students meet in the dark apartment across her landing, and were there for hours the night before Vale’s car was found.

life.news: Biscuit walked all the way to the corner and back today. She’s fourteen. We had a parade.
life.more: She’s an old rescue with three good legs and one opinionated one, and some days the corner is too far. Today she made it there and back with her tail up. I clapped. A man across the street clapped too. Biscuit accepted the applause like the queen she is.

life.news: Made a joke at the meeting that everyone laughed at and then nobody spoke to me afterwards.
life.more: The joke was true. That’s the problem with my jokes. I said what everyone was thinking about our budget and the room laughed and then looked at me like I’d set off a fire alarm. I walked Biscuit home. She thought I was hilarious. She’s my only reliable audience.

life.news: The apartment across my landing has never once had its lights on. People go in. The lights never come on.
life.more: I hear the door, I hear voices, low, several of them, and then nothing, and the strip under the door stays dark. Biscuit growls at it. Biscuit growls at nothing else in the world, not even the mailman. I’ve started to trust Biscuit on this.

gossip.says: Daria Kowalski has photographed every protest in Sunfall for eleven years on old film cameras she fixes herself. She won’t go digital. She says digital forgets. She remembers everything.
gossip.note: Carla Hadley says Daria Kowalski has photographed every protest for eleven years on old film.
gossip.ask: Carla says you’ve photographed every protest for eleven years and you say digital forgets.
gossip.answer: Digital does forget. Somebody deletes a file and it’s gone. A negative sits in a box and waits. I have eleven years of boxes. Carla is in most of them, making a sign with a joke on it nobody else got. Her signs are the best part of every archive I have.

gossip.says: Nora Hadley is no relation, before you ask. Everyone asks. She likes nuclear power and Dante and arguing. The climate group finds her exhausting. I find her the only fun person at meetings.
gossip.note: Carla Hadley says Nora Hadley is no relation and the only fun person at meetings.
gossip.ask: Carla says you’re no relation and the only fun person at meetings.
gossip.answer: No relation, unfortunately. I’d love a cousin who says what I’m thinking a beat before I think it. The group thinks I’m a heretic for liking nuclear. Carla thinks I’m a heretic for liking Dante. We get on extremely well.

women.name: Daria Kowalski
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, dark French braid, a wide bright smile, linen shirt and canvas tote

own.label: Ask about her cameras
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Old film cameras. I fix them and use them. Thirty-six frames and you have to mean every one.

own.label: Ask why she still uses film
own.player: Why film and not digital?
own.reply: Because a box of negatives can’t be deleted by an email. Digital forgets. Film waits.

own.label: Ask what she does for the collective
own.player: What do you do for the collective?
own.reply: I photograph every protest. Eleven years of them, under my bed. Every face is still there, whatever anyone would prefer now.

calls.label: Ask about the man in her protest negatives
calls.player: Who’s the man in your old protest photos?
calls.reply: From the protest against the Houellebecq evening. A man in a charity lanyard at the edge of the crowd, handing Jennifer Tate a drum. A drum, at a protest, from a man in a suit. She never mentioned where she got it. I have the negative. Negatives don’t forget.
calls.note: Daria Kowalski has a negative of a man in a charity lanyard handing Jennifer Tate a drum at the Houellebecq protest.

life.news: Got a 1950s rangefinder working. The shutter sounds like a tiny door closing. I took eleven pictures of my kitchen.
life.more: I restore old film cameras because they remember things honestly. You get thirty-six frames and you have to mean every one. I tested this one on the most boring room in my life and every picture came out like an old movie. My kitchen has never looked so important.

life.news: Someone at the collective asked why I still bother with film. I said because a box of negatives can’t be deleted by an email.
life.more: They think I’m sentimental. I’m not sentimental, I’m an archivist with a darkroom. Eleven years of protests in boxes under my bed, and every one of them still exists, and every face is still there, whatever anybody would prefer now. I find that more comforting than a cloud.

life.news: Printing old negatives from a protest years ago. There’s a man in the corner of one I don’t remember being there.
life.more: A man in a suit at the edge of the crowd, the wrong clothes for a protest, a lanyard on. I must have photographed him without seeing him. That happens. You see more in the darkroom than you did on the street. I’ve printed him larger. I keep looking.

gossip.says: April Kearney is the collective’s runner. She fixes her bicycle every single week because she rides it into the ground carrying our messages. She knows every alley in Sunfall. Nobody can follow her.
gossip.note: Daria Kowalski says April Kearney knows every alley in Sunfall and nobody can follow her.
gossip.ask: Daria says you know every alley in Sunfall and nobody can follow you.
gossip.answer: Nobody has managed yet. The canal path is too narrow for cars, and I know where the fence has a gap. Daria photographs everything and remembers everything, which is either very comforting or very frightening. She took a picture of me once mid-jump over a curb. I look like I’m flying.

gossip.says: Jennifer Tate has four megaphones. One is decorative and one makes a duck noise by accident. She’s loud, she’s sweet and she has no idea how often she’s in my photographs, right in the middle, shouting.
gossip.note: Daria Kowalski says Jennifer Tate is in the middle of most of her protest photographs.
gossip.ask: Daria says you’re in the middle of most of her protest photographs, shouting.
gossip.answer: Where else would I be? Loud isn’t dangerous, quiet is. Daria stands at the edge with an old camera and never says anything, and somehow she sees the whole thing. I’ve asked her to show me the photos. She says when you’re ready. I don’t know what that means.

women.name: Sloane Mercer
women.look: Dark skin, chestnut curly bob, gray-green eyes, hand-knitted sweater

women.name: April Kearney
women.look: Fair skin, golden-brown ringlets, a gap-toothed smile, mustard turtleneck

own.label: Ask what she does for the collective
own.player: What do you do for the collective?
own.reply: I’m the runner. Messages, posters, keys, whatever needs to be somewhere fast. I know every alley in Sunfall.

own.label: Ask about her bicycle
own.player: Do you ride a bike everywhere?
own.reply: Everywhere. It’s more tape than bicycle and I fix it every week. A new one wouldn’t know the way.

own.label: Ask about her favorite route
own.player: What’s your favorite way across town?
own.reply: The canal path. Through a gap in the fence, down by the water, and no car can follow. That’s not why I like it. It’s a little bit why I like it.

calls.label: Ask who’s been following her
calls.player: Who followed you in the gray car?
calls.reply: Two men in a gray sedan. Every time I carry something from the campaign office, it’s there. They don’t do anything. They just come along. I lose them on the canal path every time. They haven’t worked that out. I’m starting to think they don’t need to.
calls.note: April Kearney says a gray sedan follows her whenever she carries messages from the campaign office.

life.news: Beat my own record across town on the bicycle. Eleven minutes from the co-op to the river. Wind in my teeth.
life.more: I carry the collective’s messages because I know every alley and every shortcut and where the fence by the canal has a gap. Today the lights went my way and I flew. I arrived so fast the person I was delivering to thought I’d been sent by mistake.

life.news: Chain snapped on the hill. Walked the bike home in the heat. Fixed it on the kitchen floor. Again.
life.more: I ride it into the ground, so I fix it every week. It’s more tape than bicycle at this point. My roommate says I should get a new one. A new one wouldn’t know the way. This one practically steers itself down the canal path. I love it like a dog.

life.news: A gray car followed me for six blocks today. I took the canal path. It can’t fit down the canal path.
life.more: I noticed it on the second turn because it turned when I turned. Then the third. So I did my favorite trick and went through the gap in the fence and down the path by the water, and I looked back and it was just sitting at the end of the street, engine running. Then it left.

gossip.says: Isla Jameson maps hidden routes across the ridge for the water survey. She knows the desert like I know the alleys. She told the group she saw something once and then said she was mistaken. She wasn’t.
gossip.note: April Kearney says Isla Jameson maps the ridge and once took back something she saw.
gossip.ask: April says you once told the group you saw something and then said you were mistaken.
gossip.answer: I was mistaken. I said so. April thinks everyone is either brave or scared, like a bicycle is either going or stopped. Sometimes you’re just careful. She’ll understand when she’s older. Don’t tell her I said that. She’ll ride over here and tell me off.

gossip.says: Inez Morales runs the housing co-op and prints gig posters the goths pay for in drinks. She let me sleep on the co-op sofa for a month when I had nowhere. She never once mentioned it after.
gossip.note: April Kearney says Inez Morales let her sleep on the co-op sofa for a month.
gossip.ask: April says you let her sleep on the co-op sofa for a month and never mentioned it.
gossip.answer: That’s what the sofa is for. Half the people who run things on campus have slept on it at some point. April left it cleaner than she found it, and fixed the co-op’s three bicycles while she was there. Best tenant we ever had. She paid in chain oil.

women.name: Isla Jameson
women.look: Rosy fair skin, loose spiral curls, rosy cheeks, vintage windbreaker

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do for the climate group?
own.reply: I map routes across the ridge for our water survey. Where the water is, where it used to be, and who’s been taking it.

own.label: Ask about the best thing she’s found
own.player: What’s the best thing you’ve found up there?
own.reply: A spring that isn’t on any map. Real water out of a rock, a little pool, and a frog. A frog, in the desert. I sat with him for an hour.

own.label: Ask if she’s brave
own.player: Are you brave?
own.reply: I’m careful. People mix those up. Careful gets you home.

calls.label: Ask what she saw on the quarry path
calls.player: What did you see on the quarry path?
calls.reply: A white van with no plates, backed up to the old quarry, two men unloading something long and wrapped. I told the group. A week later a man I didn’t know said good morning to me by name at the trailhead. So I told the group I’d been mistaken. I wasn’t mistaken.
calls.note: Isla Jameson saw a white van with no plates unloading something wrapped at the old quarry, then took it back after a stranger greeted her by name.

life.news: Found a spring on the ridge that isn’t on any map. Real water, in the desert, coming out of a rock.
life.more: I map routes across the ridge for the group’s water survey, and today I followed a line of greener scrub up a gully and there it was, a trickle of water out of a crack, with a little pool and a frog in it. A frog. In the desert. I sat with the frog for a long time.

life.news: Got lost for three hours on the ridge with half a bottle of water. I wasn’t scared. I was a little scared.
life.more: I always tell someone where I’m going. Today the path I took wasn’t the path I said. By the time I found the road again my lips were cracked and my phone was dead. I sat in the car with the door open and drank warm water and laughed at myself. Then I drew the right path on the map.

life.news: Saw something on a quarry path I mapped. Told the group. Then I told them I’d been mistaken.
life.more: I sat with it for a week. I decided it was easier to have been mistaken. The group believed me the first time and believed me the second time. That’s the trouble with being trusted. I go up the ridge a different way now. Nobody asked why.

gossip.says: Annabel Yates is the collective’s secretary and collects old postcards of Sunfall from when it was founded. She has one of women standing on the Old Mission’s steps. She won’t say who they are. I think she knows.
gossip.note: Isla Jameson says Annabel Yates collects old postcards of Sunfall and has one of women on the Old Mission’s steps.
gossip.ask: Isla says you have an old postcard of women on the Old Mission’s steps and won’t say who they are.
gossip.answer: I don’t know who they are. That’s the honest answer. I know what they’re wearing, which is white, all of them, and I know the photographer stood very far away, like he wasn’t supposed to be there. Isla notices everything and then decides not to have. We’re both doing that.

gossip.says: Carmen Bellini from the club maps hidden trails like I do. We met at the top of a gully neither of us was supposed to be in. She had a peach. She gave me half. We swapped maps. Hers are prettier.
gossip.note: Isla Jameson says she and Carmen Bellini met at the top of a gully and swapped maps.
gossip.ask: Isla says you met at the top of a gully, gave her half a peach and swapped maps.
gossip.answer: Mine are prettier because I draw little peaches on them. Hers are better because she marks the water. I’ve started marking water too. Isla is careful in a way I’m not, and she always knows the way down. If I’m ever really lost, it’s her number I’ll call.

women.name: Kiki O’Dell
women.look: Freckled fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, thin wire-rimmed glasses, hand-knitted sweater

own.label: Ask about the open mic
own.player: You run an open mic?
own.reply: At the Furnace, for the collective. I tune everyone’s guitar, keep the list and stop the poets going over five minutes. It’s the most power I will ever have.

own.label: Ask whose cat that is in her photos
own.player: Whose cat is that?
own.reply: Judas. Not mine. He belongs to the man next door, who isn’t next door at the moment. So I feed him. He sits on the man’s pay slip like he’s guarding it.

own.label: Ask why she stopped playing at Mass
own.player: Why don’t you play at Mass anymore?
own.reply: The diocese replaced me with a program and a man with a guitar. I could have fought it. I decided my Sundays were better spent being angry somewhere comfortable.

calls.label: Ask about the empty house next door
calls.player: What happened to the man next door?
calls.reply: He kept a diary. I read it, because he’s gone and I’m nosy. The last page says he told the monsignor something he saw at the Old Mission, and the monsignor thanked him and asked him to tell nobody else. The car’s been outside since. I haven’t told anyone. I’m telling you because you’re not anyone yet.

life.news: Ran the open mic at the Furnace. Eleven acts, two of them in tune. Best night of the month.
life.more: A poet who cried, a man who played the saw, a duo who had clearly met that afternoon. I tune everybody’s guitar before they go on, which is the only reason I was invited to run it. At the end the whole room sang the one song everyone in Sunfall knows. I teach that song about twice a week. I still like it.

life.news: The empty house next door still has a car parked outside it every night. Nobody gets in. Nobody gets out.
life.more: Aurelio Baca lives there, or did. He’s the caretaker at the Old Mission. He fixed our fence for nothing, years ago, and never let us pay him. Eleven weeks ago he stopped coming home. I have a key from years ago, for his cat, so I go in every evening, water the plants and feed Judas. His coat is on the hook. His pay slip is on the table. And the car outside never moves.

life.news: The bishop’s new music program gave my old spot at Mass to a man with a guitar. He can’t tune it.
life.more: I played at St Brigid’s for years. Then the diocese sent a program with a binder and a man, and the man has a guitar he has never once tuned. Margaret Holloway sat behind me at the last Mass and said, very quietly, that it was a disgrace. It is the only thing she and I have ever agreed on. We shook hands on it.

life.news: Taught the same song for what I think is the two hundredth time today. Still like it.
life.more: Everyone who walks into the collective wanting to learn guitar wants the same song. I don’t know who decided. I’ve stopped asking. I can teach it in my sleep now, and I have, apparently, because I hummed it in a dream and woke up with my fingers on an imaginary fret. Being needed is a strange kind of happy.

gossip.says: Moth Delaney runs the Hive and feeds me at the bar when I forget to eat. My parents think she’s a friend from the collective.
gossip.note: Kiki O’Dell says Moth Delaney feeds her at the Hive when she forgets to eat.
gossip.ask: Kiki says you feed her at the bar when she forgets to eat.
gossip.answer: She forgets because she’s busy feeding somebody else’s cat. I keep a plate back for her. She always sits facing the door, like she’s waiting for a car to pull up. I’ve never asked which car.

gossip.says: Freya Castillo lives three doors down. She’s the only one on our street who’s noticed the light in the empty house next door.
gossip.note: Kiki O’Dell says Freya Castillo has noticed the light in the empty house on the mission side.
gossip.ask: Kiki says you’ve noticed the light in the empty house on your street.
gossip.answer: Kiki goes in every evening at seven. Waters, feeds, sits at his kitchen table for a while. I’ve never asked her. Somebody on our street should be doing it, and it wasn’t me. I just make sure my porch light is on when she comes out.

women.name: Annika Joseph
women.look: Freckled fair skin, brown waves with teal tips, a gap-toothed smile, corduroy jacket with enamel pins

own.label: Ask about her records
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Singers who made one album and vanished. I play them late. Somebody should remember the people who stopped.

own.label: Ask about her campaign
own.player: What does a climate campaigner actually do all day?
own.reply: Counts water. Argues with the county about the water table. Organizes marches that are mostly the same ninety people and, last time, a dog.

own.label: Ask about the car in her photos
own.player: Is that your station wagon in the photos?
own.reply: My parents’. It’s done more miles than anyone should ask of it. I’m the one in my group with a car, so I’m the one who knows where everyone went.

calls.label: Ask what really happened the night before the fire
calls.player: You said you know the whole story of that night. What is it?
calls.reply: Two people were each given half. I drove the whole thing. Vanessa and Rosa to Rosa’s place, then back. Then Vanessa and Caleb and a bag to the edge of campus. Then the rest of the bag, alone, to a flat with no lights. There’s no gray sedan in our story. There’s my parents’ station wagon. I’ve never said that out loud.

life.news: Found a record by a singer who made one album and vanished. Played it four times. Miriam banged on the ceiling, then asked what it was.
life.more: I collect singers who stopped. One album, then nothing. Somebody should remember the people who quit. Miriam Landry lives under me and we play records at each other through the floor. Tonight she lost the argument and asked for the name.

life.news: The climate march had ninety people and one very confused dog. Best turnout of the year.
life.more: We marched from the reservoir to the county building with signs about the water table. The dog joined at the second corner and stayed for the speeches. Ninety people and a dog. I’m counting the dog.

life.news: Somebody asked me again who drove who home the night before the fire. I gave the answer I always give. I’m tired of it.
life.more: I’m the one in the group who knows where everything is. Keys, bags, rides. Two people have told two different stories about that night, and both of them got half from the same person. I drove. I know the whole thing. I keep deciding not to say it.

life.news: Sat at the Lucky Cactus at sunrise again, deciding whether to leave the group. Didn’t decide. Ate pancakes.
life.more: Two years of being useful to someone who never asked how I was. I go to the diner before anyone’s awake and sit next to the booth where Dolores always sits and try to make up my mind. The pancakes are good. The decision is not getting easier.

gossip.says: Vanessa Greer recruited me. I was the first one who wasn’t in love with her. That made me useful.
gossip.note: Annika Joseph says Vanessa Greer recruited her, and that being useful to Vanessa was the job.
gossip.ask: Annika says she was the first person you recruited who wasn’t in love with you.
gossip.answer: Annika is the most useful person I have ever met. That is a compliment. Lately she hears it as something else. I don’t know why.

gossip.says: Miriam Landry lives under me. We play records at each other through the floor. It’s the best friendship I have.
gossip.note: Annika Joseph and Miriam Landry play records at each other through the floor.
gossip.ask: Annika says you two play records at each other through the floor.
gossip.answer: She plays singers who vanished. I play singers who should have. It’s a war. I’m losing and I love it.

women.name: Annabel Yates
women.look: Fair skin, a long braid to the waist, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, band T-shirt under dungarees

own.label: Ask about her postcards
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Postcards of Sunfall from when it was founded. A mud road, a horse and a hotel with a fake front. It wasn’t always like this.

own.label: Ask about being secretary
own.player: What do you do for the collective?
own.reply: I’m the secretary. I take beautiful minutes of meetings where nothing is decided. I draw little flowers in the margins.

own.label: Ask what makes her stop playing
own.player: What gets under your skin?
own.reply: People who smile too kindly. A kind smile you didn’t earn is usually a warning.

own.label: Ask about her oldest postcard
own.player: What’s the oldest postcard you have?
own.reply: Nine women on the steps of the Old Mission, in white, with a bell on a cart behind them. No date on it, which is the point of a postcard. The Daily printed the same picture once with names under it. Bea at the archive has the names. I have the faces. One of them is still alive.
own.note: Annabel Yates has a postcard of nine women on the Old Mission’s steps with a bell on a cart; Bea Hollis has the names.

calls.label: Ask about her torn journal entry
calls.player: What did your torn-out journal entry say?
calls.reply: One line. That I saw Allison Kent at a Back Row meeting, the one where they talked about the professor’s car. Allison says the Back Row is just students. The page is gone now, torn neatly. Allison sat next to me that afternoon. She smiles at me very kindly now.
calls.note: Annabel Yates wrote that she saw Allison Kent at a Back Row meeting about Vale’s car; Allison tore the page out.

life.news: Bought a postcard of Sunfall from 1911 at the stall for a quarter. Main Street was a mud road and a single horse.
life.more: I collect postcards of the town from when it was founded, because everybody here acts like Sunfall has always been the way it is. It hasn’t. It was a mud road and a horse and a hotel with a fake front. I put it on my fridge next to a photo of the same street now. The horse looked happier.

life.news: Took the minutes at a four-hour meeting. Nothing was decided. I wrote nothing was decided, beautifully.
life.more: I’m the collective’s secretary, which means I sit in every meeting with a pen and watch twelve adults agree to meet again. I have very nice handwriting. It’s wasted on nothing. Tonight I drew little flowers down the margin of the minutes. Nobody will ever read them.

life.news: A page of the campaign journal I wrote in is gone. Torn out neatly. By someone who sat next to me.
life.more: It was my entry. Just a line, about who I saw at a meeting I wasn’t supposed to be near. Now it’s gone, and the person I wrote about smiles at me every time we pass in the corridor. Very kindly. Too kindly. I’ve started writing my notes twice.

gossip.says: Rhea Cooper restores vintage dresses in a little workshop off the square. Some of them belonged to dead women from the club, and the women at the club still wear them to parties. She finds that very funny. I find it a bit haunted.
gossip.note: Annabel Yates says Rhea Cooper restores dead club women’s dresses that the club still wears to parties.
gossip.ask: Annabel says you restore dead club women’s dresses and find it funny.
gossip.answer: It is funny. They inherit the gowns and pay me to take the dead woman out of them. Lipstick on a collar, a cigarette burn, a hem let down for a dance. I fix it all and they wear them to the same parties. Annabel thinks it’s haunted. Everything at the club is haunted.

gossip.says: Sheryl Abbott at the police station collects postcards too, of towns she’s never been to, and writes them to herself. We trade at the stall. She gave me one of Sunfall from 1920 and wouldn’t take anything for it.
gossip.note: Annabel Yates says Sheryl Abbott collects postcards of towns she’s never been to and gave her one for free.
gossip.ask: Annabel says you collect postcards of towns you’ve never been to and gave her one for free.
gossip.answer: It was of Sunfall, so it was hers, not mine. I only keep places I haven’t been. Annabel collects the past and I collect the places I haven’t gone yet. Between us we’ve got everything except the present. I’m fine with that. The present is mostly paperwork.

women.name: Rhea Cooper
women.look: Freckled fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, tortoiseshell glasses, corduroy jacket with enamel pins

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I restore vintage dresses. Mostly gowns from the club, inherited from women who wore them to the same parties fifty years ago.

own.label: Ask what she notices in old clothes
own.player: Can you tell much from an old dress?
own.reply: Everything. Where the seams have stretched, where a brooch sat for years, where a hem was let down for a dance. You can clean a dress. You can’t make it nobody’s.

own.label: Ask why she keeps to herself
own.player: Why are you so private?
own.reply: Because I spend all day learning things about women from their clothes that they’d never tell me. It seems polite to keep a few of my own.

calls.label: Ask about the car outside her workshop
calls.player: Why does a gray car park outside your workshop?
calls.reply: Only on the evenings Audra Beaumont collects. She wears the dead Bluebirds’ gowns to their parties, and I restore them. A gray sedan, two men, watching my door while she’s inside. She tips me much better now. I didn’t ask why. That was the point of the tip.
calls.note: Rhea Cooper says a gray sedan parks outside her workshop on the evenings Audra Beaumont collects the dead Bluebirds’ gowns.

life.news: Got a red wine stain out of a white silk gown from 1958. Took four days. I want a medal.
life.more: I restore vintage dresses in a workshop off the square. Most of what comes in is from the club, because rich women inherit beautiful clothes and ruin them at dinner. This one had wine down the whole front. Now it’s white again. The woman will spill on it again within a month. I’ll be here.

life.news: A client wanted a dress altered to look like it had never belonged to anyone else. I said that’s not how dresses work.
life.more: Every old dress has someone in it. The way the seams have stretched, where the hem was let down, a faded spot where a brooch sat for years. You can clean it, but you can’t make it nobody’s. She took it to someone else. I hope they told her the same.

life.news: A car has started parking outside my workshop on certain evenings. Always the evenings one particular client collects.
life.more: Gray, two men, engine off. They don’t come in. They don’t look at the dresses. They look at the door. The client never mentions it. She tips very well now. Much better than she used to. I don’t like being paid for things I haven’t been told about.

gossip.says: Lucille Pembrook cooks the collective’s dinners from cookbooks a hundred years old. Last month it was mutton pudding. She laughs at everything and believes almost nothing. I trust her completely.
gossip.note: Rhea Cooper says Lucille Pembrook cooks the collective’s dinners from very old cookbooks.
gossip.ask: Rhea says you laugh at everything and believe almost nothing, and she trusts you completely.
gossip.answer: That’s the nicest thing anyone has said about me and it came from Rhea, who says almost nothing. She came to one dinner and ate the pudding in total silence and then asked for the book. She cooked it at home. She said it was better with a glass of wine. She’s right.
