gossip.says: Amber Colebrook on the police phones restores old dresses too, one a year, slowly. She came to my workshop once to ask about forties buttons and stayed three hours. We barely spoke. It was perfect.
gossip.note: Rhea Cooper says Amber Colebrook came to her workshop about buttons and stayed three hours.
gossip.ask: Rhea says you came to her workshop about buttons and stayed three hours without really talking.
gossip.answer: We talked in buttons. Shell, glass, horn, which ones survive a wash and which don’t. That’s a whole conversation if you know the language. Rhea does everything properly, which I respect, and she gave me a tin of loose buttons I’ll be using for ten years.

women.name: Tamsin Wilde
women.look: Olive skin, golden-brown ringlets, a wide bright smile, band T-shirt under dungarees

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Community art collective. I run the workshop at the underpass and I bake for our dinners. Elaborate cakes. Badly, but with enormous confidence.

own.label: Ask if art is her only job
own.player: Is art your only job?
own.reply: I do late service at the club when they need waitresses. The collective doesn’t pay and my mother’s home costs money. I carry plates past people who once gave me a scholarship. They never look up.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you close to your family?
own.reply: My father drove for the Foundation and died at the junction when I was twelve. My mother is in a home now. Her mind is going, slowly. I visit every other day. Sometimes she knows me.

own.label: Ask who her best friend is
own.player: Who’s your best friend?
own.reply: Jasmin. Since we were six. She’s held my coat at every fight I’ve ever been in. Lately I’ve started to understand what else she’d hold.

own.label: Ask why she stopped baking
own.player: Why did you stop baking?
own.reply: Everyone noticed. Nobody asked, which was kind. I’ll tell you one thing. There’s a tin in my cupboard with my last collapsed cake in it, and the lid is more interesting than the cake.

calls.label: Ask how she really is
calls.player: How are you, really?
calls.reply: Quiet. I was funny before, quick, loud. That woman is in a cupboard with the cakes. I think whoever gets me talking again will get her back. I don’t think it’ll be the police.

calls.label: Ask what’s weighing on her
calls.player: Something’s weighing on you. Tell me.
calls.reply: I worked late service that night. I saw a man in a lanyard walk a woman through the kitchen to a car with its door open. She had her hand in her pocket. She said not here. Afterward two men came to my kitchen. One said scholarship. One said mother. I told the police I saw nothing. I wrote it all inside a cake tin’s lid, in pencil.
calls.note: Tamsin Wilde saw a man in a lanyard take a woman through the gala kitchen to a waiting car; after two men threatened her scholarship and her mother’s care, she told police she saw nothing, but wrote it inside a cake tin’s lid.

life.news: Workshop at the underpass today. A little boy painted a horse with six legs and refused to fix it. Correct decision.
life.more: He said it was a fast horse. His mother wanted to paint over the extra legs and he stood in front of the wall with his arms out. We left it. It’s the best thing on the whole mural now.

life.news: My mother called me by my father’s name today. Then she apologized, very politely, like I was a stranger.
life.more: The nurse said it happens, that names come loose before faces do. I held her hand for an hour and she told me about a man who drove too fast at the junction. She didn’t know she was talking about him. I did.

life.news: Jasmin cooked for me. Burned the onions, salted it twice, made me eat all of it. Best meal of the month.
life.more: She sat on the counter and watched me finish like a prison guard. Then she washed up and sang badly the whole time. I laughed, properly, for the first time in a while. She looked so pleased she dropped a plate.

life.news: Somebody left a box of good paintbrushes at the underpass with a note: for the horse. No name.
life.more: Sable brushes, the expensive kind. The boy’s mother swears it wasn’t her. I put them on the shelf where the workshop can reach them. Maybe there are just kind people around. I’m trying to believe that again.

gossip.says: Jasmin Malik has been my best friend since we were six. She’s held my coat at every fight I’ve been in. She feeds me now. I don’t know what I’d do without her.
gossip.note: Tamsin Wilde says Jasmin Malik has been her best friend since they were six.
gossip.ask: Tamsin says you’ve held her coat at every fight.
gossip.answer: Every single one, and I’d hold more than her coat if she asked. She’s been somewhere far away lately, even sitting right next to me. I feed her and I wait. When she comes back, I’ll be the first thing she sees. That’s been the plan for years.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland’s overflow lives in our apartment. Boxes of leaflets, a bicycle, a cactus that’s definitely dead. Eden swears she’ll collect it all. Eden has been swearing that for a year.
gossip.note: Tamsin Wilde says Eden Sutherland keeps boxes, a bicycle and a dead cactus in her apartment.
gossip.ask: Tamsin says your boxes and your dead cactus are still in her apartment.
gossip.answer: The cactus is resting. And those boxes are history, every leaflet the movement ever printed. Tell Tamsin I’ll collect them when I have a home with a door that locks. She’ll laugh. Then she’ll make me a cake.

women.name: Paz Herrera
women.look: Golden-tan skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, deep dimples, hand-knitted sweater

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Climate group, direct action. I chain myself to things. I’ve been arrested twice and charmed both custody sergeants. One of them drinks with the nurse. Everyone drinks with the nurse.

own.label: Ask what she does at night
own.player: What do you do at night?
own.reply: I photograph the neon signs on the motel strip. There’s a woman who does the same from the other end. We don’t speak until the fortieth sign. Then we talk about nothing. It’s the best friendship I have.

own.label: Ask about her worst campaign
own.player: What’s your worst campaign?
own.reply: The bin fire at the recycling drive. Rebecca tells it as her worst campaign. It was me. I let her have it. It was a very good fire.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: A younger sister in the police, Monica, who promised our mother she’d look after me. A father on Brown Avenue I argue with once a week while I wash his dishes. It works. Don’t ask how.

own.label: Ask if she regrets anything
own.player: Anything you regret?
own.reply: I sat in on some meetings once. A woman called Vanessa, a louder campaign, bigger ideas. I left when the talk went quiet. Quiet is when campaigns turn into something else. I’d like to think I was in that room by accident.
own.note: Paz Herrera sat in on Vanessa Greer’s meetings and left when the talk went quiet.

calls.label: Ask if anything odd is going on
calls.player: Anything odd going on near you?
calls.reply: A gray car’s been parked under my window for two weeks. I figured it was scouting the neon. My neighbor across the landing never turns her lights on. Maybe it’s watching her. Maybe it’s watching me. Either way, I wave at it.
calls.note: Paz Herrera says a gray sedan has been parked under her window for two weeks; her neighbor Rosa Gutierrez sits in the dark across the landing.

calls.label: Ask what she’s planning
calls.player: What are you planning?
calls.reply: The co-op got a donation from a trust on the ridge. A friend told me. I set fire to bins for a living, so I’ve decided to go and find the ridge. With a camera. And a can of something. Don’t tell my sister.
calls.note: Paz Herrera learned the co-op’s donation came from a trust on the ridge and plans to go up there with a camera.

life.news: Got arrested this morning. Charmed the sergeant. Out by lunch. He bought me a sandwich.
life.more: I’d locked myself to the water board’s railing with a bicycle lock and a very good sign. They cut me loose in four minutes. The sergeant asked if I’d done this before. I said twice. He said he could tell. Then he bought me a sandwich.

life.news: Fortieth sign tonight. We finally spoke. She likes the same diner sign I do. We’re practically married.
life.more: The one with the coffee cup that only half lights up. Forty signs of silence, and then we both pointed at it at the same time from opposite ends of the strip and laughed. We talked about nothing for an hour. It was perfect nothing.

life.news: Argued with my father about the dishes. Then politics. Then my mother. In that order. Every week.
life.more: He says I’m too angry. I say he’s not angry enough. Then I wash and he dries and neither of us says anything, and that’s the part that counts. I cried on the bus home. Don’t tell him.

life.news: My sister turned up at my door in uniform, late at night, to check I was home. I was home.
life.more: Monica says she drove past and my light was on and she worried. I said a light being on is the opposite of something to worry about. She came in, ate my leftovers standing up, told me to be careful, and left. She takes promises very literally.

gossip.says: Monica Herrera is my little sister and a police officer, which is a sentence I still can’t say with a straight face. She promised our mother she’d look after me. She takes it very literally.
gossip.note: Paz Herrera says her sister Monica Herrera promised their mother she’d look after Paz.
gossip.ask: Paz says you take your promise to look after her very literally.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to. Paz chains herself to railings and charms the sergeants who cut her loose. I drive past her window on my way home. Every night. She thinks I don’t. Tell her I saw the light on and I’m glad.

gossip.says: Rebecca Shaw tells the story of the recycling drive bin fire as her worst campaign. It was mine. I let her keep it. She tells it so well.
gossip.note: Paz Herrera says Rebecca Shaw tells the recycling drive bin fire as her own worst campaign.
gossip.ask: Paz says the bin fire was hers, not yours.
gossip.answer: She would say that! It was my campaign, my bin, my disgrace. She just held the matches. Fine. She lit them. But I made the sign. Tell Paz I’ll split the credit if she splits the fine.

women.name: Agnes Castillo
women.look: Deep brown skin, box braids to the waist, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, soft cream sweater and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the parish garden
own.player: What grows in a desert parish garden?
own.reply: Roses, if you’re stubborn. Prickly pear, if you’re sensible. We grow both, which is very Catholic of us.

own.label: Ask about the ballroom dancing
own.player: You’re learning ballroom dancing?
own.reply: Yes, and I’m dreadful. It’s good for me. You have to let someone else lead, which I find very hard.

own.label: Ask what she’s worried about
own.player: You seem worried about something.
own.reply: There’s a payment in the parish books to a company I’ve never heard of. Nobody will explain it. I’ve prayed about it and I still want an answer.
own.note: Agnes Castillo found an unexplained parish payment to an unknown company.

own.label: Ask what grows best in the desert
own.player: What grows best in the desert?
own.reply: Things that wait. Seeds sit for years until the rain comes. My grandmother called it faith with roots.

own.label: Ask what else happens in the garden
own.player: What goes on in the chapel garden?
own.reply: Roses, vegetables for the pantry, and a kiln where Alma fires her pots one evening a week. On firing nights the whole garden smells like bread and stones.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your father do?
own.reply: He was the Old Mission’s last sacristan. He died there, of a stroke, in the crypt, while he was locking it. My mother still sings in the choir. She won’t go up the mission road.

own.label: Ask if she has a sister
own.player: Do you have any sisters?
own.reply: Freya. Two doors from the Old Mission, with a house full of cacti. We haven’t spoken in six years, over God. I pray for her every night. She’d hate that.

own.label: Ask what her father said at the end
own.player: What did your father say, at the end?
own.reply: He called me from the crypt, before the stroke took him. He said the bell was ringing, and that it couldn’t ring. That bell has been cracked since before my grandmother was born. I’ve told nobody but God, and now you.
own.note: Agnes Castillo’s father called her from the Old Mission’s crypt before he died, saying the cracked bell was ringing.

own.label: Ask about the payment in her accounts
own.player: Why is a strange payment in your garden accounts?
own.reply: Because nobody reads the garden accounts. Somebody chose my line on purpose to hide a payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy. I’ve prayed about it. God hasn’t told me who. I’m still asking.
own.note: Agnes Castillo says a payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy was hidden in her garden accounts.

views.dispute: There is a payment in my garden accounts to a company I had never heard of, and nobody chose the garden line by accident. I’ve prayed about it. God hasn’t told me who yet. I think the review is about the Old Mission, and the Old Mission is about my father, and I haven’t said either of those out loud until now.

life.news: The prickly pear flowered. Bright yellow, all at once, as if it had been saving it up.
life.more: Roses if you’re stubborn, prickly pear if you’re sensible. We grow both, which is very Catholic of us. The prickly pear waited three years. Things that wait grow best. My grandmother called it faith with roots.

life.news: Ballroom class. Trod on my partner four times. He said I was improving. I wasn’t.
life.more: I’m dreadful at it. It’s good for me. You have to let someone else lead, which I find very hard. Naomi from the Bluebirds is in my class and she leads with her head. Between us we’re a hazard. The instructor has started wearing steel toes.

life.news: Walked past my sister’s house. Six years since we spoke. Didn’t knock.
life.more: Freya and I were a year apart and inseparable until our father died. I prayed and she raged and we said things in a kitchen. Today the curtain moved. I don’t know if it was her. I kept walking. I’ll pray about it.

life.news: Taught a boy from the pantry to plant a seed. He checked on it every hour.
life.more: He’s seven and very serious. He put the seed in the pot like he was posting a letter, then came back every hour to see if it had answered. Seeds sit for years until the rain comes. He doesn’t have years. I watered it twice to help.

gossip.says: Bernadette Flores restores paintings at the museum and talks to them while she works. I once heard her apologize to a saint for the cold. She brings the garden her coffee grounds every week, for the roses.
gossip.note: Agnes Castillo says Bernadette Flores talks to the paintings she restores at the museum.
gossip.ask: Agnes says you talk to the paintings while you restore them, and you once apologized to a saint for the cold.
gossip.answer: He was very old and the room was very cold. You’d apologize too. They’ve been looked at for three hundred years and nobody asks how they are. Agnes talks to her roses the same way, so she can hardly judge. Hers grow. Mine just get a little brighter.

gossip.says: Sophia Moretti grows her mother’s roses in the desert, and they came up red this year. She brought me a cutting and wouldn’t let me thank her.
gossip.note: Agnes Castillo says Sophia Moretti grows her late mother’s roses.
gossip.ask: Agnes says you gave her a rose cutting and wouldn’t let her thank you.
gossip.answer: She’d have thanked me with a whole speech! Agnes is the best gardener in the parish and she doesn’t say much, so a thank-you from her is like a sermon. I just wanted Mamma’s roses in her garden too. That’s all. God bless you for asking.

women.name: Eliza Montoya
women.look: Warm brown skin, box braids to the waist, freckles across her nose, soft cream sweater and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the food pantry
own.player: What’s the food pantry like?
own.reply: Busy and quiet at the same time. People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed. That’s the real work. The cans are just the excuse.

own.label: Ask why she volunteers
own.player: Why do you give so much of your time?
own.reply: Because it was given to me first. When my family had nothing, the Sisters fed us and never once made us feel small. I owe them the rest of my life, gladly.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: You seem troubled.
own.reply: The pantry’s storeroom has a filing cabinet nobody uses, and now it’s locked and the key is gone. Someone is keeping something in a place nobody thinks to look.
own.note: Eliza Montoya says an unused filing cabinet in the food pantry’s storeroom is now locked and its key is missing.

own.label: Ask who comes to the pantry
own.player: Who comes to the food pantry?
own.reply: People you’d never guess. A nurse. A man in a suit who cried. Pride is the hardest thing anyone carries through that door.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Three little brothers, a mom who cleans, and a dad who drove the casino’s deliveries until they let him go without a reason. We had nothing once. We have a little now. The Sisters’ name is said in our house like a saint’s.

own.label: Ask about the cakes she serves
own.player: What do you serve at the pantry?
own.reply: Whatever comes in. A girl from the club brings cakes that always collapse, so I serve them in bowls and call it trifle. Nobody has ever complained.

own.label: Ask about the locked cabinet
own.player: What do you think is in the locked cabinet?
own.reply: Something Margaret is afraid of the bishop finding. Her hand goes to that cabinet when he’s mentioned, and Evelyn’s hand goes to her collar. I’ve worked out they’re the same thing. I haven’t said so. I’m saying it to you because you won’t tell.
own.note: Eliza Montoya believes the pantry’s locked cabinet holds what Margaret Holloway is hiding from the bishop, and Evelyn Rosales wears its key.

own.label: Ask what the review means for the pantry
own.player: What happens to the pantry if the review goes badly?
own.reply: Nobody from the chancery has ever come through that door. People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed, and the tins are the excuse. If the Sisters go, the pantry goes, and half of Brown Avenue finds that out in a bad month. I don’t say that to the people who come in. I’m saying it to you.

views.dispute: Nobody from the chancery has ever come through the pantry door. People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed, and that is what the review would end. The Sisters fed my family once. I owe them the rest of my life, and the bishop can review that if he likes.

life.news: A woman came into the pantry ashamed this morning and left laughing. Best can of beans I’ve ever handed over.
life.more: People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed. That’s the real work. The cans are just the excuse. Today she told me a joke about her husband and the beans. I’m not repeating it. It was very rude. I laughed till I cried.

life.news: Got a watch ticking at the repair bench. It was my practice watch, but still.
life.more: My father’s watch stopped, so I’m learning to mend them on my day off. Today the practice one ticked. Danica, who sits next to me, clapped very quietly. When I can do my father’s, I’ll tell him. Not before.

life.news: My dad’s been out of work a month now. He sits in the yard fixing things that aren’t broken.
life.more: He drove deliveries for the casino until they let him go for a reason they didn’t give. He’s a proud man. When we had nothing the Sisters fed us and never made us feel small. I’m trying to do the same for him at home. It’s harder with your own father.

life.news: A man in a suit cried in the pantry storeroom today. I’ll never say who.
life.more: Pride is the last thing to go. He came in for a parcel for a neighbor, he said. Then he sat on a box of cans and cried for ten minutes. I gave him a cup of tea and a parcel and didn’t ask whose neighbor. Everyone’s somebody’s neighbor.

gossip.says: Teresa Bellamy teaches at the parish school, and her class hamster has bitten the bishop twice. She calls it a theological position. She brings the leftover lunches to the pantry at the end of every week, in a wagon.
gossip.note: Eliza Montoya says the hamster in Teresa Bellamy’s classroom has bitten the bishop twice.
gossip.ask: Eliza says your class hamster has bitten the bishop twice, and you call it a theological position.
gossip.answer: Twice is generous. The second time the bishop put his hand straight back in. That’s faith, or it’s stupidity, and the hamster can’t tell the difference either. Eliza counts every lunch I bring in like it’s treasure. To her it is. That’s why I keep bringing them.

gossip.says: Bianca Roth from the Bluebirds learns watches at the same bench as us. She remembers everyone’s birthday. She brought me a cake on mine, and I’d never told her the date.
gossip.note: Eliza Montoya says Bianca Roth remembers everyone’s birthday.
gossip.ask: Eliza says you brought her a cake on her birthday without being told the date.
gossip.answer: Everyone brings me their form and their birthday. I remember both. People think that’s the same thing. It isn’t. Eliza’s form said nothing interesting. Her birthday is the day after the saint she’s named for. I looked it up. Of course I looked it up.

women.name: Rosalie Kemp
women.look: Pale skin, sandy shag with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, long-sleeved maxi dress

own.label: Ask about the chapel archive
own.player: What’s in the chapel archive?
own.reply: Baptisms, marriages and funerals back to when Sunfall was a mission. Every name in this town is in my books somewhere.

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: You run a book club?
own.reply: Six women, one bottle of sherry and a lot of arguing about Jane Austen. It’s the most honest room in the parish.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: Something’s troubling you.
own.reply: Our caretaker vanished without collecting his wages. A man who never missed Mass. He looked after the bell tower.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp says the chapel caretaker, who looked after the bell tower, vanished without collecting his wages.

own.label: Ask what the old records say about love
own.player: What do the old parish records say about love?
own.reply: Marriages that lasted sixty years, recorded in two lines. No photographs, no speeches. Just two names and a lifetime.

own.label: Ask about the registers
own.player: Where do you keep the old registers?
own.reply: In a fireproof room I made the parish build. Every name in Sunfall is in there, two lines per life. If the chapel burns, the town forgets who it is. Not on my watch.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: Are your parents archivists too?
own.reply: Dad kept the school’s records, Mom kept the house’s. They’re retired and spend their days cross-checking each other. It’s very romantic, in a filing sort of way.

own.label: Ask why the Old Mission was closed
own.player: Why did the parish stop using the Old Mission?
own.reply: The register for the thirtieth year: the Beaumont, Blackwood and Van Doren marriages all move to St. Brigid’s, and the priest has written that the Old Mission is closed for a reason he will not write down. A priest refusing to write something down. That’s the loudest line in the book.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp’s register shows the founding families stopped marrying at the Old Mission in the thirtieth year, for a reason the priest would not record.

own.label: Ask about the caretaker
own.player: What happened to your caretaker?
own.reply: Aurelio Baca. He kept the bell tower and the Old Mission’s keys. He never missed Mass and he never collected his last wages. Eleven weeks now. Nobody has reported him missing but me.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp says the caretaker Aurelio Baca, who kept the Old Mission’s keys, vanished eleven weeks ago without collecting his wages.

own.label: Ask about the Sisters’ charter
own.player: Do the Sisters actually have a charter?
own.reply: Sixty years ago, when the old Mass was put away, the women who kept the Watch asked the bishop of that day for one, and he gave it, because he had stood a Watch himself as a curate. It is in my registers with his signature, and I copied the page before Margaret locked the original away. If the chancery ever asks to read my books I will show them. They have never asked.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp has a copy of the Sisters’ charter, signed by the bishop of sixty years ago, who had stood the Watch himself.

views.dispute: The charter is in my registers, with the old bishop’s signature, and so is the thirtieth year, and so is a caretaker who never collected his wages. The diocese has never once asked to read my books. That tells you what the review is for better than I can.

life.news: Book club tonight. Six women, a bottle of sherry and a two-hour argument about whether Mr. Darcy is a snob. He is.
life.more: It’s the most honest room in the parish. We’ve read the same book three times and the argument gets better every year. Mrs. Ortiz says he improves. I say he learns. There’s a difference, and it took a second glass to explain it.

life.news: Found a baptism entry where the priest wrote in the margin: baby shouted at the bishop. Two hundred years ago.
life.more: Baptisms, marriages and funerals back to when Sunfall was a mission. Every name in this town is in my books somewhere, usually with no comment at all. This one had a comment. I’ve put a little paper flag on the page. He’s my favorite baby in Sunfall.

life.news: Someone asked me to change a date in a register. I said no. They didn’t like it.
life.more: A family wanted a marriage date moved so a christening three generations ago looked more respectable. I said the register says what happened. They said nobody would know. I said I would. I value respect over romance, and truth over both.

life.news: Leila came for her weekly visit and fell asleep in my armchair. I let her. She works too hard.
life.more: She comes every week to sit somewhere quiet that isn’t a cell. Today she sat down, said, this chair, and was asleep in a minute. I put a blanket over her and read for an hour. Sleeping people are very good company.

gossip.says: Leila Sayeed, the custody nurse, visits me every week to sit somewhere quiet. Today she fell asleep in my armchair. I’d never tell her she snores.
gossip.note: Rosalie Kemp says Leila Sayeed visits her every week to sit somewhere quiet.
gossip.ask: Rosalie says you fell asleep in her armchair and she let you.
gossip.answer: Did she say I snore? She did, didn’t she. She’s honest to a fault. It’s the only chair in Sunfall that doesn’t smell of the station. I patch people up at both ends of the handcuffs all week. In her apartment nobody needs patching.

gossip.says: Arielle Brooks calls me from the newspaper archive whenever she finds a name she can’t place. Between her clippings and my registers, there’s nobody in Sunfall we can’t find.
gossip.note: Rosalie Kemp says Arielle Brooks calls her to trace names between the archive and the registers.
gossip.ask: Rosalie says that between you two there’s nobody in Sunfall you can’t find.
gossip.answer: It’s true and slightly frightening. She has the births, marriages and deaths. I have what the paper said about them, which is usually a lie in a nice font. Together we’re the town’s memory. Mostly we use it to settle bets at the diner.

women.name: Bernadette Flores
women.look: Rosy fair skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, sage cardigan and long linen skirt

own.label: Ask about conserving old things
own.player: What does a conservator actually do?
own.reply: I keep beautiful things from falling apart a little longer. Paintings, vestments, people, occasionally.

own.label: Ask why new things look so cheap
own.player: Why does everything new look so cheap?
own.reply: Because we stopped making things to last. Our grandparents built for their grandchildren. We build for the next quarterly report.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: I promised my father I’d marry in the chapel where he married my mother. I nearly gave up on that promise. I’ve started believing in it again.

own.label: Ask why she repairs instead of replaces
own.player: Why repair things instead of replacing them?
own.reply: Because a mended thing has a story. A new thing just has a price. We throw away so much now, people included.

own.label: Ask about her walk to work
own.player: What’s your walk to work like?
own.reply: Past the jeweler’s on Fifth Avenue, where I don’t look in the window, because the owner has twice offered to buy the parish’s old chalice. It isn’t for sale. Nothing that old should be.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your father do?
own.reply: He was a carpenter. He built the museum’s display cases, so I work inside his hands every day. He married Mom at St. Brigid’s. On his last night he asked me to marry where he had.

own.label: Ask about the Foundation’s loan
own.player: What did the Foundation lend the museum?
own.reply: A brooch, a bell clapper, nine goblets and a book. The inventory calls the book a hymnal and marks it with a crescent. I opened it. It is not a hymnal. I closed it and said a decade of the rosary.
own.note: Bernadette Flores says the Foundation’s loan to the museum includes a bell clapper and a crescent-marked book that is not a hymnal.

own.label: Ask what the chancery wanted from the museum
own.player: Did the chancery write to the museum?
own.reply: An inventory of parish property on loan: the chalice, the vestments, two paintings of saints with half their faces gone. I wrote back that the parish’s old things are not for sale and that I am the one keeping them from falling apart. The jeweler on Fifth Avenue has asked about the chalice twice. I have started to think the two letters know each other.
own.note: Bernadette Flores says the chancery asked the museum for an inventory of parish property on loan, the same season Clara Whitmore asked twice about the parish chalice.

views.dispute: The chancery asked the museum for an inventory of the parish’s old things on loan. I wrote back that they are not for sale. A mended thing has a story and a new thing has a price, and the diocese is pricing the parish. I keep beautiful things from falling apart. That includes churches.

life.news: Saved a painting today that everyone had given up on. A saint with half her face gone. She has a face again.
life.more: I keep beautiful things from falling apart a little longer. Paintings, vestments, people, occasionally. She was two hundred years old and water had got in. Six months with a brush the width of an eyelash. She looks at me now. Kindly, I think.

life.news: Walked past the jeweler’s on the way to the museum and didn’t look in the window. Again.
life.more: The woman who runs it has offered twice to buy the parish’s old chalice. Twice I’ve said no. Now I walk past without looking, like you would past an ex. A mended thing has a story. A new thing just has a price. She only sees the price.

life.news: My sister Karina brought a tour through the museum and told them I was the museum ghost. They all waved at me.
life.more: She’s a tour guide and incorrigible. Twenty people in hats waved at me through the glass while I was cleaning a vestment. I waved back very slowly, like a ghost. One child screamed. Karina says it was her best tour ever.

life.news: Went to the chapel where my parents married. Sat where my dad sat. Didn’t cry. Then did.
life.more: I promised him I’d marry where he married my mother. I nearly gave up believing. I’ve started again. Slowly. Sitting in that pew is like mending something. You do it a stitch at a time, and one day you notice it holds.

gossip.says: My sister Karina Flores gives tours and tells tourists the cacti are fake when they ask. Then she watches them touch one. She says it’s educational.
gossip.note: Bernadette Flores says her sister Karina Flores tells tourists the cacti are fake.
gossip.ask: Bernadette says you tell tourists the cacti are fake and watch them touch one.
gossip.answer: Only the ones who ask! Whether the cacti are real, whether the desert’s always this hot, and whether I’m single. Yes, yes, and it depends on the tour. The cactus thing is a public service. They never ask again.

gossip.says: Ruth Calder from the Bluebirds wears eleven twinsets in eleven blues. I restored one of her mother’s. She cried when she saw it and blamed the dust.
gossip.note: Bernadette Flores says she restored Ruth Calder’s mother’s twinset.
gossip.ask: Bernadette says you cried over your mother’s twinset and blamed the dust.
gossip.answer: It was dust. A great deal of dust. My mother said a woman should always look as if she were about to be photographed. That twinset was the one she was last photographed in. Bernadette gave it back to me. I’ll owe her for ever, and I’ll never say so to her face.

women.name: Lucia Romano
women.look: Deep brown skin, long locs with gold cuffs, strong dark brows, blouse with a Peter Pan collar

own.label: Ask about the charity shop
own.player: What’s it like running the charity shop?
own.reply: Donated coats, donated books, donated secrets. People give the shop what they can’t keep. I sort it. I don’t ask.

own.label: Ask where she’s from
own.player: You’re not from Sunfall, are you?
own.reply: The city. My parents still live there, and they’re bewildered that their daughter runs a nuns’ junk shop in the desert. I tell them it’s a calling. They ask if the calling has air conditioning.

own.label: Ask about her collar
own.player: What’s with the Peter Pan collar?
own.reply: It’s a joke on myself. I look like a teacher from an old film, so I dress like one, and then nobody can say it first. The Sisters think it’s modest. It is. It’s also a joke.

own.label: Ask how she came to the Sisters
own.player: How did you end up with the Sisters?
own.reply: My aunt Rosaria founded the shop. She was a Sister. When she died she left me the building, the shop and a trunk I can’t open. The shop needed a Sister to run it, and the city had stopped needing me. So.

own.label: Ask if her aunt left her anything else
own.player: Did your aunt leave you anything else?
own.reply: A letter. One line: never sell to the swallow. I didn’t know what the swallow was. I’ve learned. Somebody keeps asking the diocese about our building. I keep saying no.

own.label: Ask why she cooks so much
own.player: Do you always cook this much?
own.reply: Two lunches. The shop thinks it’s one and a big appetite. The shop is kind and not clever. I’m the same. Please don’t ask me who the other one is for. I tell the truth when I’m asked plainly, and then I’d have to live with it.
own.note: Lucia Romano cooks two lunches every day and carries one up the stairs above the Sisters’ charity shop.

views.dispute: I’m from the city and I’m new to all of this. The diocese keeps writing to ask about my building. My aunt’s letter said never sell to the swallow, and I didn’t know what the swallow was, and I do now, and my answer is still no. That is the whole of my opinion and it fits on a postcard.

calls.label: Ask about her aunt’s trunk
calls.player: Did you ever open your aunt’s trunk?
calls.reply: No. The key isn’t anywhere I’ve looked, and I’ve looked everywhere except the places I can’t bring myself to. It’s in the cellar under the shop. Some nights I go down and just sit with it.

calls.label: Ask what she can see from her balcony
calls.player: What can you see from your balcony?
calls.reply: The laundromat’s yard, and a van that parks there every night with a man asleep in the front. Basil, rosemary and mint in pots. I water the herbs and pray for the man in the van. Both seem to help.

life.news: Someone donated a wedding dress today with the tags still on. I put it in the window. Three women stopped to look.
life.more: No note, no name, just the dress in a bag on the step. I don’t ask. I steamed it, put it in the window and prayed for whoever couldn’t keep it. By closing a girl had tried it on and cried. I gave her a discount the size of the whole price.

life.news: Found a love letter in the pocket of a donated coat. 1971. Still sealed.
life.more: I didn’t open it. One of the Sisters said I should. I said a sealed letter is somebody’s choice. It’s in the shop safe now, waiting for whoever comes asking. Fifty years is a long time to change your mind.

life.news: My mother rang from the city and asked when I’m coming home. I said I am home. She went quiet.
life.more: She means well. She thinks the desert took her daughter. I told her about the shop, the regulars, the herbs on the balcony. She asked if I’d made any friends. I said the Sisters. She said that’s not the same. Some days I’m not sure she’s wrong.

life.news: Sold a terrible lamp to a man who said it was exactly like his mother’s. He nearly cried. Best sale of the year.
life.more: Brass, a fringe, a shade with a hunting scene. It’s been in the back for two years. He walked in, saw it and stopped. His mother had the same one in her front room. Four dollars. He carried it out like a baby.

gossip.says: Cassandra Finch rents a room in my building and paints the sky from the roof every evening. She brings me the cake left over from her meetings. I have never once seen her not smiling.
gossip.note: Lucia Romano says Cassandra Finch paints the sky from the roof of her building every evening.
gossip.ask: Lucia says you paint the sky from the roof every evening.
gossip.answer: Every evening. Lucia leaves the roof door unlocked for me and pretends she forgot. I bring her lemon drizzle and pretend it’s left over. It never is. We’re both very bad liars, which is how I know we’re friends.

gossip.says: Sofia Delgado’s mother bakes shortbread in open war with Sister Sophia’s. Sofia carries the trays and refuses to take a side. She’d make a good diplomat.
gossip.note: Lucia Romano says Sofia Delgado’s mother and Sister Sophia Moretti are shortbread rivals.
gossip.ask: Lucia says your mom’s shortbread is at war with Sister Sophia’s.
gossip.answer: Total war. My mother says Sophia’s is too dry. Sophia says my mother’s is too sweet. Sophia and I are friends, which makes it funnier. I carry the trays and say everyone’s is wonderful. That’s my whole job at the Foundation too, honestly.

women.name: Odette Price
women.look: Olive skin, black space buns, amber eyes, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask about local radio
own.player: What’s it like working in local radio?
own.reply: Lovely and doomed. The phone-in callers are the loneliest people in town, and they’re the best part of the show.

own.label: Ask about her sketches
own.player: You sketch old shopfronts?
own.reply: Before they’re turned into vape shops. I’ve drawn eleven that are gone now. It’s a sort of memorial.

own.label: Ask about the letter
own.player: Is something worrying you?
own.reply: An unsigned letter came to my apartment. It said stop asking about the junction. I hadn’t asked about the junction yet.
own.note: Odette Price got an unsigned letter telling her to stop asking about the junction.

own.label: Ask whose voice she misses
own.player: Is there a voice you miss?
own.reply: My grandfather read the shipping forecast on local radio for thirty years. Nobody needed it in the desert. He read it anyway, like a prayer.

own.label: Ask about her sisters
own.player: Are you one of the Price sisters?
own.reply: One of three. Samantha sells houses, Bethany keeps the library, I keep the radio, which was Grandad’s. We meet once a week at the library to argue. It’s the best hour of my week.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Did your dad work at the station too?
own.reply: He sold the station’s advertising and drank it. Grandad read the shipping forecast in the desert for thirty years. I got the voice from one and the thirst for facts from neither.

calls.label: Ask what she found in the tape archive
calls.player: Found anything in the station’s old tapes?
calls.reply: A reel from forty years ago: a live broadcast from the Old Mission’s fair. Under the noise there’s a bell, which can’t be, and nine voices singing a round. Then the broadcast just stops.
calls.note: Odette Price found a forty-year-old broadcast from the Old Mission with a bell and nine voices singing, which cuts off.

calls.label: Ask what she’s found about the junction
calls.player: What have you found about the junction?
calls.reply: I hadn’t asked about it until the letter told me to stop. Now I have. The weigh station there isn’t abandoned. It’s leased. Someone keeps a light on.
calls.note: Odette Price says the weigh station at the old junction is leased, and someone keeps a light on there.

life.news: A woman rang the late show to say her cat came home after nine days. The whole switchboard cheered.
life.more: The phone-in callers are the loneliest people in town and the best part of the show. She’d rung every night for nine nights to ask if anyone had seen him. Tonight he walked in while she was on air. She cried. Chuck cried. I cried. Local radio. Lovely and doomed.

life.news: Played one of my grandfather’s old tapes. The shipping forecast, read in the desert like a prayer.
life.more: He read it on Sunfall FM for thirty years. Nobody in the desert needed to know about the North Sea. He read it anyway, slowly, every night. I play his tapes when I can’t sleep. Dogger, Fisher, German Bight. Best lullaby there is.

life.news: Another shop in Old Town became a vape shop. That’s twelve.
life.more: I draw them before they go. A cobbler, a hat shop, a tailor’s, and now a little haberdasher with a cat in the window. It’s like keeping a register of the dead, except the dead were very useful. I’ll draw this one tonight from memory.

life.news: Argued with my sisters at Bethany’s library for two hours. Best night of the week.
life.more: Samantha sells houses, Bethany keeps the library, I keep the radio. We meet every week to fight about everything. Tonight it was whether toast is a meal. It isn’t. Bethany says it is. We’ll still be arguing about it at ninety.

gossip.says: My sister Bethany Price runs the library like a secret society with late fees. She fined the mayor once. Thirty cents. He still hasn’t paid.
gossip.note: Odette Price says her sister Bethany Price fined the mayor thirty cents at the library.
gossip.ask: Odette says you fined the mayor and he never paid.
gossip.answer: Thirty cents! And he still has the book, which is the real crime. It’s a book about leadership, which is funny if you think about it. I send him a reminder card every month with a drawing of a sad owl. He knows. The owl knows.

gossip.says: Arielle Brooks at the archive found my grandfather in a newspaper from fifty years ago. A photo of him at the microphone. She brought it to the station wrapped in tissue paper.
gossip.note: Odette Price says Arielle Brooks found an old photo of her grandfather at the archive.
gossip.ask: Odette says you found an old photo of her grandfather at the microphone.
gossip.answer: In a box nobody had opened since the drought. He was leaning into the microphone like he was telling it a secret. I wrapped it in tissue because it felt like the right thing. She didn’t speak for a whole minute. I’ve never seen Odette not speak.

women.name: Arielle Brooks
women.look: Golden-tan skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, freckles across her nose, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about the newspaper archive
own.player: What do you find in the Sunfall Daily archive?
own.reply: A hundred years of the town lying to itself in very nice fonts. My favorite headline is from the drought years: Rain Expected Any Day Now. It wasn’t.

own.label: Ask about stargazing
own.player: You go stargazing in the desert?
own.reply: Every clear night. Out past the canyon the sky is so full it’s almost loud. You remember how small Sunfall is, and how small its scandals are.

own.label: Ask about the favor
own.player: Has someone asked you for a favor?
own.reply: An old friend wants me to lose a box of clippings about the old chapel’s last caretaker. She’s never asked me for anything before. That’s what worries me.
own.note: Arielle Brooks was asked by an old friend to lose archive clippings about the old chapel’s last caretaker.

own.label: Ask which star she’d name after you
own.player: If you named a star after me, which one?
own.reply: A dim one. Don’t be offended. The dim ones are the ones you only find if you’re really looking.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the Lucky Cactus. My aunt Dolores raised me and my cousin Zara at that counter after my mom left. Dolores died in the kitchen, and now my cousins run it in shifts and fight about the booth.

own.label: Ask what the archive is like
own.player: What’s it like down in the archive?
own.reply: A hundred years of the town lying to itself in very nice fonts. I know the paper better than anyone alive, which is a lonely thing to know.

own.label: Ask about the two caretakers
own.player: Is it true two caretakers vanished from the Old Mission?
own.reply: Forty years apart. The first the year of the fair, the second eleven weeks ago. Same job, same keys, same line in the parish’s wages book: never collected. The Daily ran four paragraphs the first time and nothing the second. I pulled both clippings. Rosalie at the chapel has both names. Between us there’s a pattern, and nobody has asked us to put it together.
own.note: Arielle Brooks says two Old Mission caretakers vanished forty years apart, both with wages uncollected; she has the clippings and Rosalie Kemp has the names.

calls.label: Ask about the caretaker clippings
calls.player: What’s in the box you’re meant to lose?
calls.reply: Forty years ago the Old Mission’s caretaker, a man called Baca, vanished after a night with no moon and never collected his wages. The paper ran three stories and then nothing. The third names the women seen at the chapel that week. One of them was Honoria Blackwood’s mother. I haven’t lost the box.
calls.note: Arielle Brooks says the Old Mission’s caretaker vanished forty years ago, and Honoria Blackwood’s mother was seen at the chapel that week.

life.news: Found a headline at the archive today: Rain Expected Any Day Now. From the drought. It wasn’t.
life.more: A hundred years of the town lying to itself in very nice fonts. I keep a folder of headlines that didn’t come true. Bridge To Open By Spring. Mayor Promises Fresh Start. My favorite is still the rain. Somehow it makes me love this town more.

life.news: Went stargazing past the canyon. The sky was so full it was almost loud.
life.more: You lie on the warm rock and the stars come out in layers. There’s one dim star I always look for, low on the left. I don’t know its name and I don’t want to. Out there you remember how small Sunfall is. How small its scandals are.

life.news: The cousins argued about the booth at the diner again. It’s been a year since my aunt died and nobody will sit in it.
life.more: Dolores raised me and Zara at that counter. She died in that kitchen, in a fire nobody talks about. Her booth’s by the window. Alana wants to keep it empty, Kimberly wants to sell it, Melody cries. I sit at the counter, where she put me when I was four.

life.news: An old friend asked me to lose something at the archive. I haven’t said yes.
life.more: A box of old clippings. Nothing important, she says, which is exactly what people say about important things. Archivists don’t lose things, we find them. I told her I’d think about it. I’ve been thinking about it for a week.

gossip.says: My cousin Zara Brooks walked me to school every day for six years and threatened every boy who looked at me. She has her own name tattooed on her wrist so she never forgets it. I asked why once. She said, in case you do.
gossip.note: Arielle Brooks says her cousin Zara Brooks walked her to school for six years.
gossip.ask: Arielle says you tattooed your own name on your wrist so you’d never forget it.
gossip.answer: Arielle remembers it better than I do. A lot of people lose their names in the Old Quarter. They take new ones, they become something else. I wanted mine where I’d see it every time I picked up the needle. And yes. In case she forgets it too.

gossip.says: Rosalie Kemp at St. Brigid’s keeps the registers back to when Sunfall was a mission. Every name in town is in her books. She found my great-grandmother’s baptism and read it to me over the phone like a bedtime story.
gossip.note: Arielle Brooks says Rosalie Kemp keeps the chapel registers back to the mission.
gossip.ask: Arielle says you found her great-grandmother in your registers.
gossip.answer: It’s what the books are for. Baptisms, marriages and funerals back to the mission. Her great-grandmother was baptised in a storm, and the priest wrote that in the margin. Two lines and a weather report. I read it to her because it deserved reading.

gossip.says: My cousin Kimberly Brooks runs an office, rides a motorcycle and wants to sell our aunt’s booth at the diner. She says it’s just a booth. It’s not just a booth.
gossip.note: Arielle Brooks says her cousin Kimberly Brooks wants to sell their aunt’s booth at the diner.
gossip.ask: Arielle says you want to sell your aunt’s booth at the diner.
gossip.answer: Someone has to say it. Nobody sits there. A booth nobody sits in is a shrine, and Dolores would have hated a shrine. She’d have put a family of six in it and charged them for the extra fries. I’m not selling it. I’m just saying it out loud so somebody does.

women.name: Harper Lin
women.look: Freckled fair skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, deep dimples, striped shirt and trench coat

own.label: Ask what goes into the weekend paper
own.player: What goes into the weekend paper?
own.reply: Recipes, the crossword and one serious story I fight for every single week. People only read the crossword, so I put the serious story next to it.

own.label: Ask about her old dog
own.player: Tell me about your dog.
own.reply: Pickle. Thirteen, deaf as a post, and asleep under my desk at the paper. She’s our longest-serving member of staff.

own.label: Ask about her favorite headline
own.player: What’s your favorite headline you ever wrote?
own.reply: GOAT EATS MAYOR’S SPEECH. True story. It was a very good speech, apparently. The goat agreed.

own.label: Ask about a story she never ran
own.player: Is there a story you never ran?
own.reply: One. The facts were right and it would have ruined a good woman for one bad week. I spiked it. I still don’t know if that was journalism or cowardice.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Were your parents writers too?
own.reply: Teachers. Dad taught at the parish school before Teresa Bellamy, Mom at the hill school. I was a bright, kind girl who became a bright, kind reporter, and found out that isn’t enough at the city desk.

own.label: Ask what she collects
own.player: Do you collect anything?
own.reply: Dogs and reporters. Strays, mostly. Pickle was the first and is still in charge.

calls.label: Ask who the story she spiked was about
calls.player: Who was the story you spiked about?
calls.reply: My ex-fiancé’s new wife, the week before their wedding. She’d been up at the lodge the week a man died there. Her name was Veronica Shawcross. He was voted into the family that spring and buried that winter. I still don’t know if I was being kind or a coward.
calls.note: Harper Lin says her ex-fiancé married Veronica Shawcross, was voted in, and died within the year.

life.news: Pickle woke up during a meeting today and barked once. Everyone agreed with her.
life.more: Thirteen, deaf as a post, longest-serving member of staff. She sleeps under my desk through every crisis. Today she woke up, barked at the managing editor and went back to sleep. Motion carried.

life.news: Someone sent the weekend paper a recipe for a cake with a whole lemon in it, skin and all.
life.more: Recipes, the crossword and one serious story I fight for every week. People only read the crossword, so I put the serious story next to it. I baked the lemon cake to test it. Either the best or the worst thing I’ve ever eaten. Running it anyway.

life.news: Saw my ex-fiancé in the supermarket with his wife. We both pretended to be fascinated by tins.
life.more: Five minutes reading the backs of soup tins while his wife chose pasta. I spiked a story once that would have ruined her for one bad week, and the facts were right. I’d do it again. I didn’t buy any soup. I don’t even like soup.

life.news: The crossword setter sent me a clue so good I laughed out loud in the newsroom.
life.more: I can’t tell you who sets it. Only two people in Sunfall know. The clue’s about the mayor and a goat. You’ll see it on the weekend. If you get it first time, I’ll buy you a drink. Nobody will get it first time.

gossip.says: Teresa Bellamy teaches at the parish school, in my dad’s old classroom. She sends him a drawing from one of her eight-year-olds every term. He keeps them all on the fridge.
gossip.note: Harper Lin says Teresa Bellamy took over her father’s classroom at the parish school.
gossip.ask: Harper says you send her dad a drawing from your class every term.
gossip.answer: Every term, since I took his classroom. He left me a good blackboard and a rule about never shouting before break. I send the drawings so he knows the room is still loved. This term it’s a dinosaur in a hat.

gossip.says: Fiona Blake has decided every front page in Sunfall for four years and she can’t decide what to have for lunch. I once watched her stand at a sandwich counter for eleven minutes.
gossip.note: Harper Lin says Fiona Blake can’t decide on lunch.
gossip.ask: Harper says you once stood at a sandwich counter for eleven minutes.
gossip.answer: Twelve. And I chose egg, which was wrong. I decide what Sunfall knows tomorrow and it uses up all my deciding. By lunch I’ve got nothing left. Harper brings me soup now, without asking. That’s real friendship. Or pity.

gossip.says: Hannah Webb eats at her desk, sleeps at her gran’s once a week, and has a wall of string. If she ever asks you to look at it, say yes. You’ll learn more in ten minutes than in a year of the paper.
gossip.note: Harper Lin says Hannah Webb’s wall of string is worth seeing.
gossip.ask: Harper says I should say yes if you ever show me your wall of string.
gossip.answer: Harper’s sweet. The wall isn’t for visitors yet. It’s mostly string and three stories and my gran’s shopping list, which got pinned up by accident and now feels like a clue. When it’s ready, you can see it. Bring cookies.

women.name: Delia Maher
women.look: Pale skin, twist-out coils, deep dimples, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask how she got so far so young
own.player: You’re young for an investigative reporter.
own.reply: I’m patient for a young person. That’s the trick. Everyone else my age wants to go viral. I want to be right.

own.label: Ask about her old cameras
own.player: You restore old film cameras?
own.reply: Film makes you think before you shoot. Digital lets you shoot instead of thinking. Same with opinions.

own.label: Ask about the ruined recording
own.player: What’s on the recording you’re restoring?
own.reply: A voicemail from the night of the gala. Half of it is static. The other half is a woman saying not Table 9, the kitchen.
own.note: Delia Maher is restoring a gala-night voicemail: a woman says not Table 9, the kitchen.

own.label: Ask if she ever feels too young for her job
own.player: Do you ever feel too young for your job?
own.reply: Every press conference. Old men call me sweetheart, and then they read what I wrote about them. Nobody calls me sweetheart twice.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What does your dad do?
own.reply: He was a signalman. He taught me to listen to the line for the train before you could see it. That’s all reporting is, really.

own.label: Ask where her patience comes from
own.player: Where does the patience come from?
own.reply: My mom died of something slow when I was ten. You learn patience sitting by a bed. You learn that the end comes on its own schedule, not yours.

own.label: Ask about her camera from an estate sale
own.player: Where did you get your camera?
own.reply: Daria sold it to me from an estate sale. There was a roll still inside, never developed. The estate belonged to a Bluebird husband. I haven’t developed it yet. I’m being patient again.

calls.label: Ask what the cleaned recording says
calls.player: What’s on the cleaned-up voicemail?
calls.reply: Alisha helped me clean it. After the woman says not Table 9, the kitchen, there’s a man’s voice saying a name: Marchbanks. Then a door. I won’t print until I know the woman’s name. Right beats first.
calls.note: Delia Maher’s cleaned voicemail from gala night has a man saying the name Marchbanks.

life.news: Developed a roll today that I shot a month ago. Every frame came out. Patience pays.
life.more: Film makes you think before you shoot. Thirty-six chances, and you wait weeks to find out whether you were right. Everyone my age wants to go viral. I want to be right. Today I was right thirty-six times. I’m insufferable.

life.news: An old man at the court called me sweetheart. Then he saw my notebook and didn’t again.
life.more: They always do it once. Then I ask a question they didn’t expect and they look at me properly. I keep a page in my notebook for men who called me sweetheart once. Some of them are very interesting now.

life.news: My dad’s signal box is being knocked down. He’s taking it hard.
life.more: He taught me to listen to a line for the train before you could see it. Forty years in that box. They’re replacing it with a computer in an office two towns away. I’m going to record the sound of the levers before it goes. He doesn’t know yet.

life.news: Jennifer next door finally turned her music down. She’s in love, apparently. Love is quieter than I expected.
life.more: Four megaphones, and walls like paper in our co-op. For three nights it’s been silence and humming. I knocked to check she was alive. She opened the door smiling at nothing. I’ve never wanted the megaphones back so much.

gossip.says: Jennifer Tate lives next door to me in the co-op and owns four megaphones. One of them makes a duck noise by accident. I hear it through the wall at the worst moments.
gossip.note: Delia Maher says her neighbor Jennifer Tate owns four megaphones, one of which quacks.
gossip.ask: Delia says one of your megaphones makes a duck noise.
gossip.answer: Only by accident! It’s the emergency one, which means every emergency has a duck in it now. Delia knocks on the wall when it happens. Twice for stop, three times for do it again. She always does three. Don’t let her tell you otherwise.

gossip.says: Hannah Webb at the Daily is the only other reporter in Sunfall I respect. She’s my rival. She doesn’t know I’ve read everything she’s ever written, twice.
gossip.note: Delia Maher says Hannah Webb is the only other reporter in Sunfall she respects.
gossip.ask: Delia says you’re the only other reporter in Sunfall she respects.
gossip.answer: Delia said that? She’s eighteen and she corrected my use of a semicolon in a published piece. In writing. To my editor. I respect her too, which is annoying. Tell her she still owes me a correction on the correction.

gossip.says: Alisha Benton from the police lab taught me how to clean up audio properly. She drinks her coffee black and fast, like she’s in a hurry to get back to the evidence.
gossip.note: Delia Maher says Alisha Benton taught her to clean up audio.
gossip.ask: Delia says you taught her to clean up audio.
gossip.answer: Only the basics. Filters, patience, and knowing when to stop before you make it say what you want it to. She’s quick. Quicker than some of my colleagues, don’t quote me. And my coffee’s black because two weeks-long job has no time for milk.

women.name: Zadie Foster
women.look: Light-brown skin, ash-blonde lob, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, utility vest with many pockets

own.label: Ask about reviewing music
own.player: What’s reviewing music like?
own.reply: Free tickets and a lot of enemies. Bands remember a bad review forever. One drummer still sends me a postcard every year that just says no.

own.label: Ask if she’s any good at pool
own.player: Are you any good at pool?
own.reply: Dangerously. My neighbors play for dish duty. I haven’t washed a plate in two years.

own.label: Ask about the best gig she’s seen
own.player: What’s the best gig you’ve ever seen?
own.reply: A girl with a broken guitar in the back room of the Lucky Cactus. Eleven people. She played like there were thousands. I gave her five stars and she cried.

own.label: Ask if she’d ever stop writing
own.player: Would you ever stop writing?
own.reply: Every rejection makes me want to. Then I hear a song I need to tell someone about, and I’m back. It’s less a job than an affliction.

own.label: Ask about her neighbor
own.player: Do you get on with your neighbors?
own.reply: Sienna next door teaches herself the drums very badly. I bang on the wall in time. It’s become a band. We have a name. We will never perform.

own.label: Ask if she ever played music
own.player: Did you ever play?
own.reply: Cello, in the Blue Ribbon Youth Orchestra, at twelve. Beside Hannah Webb and a girl who calls herself Salem now. I was bad at it, which is why I became a critic.

calls.label: Ask about the old orchestra programs
calls.player: What did you find in the old programs?
calls.reply: I kept the youth orchestra’s programs from the year before and the year after. The first says sponsored by Ellis Dane. The second says the Blue Ribbon Foundation. Same orchestra, same kids, different name. I never thought about it until Hannah asked.
calls.note: Zadie Foster’s old programs show the youth orchestra’s sponsor changed from Ellis Dane to the Blue Ribbon Foundation.

life.news: Got my yearly postcard from the drummer. It just says no. Eighth year.
life.more: I gave his band two stars eight years ago. Every year since, a postcard. A different town every time, the same word. No. I keep them in a shoebox. It’s the longest relationship I’ve ever had with a man.

life.news: Sienna’s drumming came through the wall again and I banged back in time. We’ve basically got a band now.
life.more: She drums when she’s stressed, I bang on the wall in time, and she started answering. Last night we did a whole song through the plaster. Neither of us has said a word about it in person. Best band in Sunfall.

life.news: A band I gave three stars sent me a cake with a three on it. In icing. I ate it. I feel terrible.
life.more: It was a good cake. A four-star cake, honestly. Writing is an affliction, not a job. You say something true about someone’s work and they remember it forever. I wrote them a note saying the cake was a four. They’ve framed it.

life.news: Beat the whole bar at pool tonight. Haven’t washed a plate since spring.
life.more: I play the neighbors for the dishes. I practice in secret at the bar on the dry river, which Linh calls cheating and I call preparation. My sink is spotless because I never use it. That’s not a metaphor. That’s my life.

gossip.says: Sienna Navarro next door paints murals and drums when she’s stressed. I bang on the wall in time. We’ve never discussed it. We’ve got about six songs now.
gossip.note: Zadie Foster says she and Sienna Navarro play music through their shared wall.
gossip.ask: Zadie says you two have six songs, played through the wall.
gossip.answer: Seven. She doesn’t count the one where I dropped a stick. We’ve never spoken about it, and if you make us speak about it, it’ll stop working. Some bands need a wall between them. Ours is load-bearing.

gossip.says: Linh Tran and I argue about every band in Sunfall. It’s mostly arguments. Some of it isn’t. Don’t ask.
gossip.note: Zadie Foster says she and Linh Tran argue about every band in Sunfall.
gossip.ask: Zadie says you two argue about every band in Sunfall, and some of it isn’t arguing.
gossip.answer: She said that? To you? Okay. Yes. It’s mostly arguments. The rest is also arguments, but closer together. She thinks a band called Gray Spoon is a three. Gray Spoon is a four. That’s all I’ll say.

gossip.says: Raven Solis does the door at gigs in the Old Quarter, and bands think she’s the merch girl until she tells them their fee. She’s the only person in the Quarter I’m scared of. She’s eighteen.
gossip.note: Zadie Foster says Raven Solis, eighteen, terrifies bands at the door.
gossip.ask: Zadie says you’re the only person in the Old Quarter she’s scared of.
gossip.answer: I just tell people the fee. They think that’s terrifying. Both are true, I suppose. Zadie came to the door once without a ticket and I made her pay. She paid. She’s been nice to me ever since. I don’t know what to say back, so I nod.

women.name: Celina Rojas
women.look: Warm beige skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, rosy cheeks, press lanyard and denim jacket

own.label: Ask what a photography assistant does
own.player: What does a photography assistant actually do?
own.reply: Carry everything, hold the reflector and get blamed for the weather. One day I’ll take the picture. Today I hold the bag.

own.label: Ask about the bicycle
own.player: How’s the bike coming along?
own.reply: It has two wheels now. Neither of them goes round. I’ve watched forty videos about chains and I understand less than when I started.

own.label: Ask about the best picture she’s helped take
own.player: What’s the best picture you’ve helped take?
own.reply: An old cowboy at the rodeo, laughing with no teeth. My boss got the credit. I got the cowboy’s number. He calls me on my birthday.

own.label: Ask what keeps her up at night
own.player: What keeps you up at night?
own.reply: Whether I’m good enough or just keen. Whether keen runs out. Whether you can tell I reread my messages six times before I send them.

own.label: Ask where she used to live
own.player: Have you always lived above your mom’s café?
own.reply: No. In the spring I had a room above the laundromat on Sunfall Road. The radiator sang at night. I left in one night and I don’t talk about why. If you’re in that room now, the third floorboard from the door creaks. Sorry.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What are your family like?
own.reply: Mom runs a café the Daily’s night staff live in. Dad rode the rodeo with Diana Moore’s first husband, until a fall. He’s in a chair now and still the funniest man in the county.

own.label: Ask about the cowboy who calls her
own.player: Who calls you on your birthday?
own.reply: An old cowboy from Dad’s rodeo days. Every year, same joke, same song, badly. I’d be devastated if he stopped.

own.label: Ask if she knows Moira Bell
own.player: Do you know Moira Bell?
own.reply: My friend. My best one, maybe. If she’s calling you a lot, that’s a bad patch, and her mom’s the one who can help. Ruth Bell. Here: {number}. Tell her Celina sent you.
own.note: Celina Rojas, Moira’s friend, gave you the number for Moira’s mother, Ruth Bell.

calls.label: Ask why she left the room above the laundromat
calls.player: Why did you leave the laundromat room in one night?
calls.reply: A letter under the door, unsigned, in handwriting I’ve since seen on the Foundation’s Christmas cards. It said my photograph of Valerie Huxley for the society page showed a woman who was unwell, that I wouldn’t take another, and that the room wasn’t safe for a girl who looked at Bluebirds through a lens. I packed while the radiator sang.
calls.note: Celina Rojas, the last tenant of the room above the laundromat, left after an unsigned letter in a Foundation hand warned her off photographing Bluebirds.

life.news: The bike has two wheels now. Neither of them goes round. Progress.
life.more: I’ve watched forty videos about chains and I understand less than when I started. A man in one of them said a bike is a conversation. Mine isn’t speaking to me. I’m thinking of giving it a name so we can start again.

life.news: The old cowboy from the rodeo rang. It’s not even my birthday. He just wanted to say hello.
life.more: My boss photographed him years ago and he’s rung on my birthday every year since. Buck Reyes. No relation to Catalina, I always have to say. Today he rang for no reason and told me about a horse he loved. I listened for forty minutes. Best call of the month.

life.news: My dad had a bad day. The chair. He doesn’t talk on bad days.
life.more: He was a rodeo rider. A fall, years ago, and now a chair. On bad days he watches old rodeo tapes with the sound off. I sit with him and hold his hand and we don’t talk. I’m good at holding things. It’s my job.

life.news: Natalie let me take the picture today. A real one. It’s going in the paper.
life.more: Carry everything, hold the reflector, get blamed for the weather. Then today she handed me the camera and said, you’ve got this one. A boy at the reservoir with a fish bigger than his arm. Page seven. I’ve bought six copies. I’m going to read it six times.

gossip.says: Natalie Cross keeps a wall of photos she’ll never print. She says some pictures are for keeping, not selling. She’s the best photographer in Sunfall and she’s sad in a way you only see if you carry her bags.
gossip.note: Celina Rojas says Natalie Cross keeps a wall of photos she will never print.
gossip.ask: Celina says you keep a wall of photos you’ll never print.
gossip.answer: She notices too much for someone who claims she only carries the bags. Yes. Some pictures are for keeping. They’re not mine to sell. Celina’s the only person who’s seen the wall and didn’t ask why. That’s why she’s going to be good.

gossip.says: Olivia Reid lived across the landing from me above the laundromat. When I was crying through the wall she used to leave cookies outside my door. We’ve never talked about it.
gossip.note: Celina Rojas says Olivia Reid used to leave cookies outside her door.
gossip.ask: Celina says you used to leave cookies outside her door when she was sad.
gossip.answer: The walls above a laundromat are cardboard with ambitions. I heard. Cookies seemed less awkward than knocking. Custard creams, because those are the emergency cookie. She left in a hurry in the spring. I hope she’s got thicker walls now.

gossip.says: Sable Marlow at the Cellar Door has a camera someone left behind after a goth night, with one photo deleted. She keeps asking around about it like it’s a lost dog.
gossip.note: Celina Rojas says Sable Marlow is asking around about a camera with a deleted photo.
gossip.ask: Celina says you’re asking around about a camera with one photo deleted.
gossip.answer: Who deletes one photo? Someone with something in it. The house photographer left it behind and I’d like to know who was in that frame before I give it back. Celina asks a lot of questions for a girl who says she only holds the bag.

women.name: Kira Henson
women.look: Warm beige skin, burgundy-dyed curls, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, cable-knit sweater and leather satchel

own.label: Ask what court reporting is like
own.player: What’s court reporting like?
own.reply: I sit in the same room as the worst things people do and write down every word. You learn to hear what people don’t say. The pauses are where the truth is.

own.label: Ask where her hidden routes go
own.player: Where do your hidden hiking routes go?
own.reply: Old mining paths, dry riverbeds, a cave nobody marks on the map. I draw them by hand, and I only share them with people I trust.

own.label: Ask about her oldest friend
own.player: Who’s your oldest friend?
own.reply: A girl from my first newsroom. We fell out for six years over nothing. Then her dad died and I was on her doorstep within the hour. That’s friendship. Turning up.

own.label: Ask if a verdict ever felt wrong
own.player: Has a verdict ever felt wrong to you?
own.reply: Once. I wrote it up straight, the way you have to. Then I walked into the desert and stayed until dark. The desert doesn’t argue.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A cabin on the canyon side with a wall of maps I drew by hand. Old mining paths, dry riverbeds. And one cave I have never marked and never will.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Who taught you shorthand?
own.reply: My father kept the county court’s records for forty years and taught me shorthand at eight. He died two years ago. My oldest friend was on the doorstep within the hour. That’s what friendship is: turning up.

calls.label: Ask about the pause in the inquest
calls.player: What did the pauses tell you in court?
calls.reply: The Sanderson inquest. The coroner asked the Foundation’s driver where he’d been that night. Nine seconds of nothing. Then an answer that was struck from the record. It’s still in my shorthand: the lodge.
calls.note: Kira Henson’s shorthand of the Sanderson inquest records that the Foundation’s driver said he had been at the lodge, an answer struck from the record.

life.news: Nine seconds of silence in court today before a witness answered. I wrote down every one.
life.more: I sit in the same room as the worst things people do and write down every word. The pauses are where the truth is. Nine seconds is a long time to decide whether to lie. I underline long pauses in red. Today’s page is very red.

life.news: Walked a dry riverbed I’d never mapped. Found an old mining cart rusted into the sand.
life.more: I draw the canyon by hand. Old paths, dry rivers, places nobody marks. The cart was full of desert flowers growing out of it. I sat with it for an hour. It’s going on the map as a small drawing. Only people I trust get the maps.

life.news: My mom’s bridge friends told her something about me that isn’t true. She believed it for a whole afternoon.
life.more: She plays bridge with Bluebird mothers and they tell her things. Today it was that I’d been seen crying outside a judge’s house. I wasn’t crying, I was sneezing. In a parking lot. Two towns away. Small towns don’t gossip. They publish.

life.news: Helen poured me a whiskey and didn’t ask a single question. Best evening in a month.
life.more: Helen Markham’s kitchen. We sit with our backs to the wall, both of us, and say very little. It’s the only room in Sunfall where nobody’s taking notes. Including me.

gossip.says: Helen Markham keeps a bottle of whiskey for people who’ve had the kind of day only she understands. I’ve had three of those days this year. She’s never asked a single question.
gossip.note: Kira Henson says Sergeant Helen Markham keeps whiskey for people who’ve had a bad day.
gossip.ask: Kira says you keep whiskey for people who’ve had the worst kind of day.
gossip.answer: Kira writes down every word in that courtroom. Somebody should give her somewhere she doesn’t have to. A glass, a kitchen and no questions. It’s the cheapest kindness I know. Don’t make it a thing.

gossip.says: Hannah Webb drinks with me and asks the best questions in Sunfall. I answer about half of them. She knows which half I’m lying about. That’s friendship.
gossip.note: Kira Henson says Hannah Webb asks the best questions in Sunfall.
gossip.ask: Kira says I’d be lucky to get half my questions answered by you.
gossip.answer: Kira answers about half, and the half she doesn’t answer is always the story. She does this little pause before she says no comment. Court reporters. They know exactly how long a pause should be.

women.name: Moira Bell
women.look: Waifish and very pale, a slim small-busted model figure, faint shadows under dark sullen eyes, bleached eyebrows, golden-brown ringlets, a small nose stud, a striped shirt under an oversized trench coat

own.label: Ask what a fact-checker does
own.player: What does a fact-checker actually do?
own.reply: I ring people and ask if they really said what they said. Most of them didn’t. I remember everything anyone tells me. It’s a gift, mostly.

own.label: Ask about teaching her cousin guitar
own.player: How are the guitar lessons going?
own.reply: He’s eleven and only wants to learn one song. I’ve taught it to him eighty times. I don’t mind. I like it when people need me.

own.label: Ask why she hates small talk
own.player: Why do you hate small talk?
own.reply: Because it’s a waste of a person. I’d rather know one true thing about you than a hundred nice ones. Tell me one true thing.

own.label: Ask what she remembers about you
own.player: What do you remember about me so far?
own.reply: Everything. What you said first, what you didn’t answer, how long you took to reply. Sorry. That came out intense. It’s the job.

own.label: Ask about her cousin
own.player: Who’s the cousin you teach?
own.reply: Ollie. Eleven. He only wants to learn one song and I’ve taught it to him eighty times. I don’t mind. I like being needed. That’s probably the problem.

own.label: Ask about her mom
own.player: What’s your mom like?
own.reply: Ruth. She cleans at the hospital and comes home with her feet in a bowl. She’s the strongest person I know and the most tired.

calls.label: Ask about the letters to the editor
calls.player: What’s in the box of letters you keep?
calls.reply: Forty letters to the editor from one man, every one in verse, every one with the same return address: the apartment above the old Rialto. I keep the envelopes. I remember everything, so I remember where he lives.
calls.note: Moira Bell keeps Theon’s forty letters to the editor; they all come from the apartment above the old Rialto.

calls.label: Ask about her dad
calls.player: What happened to your dad?
calls.reply: He was a signalman. He died on the line when I was nine. I saved a voicemail from the week before: he’d be late because the Foundation’s truck was on the crossing again and he had to log it. I rang the Foundation. They said there was no truck. I remember everything.
calls.note: Moira Bell’s late father logged a Foundation truck on the railway crossing the week before he died; the Foundation denies it.

life.news: Taught my cousin Ollie his one song for the eighty-first time. He nearly got the middle bit.
life.more: He’s eleven and only wants to learn one song. I’ve taught it to him eighty-one times. I don’t mind. I like it when people need me. Today he got the middle bit right and looked at me like he’d won a war. I clapped like an idiot.

life.news: My mom came home from the hospital with her feet in pieces. Double shift again.
life.more: She cleans at the hospital. Twelve hours, then home with her feet in a bowl of hot water while I read her the paper. Tonight I read her a story I’d checked and she said, you made that one honest. Nicest thing anyone’s ever said about my job.

life.news: Rang a man today to check a quote. He swore he’d never said it. I played him the recording.
life.more: I ring people and ask if they really said what they said. Most of them didn’t. He went quiet, then said, well, I didn’t mean it. Which is different. I wrote that down too. I remember everything anyone tells me. It’s a gift, mostly.

life.news: A woman I rang to check a fact sent me a thank-you card. Nobody ever thanks a fact-checker.
