life.more: I’d caught a mistake that would have said she’d died. She hadn’t. Her sister had seen an early draft and screamed. We fixed it in time. She sent a card with a drawing of a very alive woman on it. It’s on my wall.

gossip.says: My cousin Catherine Bell is a Bluebird. The rich Bells. Our families haven’t sat at the same table in ten years. She plays tennis at the club like she’s trying to kill the ball.
gossip.note: Moira Bell says her cousin Catherine Bell is a Bluebird, and the families haven’t spoken in ten years.
gossip.ask: Moira says your two families haven’t sat at the same table in ten years.
gossip.answer: Ten years and two months. Moira would know the days. It wasn’t her fault and it wasn’t mine. Our fathers fell out over money, which is the only kind of falling out rich families have. I’d sit at her table. Tell her that. Don’t tell her I said it first.

gossip.says: Celina Rojas is my best friend at the paper. She rereads every message six times before she answers. If she hasn’t replied, she’s on read number four. Be patient.
gossip.note: Moira Bell says Celina Rojas rereads every message six times.
gossip.ask: Moira says you read every message six times before replying.
gossip.answer: Five! Sometimes five. Okay, six. I want to get it right. Moira remembers every word anyone has ever said, so she never needs to reread anything. Between us we make one normal person.

gossip.says: Fiona Blake, my editor, looks after me like a mother hen. When I had a bad week she rang my mom herself. Don’t tell anyone. Editors are supposed to be terrifying.
gossip.note: Moira Bell says her editor Fiona Blake called her mom during a bad week.
gossip.ask: Moira says you called her mom when she was having a bad week.
gossip.answer: She’s the best fact-checker I’ve ever had and she was running on no sleep. Somebody had to ring Ruth. Editors are supposed to be terrifying, yes. I’m terrifying to everyone except the ones who are actually good.

women.name: Talia Farouk
women.look: Light olive skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, tortoiseshell glasses, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask about her travel column
own.player: What do you write about in your travel column?
own.reply: Places nobody visits on purpose. A motel with one working sign, a diner with the best pie for two hundred miles. Readers send me hate mail and then go there.

own.label: Ask about her forgotten records
own.player: What kind of records do you collect?
own.reply: Ones nobody else remembers. Singers who made one album and vanished. I like to think somebody somewhere is still singing in the shower, unaware they’re a cult classic.

own.label: Ask what she’s skeptical of
own.player: What are you skeptical of?
own.reply: Hidden gems. Every hidden gem has a gift shop now. The real ones don’t know they’re hidden.

own.label: Ask where she feels at home
own.player: Where do you feel most at home?
own.reply: On a bus at night, with nowhere to be for six hours. Everyone else calls it travel. I call it the only time my head is quiet.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Does travel run in your family?
own.reply: Grandad drove the first bus route from Sunfall to the coast. Dad runs what’s left of it: two coaches and a timetable. I grew up asleep across the back seats.

own.label: Ask where the best pie is
own.player: Where’s the best pie in the county?
own.reply: A diner two hundred miles from here with a waitress who calls everyone sugar. I won’t print the name. Some things should only be found.

calls.label: Ask about her letter
calls.player: What did your unsigned letter say?
calls.reply: That the weigh station at the old junction is private property. It isn’t. I checked. It belongs to the county and it’s leased to a trust. Someone wanted me to think it was none of my business, which is how I knew it was.
calls.note: Talia Farouk found that the weigh station at the old junction belongs to the county and is leased to a trust.

life.news: Rode the night coach to the coast and back. Six hours with nowhere to be. My head is quiet.
life.more: Everyone else calls it travel. I call it the only time my head is quiet. My grandfather drove the first route from Sunfall to the coast, and my dad runs what’s left: two coaches and a timetable. I sit at the back with headphones and a record nobody remembers.

life.news: Found a singer who made one album and vanished. Her best song is about a gas station in the rain.
life.more: I collect them. Singers who made one record and disappeared. This one recorded in a garage in the desert and was never heard of again. The song is about falling in love with a man pumping gas. It’s perfect. I want to find her. I won’t. That’s the point.

life.news: Got hate mail about my column on the dry lake. Then three of them went.
life.more: Places nobody visits on purpose, that’s my beat. Readers send me furious letters, then go there with their families. One sent a photo of himself at the dry lake captioned: you were right, curse you. I’ve pinned it up. It’s my best review.

life.news: Dad let me drive the coach round the depot. I’m a terrible driver and he laughed for the first time in months.
life.more: My mom died when I was twenty and he went quiet. Today he put me in the driver’s seat of the old coach and I hit a cone, very slowly. He laughed until he had to sit down. I’ll hit a hundred cones if it does that.

gossip.says: Odette Price at Sunfall FM plays her grandfather’s shipping forecast tapes when she can’t sleep. We’ve never met. I’ve rung her show three times under a fake name.
gossip.note: Talia Farouk says she’s rung Odette Price’s radio show three times under a fake name.
gossip.ask: Talia says she’s rung your show three times under a fake name.
gossip.answer: Has she? Oh, now I need to know which ones. The woman who wanted to talk about lighthouses? The man with the very bad accent? Tell her she can ring under her own name. The lonely callers are the best part of the show. She doesn’t have to be lonely to ring.

gossip.says: Linh Tran wrote a scene in her novel about a night coach and got it so right I checked whether she’d been on my dad’s bus. She hasn’t. She just knows things.
gossip.note: Talia Farouk says Linh Tran wrote a night coach scene so accurately it was eerie.
gossip.ask: Talia says you wrote a night coach scene so right she thought you’d been on her dad’s bus.
gossip.answer: I’ve never been on it! I made it up. The man who eats an orange very slowly in the dark, the woman asleep against the window. Talia says they’re real. I’m starting to think the town is writing me. Don’t sit next to me on a bus. You’ll end up in it.

women.name: Mara Winters
women.look: Light-brown skin, long red curls, strong dark brows, chambray shirt and chinos

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I’m the Daily’s sports desk. All of it. In Sunfall that means the rodeo, the women’s five-a-side and the reservoir regatta. I always leave the score until the end. People hate it. They keep reading.

own.label: Ask what she collects
own.player: Do you collect anything?
own.reply: Vintage sports postcards. The regatta in its first year, the rodeo’s founding, teams nobody remembers holding cups with names nobody uses anymore. A whole wall of them.

own.label: Ask how she keeps fit
own.player: How do you stay in shape?
own.reply: I run and I box at Lauren Bishop’s gym. She shouts at me in a way I find extremely motivating. Then I drink with the rodeo crowd and undo all of it.

own.label: Ask if she’s seeing anyone
own.player: Are you seeing anyone?
own.reply: A bull rider. Lovely forearms, terrible spelling, eight seconds of genius at a time. I don’t expect to keep him. That’s half the fun.

own.label: Ask about the trophy on her wall
own.player: What’s that trophy on your wall?
own.reply: A youth football cup I won at twelve. That year it was called the Dane Cup. The next year it was the Blue Ribbon Shield. Same cup, new name. I have both photographs. Nobody else seems to think that’s strange.
own.note: Mara Winters won the Dane Cup at twelve; the next year the same cup was renamed the Blue Ribbon Shield, and she has photographs of both.

calls.label: Ask what she’s researching
calls.player: What are you working on?
calls.reply: The regatta, backwards. Fourteen years ago a man drowned at it and the Daily ran two paragraphs. The boat-hire owner said the boat had been tampered with. It was closed as misadventure. And I’ve got a postcard from that year with the boat in it and a woman on the jetty beside it in a striped top, the night before.
calls.note: Mara Winters is researching a drowning at the reservoir regatta fourteen years ago, closed as misadventure; her postcard from that year shows a woman in a striped top beside the boat the night before.

calls.label: Ask if anyone’s trying to hire her
calls.player: Anyone trying to hire you?
calls.reply: The club asked if I’d like to be the regatta’s official historian. Access, a title, a dinner. Very generous. Very sudden. I said I’d think about it, which is what I say when I already know.

life.news: Women’s five-a-side final tonight. The police beat the campus in the last minute. I’ve been screaming. I’m a journalist. I’m impartial.
life.more: Penalty in the last minute, keeper guessed wrong, and the whole police bench ran onto the field in their socks. The campus girls were furious and gracious in that order. I wrote six hundred words and left the score until the final line. Of course I did.

life.news: A bull at the rodeo stopped mid-buck and just stood there looking at the crowd. Nobody knew what to do.
life.more: The rider sat on him like a man waiting for a bus. The clown tiptoed up. The bull looked at the announcer’s booth for a long time, then trotted back to the chute on his own. Best story I’ve filed all year and it’s about nothing.

life.news: Lauren Bishop made me do burpees until I saw God. God was not impressed either.
life.more: I came in hungover from the rodeo and she could tell from the door. Forty burpees, then forty more because I made a joke. I lay on the mat afterward and she stood over me and said same time next week. I said yes. I always say yes.

life.news: Found a postcard of the very first rodeo at a market. The man selling it had no idea. Two dollars.
life.more: Sepia, a cowboy midair, the stands half built behind him. On the back someone wrote: wish you could see this, it’s going to be something. It was. I’m framing it for the middle of the wall.

gossip.says: Audrey King sells the tickets at the rodeo and knows every rider’s secrets. We drink together after. She talks, I listen, I never print a word. That’s the deal.
gossip.note: Mara Winters says Audrey King sells the rodeo tickets and knows every rider’s secrets.
gossip.ask: Mara says you know every rider’s secrets.
gossip.answer: Every one, and the bulls’ too. Mara’s the only reporter I drink with, because she never writes it down. She tells it back to me later, better than I told it. It’s like hearing your own life on the radio. Tell her the next round’s hers.

gossip.says: Lauren Bishop runs the gym where I box. She shouts at me in a way I find extremely motivating, and she can spot a hangover from across the room.
gossip.note: Mara Winters says she boxes at Lauren Bishop’s gym.
gossip.ask: Mara says you can spot her hangovers from across the room.
gossip.answer: From the parking lot, actually. She comes in after the rodeo smelling like beer and hay and thinks a smile will save her. It doesn’t. Forty burpees. She thanks me after, which is the only reason I don’t charge her double.

women.name: Ashley Grant
women.look: Fair skin, brown waves with teal tips, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, cable-knit sweater and leather satchel

own.label: Ask about filming the news
own.player: What do you do for the TV bureau?
own.reply: I’m the camera. Nine years of men at podiums and cars in ditches, and now and then a sunset nobody asked for.

own.label: Ask what she does on long shoots
own.player: What do you do when a shoot drags on?
own.reply: Restore vintage dresses in the back of the van. Hems, buttons, beading. Stakeouts are very good for beading.

own.label: Ask what happens to footage nobody uses
own.player: What happens to the footage that doesn’t make the news?
own.reply: Most of it gets wiped. Mine doesn’t. I keep the rushes. You never know what you filmed until later.

calls.label: Ask about her gala footage
calls.player: Did you film the gala?
calls.reply: For the regional news. They used forty seconds of the band. I have three hours, including the kitchen corridor when the service door opened. A few days later a typed letter came to the bureau: you’ve filmed enough. I haven’t watched the corridor part again. I’m scared to.
calls.note: Ashley Grant filmed three hours of the gala, including the kitchen corridor, and got an unsigned letter telling her to stop.

life.news: Filmed a sunset over the reservoir for the weather segment. The producer cut it to four seconds. I watched the whole thing twice.
life.more: I’ve been the bureau’s camera for nine years. Most of what I shoot is a man at a podium or a car in a ditch. Tonight I got eleven minutes of the reservoir going gold, then pink, then gone. Four seconds made the broadcast. The other ten minutes and fifty-six are mine.

life.news: The news van broke down on the state road. I sat in the back for two hours sewing a hem by flashlight.
life.more: I keep a vintage dress in a bag in the van, always one I’m restoring, for exactly this. Breakdowns, stakeouts, a council meeting that runs four hours. The tow truck driver asked what I was making. I said patience. He said he’d heard of it. He hadn’t.

life.news: Got a letter at the bureau with no name on it. One line. You’ve filmed enough.
life.more: Typed, folded once, no stamp, so somebody walked it in. I’ve filmed a lot of things. I don’t know which one is enough. I put it in the bag with the dress. I’m going to keep filming, obviously. I just look over my shoulder now when I do it.

gossip.says: Nadine Wells at the radio station bakes birthday cakes for the lonely callers on the phone-in. They’re terrible cakes. She drives them round anyway. The callers cry. Good crying.
gossip.note: Ashley Grant says Nadine Wells bakes birthday cakes for the radio station’s lonely callers.
gossip.ask: Ashley says you bake birthday cakes for the lonely callers and drive them round.
gossip.answer: They are terrible cakes, she’s right, and that’s part of it. A perfect cake from a shop says somebody paid. A wonky cake from me says somebody tried. Ashley filmed me delivering one once for a segment. They never aired it. She kept it.

gossip.says: Natalie Cross takes photographs for the Daily from across the road, always across the road, like she doesn’t want to be in the picture. She sees more from there than I do from the front.
gossip.note: Ashley Grant says Natalie Cross always shoots from across the road.
gossip.ask: Ashley says you always shoot from across the road and see more from there.
gossip.answer: You do see more. The people at the front perform for the camera. The people across the road forget you’re there. Ashley stands at the front with a camera on her shoulder like a bazooka and somehow everyone still trusts her. I don’t know how she does it.

women.name: Nadine Wells
women.look: Pale skin, a sleek low bun, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about the phone-in callers
own.player: What do you do at the radio station?
own.reply: Research for the phone-in. Potholes, council meetings, and the loneliest callers in Sunfall. I know all their names.

own.label: Ask about the cakes
own.player: Is it true you bake for the callers?
own.reply: Birthday cakes, for the lonely ones. They’re terrible cakes. That’s the point. A wonky cake says somebody tried.

own.label: Ask what she won’t give up on
own.player: What will you never give up?
own.reply: A layer cake. One day one of them will stand up straight. I’ll know peace then.

calls.label: Ask what her old friend wanted
calls.player: What did your friend from school want from the station?
calls.reply: The tape archive index. Every recording Sunfall FM has kept for forty years, with dates. She works at the club now, the youngest of the Bluebirds. She said it was for a history project. Somebody at the club wants to know what we’ve still got. I haven’t given it to her.
calls.note: Nadine Wells says a young Bluebird asked her for Sunfall FM’s tape archive index.

life.news: Delivered a birthday cake to a man who calls the phone-in every night. He’s ninety. He said nobody’s made him a cake in thirty years.
life.more: It was a lemon cake and it leaned like a tower in Italy. He didn’t care. He put a candle in it himself and made me sing. I sang badly. He sang worse. We ate the whole leaning side. I cried in the car. Good crying. Then I went back to work and researched a story about potholes.

life.news: My cake for the producer’s birthday collapsed in the oven. I iced it anyway. It looked like a car crash.
life.more: Three layers, chocolate, very ambitious. The middle sank like a sinkhole. I filled it with frosting and called it a crater cake. Everyone ate it. The producer said it was the most honest thing the station has ever produced. I think it was an insult. I’m taking it as a compliment.

life.news: An old friend from school asked me for something strange today. A copy of the station’s tape index. Just the list.
life.more: We haven’t spoken in years, and now she works at the club in a twinset and pearls and wants to know what tapes we keep. She said it was for a history project. She’s never done a history project in her life. I said I’d think about it. I’m thinking about it.

gossip.says: Felicity Stone runs the Desert Ledger, the free weekly, and she gets up before dawn to look at birds on the dry river. She’s quick to laugh and slow to trust. She trusted me after a year. I felt like I’d won something.
gossip.note: Nadine Wells says Felicity Stone runs the Desert Ledger and birdwatches on the dry river before dawn.
gossip.ask: Nadine says it took you a year to trust her, and she felt like she’d won something.
gossip.answer: She had won something. A year is quick, for me. Nadine is impossible not to like, which is exactly why I took so long. People who are easy to like are usually selling something. She was selling cake. Terrible cake. I trust her completely now.

gossip.says: Odette Price is my boss at Sunfall FM. She’s drawn eleven shopfronts before they became vape shops, and she answers the loneliest callers in town like they’re the most important people alive. To her they are.
gossip.note: Nadine Wells says Odette Price answers the radio station’s loneliest callers like they’re the most important people alive.
gossip.ask: Nadine says you answer the loneliest callers like they’re the most important people alive.
gossip.answer: Because for the three minutes they’re on air, they are. Local radio is lovely and doomed, and I intend to enjoy every minute before it goes. Nadine bakes them cakes. I’d never have thought of the cakes. That’s why I hired her.

women.name: Ellen Yamada
women.look: Fair skin, brown waves with teal tips, gold hoop earrings, press lanyard and denim jacket

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What does an archive researcher do all day?
own.reply: I index what the reporters bring down. A hundred years of Sunfall in boxes. Nobody indexes what they don’t bring, so I’ve started going to see for myself.

own.label: Ask if she takes pictures
own.player: Do you take pictures?
own.reply: Neon. The Lucky Cactus, the motel strip, the casino sign, all shot from my car on the way home. My apartment walls are covered in it. It’s like living inside a jukebox.

own.label: Ask who she works with
own.player: Who do you work with down there?
own.reply: Arielle Brooks. I trained her. She reads every headline like it’s lying to her, which it usually is. Best student I’ve had. Only student I’ve had.

own.label: Ask about the boldest thing she’s done for work
own.player: What’s the most adventurous thing you’ve done for work?
own.reply: I borrowed the photo desk’s camera and went to the goth night at the Cellar Door, on a night with no moon, to find out what the flyers meant. I took forty pictures. I deleted one.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What does your family do?
own.reply: My dad’s a retired engineer. He built the Foundation’s lodge up on the ridge, thirty years ago. He’s never talked about it. Lately he drives up there at night and sits in his car outside the gate. I followed him once.

calls.label: Ask what was in the picture she deleted
calls.player: What was in the picture you deleted?
calls.reply: My dad. At the back of the goth night, in his coat, watching the girls in the circle. I couldn’t read his face. I’ve known that face for thirty-four years.
calls.note: Ellen Yamada deleted a photograph of her father, Ken Yamada, watching the circle’s girls at the back of a goth night at the Cellar Door.

calls.label: Ask what her dad said about the lodge
calls.player: What did your dad say about the lodge?
calls.reply: He said he poured the lodge’s cellar floor himself, and he knows what’s under it. He wouldn’t say more. The Daily printed a plan of that cellar years ago, in a feature about the Foundation’s new retreat. I have it in a box.
calls.note: Ellen Yamada’s father poured the lodge’s cellar floor and says he knows what is under it; the Daily’s archive holds a printed plan of the cellar.

life.news: Shot the casino sign tonight with half its letters out. It says CAS NO. Best picture I’ve taken all year.
life.more: I sat in the car for twenty minutes waiting for the I to flicker back on, and it never did. CAS NO. It’s going on the wall above the bed. Every town needs a sign that tells the truth by accident.

life.news: Found a box in the archive with no label, full of photos of the same parking lot over thirty years. Who does that?
life.more: Same angle, same lamp post, once a year. The cars change, the lot doesn’t. No name, no note. I’ve indexed it under Mysteries, Pleasant. Arielle says that isn’t a category. It is now.

life.news: Followed my dad’s car again tonight. Turned around halfway. I couldn’t do it.
life.more: He went up the ridge road again, late. I got as far as the bend by the reservoir and turned back. Some things you want to know, and some things you want to have known. I don’t know which one this is yet.

life.news: A drink at the Vestry after work, alone, with a good book and a bartender who leaves you alone. Perfect night.
life.more: The bar in the old church, with the hum in the walls that everyone says is a ghost. I think it’s the plumbing. Either way, it’s company. Two chapters, one drink, nobody asked me anything. I may move in.

gossip.says: Arielle Brooks reads every headline in the archive like it’s lying to her. I trained her. Best student I’ve ever had.
gossip.note: Ellen Yamada trained Arielle Brooks at the Daily’s archive.
gossip.ask: Ellen Yamada says she trained you, and you’re her best student.
gossip.answer: I’m her only student. She’ll tell you that too, eventually. Ellen taught me that a headline is a guess somebody got paid for. She also taught me to go and look. She goes and looks at things nobody should. I worry about her.

gossip.says: Sable Marlow runs the Cellar Door and mops it more than she enjoys it. She’s glamorous for ten minutes a night. I saw the ten minutes once.
gossip.note: Ellen Yamada says Sable Marlow runs the Cellar Door.
gossip.ask: Ellen says you’re glamorous for ten minutes a night and mopping for the rest.
gossip.answer: Ten minutes if the bar’s quiet. The rest is mops and a bucket and a man asleep in the restroom. Ellen came in once with a camera, very brave, very out of place. I stood in her way all night. She got past me anyway. I respect that.

women.name: Felicity Stone
women.look: Fair skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about the paper she edits
own.player: What’s the Desert Ledger?
own.reply: The free weekly. Lives on ads, mostly from people who hate being written about. Every week I decide how brave we can afford to be.

own.label: Ask what she does before work
own.player: What do you do before work?
own.reply: Birdwatch on the dry river with a thermos. It’s the only quiet hour in my day, and the birds don’t buy ad space.

own.label: Ask why she’s slow to trust
own.player: Why does it take you so long to trust people?
own.reply: Because the people who are easiest to like are usually selling something. It took me a year with my best friend. She was selling cake.

calls.label: Ask about the ruined tape
calls.player: Whose voice is missing from your tape?
calls.reply: Elena Cross. I interviewed her for the Ledger the week before the gala, about the scholarship money. She said something about a second set of books. Now the tape is chewed and her voice is hiss. I can hear myself asking the question. I can’t hear what she answered.
calls.note: Felicity Stone interviewed Elena Cross the week before the gala; the tape is ruined where Elena spoke about a second set of books.

life.news: Saw a great blue heron on the dry river at dawn. It just stood there being enormous. I forgot to breathe.
life.more: I go out before work with binoculars and a thermos, and some mornings Penelope comes and gasps at everything. Today it was just me and this heron the size of a coat rack, standing in a puddle like it owned the river. It did. I just visited.

life.news: An advertiser pulled out of the Ledger because of one story. Half a page, gone. We’re a free paper. We needed that half page.
life.more: The Desert Ledger lives on ads. Most of them come from people who don’t like being written about. So every week I decide how brave we can afford to be. This week we were a bit braver than we could afford. I ate noodles for dinner. I’d do it again.

life.news: Found an old tape in the Ledger’s cupboard. It’s an interview I did. The tape is chewed up. I can hear my own voice and nobody else’s.
life.more: I don’t remember it being damaged. I remember the interview very well. Now the other woman’s voice is just a hiss. It’s like she’s been erased and I’m talking to nobody. I want it fixed. I don’t know anyone who fixes tapes.

gossip.says: Leanne Dalton is the Daily’s best investigative reporter and she volunteers at the Sisters’ thrift shop every week. She says it’s for charity. She keeps looking at the cellar door.
gossip.note: Felicity Stone says Leanne Dalton volunteers at the Sisters’ thrift shop and keeps looking at the cellar door.
gossip.ask: Felicity says you volunteer at the thrift shop and keep looking at the cellar door.
gossip.answer: I volunteer for charity. I also have eyes. The Sisters have a cellar, and a cellar in a building that old has things in it nobody has catalogued. I’ve priced eleven hundred coats waiting for an invitation downstairs. Felicity notices everything. That’s why she edits a paper and I just write for one.

gossip.says: Penelope Kline from the club birdwatches with me on the dry river. She gasps at everything. A sparrow, a heron, a plastic bag she thought was an egret. She makes mornings better.
gossip.note: Felicity Stone says Penelope Kline birdwatches with her and gasps at everything.
gossip.ask: Felicity says you gasp at everything, including a plastic bag you thought was an egret.
gossip.answer: It was a very convincing plastic bag. It moved like an egret. Felicity laughed so hard she dropped her thermos in the river. She never gasps at anything. She just writes it in a little book. I’m going to make her gasp one morning. It’s a long-term project.

women.name: Leanne Dalton
women.look: Freckled fair skin, a sleek low bun, a beauty mark above her lip, striped shirt and trench coat

own.label: Ask about investigative work
own.player: What’s investigative journalism actually like?
own.reply: Ninety percent waiting, nine percent paperwork, one percent knocking on the right door at the right moment. I live for the one percent.

own.label: Ask about the Sisters’ thrift shop
own.player: What do you do on your days off?
own.reply: Volunteer at the Sisters’ thrift shop. Pricing coats. It’s very calming. It also has a cellar I’d love to see.

own.label: Ask about her sources
own.player: How do you look after your sources?
own.reply: You make them a promise and you keep it, even when it costs you the story. Especially then.

calls.label: Ask about the bursary with the scrubbed name
calls.player: Whose name was taken off your college bursary?
calls.reply: A donor from the club. Augustus Pell’s circle funds half the scholarships in the county, and when one of their names gets awkward, the plaques get sanded. Mine was sanded the same year the Foundation’s accounts were audited. I’ve got the old brochure with his name on it. I kept everything.
calls.note: Leanne Dalton says her college bursary’s donor name was sanded off the plaque the year the Foundation was audited.

life.news: A story I’ve been working on for a year finally went to print. My name on page one. I had a hot dog to celebrate.
life.more: Investigative work is ninety percent waiting and nine percent paperwork and one percent knocking on a door at the right moment. Today the one percent paid off. I walked to the hot dog cart by the courthouse and ate two and said nothing to anyone. That’s the best feeling in the world.

life.news: A source stopped returning my calls. Nice woman. She sounded scared on the last one.
life.more: You make people a promise when they talk to you: I’ll protect you. Then sometimes somebody else makes them a bigger promise, or a worse one, and they go quiet. I sent her a card with no name on it. I hope she knows it’s from me. I hope she’s fine.

life.news: The college bursary I won at nineteen has a different name on it now. Somebody scrubbed the donor’s name off the plaque.
life.more: I went back to give a talk, and the plaque outside the library has a smooth patch where a man’s name used to be. Nobody at the college could tell me who. They looked at me like I’d asked about the weather on the moon. I paid my way through college with that man’s money. I’d like to know who he was.

gossip.says: Mina Kerr reviews the Old Quarter’s nights for the Night Wire and plays five-on-five against the police on Sundays. She’s private and very sharp. Her reviews make bands cry. Sometimes in a good way.
gossip.note: Leanne Dalton says Mina Kerr’s music reviews make bands cry.
gossip.ask: Leanne says your reviews make bands cry, sometimes in a good way.
gossip.answer: Only the bands that deserve it, either way. Leanne asked me once how I decide what to say, and I said, the truth, then I cut half of it. She said that’s all journalism is. She’s right. She also tackles harder than anyone on the police team. Not that she plays. She watches.

gossip.says: Hannah Webb is the best young reporter at the Daily and I taught her almost everything. She has three stories going and thinks two of them are the same story. She’s probably right. She usually is.
gossip.note: Leanne Dalton says she taught Hannah Webb almost everything.
gossip.ask: Leanne says she taught you almost everything, and you’re usually right.
gossip.answer: Almost everything. She didn’t teach me to stop, because she doesn’t know how either. Leanne taught me to wait outside a door for six hours with a sandwich and a question. Most of my stories are that sandwich. I owe her more than she lets me say.

women.name: Mina Kerr
women.look: Pale skin, long wavy hair with gold clips, thin wire-rimmed glasses, press lanyard and denim jacket

own.label: Ask about her reviews
own.player: What do you write about?
own.reply: Music in the Old Quarter for the Night Wire. I tell the truth, then I cut half of it. People call that cruel. It’s the kind half I cut.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do when you’re not reviewing?
own.reply: Five-on-five soccer on the campus team against the police. It’s the only time I get to shove a detective.

own.label: Ask why she’s so private
own.player: Why don’t you talk about yourself much?
own.reply: Because I spend all night writing about other people’s feelings. I’m out by the time I get to mine.

calls.label: Ask about the letter under her door
calls.player: What did the letter under your door say?
calls.reply: That a reviewer who writes about the Midnight Rite won’t be reviewing anything. I’d never heard of the Midnight Rite. I’d never written about it. Now I can’t stop thinking about it. That’s the thing about warnings. They’re also invitations.
calls.note: Mina Kerr got an unsigned letter warning reviewers off the Midnight Rite.

life.news: Reviewed a band at the Furnace that nobody had heard of. Five stars. They called me crying. I hung up before I cried too.
life.more: Three girls with one amp and a drum machine held together with tape, playing to twenty people like it was a stadium. I gave them five stars and said exactly why, sentence by sentence. Their bassist rang the Night Wire’s phone and couldn’t speak. I said good night, quickly. I don’t do feelings on the phone.

life.news: Wrote a bad review. Accurate. Fair. The singer threw a drink at me in the bar. It was a good drink.
life.more: I tell the truth and then I cut half of it, which most people think is cruelty. It’s kindness. You should read the half I cut. Tonight I got a gin and tonic down my jacket. I went home, changed, and wrote the next review exactly the same way.

life.news: Got a letter at my apartment. No stamp, no name. It said a reviewer who writes about certain nights won’t be reviewing anything.
life.more: Somebody walked up three flights of stairs to put it under my door. I didn’t write about any certain nights. I don’t know which nights are certain. I’ve put a chair under the door handle. I’ve started taking the long way home.

gossip.says: Rosie Nolan is thirty-six and still an assistant on the photo desk, by choice. She says she’d rather hold the bag for the young ones than put her name on a picture. She plays drums at the Furnace after hours. Loudly.
gossip.note: Mina Kerr says Rosie Nolan stays an assistant on the photo desk by choice and plays drums after hours.
gossip.ask: Mina says you stay an assistant on purpose and play drums after hours, loudly.
gossip.answer: Loudly is the only way I know how. And yes, by choice. Names on pictures get you letters under the door. Holding the bag gets you a quiet life and a drum kit. Mina has a name on everything she writes. I worry about her. I don’t tell her that.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster is my rival and my senior at the Night Wire. Free tickets and a lot of enemies. She’s been reviewing the Old Quarter since before I could legally drink in it. I’m going to beat her. Eventually.
gossip.note: Mina Kerr says Zadie Foster is her rival at the Night Wire and she’s going to beat her eventually.
gossip.ask: Mina says you’re her rival and she’s going to beat you, eventually.
gossip.answer: Eventually is the right word. She’s good. Better than I was at her age, which I resent and admire in equal amounts. She cuts half of every review and the half she cuts is always the half I’d have kept. One of us is right. I suspect it’s her. Don’t tell her.

women.name: Rosie Nolan
women.look: Porcelain skin, ash-blonde lob, a gap-toothed smile, black turtleneck and blazer

own.label: Ask why she stays an assistant
own.player: What do you do at the paper?
own.reply: I’m the photography assistant. Thirty-six, by choice. I carry the bag and hold the reflector and I never get letters under my door.

own.label: Ask what she does after hours
own.player: What do you do after work?
own.reply: Drums, at the Furnace after closing. Forty minutes of hitting everything I couldn’t hit all day. The cleaner claps with her mop.

own.label: Ask about the young photographers
own.player: Do you mentor the young ones?
own.reply: I hold them when their pictures get spiked and lie that it doesn’t matter. It always matters. They figure that out on their own.

calls.label: Ask what her friend at the club wants
calls.player: What favor did your friend at the club ask for?
calls.reply: To look at some pictures, somewhere private. Photos from the gala, I think, from the club’s own photographer. She wants to know if they’ve been doctored. She thinks somebody’s been taken out of one. She sounded very frightened for a woman in silk.
calls.note: Rosie Nolan says a friend in the club’s press office wants her to check whether someone was removed from a gala photograph.

life.news: Played the drums at the Furnace after closing. Forty minutes. Nobody there but the cleaner. She clapped with her mop.
life.more: Nixie lets me use the kit after the doors shut, and I hit everything I couldn’t hit all day. Thirty-six years old, an assistant by choice, with forearms like a docker. The cleaner asked if I was in a band. I said I’m in a band of one. She said that’s the best kind. I adore her.

life.news: A young photographer cried in the darkroom because her picture got spiked. I held her and lied that it didn’t matter.
life.more: It did matter. It was a good picture and an editor spiked it to keep a donor happy. I’ve seen it a hundred times. That’s why I stay an assistant: I’d rather carry the bag and hold the girls who cry than be the name the donor complains about. Some days I wonder if that’s cowardice.

life.news: An old friend rang me from the club’s press office. She wants a favor. She wouldn’t say what over the phone.
life.more: We were assistants together twenty years ago. She went to the club and wears silk now and gets her hair done every week. I stayed and got forearms. She said, I need you to look at some pictures for me, not here. I said where. She said I’ll tell you. She hasn’t.

gossip.says: Susie Mathers sits in the county court writing down every word and laughs at the wrong moments. She’s learning Italian from her girlfriend’s recipe cards. She once borrowed our camera and brought it back one frame short.
gossip.note: Rosie Nolan says Susie Mathers borrowed the photo desk camera and brought it back one frame short.
gossip.ask: Rosie says you borrowed the photo desk camera and brought it back one frame short.
gossip.answer: One frame. I took a picture I shouldn’t have and then I thought better of it. Rosie noticed in four seconds, held the camera up to the light, looked at me, and said nothing. She’s never said a word about it. That’s why everyone trusts her with their worst pictures.

gossip.says: Celina Rojas is the youngest on the photo desk. She carries everything and gets blamed for the weather. She rides a bicycle neither wheel of which goes round. I’m teaching her everything I know except how to stay.
gossip.note: Rosie Nolan says she’s teaching Celina Rojas everything except how to stay an assistant.
gossip.ask: Rosie says she’s teaching you everything except how to stay.
gossip.answer: She means she wants me to leave and be a real photographer. She says it like it’s a threat. Rosie carries more bags than I do and she’s twice my age and she never once complains about the weather. I’m going to name my first exhibition after her. She’ll hate it.

women.name: Susie Mathers
women.look: Rosy fair skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, tortoiseshell glasses, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about court reporting
own.player: What’s it like being a court reporter?
own.reply: You write down every word in the same room as the worst things people do. The words are easy. The pauses are where the truth is.

own.label: Ask about learning Italian
own.player: Are you learning a language?
own.reply: Italian, from my girlfriend’s nonna’s recipe cards. I can make a perfect risotto. I can’t ask for directions.

own.label: Ask if she gets in trouble at work
own.player: Do you ever get in trouble at work?
own.reply: I laugh at the wrong moments. In a silent courtroom. The judge has a look. I’ve had the look twice.

calls.label: Ask about the picture she deleted
calls.player: Who was in the court’s public gallery?
calls.reply: At Dale Pruett’s missing person hearing. Two men from the club’s board, sitting in the back of the public gallery, in the same row, not looking at each other. Board members don’t come to bail hearings. I took the picture and deleted it. I can still see it.
calls.note: Susie Mathers saw two board members in the court’s public gallery at Dale Pruett’s hearing.

life.news: Cooked a risotto from Noreen’s recipe card in Italian. Understood every word. Well, most words. Well, the pictures.
life.more: Noreen’s nonna writes her recipes in very small Italian with drawings of the pan in the margin. I translated it with a dictionary and a lot of hope. It came out creamy and perfect. Noreen ate two bowls and said brava. I nearly proposed. I didn’t. I washed up instead.

life.news: Laughed in court today. At the wrong moment. The judge looked at me over his glasses for a full ten seconds.
life.more: A witness said something that was funny in the way only true things are funny, and I laughed before I could stop. One snort, in a silent courtroom. I write down every word for a living. I can’t write down my own snort. The judge didn’t either. I checked the transcript. He was kind.

life.news: Took a picture of the court’s public gallery with the photo desk’s camera. Then I deleted it. I don’t really know why.
life.more: It was during a dull bail hearing, and I looked up and saw who was sitting in the gallery, and something about them being there made my neck cold. I took the shot without thinking. Then I deleted it in the bathroom. I still remember the picture perfectly. That’s the problem.

gossip.says: Gina Fowler sits next to Moira Bell in the fact-checkers’ corner and makes collages out of the copy that gets spiked. She’s poised, she’s fierce and her collages say more than the stories did.
gossip.note: Susie Mathers says Gina Fowler makes collages out of spiked copy.
gossip.ask: Susie says you make collages out of the stories that get spiked.
gossip.answer: They deserve somewhere to go. Somebody wrote those sentences and checked them and then a man upstairs decided the town didn’t need to know. So the town gets to know in a collage on my wall. Susie laughs at all the wrong moments in court. It’s the bravest thing in that building.

gossip.says: Kira Henson is my boss in the county court. She writes down every word and says the pauses are where the truth is. She maps canyon trails and only shares them with people she trusts. She hasn’t shared one with me yet.
gossip.note: Susie Mathers says Kira Henson only shares her canyon trails with people she trusts.
gossip.ask: Susie says you only share your canyon trails with people you trust, and you haven’t shared one with her yet.
gossip.answer: Not yet. She laughs in court. A woman who laughs in court will laugh on a narrow ledge and fall off it. When she can sit through a whole sentencing without making a sound, she gets a trail. She’s close. She’s very close. Don’t tell her.

women.name: Gina Fowler
women.look: Freckled fair skin, loose spiral curls, rosy cheeks, utility vest with many pockets

own.label: Ask about her collages
own.player: What do you make in your spare time?
own.reply: Collages, from stories the Daily kills. The true sentences, glued into pictures. You can read every word if you get close enough.

own.label: Ask about fact-checking
own.player: What does a fact-checker do?
own.reply: Rings people and asks if they really said what they said. Half of them didn’t. The other half wish they hadn’t.

own.label: Ask about her cousins
own.player: Do you have family in town?
own.reply: Two cousins who haven’t spoken in a year. A tour guide and a Sister. I love them both. I’m going to lock them in my kitchen.

calls.label: Ask about Moira’s voicemails
calls.player: What’s on Moira’s voicemails?
calls.reply: Moira’s bad week. She rang everyone, me too, and I saved the messages on an old tape. In the third one she says a name, then a street, then she stops, like somebody walked in. The tape is warped right there. I want it restored. I think there’s a fact in it.
calls.note: Gina Fowler saved Moira Bell’s voicemails; in one Moira names someone and a street before stopping.

life.news: Finished a collage from a month of spiked stories. Called it Things Sunfall Didn’t Need To Know. It’s my best one.
life.more: Every story that gets killed at the Daily ends up on the spike, and I take them home. Then I cut them up and glue them into pictures, the true sentences into shapes. This one is a desert with a big eye in the sky. You can read every word if you get close. Most people don’t get close.

life.news: Moira had a bad week. I listened to her voicemails at my desk and couldn’t help her. I can’t stop hearing them.
life.more: She sits across from me and checks facts so carefully you could set a clock by her, and then she had a week where everything came apart, and she rang everyone. Me too. I saved the messages. I don’t know why. I think there’s something in them she meant to say and didn’t.

life.news: My cousins asked me to dinner on the same night. Karina and Bernadette. They haven’t spoken in a year. Neither knows about the other’s invite.
life.more: One’s a tour guide who tells tourists she’s single for tips. The other is a Sister of Mercy who restores paintings at the museum. They fell out over something neither will tell me. Now I have two dinners and one night. I’m going to make them both come to mine. Wish me luck.

gossip.says: Wendy Chalmers writes the Ledger’s travel column and keeps a journal of every road in the county with how long it takes. She’s Talia Farouk’s rival. They’ve never been in the same room. I’d sell tickets.
gossip.note: Gina Fowler says Wendy Chalmers keeps a journal of every road in the county and is Talia Farouk’s rival.
gossip.ask: Gina says you keep a journal of every road in the county and you’re Talia Farouk’s rival.
gossip.answer: Rival is a strong word. I’ve just been to more places than her and written about them better. Talia goes to places nobody visits on purpose. I go to places people should visit and tell them how long it takes. Gina makes collages. She’s the only person who’s ever read my column all the way through.

gossip.says: Moira Bell sits across from me in the fact-checkers’ corner. She rings people and asks if they really said what they said. She remembers everything anyone tells her. Almost everything. She had a bad week. I kept her voicemails.
gossip.note: Gina Fowler says she sits across from Moira Bell and kept her voicemails from a bad week.
gossip.ask: Gina says she kept your voicemails from your bad week.
gossip.answer: She kept them? Of course she did. She keeps everything and cuts it up and glues it into something beautiful. I don’t remember everything I said that week. That’s the first time I can say that. If she wants to listen, she can. Tell her to tell me if I said anything true.

women.name: Wendy Chalmers
women.look: Freckled fair skin, burgundy-dyed curls, a wide bright smile, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about her travel journal
own.player: What’s in your journal?
own.reply: Every road in the county, with how long it takes. People deserve to know if a place is worth forty minutes.

own.label: Ask about her column
own.player: What do you write for the Ledger?
own.reply: The travel column. Ghost towns, canyon light, the best pie on the state road. It gets cut for mattress ads.

own.label: Ask about her rival
own.player: Do you have a rival?
own.reply: Talia Farouk at the Daily. We’ve never met. She writes beautifully about bus stations. I take it very personally.

calls.label: Ask about the name on her travel award
calls.player: Whose name was taken off your travel award?
calls.reply: The original certificate says the Augustus Pell Travel Award, in gold. The reissued one says The Foundation Travel Award. They changed it the year the Foundation’s accounts went to the auditors. Every award they gave out that year has been reissued with no name. I checked four.
calls.note: Wendy Chalmers says the Foundation reissued its awards without Augustus Pell’s name the year its accounts were audited.

life.news: Drove a dirt road to a ghost town nobody writes about. Forty minutes from the highway. One saloon, one dog, perfect.
life.more: I keep a journal of every road in the county with how long it takes, because nobody else bothers, and people deserve to know if a place is worth forty minutes. This one was worth four hours. The dog walked me round the whole town like a tour guide. He wanted a sandwich. He got one.

life.news: Wrote the best column of my career about a canyon. The editor cut it to make room for a mattress ad.
life.more: Eight hundred words about light on red rock at the end of the day, and I lost three hundred of them to a man promising a better night’s sleep. I read the ad. It was a very bad ad. Nobody will sleep better. I will be sleeping worse, out of spite, for a week.

life.news: The travel bursary I won at eighteen was named for a man. The name isn’t on the certificate anymore. They reissued it.
life.more: I asked for a copy for my wall, and the new one just says The Foundation Travel Award. No name. I have the original in a drawer and it has his name in gold. I didn’t think about it at the time. I’m thinking about it now.

gossip.says: Jules Moreland is nineteen and works the sports desk under Mara Winters. She runs a film night at the drive-in’s reopened screen and overthinks every headline. She’s going to be very good. She doesn’t believe me.
gossip.note: Wendy Chalmers says Jules Moreland runs a film night at the drive-in and overthinks every headline.
gossip.ask: Wendy says you overthink every headline and you’re going to be very good.
gossip.answer: I don’t believe her because she says it to everyone, but she says it in a very specific way to me, so maybe. The drive-in is the best thing in Sunfall. Wendy came once and timed how long it took to get there from three directions. She’s a lot. I love her.

gossip.says: Talia Farouk writes travel for the Daily and goes to places nobody visits on purpose. She’s my rival. We’ve never been in the same room. She writes beautifully about bus stations, which is very annoying of her.
gossip.note: Wendy Chalmers says Talia Farouk is her rival and writes beautifully about bus stations.
gossip.ask: Wendy says you’re her rival and you write beautifully about bus stations.
gossip.answer: Bus stations are the only honest buildings left. Nobody performs in a bus station. Wendy writes about places people should go, with times. I write about places nobody should go, with feelings. We are both right. I’ve read every column she’s ever written. Please never tell her.

women.name: Jules Moreland
women.look: Pale skin, ash-blonde lob, thin wire-rimmed glasses, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about the drive-in
own.player: What do you do outside the paper?
own.reply: Run a film night at the old drive-in. Two hundred cars, one screen, and a projector I talk to like a horse.

own.label: Ask about the sports desk
own.player: What’s it like on the sports desk?
own.reply: The rodeo, the five-on-five league and the regatta. I write eleven headlines and they use the first one.

own.label: Ask if she overthinks
own.player: Do you overthink things?
own.reply: Every single thing. I’ve rewritten this reply four times. This is the fourth.

calls.label: Ask what she saw at the Cemetery Chapel
calls.player: What did you see at the Cemetery Chapel?
calls.reply: I was there late with a boy. Don’t ask. We saw men with shovels and a lantern, by the far wall where the white flowers are. No priest, no family. They put something in the ground and patted it flat. Then a letter came telling me my chapel column won’t run. I hadn’t written it.
calls.note: Jules Moreland saw men bury something by the far wall of the Cemetery Chapel at night, with no priest or family.

life.news: Ran film night at the drive-in. Two hundred cars. The projector didn’t break once. I cried in the booth.
life.more: They reopened the old drive-in screen at the edge of town, and I run a film night there for the Daily with Coraline doing the sound. Tonight the whole lot honked at the end like a stadium. I sat in the projection booth with the reel still spinning and cried into my popcorn. Best night of my life.

life.news: Wrote a headline about the regatta. Rewrote it eleven times. They used the first one.
life.more: I overthink every headline. Every single one. I tried eleven versions about rowing and puns about oars and something clever about the reservoir, and Mara read the first one over my shoulder and said that one. It was the boring one. It was right. I hate that it was right.

life.news: Got a letter at my apartment about a column I haven’t written yet. Telling me not to write it.
life.more: I only had the idea for it in my head. I hadn’t typed a word. I hadn’t told anybody but Mara. The letter said, the column about the chapel will not run. No name. How do you know about a column that doesn’t exist? I haven’t slept well since.

gossip.says: Imogen Reyes is the quietest researcher at the radio station. She paints watercolors of Brown Avenue and watches everyone like she’s reading a weather report. She’s nineteen like me. She knows things.
gossip.note: Jules Moreland says Imogen Reyes watches everyone like she’s reading a weather report.
gossip.ask: Jules says you watch everyone like you’re reading a weather report.
gossip.answer: I’m not reading a weather report. I’m reading people. They’re easier than weather and they change faster. Jules thinks too much about everything and says all of it out loud, which is the opposite of me. We have lunch together and I don’t have to say anything. It’s perfect.

gossip.says: Mara Winters runs the sports desk and taught me that the boring headline is usually the right one. She collects postcards of games nobody remembers. She won a football cup as a kid and still has the medal on her keys.
gossip.note: Jules Moreland says Mara Winters taught her that the boring headline is usually right.
gossip.ask: Jules says you taught her that the boring headline is usually the right one.
gossip.answer: It is. Nobody reads a pun about oars. They read who won. Jules writes eleven versions of everything and the first one is always the best, because it comes from her gut before her brain gets involved. One day she’ll trust her gut. Then she’ll take my job.

women.name: Pearl Hartley
women.look: Rosy fair skin, glossy black ponytail, a small nose stud, chambray shirt and chinos

own.label: Ask about her job
own.player: What do you film?
own.reply: The bulletin’s soft pieces. Bake sales, the drive-in, the bear. My father filmed riots and lost an eye. I film bake sales on purpose.

own.label: Ask about the shelf in her photo
own.player: What’s on that shelf behind you?
own.reply: Roadside souvenirs. A plastic alien, a snow globe with a gas station in it, a spoon from a town of nine people. Every one cost a dollar. They’re priceless.

own.label: Ask why she’s so calm
own.player: How are you always this calm?
own.reply: I decided panicking was a luxury. Also, I’m usually three moves ahead. It helps.

calls.label: Ask about the lodge dinner
calls.player: Are you going to film the lodge dinner?
calls.reply: I am. Warmly, like they asked. But I’m leaving my own camera running in the van, pointed at the cellar door. Not the bureau’s. Mine. If anything comes out of it, you’ll be the first person I ring.

life.news: Filmed the Sisters’ bake sale for the bulletin. Came home with four minutes of footage and a bag of shortbread.
life.more: I do the soft pieces. The bear, the drive-in reopening, bake sales. A camera is a thing people hit, my father says, so I film things nobody wants to hit. Today the shortbread was so good I forgot to change the battery.

life.news: Found a snow globe at the market with a gas station inside it. Best dollar I’ve spent this year.
life.more: I collect odd roadside souvenirs. A plastic alien, a spoon from a town of nine people, and now a gas station in a snow globe. Nixie Adler found the same stall ten minutes after me. She’s still angry.

life.news: An old friend asked me to film a charity dinner at the lodge. Warmly, she said. Nobody says warmly unless they mean something else.
life.more: Nina and I knew each other in the city years ago. She went into consulting and now she works for a trust with a lot of money. She wants the bureau’s camera at the lodge’s dinner, as a favor, warmly. I said I’d think about it. I’ve been filming for nine years. I know what warmly means.

life.news: Watched my bake sale footage back and found four seconds I can’t explain. A woman at the back of the hall. I keep rewinding.
life.more: A woman in a headscarf, buying shortbread at the back of St Brigid’s hall. Four seconds. I didn’t notice her when I filmed it. Now I can’t stop noticing her. I showed Ashley and nobody else.

gossip.says: Ashley Grant does the real news at the bureau. I do the bake sales. Somebody has to be the calm one.
gossip.note: Pearl Hartley films the soft pieces at the bureau; Ashley Grant does the hard news.
gossip.ask: Pearl says she’s the calm one at the bureau.
gossip.answer: She is. I keep the tapes, she keeps me. She’s always three moves ahead and she never tells me what the moves are.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler and I fight over the same souvenir stall at the market. She lost the snow globe. She’s still not over it.
gossip.note: Pearl Hartley and Nixie Adler fight over the same souvenir stall at the market.
gossip.ask: Pearl says you lost the snow globe to her.
gossip.answer: She got there ten minutes early. That is not winning, that is cheating. I’m getting the alien next time. Tell her.

women.name: Imogen Reyes
women.look: Light-brown skin, honey-blonde beach waves, rosy cheeks, press lanyard and denim jacket

own.label: Ask what she paints
own.player: Do you paint?
own.reply: Watercolors of Brown Avenue. You can’t fix watercolor. One stroke and it’s there forever. I like that.

own.label: Ask what she researches at the station
own.player: What do you do at the radio station?
own.reply: Research. I find out things nobody asked about. Then I decide whether to tell anyone.

own.label: Ask why she doesn’t make small talk
own.player: Why are you so quiet?
own.reply: I’m terrible at small talk. In a crisis I’m perfect. Ask me something that matters.

calls.label: Ask about the picture she deleted
calls.player: What was the picture you deleted?
calls.reply: My sister Catalina, at the gate to the lodge on the ridge road, in her good dress, with a man from the club’s board holding the car door. She’d told us she was at the library. They’re going to offer her a husband. My family will say yes. She hasn’t worked that out yet.
calls.note: Imogen Reyes photographed her sister Catalina at the lodge gate with a board member, then deleted it.

life.news: Painted Brown Avenue in watercolor at dusk. The light on the laundromat came out exactly right. I kept it.
life.more: You can’t fix watercolor. One stroke and it’s there forever. That’s why I like it. I sat on the curb outside our house with my paints and did the whole street, my mother’s washing on the line, the neighbor’s dog. My mother said it looked like home. I think that’s the best review I’ll ever get.

life.news: Family dinner. Everyone talked about my sister’s future. Nobody asked her what she wanted.
life.more: Catalina is the clever one, the scholarship one, the one who’s going places. At dinner my mother and aunts talked about her like a stock that was going up. Catalina smiled and said nothing. I squeezed her hand under the table. She didn’t know what it meant. I did.

life.news: Borrowed the station’s camera for a story and took a picture I shouldn’t have. I deleted it. My hands shook.
life.more: I was taking pictures of the ridge road for a piece about potholes, and through the long lens I saw someone I know at a gate I didn’t expect. I took the picture before I understood it. Then I understood it. Then I deleted it, standing in the road, with a truck honking at me.

gossip.says: Bea Hollis indexes old tapes at the Daily’s archive and sings alto in a little choir. She’s the only person who can solve the hardest crossword in the paper. She solves it in pen.
gossip.note: Imogen Reyes says Bea Hollis solves the Daily’s hardest crossword in pen.
gossip.ask: Imogen says you solve the hardest crossword in the paper in pen.
gossip.answer: In pen, yes. If you’re going to be wrong, be wrong in ink and own it. The setter writes clues like she’s whispering to one person, and I’ve decided that person is me. Imogen sat with me in the archive once for four hours without speaking. Best company I’ve ever had.

gossip.says: Catalina Reyes is my eldest sister. She keeps a journal of a trip she hasn’t taken yet. She thinks she’s the one who knows what’s going on in our family. She’s the only one who doesn’t.
gossip.note: Imogen Reyes says her sister Catalina is the only one who doesn’t know what’s going on in their family.
gossip.ask: Imogen says you’re the only one in your family who doesn’t know what’s going on.
gossip.answer: That’s Imogen being mysterious. She’s been doing it since she was small. She squeezes my hand at dinner and won’t tell me why. If there’s something going on in my family, I’ll find out. I always do. I’m the one with the plan. Tell her to just say it.

women.name: Bea Hollis
women.look: Pale skin, short silver-dyed crop, gold hoop earrings, press lanyard and denim jacket

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: Do you sing?
own.reply: Alto, in a small choir of nine. We sing rounds in the old stone church. The building sings back.

own.label: Ask about the archive
own.player: What do you do at the archive?
own.reply: Index forty years of tapes the Daily kept. Half are labeled wrong. One labeled lunch is a mayor resigning.

own.label: Ask about her hobbies
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: The crossword, in pen. If you’re going to be wrong, be wrong in ink and own it.

own.label: Ask what happened to St. Brigid’s bell
own.player: Whatever happened to St. Brigid’s old bell?
own.reply: Lent to the town for the founders’ fair, forty years ago, by a bishop who liked the founders’ dinners. Nine women sang under it, the broadcast was cut, and the bell never went back up the tower. The diocese’s receipt says sold. The caretaker who rang it that day never collected his wages. I have the reel. The reel has the bell on it. I can’t prove where the bell is. I have a guess, and it has a dining room.
own.note: Bea Hollis says St. Brigid’s bell was lent for the founders’ fair forty years ago and never came back; the diocese’s receipt says sold, and the caretaker who rang it vanished.

calls.label: Ask about the recording of the round
calls.player: What’s the old recording you want restored?
calls.reply: The founders’ fair, forty years ago. Nine women singing a round, no names on the box. It warps in the middle, right where the tune changes into something I don’t recognize. I’ve asked the Sisters. They went very quiet and said it was a hymn. It isn’t a hymn.

life.news: Our little choir sang a round in the old church and the echo came back like a second choir. I got goosebumps.
life.more: Nine of us, one alto part, mine, in a stone church with terrible heating and perfect acoustics. We sang a round, and when we stopped, the building kept singing for three seconds. Nobody moved. The conductor didn’t say anything. That was the whole review.

life.news: Indexed four hundred tapes today. Two hundred were labeled wrong. One was labeled lunch.
life.more: The Daily kept every recording it ever made and labeled them like a squirrel hiding nuts. My job is to find out what’s actually on them. Today’s highlight was a tape marked lunch that turned out to be a mayor resigning. I’m going to rename it. Lunch was more accurate.

life.news: Found a recording from the founders’ fair, forty years ago. Nine voices singing a round. Ruined in the middle.
life.more: Nine women, no names on the box, singing an old round in harmony. It’s beautiful for two minutes, and then the tape warps and the voices stretch and go strange. I want it restored more than anything I’ve ever wanted at work. I want to know who they were.

gossip.says: Tova Lindqvist runs the Night Wire, the campus late paper, at twenty. She cooks for her whole staff from strange old cookbooks. She’s printed stories the Daily wouldn’t touch. She’s the bravest editor in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Bea Hollis says Tova Lindqvist printed stories in the Night Wire that the Daily wouldn’t touch.
gossip.ask: Bea says you’ve printed stories the Daily wouldn’t touch and you’re the bravest editor in Sunfall.
gossip.answer: I’m not brave, I just don’t have advertisers. It’s easier to be brave when nobody’s paying you to be quiet. Bea indexes every tape the Daily kept, and she knows exactly what they decided not to run. If she ever gives me her list, then I’ll be brave.

gossip.says: Harriet Boyle at the police archive sets the Daily’s cryptic crossword under a made-up name. Nobody knows but me. I solve every one. I think she’s started writing the clues for me.
gossip.note: Bea Hollis says Harriet Boyle secretly sets the Daily’s crossword, and she solves every one.
gossip.ask: Bea says you secretly set the Daily’s crossword, and she solves every one.
gossip.answer: Nobody is supposed to know that. Of course it’s Bea. She solves them in pen, I’ve heard. Fine. Yes. I have started writing a few clues just for her. It’s the only conversation I have that nobody else can overhear. It’s very nice. Please don’t ruin it.

women.name: Tova Lindqvist
women.look: Fair skin, jet-black waist-length hair, thin wire-rimmed glasses, black turtleneck and blazer

own.label: Ask about the Night Wire
own.player: What’s the Night Wire?
own.reply: The campus late paper. A basement, a press older than my parents, and two thousand copies a week. I’ve run it since I was nineteen.

own.label: Ask what she cooks
own.player: Do you cook?
own.reply: For my whole staff, from strange old cookbooks. Stew from 1910. Pudding from a war. They eat on the floor. It’s a newsroom tradition now.

own.label: Ask about complaints
own.player: Do people complain about your paper?
own.reply: Constantly, from both sides, on the same day. If everybody’s angry I’m probably doing it right.

calls.label: Ask about the name on her office door
calls.player: Whose name is painted over on your office door?
calls.reply: Founded with the support of Augustus Pell, in gold, under fresh white paint. Somebody painted it over the summer the Foundation’s books went to the auditors. Every plaque on campus with his name got the same treatment that summer. I have pictures of six.
calls.note: Tova Lindqvist found Augustus Pell’s name painted over on the Night Wire’s door and six other campus plaques.

life.news: Printed the Night Wire at three in the morning and the press didn’t jam. I kissed the press. On the side.
life.more: The Night Wire is the campus late paper and I’ve run it since I was nineteen, out of a basement with one press older than my parents. Tonight it ran clean, two thousand copies, no jam. I gave the staff a stew from a 1910 cookbook. They ate it on the floor. Best newsroom in America.

life.news: A student complained my paper was too political. Then another complained it wasn’t political enough. Same day.
life.more: If both sides are angry you’re probably doing journalism. If neither side is angry you’re doing the Desert Ledger. I wrote both of them very polite replies and ate a whole sleeve of cookies. Being the editor at twenty means being the adult in a room full of other twenty-year-olds.

life.news: There’s a name painted over on the Night Wire’s office door. The paint is newer than the door. I scraped a corner off.
life.more: Under the white paint, gold letters. Founded with the support of, and then a first name. I stopped scraping. I don’t know why. Something about seeing it come through the paint like a face in a window. I painted it back over. I took a picture first.

gossip.says: Polly Dashwood is the Ledger’s only investigative reporter. She takes ballroom dancing, very earnestly, and got humiliated at a press lunch by a man from the club in front of the whole county. She came back to work the next day. That’s brave.
gossip.note: Tova Lindqvist says Polly Dashwood was humiliated at a press lunch and came back to work the next day.
gossip.ask: Tova says you got humiliated at a press lunch and came back to work the next day.
gossip.answer: Where else would I go? Home, to cry into a cushion? I did that for one evening. Then I put on my dancing shoes and went to my class and did a very aggressive foxtrot. Tova printed my story when the Ledger wouldn’t. I’d follow that girl into a fire.

gossip.says: Delia Maher wrote the donor-lounge story I printed in the Night Wire. She’s eighteen, she shoots on film, and she has a voicemail from gala night she plays to nobody. She’s the best young reporter in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Tova Lindqvist says she printed Delia Maher’s donor-lounge story in the Night Wire.
gossip.ask: Tova says you’re the best young reporter in Sunfall and she printed your donor-lounge story.
gossip.answer: She printed it when nobody else would and she paid me in stew. It was a good stew. Tova runs a newsroom out of a basement with a press that jams if you look at it. She’s the only editor who’s ever said yes to me first and asked questions after.

women.name: Polly Dashwood
women.look: Freckled fair skin, chestnut curly bob, thin wire-rimmed glasses, cable-knit sweater and leather satchel

own.label: Ask about her dancing
own.player: Do you dance?
own.reply: Ballroom, at the studio in the Quarter. Foxtrot, waltz, a very earnest tango. It’s the one place nobody asks about my work.

own.label: Ask about investigating for the Ledger
own.player: What do you do at the Ledger?
own.reply: I’m its only investigator. Which means I investigate everything, alone, for a free paper that runs mattress ads.

own.label: Ask what she does when someone is cruel
own.player: What do you do when someone humiliates you?
own.reply: Smile, finish my soup, every spoonful, and then go and do my job better than they do theirs.

calls.label: Ask about the press lunch
calls.player: What happened at the Foundation’s press lunch?
calls.reply: Augustus Pell asked me, in front of every paper in the county, whether I’d been told how to read a balance sheet yet. I had asked him about the scholarship accounts. Everybody laughed. A week later an apology came, unsigned. Nobody apologizes unless you were close.
calls.note: Polly Dashwood asked Augustus Pell about the scholarship accounts at a press lunch; he humiliated her, and an unsigned apology followed.

life.news: Danced a whole foxtrot without looking at my feet. The teacher said, finally. I nearly cried.
life.more: The ballroom studio in the Quarter is the one place nobody asks me about my stories. You just count and turn and hold your frame. Tonight I did the whole thing with my chin up and my eyes on my partner. He was eighty. It was the most romantic moment of my month.

life.news: A man from the club humiliated me at a press lunch. In front of the whole county. I smiled and ate my soup.
life.more: He asked me a question about my own story as if I were a child who had wandered into the room, and the whole table laughed, and I smiled and ate my soup, very slowly, every spoonful. Then I went to the bathroom and shook. Then I went back and finished the soup. It was cold. I finished it.

life.news: Got a letter after the lunch. Unsigned. Apologizing. It was worse than the lunch.
life.more: Typed on good paper, delivered by hand. We regret any distress caused at the luncheon. That’s all. No name, no reason. An apology from nobody is a warning from somebody. I’ve kept it in my desk. I look at it when I need to be angry.

gossip.says: Marnie Quill is the youngest reviewer in the Old Quarter and she’s in love with every venue manager and most of the bands. She repairs watches on her day off with a bench full of women. She’s pure sunshine.
gossip.note: Polly Dashwood says Marnie Quill is in love with every venue manager and most of the bands.
gossip.ask: Polly says you’re in love with every venue manager and most of the bands.
gossip.answer: Not every venue manager. Most. And only the bands that deserve it. Polly says I’m sunshine like it’s a diagnosis. She’s the most earnest person I’ve ever met. She dances the foxtrot like it’s a court case. I mean that as the highest compliment.

gossip.says: Lara Newsome takes ballroom at the same studio as me. She waltzes like she’s marching on city hall. Our teacher is eighty and has given up on both of us. We practice together in the parking lot.
gossip.note: Polly Dashwood says she and Lara Newsome practice ballroom together in the parking lot.
gossip.ask: Polly says you two practice ballroom together in the parking lot.
gossip.answer: We do, and the teacher doesn’t know, so if you tell her I’ll deny it. Polly leads like she’s cross-examining me. It works, weirdly. We had a crowd once. Two men and a dog. The dog was the only one who clapped.

women.name: Marnie Quill
women.look: Pale skin, a high curly ponytail, tortoiseshell glasses, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask about reviewing
own.player: What do you write about?
own.reply: Music in the Old Quarter. I love every band. My editor says that’s not how reviewing works. I disagree.

own.label: Ask what she does on her day off
own.player: What do you do on your day off?
own.reply: Fix old watches at a bench with four other women and very tiny screwdrivers. When one ticks, we cheer.

own.label: Ask who she has a crush on
own.player: Do you have a crush on anyone?
own.reply: Every venue manager in the Old Quarter. Most of the bands. A couple of the bartenders. You’re in the running.

calls.label: Ask about the show her friend wants reviewed
calls.player: What show did your friend want you to review?
calls.reply: She wants me to review the Midnight Rite like a gig. A date, a meeting place, wear black. We were in the youth orchestra together, in matching blue bows. She said it’s the most beautiful music I’ll ever hear. She said it like she was frightened of it.
calls.note: Marnie Quill’s friend from the youth orchestra wants her to review the Midnight Rite like a gig.

life.news: Got an old wristwatch ticking at the bench today. Four women cheered. One of them cried. I cried too.
life.more: On my day off I go to a watch bench with a bunch of women and we fix old things very slowly with tiny screwdrivers. I’ve been on this one for a month. Today it ticked. It sounded like a heartbeat. I held it up and everyone clapped. I’m going to give it back to the old man who owns it tomorrow.

life.news: Wrote a gushing review of a band. My editor said I can’t give everyone five stars. I said but they were all good.
life.more: I love every band, that’s the problem. I go out every night to a room full of people trying, and I come home and want to tell the world. Zadie says a reviewer needs teeth. I have teeth. I just use them to smile. I’ve been told to be meaner. I’ll try. I won’t.

life.news: An old friend from the youth orchestra asked me to review a show. She wouldn’t say where. Just a date and a place to meet.
life.more: We played violin together when we were small, in the club’s youth orchestra, in matching blue bows. Now she’s very grown up and very serious and she wants me to review a show that isn’t in any listing. She said I’ll understand when I see it. I’m not sure I want to understand.

gossip.says: Corinne Gale takes pictures for the Ledger and runs a book club of women who read what the club’s book clubs won’t. She’s blunt. She told me my last review was gushing. She bought me a drink after. She’s like that.
gossip.note: Marnie Quill says Corinne Gale runs a book club of women who read what the club’s book clubs won’t.
gossip.ask: Marnie says you run a book club for women who read what the club won’t, and you told her she gushes.
gossip.answer: She does gush. It’s her best quality and her worst review style. My book club reads things that make you angry and then we drink wine and get less angry. The club’s book clubs read things that make you sleepy. Marnie came once and loved every book. Of course she did.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler runs the Furnace and she’s the scariest venue manager in the Old Quarter. She once threw a man out by his own belt. I’m a little bit in love with her. Don’t tell her. She’d throw me out too.
gossip.note: Marnie Quill says Nixie Adler is the scariest venue manager in the Old Quarter.
gossip.ask: Marnie says you’re the scariest venue manager in the Old Quarter and she’s a little in love with you.
gossip.answer: Everyone’s a little in love with me. It’s the eyeliner. Marnie is the only reviewer who comes to every single show and stands at the front and dances. The bands love her. I let her in free. If anyone ever bothers her, they leave by their own belt.

women.name: Corinne Gale
women.look: Rosy fair skin, platinum pixie cut, strong dark brows, chambray shirt and chinos

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: Are you in a book club?
own.reply: I run one. We read the books the club’s book clubs won’t touch. Angry books, sad books, books where the woman wins.

own.label: Ask about her photography
own.player: What do you photograph for the Ledger?
own.reply: Whatever the Daily leaves behind. One pass, a borrowed camera and a bus ticket. My pictures are better. They print theirs.

own.label: Ask why she’s so blunt
own.player: Are you always this blunt?
own.reply: Yes. It saves time. Then I buy you a drink, so it evens out.

calls.label: Ask about the photo she deleted
calls.player: What was in the reflection you deleted?
calls.reply: The gala, on the Ledger’s one pass. A shot through the dining room window, and in the glass, faint, me with my camera, and behind me two men walking a woman in a blue dress toward the kitchen. I panicked and deleted it. I deleted myself. I deleted her too.
calls.note: Corinne Gale deleted a gala photograph whose reflection showed two men walking a woman in a blue dress toward the kitchen.

life.news: My book club finished a novel about a woman who leaves her husband and opens a bar. Six women. Six standing ovations.
life.more: We read what the club’s book clubs won’t touch. Angry books, sad books, books where the woman wins and nobody apologizes. Tonight we drank too much and argued about the ending and one woman said she was going to leave her husband too. She was joking. Mostly. I bought her a drink.

life.news: Got one pass to cover a big event for the Ledger. One. The Daily got six. I took the bus there in my good shoes.
life.more: The Ledger is the free paper, so we get the leftovers. One pass, a borrowed camera and a bus ticket. I stood at the back between a plant and a fire exit and shot the whole thing over the heads of the Daily’s six photographers. My pictures were better. They printed theirs.

life.news: Took a photo at a party and realized afterwards I was in it, reflected in a window. I deleted it. The only time I’ve ever deleted myself.
