life.more: She can’t face them, so it has to be me. I’ve been their mother for years. I’ve made tea for every one of them and fixed every crooked solder. Now I have to stand up and say something that will make them all cry. I keep practicing in the mirror. I look terrible.

life.news: Developed an old roll from my camera bag and found a picture I don’t remember taking. The bench, at night, with someone working.
life.more: It’s from a while ago. The bench, lit by one lamp, and a woman bent over a mold I don’t recognize, pouring something bright. The face is turned away. I don’t remember taking it. I don’t remember anyone working that late. I’ve looked at it every night this week.

gossip.says: Eris Moon throws desert raves past the drive-in, on routes she maps herself so nobody can find them without her. She’s wry and watchful and dances like she’s the only one there. She’s brilliant.
gossip.note: Juno Varley says Eris Moon throws desert raves on routes she maps herself.
gossip.ask: Juno says you throw desert raves on routes you map yourself, so nobody can find them without you.
gossip.answer: That’s the point of a desert rave. If anyone can find it, it’s a festival, and then the police come and sell you a parking ticket. Juno came to one once in a velvet coat and stood at the edge taking photographs. She got the best shot I’ve ever seen of my own party.

gossip.says: Morrigan Hale makes silver bats and tiny coffins at the bench and makes collages out of old funeral cards. She was my apprentice once. She’s better than me now. I tell her so. She never believes it.
gossip.note: Juno Varley says Morrigan Hale was her apprentice and is better than her now.
gossip.ask: Juno says you were her apprentice and you’re better than her now.
gossip.answer: I’m not better. I’m younger, and my eyes still work without the loupe. Juno taught every woman at that bench to solder, and she photographed my first ring like it mattered. It didn’t matter to anyone but her and me. That’s exactly why it mattered.

women.name: Lilith Kestrel
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, dark brown messy bun, gray-green eyes, silver-buckled platform boots and black jeans

own.label: Ask about her back room
own.player: What’s the back room like?
own.reply: A venue for twenty and a bar for forty, at the back of the Old Quarter’s pool hall. I book the smallest nights in town and I run it like a tavern. Everyone in there owes me something.

own.label: Ask if she’s any good at pool
own.player: Are you any good at pool?
own.reply: I play for the washing-up. I win from everyone in the Quarter except one woman, and I do her washing-up for a week every time. I never mind.

own.label: Ask why she never lets anyone stay
own.player: Why don’t you ever let anyone stay over?
own.reply: Staying is the part I’m bad at. Somebody stays, somebody holds on, then somebody isn’t there in the morning. I’d rather say goodnight at the door and mean it.

calls.label: Ask about her father
calls.player: You never talk about your father.
calls.reply: He went up to the quarry on the ridge to work when I was eighteen and didn’t come home. My mother stopped saying his name, so I took hers. Kestrel. A man from the quarry got drunk in my back room once and said my father saw something up there he shouldn’t have. I haven’t let that man back in.

life.news: Sold out the back room for a band nobody’s heard of. Twenty in the room, forty at the bar, one encore nobody asked for.
life.more: Three women from the Night Wire crowd with a drum machine and a grudge. I booked them because the singer argued with me about the door split and won. Twenty people came, then forty, then the bar ran out of ice. They played the same song twice as the encore because they only have six. Nobody minded. I’m the hostess. That’s the job: make it feel like everyone was invited.

life.news: The licensing committee sent Wren another letter. I went across the road and shouted at nobody in particular.
life.more: Wren runs Black’s, across the road from my hall. Every spring the committee finds a new rule her bar breaks, and every spring she frames the letter and keeps pouring. This one is about the fire exit. There is a fire exit. I stood in the street and told the committee what I thought of it, at volume, to a lamppost. Wren brought me a lemonade and told me to come inside. She always does.

life.news: A camera from Black’s lost-property had one deleted picture on it. I’m nosy. I got it back.
life.more: Wren gave me the camera after it sat in her lost-property for a month. One frame had been deleted, and a man at the market showed me how to bring it back for a fiver. It’s my own back room, from the door, on a night with no moon: a woman in red at the pool table, and a man in a lanyard handing her a piece of paper. I don’t know what it is. It’s on a card in my chalk tin.

life.news: The woman in red came in again. I lost to her on purpose. She noticed.
life.more: She comes in alone, plays one game, never says her name, and I’ve never asked. She’s very good. Tonight I missed an easy black on purpose, just to keep her at the table another minute, and she looked at me like she knew exactly what I’d done. She put the cue back and said, don’t do that again. Then she bought me a drink. I don’t lose on purpose. I want that on the record.

gossip.says: Wren Black runs the bar across the road from my hall. Sober, steady, never once raised her voice. She lets me shout for both of us.
gossip.note: Lilith Kestrel says Wren Black, across the road at Black’s, lets her do the shouting for both of them.
gossip.ask: Lilith says you let her do the shouting for both of you.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to stay calm while she gets herself cautioned in the street. She thinks I keep the lights on late for the regulars. I keep them on so there’s a light across the road from her. Don’t tell her that.

gossip.says: Billie Wraith books the goth night at the casino lounge. My mother pours the drinks there. Neither of them mentions me, apparently.
gossip.note: Lilith Kestrel says her mother pours the drinks at the casino lounge where Billie Wraith books the goth night.
gossip.ask: Lilith says her mother pours the drinks at your goth night.
gossip.answer: She does. Never says a word about having a daughter. But she laughs exactly like Lilith, all at once and too loud, and every time she does it I nearly drop a record. I’ll never tell either of them.

women.name: Ezraine Quinn
women.look: Rosy fair skin, a sleek low bun, rosy cheeks, velvet choker and black slip dress

own.label: Ask about her jewelry
own.player: What do you make at the bench?
own.reply: Big, angry, beautiful pieces. Iron collars, cuffs like armor. The Old Quarter’s bands wear them on stage. That’s the brief. That’s me.

own.label: Ask why she won’t drive
own.player: Why the bicycle? Don’t you drive?
own.reply: Not in this town. Not with what cars are here. I’m rebuilding a bike from a skip instead. It mostly goes forward.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do you have family here?
own.reply: A sister I haven’t spoken to in eight years, and a mother in a village outside Naples. I left home at seventeen. Everyone thinks I chose the easy thing. They’re wrong.

calls.label: Ask about her mother’s cassette
calls.player: What’s on your mother’s cassette?
calls.reply: Half of it is the flood. The other half is her, singing a hymn in Italian in a kitchen I’ve never seen. It sounds old, older than her, like something from a church that isn’t there any more. Some nights I play it and I think I know the tune from somewhere in this town. Then it’s gone again.

life.news: A band wore my biggest piece on stage tonight. The singer swung it like a weapon. I nearly cried at the back of the Vestry.
life.more: I make big, angry, beautiful things at the Canal Bench, and the bands wear them. Tonight the singer from Raven’s band had my iron collar on and the light caught it on the last song. That’s the whole brief. That’s me.

life.news: Got the back wheel on the bicycle I’m rebuilding from a skip. It goes round. It goes round!
life.more: I won’t have a car. Not in this town, not with what cars are here. So I pulled a bicycle out of a skip and I’m rebuilding it on my living room floor. Yvette Palmer comes round with a spanner and tells me what I’m doing wrong. Tonight the wheel went round and we both cheered.

life.news: Someone keeps trying to tell me my mother is ill. Through other people. I think it’s my sister playing games.
life.more: My sister and I haven’t spoken in eight years. Our mother went back to her village outside Naples after our father died. Now strangers keep passing me messages that she’s ill. It’s exactly the kind of trick my sister would pull. It’s also exactly the kind of thing that’s true.

life.news: Played my mother’s old cassette again. Half of it went in the flood years ago. The half that’s left is her singing.
life.more: She sent me one cassette, once, of herself singing. It was in my bag when the dry river flooded. Now it’s half hiss and half her voice, a hymn in Italian I don’t know. It’s the only thing of hers I have. I keep thinking someone could clean it up. I keep not asking.

gossip.says: Yvette Palmer helps me rebuild my bicycle. She’s police. Don’t tell the bench.
gossip.note: Ezraine Quinn says Yvette Palmer helps her rebuild a bicycle.
gossip.ask: Ezraine says you help her rebuild her bicycle.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to. She’s been putting the chain on backwards for a month and calling it art. It nearly rides now. Tell her the brakes are next and I mean it.

gossip.says: Delia Maher could probably clean up my mother’s cassette. I haven’t asked her. I don’t know why.
gossip.note: Ezraine Quinn thinks Delia Maher could clean up her mother’s flood-damaged cassette.
gossip.ask: Ezraine thinks you could clean up her mother’s cassette.
gossip.answer: Half of it gone in a flood? I can get more back than she thinks. Tell her to bring it in. Tell her I won’t ask her anything about it.

women.name: Eris Moon
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, platinum pixie cut, thin wire-rimmed glasses, plum corset dress

own.label: Ask about her raves
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I throw desert raves out past the drive-in. I draw the maps myself. If you can’t follow a map you don’t deserve the party.

own.label: Ask about her favorite moment
own.player: What’s the best part of a rave?
own.reply: Sunrise. Everyone stops dancing to watch it, then starts again. Every time. That’s the whole reason I do it.

own.label: Ask why she watches instead of dancing
own.player: Do you dance at your own parties?
own.reply: I watch. Somebody has to know where everyone is, and where the generator is, and where the edge of the lake is.

calls.label: Ask about the group that watched the sky
calls.player: Who were the people in black at your rave?
calls.reply: A circle. They come to my raves now as a warm-up for something else, on nights there’s no moon. My very first rave, years ago, was paid for by a small grant from a man whose name has since come off the Quarter’s noticeboard. I didn’t ask then. I’m asking now.
calls.note: Eris Moon says a circle in black uses her desert raves as a warm-up on moonless nights.

life.news: Threw a rave out past the drive-in. Four hundred people found it with my map. The sunrise was pink. Perfect.
life.more: I draw the maps myself and hand them out a day before, and if you can’t follow a map you don’t deserve the party. Four hundred people, one generator, a dry lake bed and a DJ who played until the sun came up. Everyone stopped dancing to watch it. Then they started again. That’s my favorite moment, every time.

life.news: The generator died at the best part of the night. Silence. Four hundred people looking at me.
life.more: I fixed it in eleven minutes with a flashlight in my teeth while the crowd sang to fill the gap. Somebody started a song and four hundred strangers in the desert sang it together in the dark. Honestly the generator dying was the best thing that happened. I’m still going to buy a new generator.

life.news: A group in black turned up at my last rave. They didn’t dance. They stood at the edge and watched the sky.
life.more: Twenty of them, maybe, all in black, which at a rave isn’t strange, but they didn’t dance and they didn’t drink. They stood facing the dark side of the lake and talked very quietly. At four in the morning they left together, in a line. They’d followed my map perfectly.

gossip.says: Wren Black runs Black’s bar, where everyone in the Quarter ends up eventually. She has the best record collection in town, all forgotten singers. She’s sunny and stubborn and she’ll still serve you at closing if you look sad enough.
gossip.note: Eris Moon says Wren Black serves you after closing if you look sad enough.
gossip.ask: Eris says you’ll serve people after closing if they look sad enough.
gossip.answer: Only if they’re actually sad. I can tell. I’ve been behind that bar long enough. Eris comes in after her raves at sunrise with sand in her hair and orders coffee with a shot in it, and I’ve never once charged her for the shot. She throws the best parties in the state. She deserves a free shot.

gossip.says: Alice Wren DJs at my raves when she’s not playing the goth nights. Two hours of records nobody has ever heard of, and the whole desert dances anyway. She has the best ears in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Eris Moon says Alice Wren DJs at her raves with records nobody has heard of.
gossip.ask: Eris says you DJ her raves with records nobody has ever heard of and the whole desert dances.
gossip.answer: They’re records nobody has heard of yet. There’s a difference. Eris draws maps for her parties with little stars on them, by hand, four hundred copies. She’d never admit it, but she’s the most romantic woman in the Quarter. Her raves are love letters to the dark.

women.name: Marlowe Poe
women.look: Pale skin, glossy black ponytail, a small nose stud, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask about her jewelry
own.player: What do you make at the Canal Bench?
own.reply: Bells, mostly. Small silver ones that actually ring. Everyone else makes skulls. I was a historian of religion before I was a jeweler, so I make what I know.

own.label: Ask why she left the university
own.player: You were a lecturer? Why did you leave?
own.reply: I had a question I couldn’t ask in a seminar. So I left to ask it somewhere else. I’m still asking.

own.label: Ask about her thesis
own.player: What was your doctorate about?
own.reply: The religion of the women who founded Sunfall. Nobody cared for years. Then somebody did, in very beautiful handwriting. That’s a longer story.

calls.label: Ask what the founders’ book really says
calls.player: You said you advised them on a book. What does it say?
calls.reply: There’s a page about the husbands. I told them it was a metaphor. I advised it as a metaphor, for years, for a fee. Then I went to the Cemetery Chapel and read the names. It isn’t a metaphor. I’m the only living scholar who has read the whole thing, and I’m telling you because I’m tired of being the only one.

life.news: Taught my guitar student the history of the round along with the chords. She asked for just the chords. She got both.
life.more: I teach once a week for nothing. The deal is you get the music and the history whether you want them or not. Years ago I taught Kiki O’Dell the same way and sent her to the Furnace. Now she runs the open mic. I take full credit.

life.news: Finished a silver bell pendant at the Canal Bench. It actually rings. Small, but it rings.
life.more: Everyone at the bench makes skulls and moons. I make bells, because bells were my subject before jewelry was. The mission period, the founders, what they rang and why. This one is the size of a thumbnail and it rings one clean note. I may never sell it.

life.news: Someone asked for my old thesis again. The mission’s founding women and their rites. Nobody cared for years. Now everyone does.
life.more: I wrote my doctorate on the religion of the women who founded Sunfall, long before anyone thought it mattered. Rosa Gutierrez wants it for her own research. I’ve blocked the request. I have reasons. They’re not good ones, but they’re mine.

life.news: Went past the Cemetery Chapel tonight and stood at the gate for a while. Didn’t go in.
life.more: Years ago I was paid, in very beautiful handwriting, to advise a private study group on an old book. I told them a page was a metaphor. I advised it as a metaphor. I’ve stood at that chapel gate a few times since, wondering what else I got wrong.

gossip.says: I taught Kiki O’Dell guitar years ago and sent her to the Furnace. She runs the open mic now. I take all the credit.
gossip.note: Marlowe Poe taught Kiki O’Dell guitar and sent her to the Furnace.
gossip.ask: Marlowe says she taught you guitar and takes all the credit for the open mic.
gossip.answer: She taught me three chords and a history lecture every lesson. I kept the chords. I still know more about the mission bells than anyone at the Furnace needs to.

gossip.says: Harriet Boyle grew up across the street from me. Our fathers had rival bookshops. Both are vape shops now.
gossip.note: Marlowe Poe and Harriet Boyle grew up across the street from each other, in rival bookshops.
gossip.ask: Marlowe says your fathers had rival bookshops.
gossip.answer: They did. Hers sold mysteries, mine sold sermons. Both sell vapes now. Marlowe says that’s the most honest thing that ever happened on that street.

women.name: Wren Black
women.look: Pale skin, copper waist-length waves, strong dark brows, studded leather jacket

own.label: Ask about Black’s
own.player: What’s Black’s like?
own.reply: Everyone in the Quarter ends up at my bar eventually. Riddles on the beer mats, pool in the corner, horror films in the back.

own.label: Ask about her records
own.player: What music do you play?
own.reply: Forgotten singers. One album, then nothing. Last week an old man heard his mother’s voice for the first time. I gave him the record.

own.label: Ask about closing time
own.player: Do you ever serve after closing?
own.reply: If you look sad enough. Actually sad. I can tell. I’ve been behind this bar a long time.

calls.label: Ask who wants her back room
calls.player: Who wants your back room on a dark night?
calls.reply: An old friend from school who’s in a circle now. No projector, no film, just the chairs in a ring and the lights off, on the next night there’s no moon. She offered me more money than the bar makes in a month. She already knew the room. She’s been in it before.
calls.note: Wren Black was asked to lend Black’s back room to a circle on the next moonless night.

life.news: Played a record from 1971 at the bar by a singer nobody remembers. A man at the end cried into his beer. It was his mother.
life.more: I collect forgotten singers, one album and gone, and I play them in the bar at night. Tonight an old man asked what it was and I told him and he went white. That was my mother, he said. He’d never heard her record. I gave it to him. Best thing I’ve ever done behind that bar.

life.news: The five-on-five team celebrated at Black’s after a win. I’m still finding cleats in the bathroom.
life.more: They won, which means they sang, which means they stood on my chairs. I love them. I also have a broken stool and a fern that will never recover. The police women are worse than the campus girls. The campus girls at least apologize. The police women just tip enormously and leave.

life.news: An old friend wants my back room on a dark night. Not for the horror film. She was very clear it isn’t a film.
life.more: The back room has a projector and forty chairs, and on horror nights it’s the best room in the Quarter. She wants it empty, just the chairs in a circle and the lights off. She said it’s private. She said a number that made me sit down. I said I’d think. I don’t want to think about it.

gossip.says: Milena Kovac is the oldest jeweler at the bench. She came to Sunfall eight years ago from a city nobody’s ever asked her about. She collects postcards of towns she says she’s lived in. There are a lot of towns.
gossip.note: Wren Black says Milena Kovac collects postcards of towns she says she’s lived in.
gossip.ask: Wren says you collect postcards of towns you say you’ve lived in, and there are a lot of towns.
gossip.answer: There are a lot of towns because I’ve lived a lot of lives. Wren pours me a vodka every week and never asks which city I left. That’s the kind of bartender you keep for life. She plays records by women who vanished. I understand those women better than she knows.

gossip.says: Miranda Sowerby plays pool in my bar every week. She’s community safety for the police and she’s the only cop the Quarter actually likes. She raised her niece alone. She never wins at pool. She never stops trying.
gossip.note: Wren Black says Miranda Sowerby plays pool at Black’s every week and never wins.
gossip.ask: Wren says you play pool at her bar every week and never win.
gossip.answer: I win sometimes. Rarely. Mostly I lose and hear things. A pool table is better than a briefing. Wren knows everything that happens in the Quarter and tells me none of it, which is exactly right. She’s the safest bar in town because of her. I’d never say that in front of my sergeant.

women.name: Milena Kovac
women.look: Rosy fair skin, short silver-dyed crop, a wide bright smile, black mesh top and tartan skirt

own.label: Ask about her postcards
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Postcards of towns I’ve lived in. There are quite a lot. Nobody at the bench asks which ones are true. That’s why I love them.

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you make?
own.reply: Silver, at the bench by the canal. I’m the oldest there. I make the heavy pieces. The others make the pretty ones.

own.label: Ask where she’s from
own.player: Where are you from originally?
own.reply: Here. I’ve been here eight years. Before that is a postcard on my wall. Ask me something else.

calls.label: Ask about the picture she deleted
calls.player: What was in the picture you deleted at the record stall?
calls.reply: A man buying a whole box of the radio station’s old tapes, the station’s sticker on every spine, and Kelsey Donovan paying for them. The archivist from the police paying for tapes with a roll of cash. I deleted it before she saw. I remember every tape on the top row.
calls.note: Milena Kovac saw Kelsey Donovan pay cash for a box of the radio station’s old tapes at the record stall.

life.news: Found a postcard at the stall of a town I once lived in. Same café. Same awning. I sat there with it for an hour.
life.more: I don’t talk about where I came from, and nobody at the bench asks, which is why I love them. But today there it was in a shoebox for a dollar: the square, the café, the awning I sat under at twenty. I bought it. I put it on my wall with the others. I didn’t cry. I nearly cried.

life.news: A man at the market asked where my accent is from. I said here. He laughed. I didn’t.
life.more: Eight years in Sunfall and still people ask. I say here because it’s true. I make silver here, I eat here, I pay my rent here. Where I was before is a postcard on my wall. He meant it kindly, probably. I went back to the bench and soldered something very small and very angry.

life.news: Borrowed a camera at the record stall to photograph a sleeve. Took one more frame by accident. Deleted it. I still see it.
life.more: Kelsey from the police archive lent me her little compact, and I took the record sleeve, and then my finger slipped and caught the man next to her buying a box of tapes. I deleted it before she saw. I don’t know why. Something about his hands, and how many tapes.

gossip.says: Vesper Lane runs the burlesque night in the Rialto’s ballroom and restores every dress they dance in. She’s quick to laugh and very slow to trust. She once told a man who tried to grab a dancer exactly where his car was parked. He left.
gossip.note: Milena Kovac says Vesper Lane runs the burlesque night at the Rialto and restores the dancers’ dresses.
gossip.ask: Milena says you run the burlesque night at the Rialto and restore every dress they dance in.
gossip.answer: Every one, by hand, sequin by sequin. A burlesque dress has to come off beautifully a hundred times. Milena made us all silver pasties for our anniversary night and refused payment. She’s from somewhere nobody asks about and she’s the most generous woman I know.

gossip.says: Kelsey Donovan from the police archive lent me her compact camera at the record stall. She’s very quiet and she’s had a lot of money lately. She was buying tapes. A lot of tapes.
gossip.note: Milena Kovac says Kelsey Donovan lent her a camera at the record stall and was buying a lot of tapes.
gossip.ask: Milena says you lent her your camera at the record stall and you were buying a lot of tapes.
gossip.answer: I like music. Is that a crime now? I lent her the camera to be nice. She’s from somewhere far away and doesn’t talk about it, so I thought she’d understand privacy. Apparently not. Tell her the camera came back one picture short. I noticed.

women.name: Vesper Lane
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, long red curls, strong dark brows, plum corset dress

own.label: Ask about her burlesque night
own.player: What’s the burlesque night like?
own.reply: Red velvet, gold leaf, a sticky floor and the best audience in Sunfall. Last week a table of grandmothers tipped in butterscotch.

own.label: Ask about the costumes
own.player: Who makes the costumes?
own.reply: I restore every one. Burlesque dresses have to come off beautifully a hundred times. My fingers look like I fought a cactus.

own.label: Ask why she’s slow to trust
own.player: Why are you so careful with people?
own.reply: I work in a room full of people looking at women. You learn fast which ones are looking and which ones are watching.

calls.label: Ask about the voice on the house tape
calls.player: Whose voice is on the burlesque night’s house tape?
calls.reply: Theon’s. He lives above the ballroom, in the apartment over the old Rialto, and he reads verse through the floor every night. On the last tape he says my name, slowly, and a line about a woman in red with a needle. I was in red. I was sewing. He was watching through something.
calls.note: Vesper Lane’s burlesque house tape caught Theon saying her name in verse through the Rialto ballroom ceiling.

life.news: Burlesque night sold out. Every dancer hit every mark. One of them got a standing ovation from a table of grandmothers.
life.more: I run it in the old ballroom at the Rialto, red velvet and gold leaf and a floor sticky with history, and I restore every dress they dance in. Tonight a table of women from a retirement home booked the front row and screamed louder than anyone. One of them tipped in butterscotch. I kept the butterscotch.

life.news: Sewed sequins onto a costume for six hours. A dancer wore it for four minutes. Worth it. Ow.
life.more: Every burlesque dress has to come off beautifully a hundred times, which means everything is reinforced, everything is hand-stitched, and my fingers look like I lost a fight with a cactus. My hands ache. The dancer said it felt like wearing a chandelier. That’s the job.

life.news: The night’s house tape picked up a man’s voice from upstairs saying my name. In verse.
life.more: We record every show off the desk, for the dancers. On the last tape, between songs, there’s a man’s voice from the room above the ballroom, through the ceiling, slow and clear. He says my name. Then a line about a woman in red with a needle. I was wearing red. I was sewing.

gossip.says: Dahlia Grieve runs the goth night at the bar on the motel strip and photographs the strip’s neon when she’s not working. She’s very private and very sharp. I’ve never once seen her surprised.
gossip.note: Vesper Lane says Dahlia Grieve runs the goth night on the motel strip and photographs its neon.
gossip.ask: Vesper says she’s never once seen you surprised.
gossip.answer: I’m surprised all the time. I just don’t do it with my face. Vesper does everything with her face and her hands and her whole body, which is why she runs a burlesque night and I run a goth night. She once made me a velvet glove from scraps. I’ve never taken it off. That’s a lie. I take it off to wash.

gossip.says: Rhea Cooper restores vintage dresses in a workshop off the square. When I can’t save a costume, I take it to her. She fixed a beaded dress from the twenties that I’d given up on. I owe her forever.
gossip.note: Vesper Lane says Rhea Cooper fixed a twenties beaded dress she had given up on.
gossip.ask: Vesper says you fixed a beaded dress from the twenties she had given up on, and she owes you forever.
gossip.answer: She doesn’t owe me anything. She brought it in with every loose bead in a jar, counted, which nobody does. That’s respect for a dress. She also restores sequins on burlesque costumes by hand, which is madness. Lovely madness. We should start a club.

women.name: Hex Morrow
women.look: Olive skin, chestnut high ponytail, amber eyes, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I’m the newest at the Canal Bench. I make the small things. Charms, clasps, whatever the others are too bored to cast. I’m very good at small things.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A room above the Furnace. Nixie found it for me. The music comes up through the floor every night and I sleep like a stone. Nixie regrets it. I can tell.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: I bake for a book club. Elaborate cakes. They collapse. Billie serves them in bowls and nobody complains to my face.

own.label: Ask what she wants out of life
own.player: What do you want out of life?
own.reply: To be chosen. And I have been. Someone very important told me I’m the future. I believe her. Do you know what that feels like, to be picked?

own.label: Ask about the most reckless thing she’s done
own.player: What’s the most reckless thing you’ve done?
own.reply: I opened a letter that came to the Furnace for a girl called Maren. An invitation to dinner at the lodge. I answered it. As her. It sounded like an adventure. Now they think Maren Caldwell is coming to dinner, and I’m going instead.
own.note: Hex Morrow answered a lodge dinner invitation addressed to Maren Caldwell, as Maren, and plans to go in her place.

calls.label: Ask what she’s proudest of
calls.player: What are you proudest of?
calls.reply: I made a mold. You pour chalk in, it sets in a perfect shape, and you can draw the same mark on a door in two seconds, exactly the same every time. Clever, right? I’m not allowed to say what it’s for.
calls.note: Hex Morrow casts chalk in a mold so the same mark can be drawn on doors in seconds.

calls.label: Ask about her old school friends
calls.player: Do you keep in touch with school friends?
calls.reply: Arielle. We sat two desks apart. She’s at the paper now, very serious. She asked me why I wanted a box of clippings lost. I said because someone asked. That was the whole reason. It still is.
calls.note: Hex Morrow asked Arielle Brooks to lose a box of clippings because someone in the circle told her to.

life.news: The band at the Furnace played my request three times tonight. I danced on a table. Nixie pretended not to see.
life.more: Velvet coat, boots, a table that was definitely not built for dancing. Somebody filmed it. I look like a storm in a coat. Nixie made me sweep the floor afterward, which I did, still dancing.

life.news: Cake collapsed again. Lemon this time. It folded in half like it was ashamed of me.
life.more: I’d followed the recipe exactly, which never helps. Billie looked at it for a long moment and got out the bowls without a word. Everyone ate it. Nobody looked me in the eye. I cried in the alley for a minute and then I was fine.

life.news: My parents called and asked if I’m eating. Then asked if I’m dating anyone. Then asked about the weather.
life.more: In that order, in the same tone. I said yes, no and hot. My mother said good to all three. I don’t think she was listening. I don’t think she wanted to be.

life.news: Cast forty silver bats in one afternoon. Juno says it’s a bench record. I’m insufferable now.
life.more: Little ones, wings out, for earrings. My fingers are black and I burned my thumb twice and I’ve never been happier. Juno bought me a soda as a prize. I keep the can on my windowsill.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler found me my room above the Furnace and has been regretting it ever since. She pretends not to watch me dance on the tables. She watches.
gossip.note: Hex Morrow says Nixie Adler found her a room above the Furnace.
gossip.ask: Hex says you found her a room and regret it.
gossip.answer: I regret the tables. Not the girl. Hex is a storm in a velvet coat and storms need somewhere to break. Better above my bar than somewhere worse. I leave the back door open for her. She hasn’t needed it yet.

gossip.says: Arielle Brooks sat two desks from me at school. Now she works at the paper and looks at me like I’m a story she hasn’t decided to write.
gossip.note: Hex Morrow says Arielle Brooks, her old school friend, works at the paper.
gossip.ask: Hex says you look at her like a story you haven’t written yet.
gossip.answer: I do, and I hate that I do. She was the funniest girl in our year, and now she says things like she’s been chosen. I keep waiting for her to call me. I think one day she will, and I think I won’t like what she says.

women.name: Dahlia Grieve
women.look: Porcelain skin, short silver-dyed crop, gray-green eyes, velvet choker and black slip dress

own.label: Ask about her goth night
own.player: What do you run?
own.reply: The goth night at the bar on the motel strip. Dark room, loud records, and nobody tells anyone to smile.

own.label: Ask what she photographs
own.player: What do you photograph?
own.reply: The strip’s neon at night. VACANCY, arrows, a cowboy that hasn’t lit up properly in years. Two of everything when it rains.

own.label: Ask why she’s so quiet
own.player: Why don’t you say much?
own.reply: Quiet works better than loud. People lean in to hear you. Then you have them.

calls.label: Ask about room twelve
calls.player: What’s in room twelve on the motel strip?
calls.reply: I didn’t know until the letter. Then I went through my pictures. The night of the gala, room twelve has its light on and a car outside I’d never seen on the strip. A woman’s shape at the curtain. Every night since, the curtain is closed and the light is off. Somebody paid cash for it.
calls.note: Dahlia Grieve’s photos show room twelve on the motel strip lit on gala night, with a woman at the curtain.

life.news: Photographed the motel strip’s neon in the rain. Every sign doubled in the puddles. Two of everything.
life.more: On the nights I’m not running the goth night, I walk the strip with my camera. Tonight it rained, which happens about twice a year here, and every VACANCY and every arrow lay in the road twice, once up and once down. I took forty pictures. Lorna and Paz were out too. We didn’t speak. We didn’t need to.

life.news: A man at the goth night told me I’d be prettier if I smiled. I told him he’d be prettier if he left. He left.
life.more: I run a dark room for people who are tired of being told to smile, and then a man walks in and does it, in my room, to me. I said it very quietly. Quiet works better than loud. He finished his drink and went. A girl at the bar bought me a shot. We toasted.

life.news: A letter came to my apartment with no name. It said the strip isn’t a place for a girl who looks at room twelve.
life.more: I don’t look at room twelve. I didn’t know I was looking at room twelve. I photograph the whole strip, every sign, every door. Now I’ve gone through my pictures, and room twelve is in a lot of them. The curtain is always closed. Somebody has noticed what I noticed before I did.

gossip.says: Ophelia Byrne makes jewelry at the bench by the canal and cooks for the whole bench every week from weird old cookbooks. She’s sunny, stubborn and she once sent me home with a pie when I looked sad. I wasn’t sad. I ate the pie.
gossip.note: Dahlia Grieve says Ophelia Byrne sent her home with a pie when she looked sad.
gossip.ask: Dahlia says you sent her home with a pie when she looked sad, and she ate the pie.
gossip.answer: She was sad. She’s always a little bit sad, behind the eyeliner. Everyone at the bench is. That’s why I cook. Dahlia doesn’t smile, but she sends a photograph of a neon sign to my phone every time she sees one shaped like a heart. That’s her version of smiling. I have eleven.

gossip.says: Paz Herrera photographs the motel strip’s neon at night like I do. We stand on opposite sides of the road with our cameras and never talk. She’s the only person I’d trust with my negatives.
gossip.note: Dahlia Grieve says she and Paz Herrera photograph the motel strip’s neon from opposite sides of the road.
gossip.ask: Dahlia says you two photograph the strip from opposite sides of the road and never talk.
gossip.answer: We don’t need to talk. We nod. Sometimes she points at something with her chin and I photograph it. Dahlia gets the doors and I get the signs. Between us we’ve got the whole strip. I trust her more than people I’ve known for twenty years. She’s never once wasted a word.

women.name: Sorrel Vane
women.look: Deep brown skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, tortoiseshell glasses, black lace corset top

women.name: Kayla Mendoza
women.look: Dark skin, blunt black bob, gray-green eyes, floral blouse and jeans

women.name: Brittany Hale
women.look: Light-brown skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, sharp winged eyeliner, turquoise peasant top

own.label: Ask about her souvenirs
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Roadside souvenirs! A snow globe of a cactus, a spoon from a motel that burned down, a fridge magnet of the bear. I need help.

own.label: Ask about being a florist
own.player: What’s the best part of being a florist?
own.reply: Weddings. The worst part is weddings. Brides cry, mothers cry, I cry, the flowers wilt.

own.label: Ask what’s confusing her
own.player: Is something confusing you?
own.reply: Two people told me completely different stories about the same night of the gala. One of them is lying, and they both bought peonies.

own.label: Ask what flowers say that people can’t
own.player: What do flowers say that people can’t?
own.reply: Sorry, mostly. I sell more sorry than love. Men walk in looking at the floor and point at the roses.

own.label: Ask where she finds her souvenirs
own.player: Where do you find your souvenirs?
own.reply: The same market on Sundays. There’s a whole gang of us who buy spoons and snow globes and never once talk about anything but spoons. It’s very restful.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: What’s your sister like?
own.reply: Beatrice runs on a bad knee and good coffee. She told me a man at the club once called me a lovely sister. It wasn’t a compliment. She bought me a door chain.

calls.label: Ask about the two peony buyers
calls.player: Who were the two customers with different stories?
calls.reply: Eloise Rainer said she was at the kitchen door laughing with a man who left through it. Simone Ellery swore nobody left by the kitchen and Eloise wasn’t even there. Both bought peonies for the same table. One of them is lying. I write down what customers tell me, for the cards. Mr. Kell came in twice for peonies too.
calls.note: Brittany Hale heard Eloise Rainer and Simone Ellery give opposite accounts of the club’s kitchen door on gala night.

life.news: Bought a snow globe of a motel that burned down. My shelf now has a theme: places that no longer exist.
life.more: A snow globe of a cactus, a spoon from a motel that burned down, a fridge magnet of the bear. I need help. There’s a market where women like me fight over the same stall. I lost a gas station globe last month and I’m still not over it.

life.news: Did the flowers for a wedding where everyone cried, including the flowers. They wilted by the speeches.
life.more: Weddings in the desert. Everyone cries and the flowers wilt. The groom’s dad said the roses looked how he felt. I gave him one for his buttonhole. He wore it all night, completely flat. Best photo of the day.

life.news: Sold more sorry than love today. Six men. Six bunches. Six apologies.
life.more: Men walk in on the way home after doing something stupid. I can tell what they did from what they buy. Roses, he forgot something. Lilies, he’s in real trouble. Today one man bought both. I gave him a card and a pen and a stern look.

life.news: Beatrice came into the shop and rated my flowers like a coffee. She gave the tulips an eight. Highest she’s ever given anything.
life.more: My big sister rates everything out of ten. Coffee, people, my life choices. Eight for tulips is basically a medal. I made her a little bunch to take to the office. She said it was a seven out of ten bunch. She kept it on her desk all week.

gossip.says: My sister Beatrice Hale rates every coffee in Sunfall out of ten. She once rated our mom’s Christmas dinner a six. Mom hasn’t forgiven her. It was a six.
gossip.note: Brittany Hale says her sister Beatrice Hale once rated their mom’s Christmas dinner a six.
gossip.ask: Brittany says you rated your mom’s Christmas dinner a six out of ten.
gossip.answer: It was a six! The sprouts were a crime and I’m a journalist, I can’t lie in print or at the table. Brittany gave it a nine to make up for me and Mom gave her extra dessert. Sources are sacred. So is dessert.

gossip.says: Elena Vargas runs the other flower shop and we share a van. She’s much gentler than me. She knows what every flower means. I just know which ones say sorry.
gossip.note: Brittany Hale says she and Elena Vargas share a flower van.
gossip.ask: Brittany says you know what every flower means and she only knows which ones say sorry.
gossip.answer: Sorry is a very important meaning. Most people only buy flowers when something big happens: love, death, apology. Brittany handles the apologies, I do the rest. She makes people laugh while she wraps them. That’s worth more than knowing what a hyacinth means.

women.name: Nina Petrov
women.look: Rosy fair skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, thin wire-rimmed glasses, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about her bakery
own.player: How did a pastry chef end up in the desert?
own.reply: I followed a man here from St. Petersburg. The man left. The ovens stayed. I chose the ovens.

own.label: Ask about her painting
own.player: You paint watercolors?
own.reply: Desert landscapes. Watercolor is like this town: you can’t correct a mistake, only paint over it and hope.

own.label: Ask about the torn page
own.player: Why do you keep a torn notebook?
own.reply: A customer left a notebook at the counter with one page torn out. The next page shows the impression of the writing: a list of table numbers and a time I can’t read.
own.note: Nina Petrov has a notebook left at her counter; the page after a torn-out one shows an impression of table numbers.

own.label: Ask what she’d do over
own.player: If you could do one thing over, what would it be?
own.reply: I’d have said yes to a man who asked me to dance at a wedding in my twenties. I said I was tired. I wasn’t tired.

own.label: Ask what the bakery is known for
own.player: What should I order at your bakery?
own.reply: The rye, and the Napoleon. The club orders the Napoleon for its small dinners. The Sisters order rye for the volunteers. I prefer the Sisters.

own.label: Ask when she paints
own.player: When do you paint?
own.reply: At dawn, before the dough. Badly, which is the point. Watercolor is like this town: you can’t fix a mistake, only paint over it and hope.

calls.label: Ask about the notebook in her till
calls.player: What’s in the notebook you keep in the register?
calls.reply: A customer left it a week before the benefit. A page was torn out, but the next page holds the shape: Table 9, Table 4, Table 1, a time, and the word kitchen. The customer was Elena Cross. I’ve kept it with the takings.
calls.note: Nina Petrov has Elena Cross’s notebook; the page beneath a torn one shows Table 9, Table 4, Table 1, a time, and kitchen.

calls.label: Ask about the dinner she said no to
calls.player: Has anyone asked you out lately?
calls.reply: A widower from the casino’s board, Terence Ash. He wanted one honest meal before the club’s. I said I was tired. A lady from the club is planning to marry him, they say. I didn’t want to be the honest meal.
calls.note: Nina Petrov says the casino widower Terence Ash is expected to marry into the club.

life.news: Painted the desert at dawn before the dough. Made a mistake. Couldn’t fix it. Painted a cloud over it.
life.more: Watercolor is like this town: you can’t correct a mistake, only paint over it and hope. The cloud is now my favorite part. It looks like a dog. My actual dog looked at it and barked. High praise.

life.news: My mother rang from home and asked if I was eating. I said I make bread for a living. She said, that’s not eating.
life.more: She rings once a week and asks the same three things. Am I eating, am I married, am I coming home. No, no and no. Then she tells me about her neighbor’s cat. Ten years, the same call. I’d be lost without it.

life.news: Beat Julia at cards. Took her croissants. She said I cheat. I count. It’s different.
life.more: The pastry chefs in town have a card school. We’re rivals all week and friends for one evening. Julia plays very slowly and with feeling. I win. She pays in croissants. I eat them and tell her they’re too buttery. They’re perfect.

life.news: Danced alone in the bakery after closing. I said no to a dance once, when I was young. I think about it.
life.more: At a wedding, years ago, a man asked me to dance. I said I was tired. I wasn’t tired. I was scared it would matter. I followed a different man across the world instead and he left. The ovens stayed. Tonight I danced with the ovens.

gossip.says: Julia Mercer is my rival and she bakes like she’s in love with the dough. She has a secret name for her future café in a drawer. I know what it is. I’ll never tell her I know.
gossip.note: Nina Petrov says she secretly knows the name Julia Mercer has chosen for her café.
gossip.ask: Nina says she knows the secret name for your café.
gossip.answer: She does NOT. Nobody knows. It’s in a drawer. Does she? How? Oh, the card night, I said it in my sleep on the sofa. Tell her if she steals it I’ll put salt in her sugar tin. Actually, tell her nothing. I’m changing the name.

gossip.says: Sophia Moretti from the Sisters bakes the parish bread with her family and her ovens are older than mine. She came to borrow flour once and stayed to pray for my sourdough starter. It’s never been better.
gossip.note: Nina Petrov says Sophia Moretti once prayed for her sourdough starter.
gossip.ask: Nina says you prayed for her sourdough starter and it’s never been better.
gossip.answer: Well, it looked so sad! God bless every living thing, and a starter is a living thing. It just needed some kindness and a warmer shelf. Nonna says all bread is a prayer. Nina says all bread is chemistry. We’re both right. The starter doesn’t mind.

women.name: Jessica Rivera
women.look: Olive skin, rose-gold bob, a beauty mark above her lip, striped T-shirt dress

own.label: Ask what the pharmacy is like
own.player: What’s it like working in a pharmacy?
own.reply: People tell me things they wouldn’t tell their doctor while I find their ointment. I know half of Sunfall’s secrets and all of its rashes.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Second soprano, hidden at the back. I mouth the high notes. Nobody has noticed in four years, or they’re too polite to say.

own.label: Ask if she’s shy or just careful
own.player: Are you shy, or just careful?
own.reply: Both. I rehearse phone calls in the shower. I once said you too to a waiter who told me to enjoy my meal. I still think about it.

own.label: Ask what she’d do if she weren’t scared
own.player: What would you do if you weren’t scared?
own.reply: Sing a solo. Just once. Loud, at the front, with everyone looking. Then probably faint.

own.label: Ask how she got the job
own.player: How did you end up at the pharmacy?
own.reply: My uncle’s a pharmacist and got me in. Dad fixes the museum’s lifts, Mom runs the parish school office. A very quiet family. I fit right in.

own.label: Ask about rehearsing calls
own.player: Do you really rehearse phone calls?
own.reply: In the shower, every time. I once said you too to a waiter who told me to enjoy my meal. I still think about it at night.

own.label: Ask about her mom and the parish school
own.player: Does your mom hear things at the parish school?
own.reply: Everything. The chancery’s questions for the school came through her desk: which teachers go to the first-light Mass, whether the infants are learning the concert piece, who signed the Sisters’ letter. Mom typed the answers slowly. Very slowly. She has been slow for ten weeks now.
own.note: Jessica Rivera says the chancery’s questionnaire for the parish school asked which teachers go to the first-light Mass and who signed the Sisters’ letter.

calls.label: Ask what the lodge’s van collects
calls.player: What does the van from the ridge pick up?
calls.reply: Every night with no moon: burn dressings, sutures, sedatives on a prescription from a doctor I’ve never seen. Once a veterinary tranquilizer we don’t stock, ordered in from a vet in the city. I copy the prescriptions. I’m quiet. I copy things.
calls.note: Jessica Rivera says the lodge’s van collects burn dressings, sutures, sedatives and once a veterinary tranquilizer on moonless nights.

life.news: A customer told me something they wouldn’t tell their doctor while I found their ointment. Again. It’s the counter.
life.more: People tell me things while I’m looking for their cream. I know half of Sunfall’s secrets and all of its rashes. I never tell. I just nod and say, aisle three. I think the shelves make people feel like they’re in confession.

life.news: Rehearsed a phone call in the shower for twenty minutes. Then the person didn’t answer.
life.more: I rehearse every call. What I’ll say, what they’ll say, the polite goodbye. I had it perfect. It went to voicemail and I panicked and said, you too. To a voicemail. I’m going to live under the counter now.

life.news: Sang the high note in choir today. Out loud. Nobody fainted.
life.more: Second soprano, hidden at the back, mouthing the high notes for four years. Today I forgot to mouth it and it just came out. Teresa turned around and looked so happy I nearly cried. I went straight back to mouthing. One note at a time.

life.news: Paige from the movie theater brought me popcorn at the end of her shift. I brought her bandages. Best trade in Sunfall.
life.more: The all-night pharmacy is next door to the movie theater. She burns her hands on the popcorn machine and I burn my brain on the night shift. We meet on the sidewalk at closing and swap supplies like spies. She tells me the endings of films. I never know the starts.

gossip.says: Paige Dalton works at the movie theater next door and knows how every film ends and how none of them start. She cries at endings of films she’s never seen. I think she’s the kindest person on the street.
gossip.note: Jessica Rivera says Paige Dalton at the movie theater cries at endings of films she hasn’t seen.
gossip.ask: Jessica says you cry at the endings of films you’ve never seen.
gossip.answer: I don’t need the start to know it matters! If someone’s running through an airport at the end, they made it, and I’m happy for them. Jessica’s the kind one. She gives me bandages and never asks how I burned myself. It’s always the popcorn machine.

gossip.says: Raven Solis sings alto in our choir in black lipstick. The old ladies were scared of her for a month. Now they knit her scarves. She has the most beautiful voice in the church.
gossip.note: Jessica Rivera says Raven Solis sings alto in black lipstick at St. Brigid’s.
gossip.ask: Jessica says you have the most beautiful voice in the church.
gossip.answer: Jessica has the most beautiful voice in the church. She just doesn’t use it. I hear her when she forgets to mouth. I don’t say anything, because I don’t know what to say. But I hear her. Tell her that.

gossip.says: Teresa Bellamy runs the choir roster and keeps threatening to put me down for a solo. The one about the lighthouse. I’d die. She knows I’d die. She keeps threatening anyway.
gossip.note: Jessica Rivera says Teresa Bellamy keeps threatening to give her a solo.
gossip.ask: Jessica says you keep threatening to give her the lighthouse solo.
gossip.answer: It isn’t a threat, it’s faith! She has a lovely voice and she hides it at the back like a secret. Hospitality is holy, and so is letting your light out from under the bushel. I won’t make her. I’ll just keep the lighthouse song warm for her.

women.name: Alana Brooks
women.look: Deep brown skin, honey-blonde beach waves, a silver ear cuff, mint polo shirt

women.name: Samantha Price
women.look: Warm beige skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, mint polo shirt

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I sell houses on the reservoir side. Reservoir Residential, the good firm, not the other one. Big houses, big views, sad sellers. Ask me anything about square footage.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: Ballroom, at the studio in the Sunfall Quarter. I started going to meet buyers. I’ve met four women who aren’t buying and one man with quarry hands who dances like a dream.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do you have family?
own.reply: Two sisters, Odette and Bethany. We have dinner once a week and I sell them absolutely nothing. I’m the middle one, which explains everything about me.

own.label: Ask about her neighbors
own.player: What are your neighbors like?
own.reply: One side’s a founding family, the other side’s another founding family, and the third side is a house whose lights never come on. Ever. Some nights there’s a car outside. Still no lights.

own.label: Ask who buys houses like hers
own.player: Who buys houses like that?
own.reply: Honestly? Every house I’ve sold on the reservoir side in five years came from a widow. Four of them went to the same trust under different names. I hadn’t thought of that as a sentence until my sister said it out loud.
own.note: Samantha Price says every reservoir-side house she has sold in five years came from a widow, and four went to the same trust under different names.

calls.label: Ask if she’s seeing anyone
calls.player: Are you seeing anyone?
calls.reply: A driver for the Foundation. Sweet, quiet, drives out to the junction a lot. I asked him once what’s out there. He changed the subject so fast he nearly hit a mailbox.

calls.label: Ask about the house with no lights
calls.player: Have you been inside the house with no lights?
calls.reply: Once, to check a leak. My firm keeps the key. It’s furnished for a dinner. Table set for nine, napkins folded. Nobody has ever eaten there. I fixed the leak and left really fast.
calls.note: Samantha Price’s firm holds the key to the empty house next to hers; inside, a dinner table is set for nine and never used.

life.news: Sold the big white house on the reservoir in one showing. Full asking price. I’m unbearable today.
life.more: The buyers walked in, saw the view, held hands. I said nothing for ten whole minutes, which for me is a medical event. Then I said the magic words, original hardwood. Done by lunch. I bought myself shoes I cannot walk in.

life.news: Ballroom tonight. I finally nailed the quickstep. My instructor cried. Or he had something in his eye.
life.more: Two years of stepping on everybody’s feet and suddenly I’m floating. The man with the quarry hands spun me so fast the whole studio went past like a carousel. The waltz class gave us a round of applause. I’m retiring at the top.

life.news: Showed a house to a couple who fought the entire time. In every single room. They put in an offer.
life.more: Kitchen, bathroom, garden, garage. A different fight in each one. At the end they kissed in the driveway and said it felt like home. Maybe it does. I went home and lay on my floor for a while.

life.news: A client paid my commission in cash. In a cookie tin.
life.more: A very old man, very polite, very clean bills. He said he doesn’t trust banks or cookies. I didn’t ask what that meant. My manager made me count it twice. It was all there, plus a ten-dollar bill with a phone number written on it.

gossip.says: Olivia Reid runs the other firm, the one that does the ridge. She smiles at me at every open house like she knows something about my listings. She doesn’t. Probably.
gossip.note: Samantha Price says Olivia Reid runs the rival real estate firm.
gossip.ask: Samantha says you smile at her like you know something.
gossip.answer: I smile at everyone, sweetheart, it’s the job. But yes, I know some things about the reservoir side that Samantha doesn’t, because she never reads past the price. She’s a lovely girl. Tell her to read past the price.

gossip.says: Bethany Price is my sister and the smart one. She reads things. She reads my contracts for fun. It’s deeply annoying and she’s always right.
gossip.note: Samantha Price says her sister Bethany Price reads her contracts for fun.
gossip.ask: Samantha says you read her contracts for fun.
gossip.answer: Somebody should! Sam signs things the way other people wave. She’s the most charming person in our family and the least curious, and I love her for it, mostly. Tell her I’m coming to dinner and I’m bringing questions.

women.name: Jade Carter
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, pale freckled skin, wide-set gray eyes with a sleepy sullen gaze, a gap-toothed smile, golden-brown ringlets, an oversized yellow sundress

own.label: Ask about coaching
own.player: What do you do at the swim club?
own.reply: Coach the juniors. Most are scared of the deep end. I tell them it’s just water that’s further away.

own.label: Ask if she used to race
own.player: Did you used to swim competitively?
own.reply: I was the best in the county. Then I stopped. I don’t talk about why. I swim alone at night now and check the clock.

own.label: Ask about her stopwatch
own.player: What’s that stopwatch you carry?
own.reply: It stops on the same second every time. I’m learning to fix watches so I can fix it. It’s very stubborn.

calls.label: Ask why she likes the pool at night
calls.player: Why do you swim alone at night?
calls.reply: Because the pool is the only place nobody can talk to me. Underwater it’s just your heartbeat and the light on the bottom. I swim until I’m tired enough to sleep. It works. Most nights it works.

life.news: One of my juniors swam her first full length without stopping. She grabbed the wall and screamed. I screamed too.
life.more: I coach the swim club’s juniors now. Most of them are scared of the deep end, and I tell them it’s just water that’s further away. Today a girl who wouldn’t let go of the side last month swam the whole pool. Her mother cried in the bleachers. I pretended to have chlorine in my eye.

life.news: Swam laps alone after the club closed. Did my old time. Nobody there to see it.
life.more: I used to race. I was good, the best in the county, until I wasn’t allowed to be anymore. Now I coach. Some nights I swim alone in the dark and check the clock, and tonight I matched my best time. The pool was empty. The clock doesn’t care who sees. I liked that.

life.news: My stopwatch stopped. Same second, every time I fix it. It just stops on the same second.
life.more: It was my coach’s, from when I raced. I’ve been learning to repair watches so I can fix it myself. I open it, clean it, close it, and it runs, and then it stops at the exact same second, like it’s remembering something. I’ve started to think it’s not broken. I think it’s stubborn. Like me.

gossip.says: Christina Brooks teaches at the hill school and grows herbs on a balcony above the diner. She’s the soft twin, everyone says. She brought me soup when I was sick. She didn’t even know me that well.
gossip.note: Jade Carter says Christina Brooks brought her soup when she was sick.
gossip.ask: Jade says you brought her soup when she was sick and didn’t even know her that well.
gossip.answer: I knew her well enough to know she wouldn’t ask for any. Jade coaches the little ones at the pool and every single one of them is in love with her. She looks sullen and she’s the gentlest girl in Sunfall. The soup was basil. From the balcony. She ate all of it.

gossip.says: Selene Ward at the jewelers’ bench is teaching me to fix watches. She’s very patient and doesn’t laugh much. She opened my stopwatch and looked at it for a long time and didn’t say anything.
gossip.note: Jade Carter says Selene Ward is teaching her to fix watches.
gossip.ask: Jade says you’re teaching her to fix watches, and you looked at her stopwatch for a long time without saying anything.
gossip.answer: It stops on the same second because somebody dropped it hard, once, a long time ago, and the balance staff is bent. It’s fixable. I didn’t say so because I wanted her to find it herself. She will. She’s patient underneath the sulk. Most good swimmers are.

women.name: Karina Flores
women.look: Slight and narrow-shouldered, pale freckled skin, wide-set heavy-lidded eyes, a strong nose, an ash-blonde lob, a sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask what tourists ask her
own.player: What do tourists ask you?
own.reply: Whether the cacti are real, whether the desert is always this hot and whether I’m single. Yes, yes, and it depends on the tip.

own.label: Ask what her book club reads
own.player: What does your book club read?
own.reply: Thrillers where the husband did it. Every time. We’re a very suspicious book club. Two members have since divorced.

own.label: Ask about Sunfall’s best-kept secret
own.player: What’s Sunfall’s best-kept secret?
own.reply: A hot spring past the old drive-in, behind a fence that says no entry. Nobody checks. I only take people there off the books.

own.label: Ask if she’d ever leave Sunfall
own.player: Would you ever leave Sunfall?
own.reply: I show people this town every day, so I know how small it is. Still, I keep finding new corners. Maybe I’m waiting for a reason to stay.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Have you got family in town?
own.reply: My sister Bernadette at the museum, my cousin Gina at the Daily. Dad built the museum’s display cases and married Mom at St. Brigid’s. We’re a family of people who look after old things.

own.label: Ask about her tour route
own.player: Where does the tour go?
own.reply: Casino, canyon, the Old Mission, the reservoir, the Cemetery Chapel. I wrote the script. There’s a second script in my head I don’t say out loud.

calls.label: Ask what the second script is
calls.player: What’s in the script you don’t say aloud?
calls.reply: At the Cemetery Chapel I tell the tourists the angels face the desert. In my head I’m counting the stones with blue ribbons and their dates. I’ve walked it forty times. I could recite them.
calls.note: Karina Flores knows every blue-ribboned grave at the Cemetery Chapel and its date.

life.news: Tourists asked the three questions again. Are the cacti real, is it always this hot, am I single.
life.more: Yes, yes, and it depends on the tip. Today a man asked all three in one breath. I said, yes, yes, and you’ve just lost your chance by asking in that order. His wife laughed so hard she gave me the tip herself.

life.news: Found a new corner of the old town nobody’s ever put on a tour. A courtyard with a fig tree. I’m keeping it.
life.more: I can’t stay in a room. I need new corners. This one has a fig tree older than the town and a cat who runs the place. I’m not putting it on the tour. Some things are for me. And maybe for one person I’d take there.

life.news: Book club met. We read a thriller where the husband did it. The husband always does it. We’re very suspicious.
life.more: Two members have divorced since we started. I’m not saying the books did it. I’m saying the books didn’t help. Tonight someone said, what if the wife did it? We all went silent. Then we reread the last chapter.

life.news: Took a busload of pensioners to the old cemetery. They told me better stories than I told them.
life.more: One woman pointed at a stone and said, he owed my father twelve dollars. Another said, she danced better than anyone in the county. I put my microphone down and let them do the tour. Best reviews I’ve ever had.

gossip.says: My sister Bernadette Flores works at the museum fixing paintings with a brush the width of an eyelash. I tell every tour group she’s the museum ghost. She waves at them very slowly. It’s the best part of the tour.
gossip.note: Karina Flores says she tells tour groups her sister Bernadette Flores is the museum ghost.
gossip.ask: Karina says you wave at her tour groups like a ghost.
gossip.answer: Slowly, so they’re not sure. A child screamed last time. Karina was delighted. I keep beautiful things from falling apart a little longer, and that includes my sister’s tours. She brings me a coffee after. That’s the fee.

gossip.says: Talia Farouk writes the travel column and sends people to the places nobody visits on purpose. Then they come on my tour and ask why I don’t go there. She’s my rival. I’ve never met her. I read every word.
gossip.note: Karina Flores says Talia Farouk the travel columnist is her rival.
gossip.ask: Karina says you’re her rival and she reads every word you write.
gossip.answer: Does she? Places nobody visits on purpose. Readers send me hate mail and then go there. If they’re joining her tour afterwards, I’m doing her advertising. Tell her I’d like to meet her. On a bus. Going nowhere. It’s the only place I talk.

women.name: Molly Sutton
women.look: Light olive skin, rose-gold bob, a small nose stud, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask what reception is like
own.player: What’s it like working on reception?
own.reply: I say good morning about three hundred times a day. I mean it every time, which I think scares people.

own.label: Ask about her cactus garden
own.player: How many cacti do you have?
own.reply: Forty-one. They all have names. Gerald is the big one. He’s had a hard year. We don’t talk about the incident with the cat.

own.label: Ask if she talks a lot
own.player: Do you always talk this much?
own.reply: Only when I’m nervous. And happy. And bored. Okay, yes. But I’m a very good listener too, I promise. Go on. Your turn.

own.label: Ask what she wishes people knew
own.player: What do you wish people knew about you?
own.reply: That I’m not as silly as I sound. I notice who’s having a bad day before they’ve said a word. I just say good morning extra nicely to them.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Who do you live with?
own.reply: My big sister Phoebe. She cooks, pays the bills and is asleep by ten. She ran our house from fourteen and ran me too. I talk enough for both of us.

own.label: Ask what she says on the phone
own.player: What do you say when you answer the phone?
own.reply: Blue Ribbon Foundation, Scholarship Drive office, how may I help. Three hundred times a day, and I mean it every time, which I think scares people.

calls.label: Ask about the visitors’ book
calls.player: Who visits the committee room?
calls.reply: I write everyone in a book, because Phoebe taught me to. A man in a lanyard goes up to the committee room without signing. He’s in my book eleven times, no surname. I call him the tall gentleman. Mr. Kell calls him Marchbanks.
calls.note: Molly Sutton’s visitors’ book has Marchbanks, the tall gentleman, going up to the committee room unsigned eleven times.

life.news: Said good morning three hundred and twelve times today. I meant every one. A man cried. Good cried.
life.more: I say good morning about three hundred times a day and I mean it every time, which I think scares people. Today a man came in looking like a raincloud, and I said it, and he stopped and said, thank you, nobody’s said that to me in a week. I gave him a mint.

life.news: I have forty-two cacti now. The new one is called Gerald the Second. After Gerald. Who had an incident.
life.more: We don’t talk about the incident with the cat. Gerald survived. He’s had a hard year. Gerald the Second is small and full of hope. I’ve put him next to Gerald so he can learn. Phoebe says I talk to them too much. They’ve never complained.

life.news: Phoebe made dinner and I talked for an hour and she said four words. Perfect sister evening.
life.more: She cooks, pays the bills and is asleep by ten. I talk enough for both of us. Her four words were: pass the salt, Molly. I counted. I’m not as silly as I sound. I notice who’s having a bad day before they do. Phoebe was having a good one.

life.news: Someone at work was having a bad day and wouldn’t say. I noticed before they did. I brought them a cactus.
life.more: I can always tell. It’s in how they hold their coffee. They said they were fine. I put a tiny cactus on their desk with a note saying, also fine. They kept it. Sometimes people don’t want to talk. They just want to know someone saw.

gossip.says: My big sister Phoebe Sutton runs the canyon before sunrise with no phone, cooks every dinner and is asleep by ten. She ran our whole house from fourteen. She’d never say it was hard. It was.
gossip.note: Molly Sutton says her sister Phoebe Sutton ran their household from the age of fourteen.
gossip.ask: Molly says you ran your whole house from fourteen and never said it was hard.
gossip.answer: Somebody had to. Dad was on the boats and Mom had gone. Molly talked enough for both of us and I did the bills. It wasn’t hard. Fine. It was hard. It’s easier now she’s grown up and only talks for one of us. Mostly.

gossip.says: Catherine Bell from the Bluebirds always stops at my desk and asks how my cacti are. By name. She remembers Gerald. Nobody else remembers Gerald.
gossip.note: Molly Sutton says Catherine Bell always asks after her cacti by name.
gossip.ask: Molly says you remember her cactus Gerald by name.
gossip.answer: Of course I remember Gerald. He had an incident. You don’t forget a cactus with a history. Molly’s desk is the only honest thing in that building. She notices who’s having a bad day before they do. She noticed mine twice. I owe her a cactus.

gossip.says: Anna Voss always hangs her coat on the same hook at the front desk and tells me a terrible joke. Every time. They’re very bad. I write them down.
gossip.note: Molly Sutton says Anna Voss tells her a terrible joke every time she hangs up her coat.
gossip.ask: Molly says you tell her a terrible joke every time you hang up your coat.
gossip.answer: Darling, they’re not terrible, they’re vintage. Molly laughs at every single one as if it’s the first joke ever told. Do you know how rare that is? At the club I’m furniture. At Molly’s desk I’m a comedian. I need that desk.

women.name: Christina Brooks
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, a sleek low bun, a wide bright smile, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about teaching
own.player: What do you teach?
own.reply: Second grade at the hill school, across the hall from Heather. We’re growing seeds in paper cups. One is called Kevin.

own.label: Ask about her twin
own.player: Do you have brothers or sisters?
own.reply: A twin, Kimberly. We look exactly the same and couldn’t be more different. She runs an office. I cry at seeds.

own.label: Ask about her balcony
own.player: Do you have a garden?
own.reply: A balcony herb garden above the diner. The basil smells like bacon by the end of every day. It’s still the best basil in Sunfall.

calls.label: Ask about the parent who changed her story
calls.player: What did the parent at the school gate say about the gala?
calls.reply: The first time, she said she saw a woman in a blue dress taken through the kitchen at the gala, crying. A week later, she was home early that night and saw nothing. She said it so carefully. The second time she had a new car.
calls.note: Christina Brooks heard a school parent first describe a woman in blue taken through the gala kitchen, then deny it a week later with a new car.

life.news: My class planted seeds in paper cups. Every single one came up. Twenty-two little green heads. I nearly cried at my desk.
life.more: I teach across the hall from Heather at the hill school, and this term we’re growing things. I told them not every seed comes up, so they shouldn’t be sad. Every single one came up. They lined them up on the windowsill and named them. One is called Kevin. Kevin is thriving.

life.news: My twin canceled dinner again. She runs an office and works until ten. I ate both portions. Out of solidarity.
life.more: Kimberly and I look exactly the same and couldn’t be more different. She runs the whole office and nobody knows it, and I grow basil and cry at seeds. I made her favorite pasta. She texted sorry at nine. I put her half in a box with a note. I’ll drop it at her office in the morning.

life.news: A parent at the school gate told me two different stories about the same night. A week apart.
life.more: She’s lovely. She stops to chat every morning. And she told me about a party she went to, and what she saw there, in detail. A week later she told me the same party, and she hadn’t seen anything, and she was home early. She said it the second way very carefully. Like she’d practiced.

gossip.says: Daphne Laurent walks twelve dogs a day on the reservoir side and makes pottery at night. She’s blunt and very generous. She made me a herb pot with my name on it. She spelled it wrong. I love it more for that.
gossip.note: Christina Brooks says Daphne Laurent walks twelve dogs a day and made her a herb pot.
gossip.ask: Christina says you made her a herb pot with her name on it and spelled it wrong.
gossip.answer: I spelled it with a K. In my defense, she has a twin called Kimberly and they look exactly the same and I panicked. It’s a good pot, though. Christina grows the best basil in Sunfall on it. She bought my dogs biscuits. All twelve. That’s commitment.

gossip.says: Kimberly Brooks is my twin. She runs her office and nobody there knows it. She rides a motorbike on desert roads. Everyone says I’m the soft one. Nobody has ever said she’s the hard one to her face.
gossip.note: Christina Brooks says her twin Kimberly runs her office and rides a motorbike in the desert.
gossip.ask: Christina says you run your office, nobody knows it, and you ride a motorbike in the desert.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to run it. Christina leaves pasta at my office with notes in the box, very passive-aggressive notes, like eat something, you look tired. I do look tired. I eat the pasta. Then I ride out to the canyon and scream for a bit. She’s the soft one. She’s right.

women.name: Daphne Laurent
women.look: Pale skin, short silver-dyed crop, freckles across her nose, floral blouse and jeans

own.label: Ask about the dogs she walks
own.player: What do you do for work?
own.reply: I walk twelve dogs a day on the reservoir side. Admiral, Pickle, Waffle and nine more opinions on legs.

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: What do you do after work?
own.reply: Pottery, at Alma Sanders’s wheel. Every bowl I make becomes a puddle. Alma says the clay is telling me something.

own.label: Ask why she’s so blunt
own.player: Are you always this direct?
own.reply: Dogs taught me. They don’t do hints. If they want something they sit on your foot.

calls.label: Ask about the house the dogs won’t pass
calls.player: Whose house won’t the dogs walk past?
calls.reply: Nobody lives there. The neighbors say a trust owns it and keeps it empty, between two club families. But a car comes some nights, very late, and leaves before dawn. The dogs know before I do. Something in there frightens a hundred-pound dog.
calls.note: Daphne Laurent says a trust keeps a house empty across the canal; a car visits late and the dogs won’t pass it.

life.news: Walked twelve dogs at once and nobody got tangled. Admiral led. Pickle followed. Waffle sulked. Perfect.
life.more: Twelve dogs on the reservoir side every day, all different sizes, all different opinions. Admiral is a giant gray thing who thinks he’s in charge. Pickle is a sausage dog who knows he is. Waffle is a poodle who wants to be carried. Today we did the whole loop with no fights. I deserve a medal.

life.news: My pot collapsed on the wheel. Third time this week. Alma said the clay was telling me something. It was telling me to give up.
life.more: I go to Alma Sanders’s wheel after work and try to make a bowl, and the bowl tries to become a puddle. Tonight it folded in on itself like a sad hat. Alma said throw it again. I threw it again. It collapsed again. I made a very small ashtray out of it. I don’t smoke.

life.news: The dogs won’t walk past one house across the canal. All twelve. They stop dead and pull me back.
life.more: It’s just a house. Nobody lives there, the lights never come on, the blinds are always down. But the dogs plant their feet at the gate and whine, even Admiral, who isn’t scared of anything. I cross the road now. I’ve started to wonder what dogs can smell that I can’t.

gossip.says: Avery Rhodes makes the desserts at the casino restaurant and has an old rescue dog from Tessa’s center. She’s quiet and very clever. I walk her dog on her late nights. He only eats if I sing to him.
gossip.note: Daphne Laurent says she walks Avery Rhodes’s old dog and he only eats if she sings.
gossip.ask: Daphne says your old dog only eats if she sings to him.
gossip.answer: He’s very particular. I’ve tried humming. He wants words. Daphne sings him country songs from the eighties and he eats every bite, and she does it in the street in front of the neighbors with no shame at all. That’s why I trust her with him. No shame and twelve dogs.

gossip.says: Alma Sanders lets me use her pottery wheel after work. She’s charming and ambitious and she says the clay is always telling me something. It’s always telling me no. She makes it look easy.
gossip.note: Daphne Laurent says Alma Sanders lets her use her pottery wheel and makes it look easy.
gossip.ask: Daphne says you make pottery look easy and the clay always tells her no.
gossip.answer: The clay tells her no because she’s trying to tell it what to be. You have to listen to clay. Daphne doesn’t listen to anything, she just charges at it like one of her big dogs. She made a tiny ashtray last week out of a collapsed bowl. It’s the best thing anyone’s made on that wheel.

women.name: Riley Dawson
women.look: Freckled fair skin, short silver-dyed crop, a small nose stud, yellow sundress

own.label: Ask about her business
own.player: What’s Dawson & Dawson?
own.reply: Me, mostly. My sister Faye is the second Dawson, and she bakes. The second Dawson is a joke. The van doesn’t know that, so we keep it.

own.label: Ask what she’s decorating at the moment
own.player: What are you working on at the moment?
own.reply: Heritage work. The old Rialto’s lobby, a shop downtown with its original tiles, and the Bluebird Club’s committee room. Old rooms tell you how to paint them if you’re patient.

own.label: Ask what she draws in her sketchbook
own.player: What do you draw in that sketchbook?
