own.reply: Shopfronts, before they’re gone. I’ve drawn the old cobbler’s from the curb outside the laundromat. Funny thing: I’ve seen other women sketching the same cobbler’s from different curbs. We’ve never spoken. It’s like a club with no meetings.

own.label: Ask if there’s someone special
own.player: Is there someone in your life?
own.reply: A river man. Which in Sunfall means a boy who rents out boats on the reservoir. He smells of engine oil and sunscreen, and he’s the kindest person I know. Don’t tell him I said that.

own.label: Ask if decorating runs in the family
own.player: Is decorating a family thing?
own.reply: My dad did the Bluebird Club’s rooms for thirty years. He fell from a ladder in the lodge’s dining room when I was little. The club called it an accident and paid for everything. I could paint a straight line at eight. I took the firm.

own.label: Ask if anything strange happened at the club
own.player: Did anything strange happen while you worked at the club?
own.reply: They asked me to leave the committee room at a certain hour, and I did. Then I came back for my brushes, because I don’t leave tools. They were still in there. Nine of them around the table, and a woman in a creased linen suit holding an envelope. I told the club I’d left when asked. I told my sister the truth.
own.note: Riley Dawson went back to the Bluebird Club’s committee room for her brushes and saw nine people at the table and a woman in a creased linen suit holding an envelope.

calls.label: Ask about the pictures in the committee room
calls.player: What are the pictures on the committee room walls like?
calls.reply: Collages. I took them down to paint and put them back, twice. The second time I looked properly. I’ve got one made of receipts in my kitchen, by Daisy Chen, so I know a story when it’s glued. Those ones are stories. I just don’t know whose.

calls.label: Ask about her dad’s accident
calls.player: What happened after your dad’s accident?
calls.reply: The club paid my mom. Generously, everyone said. And she signed something. She keeps the paper in a cookie tin under her bed. She says nobody has ever asked her about it. I think she wants somebody to.
calls.note: Riley Dawson says the club paid her mother after her father’s fall in the lodge’s dining room, and her mother signed a paper she still keeps.

life.news: Painted a ceiling today without a single drip. Thirty feet up. Nobody saw. Tell me I’m amazing.
life.more: The Rialto lobby. Plaster roses all the way around and a sky in the middle that somebody painted in 1931. I matched the blue by eye. Faye says nobody looks at ceilings. That’s the point. You do it right for the one person who looks up.

life.news: Faye brought home a cake that failed. It looks like a hat. It tastes incredible.
life.more: She bakes for a group of pastry chefs who bet on each other’s cakes. When one collapses, it comes home to me. Tonight’s was meant to be a cathedral. It’s a hat. We ate half of it with spoons, standing at the counter.

life.news: Drove past the lodge today on a job. Didn’t go in. I never do.
life.more: My dad worked there for years. That’s where he fell. The club paid for everything and sent flowers. I’ll paint any room in Sunfall but that one. Faye says that’s not very professional. I say it’s the most professional thing I do.

life.news: Took the van to the reservoir after work and got rowed around by my favorite boat man. Sunset. Engine oil. Perfect.
life.more: He can’t row in a straight line to save his life, which is funny for a boat man. We went in circles for an hour and talked about nothing. I’d paint that sky if anyone would believe the colors.

gossip.says: Nina Petrov runs the bakery in Old Town. She followed a man here from St Petersburg, the man left, and she kept the ovens. I redid her shop last spring. She wanted it to look like nobody had touched it in a hundred years. Hardest job I’ve ever done.
gossip.note: Riley Dawson says Nina Petrov followed a man from St Petersburg, and when he left she kept the ovens.
gossip.ask: Riley says you followed a man here from St Petersburg, and when he left you kept the ovens.
gossip.answer: The ovens never once told me they needed space. Riley made my shop look a hundred years old in three weeks, which is a talent and also an insult, and I paid her in bread for a month. She still comes in every weekend. She says it’s for the bread. It is mostly for the bread.

gossip.says: A woman from the police records office sketches the same old cobbler’s that I do, from across the street. Cassidy Boone. We nod. We’ve never spoken. It’s perfect.
gossip.note: Riley Dawson says Cassidy Boone sketches the same old cobbler’s shop she does.
gossip.ask: Riley says you sketch the same cobbler’s she does, from across the street.
gossip.answer: The cobbler’s downtown, before they knock it down. I take the curb by the bus stop. She takes the laundromat side. We nod and never talk. It’s the best friendship I have. Don’t ruin it by introducing us.

women.name: Lacey Wilson
women.look: Deep brown skin, twist-out coils, a small nose stud, red gingham shirt

women.name: Avery Rhodes
women.look: Pale skin, black space buns, amber eyes, turquoise peasant top

own.label: Ask about the casino’s desserts
own.player: What do you do at the casino?
own.reply: Pastry chef in the restaurant. Sugar cages, chocolate domes, things that look like jewelry for people who wear real jewelry.

own.label: Ask about her dog
own.player: Do you have pets?
own.reply: An old rescue from Tessa’s center. Gray eyes, one floppy ear, and he only eats if Daphne sings to him. I can’t sing.

own.label: Ask why she’s so private
own.player: Why do you keep to yourself?
own.reply: I work in a casino. Everyone there is pretending. I’d rather not pretend, so I just don’t say much.

calls.label: Ask about the van at the kitchen door
calls.player: What’s the van outside the casino kitchen?
calls.reply: A white van with the Foundation’s ribbon on the door, on goth nights, at closing. It backs up to our kitchen and things are carried out. Crates, heavy, under cloths. Last time one of the men in the lounge’s goth night helped load it, wearing his charity lanyard under his coat.
calls.note: Avery Rhodes sees a Foundation van load crates out of the casino kitchen on goth nights.

life.news: Made a sugar cage over a chocolate dome for the casino’s high rollers. It cracked perfectly at the table. Somebody gasped.
life.more: You spin the sugar into threads and drape it into a cage, and then the waiter pours hot sauce on it and it melts open like a flower. I watched from the kitchen door. A woman in diamonds gasped. I went back to my station and smiled at the oven for a full minute.

life.news: My old dog wouldn’t eat today. I sat on the floor with him for an hour. He ate one biscuit. I counted it as a win.
life.more: He came from Tessa’s rescue center already old, with gray around his eyes and one ear that doesn’t stand up. Some days he eats and some days he just looks at me like he’s apologizing. Tonight he ate one biscuit from my hand. I’ll take one. I’ll take any number.

life.news: There’s a van outside the casino kitchen door on the nights the lounge runs its goth night. Not the delivery van.
life.more: Our delivery van is green. This one is white, newer, with the Foundation’s little ribbon on the door, and on goth nights it backs up to our kitchen at closing. Nobody unloads anything into the kitchen. Something gets loaded out. Nobody tells the pastry chef anything.

gossip.says: Summer Barton works at the pharmacy on Sunfall Road and restores old film cameras, very badly, with great patience. Nothing fazes her. She once caught a shoplifter by just saying excuse me, very mildly.
gossip.note: Avery Rhodes says Summer Barton caught a shoplifter by saying excuse me, very mildly.
gossip.ask: Avery says you caught a shoplifter just by saying excuse me, very mildly.
gossip.answer: He put the vitamins back and apologized and left. People hate being noticed politely. It’s worse than shouting. Avery makes desserts that look like jewelry and then watches people eat them from the kitchen door like a cat. She’s very private and very kind. She gave me a sugar flower once. I’ve still got it.

gossip.says: Tessa Larkin at the rescue center gave me my old dog. She calls every month to ask how he is. Every month. She remembers his name and his ear and how he likes his biscuits.
gossip.note: Avery Rhodes says Tessa Larkin calls every month to ask after the dog she gave her.
gossip.ask: Avery says you call every month to ask about her dog.
gossip.answer: Of course I do. He waited at the center for two years because he’s old and his ear doesn’t stand up, and then a pastry chef came in and sat on the floor with him for an hour. I knew then. She tells me how much he ate. I write it down. He’s doing well, mostly. She’s doing well, too, I think, because of him.

women.name: Summer Barton
women.look: Pale skin, auburn shag with a curtain fringe, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, mint polo shirt

own.label: Ask about the pharmacy counter
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I’m a pharmacy assistant on Sunfall Road. I know half the town’s secrets and all of its rashes.

own.label: Ask about her hobby
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: Restore old film cameras, badly, with tape. Daria from the collective sighs at me. Lovingly.

own.label: Ask if anything fazes her
own.player: Does anything ever rattle you?
own.reply: Not much. I say excuse me very mildly and people fall apart. It’s a superpower.

calls.label: Ask about the double prescription
calls.player: Who bought the same prescription twice and changed her story?
calls.reply: The first time, she said she’d dropped her pills running from the club’s kitchen corridor on gala night, after what she saw. The second time, she’d never been to the gala at all. Same prescription, both times cash. Her hands shook less the second time.
calls.note: Summer Barton says a customer first said she fled the gala kitchen corridor, then denied going to the gala, paying cash both times.

life.news: Got an old Polaroid camera working. Took one picture of the pharmacy cat. It came out perfect. I’ve framed it.
life.more: I restore old film cameras very badly and very slowly. Daria from the collective helps me, which means she sighs at me in a loving way while I break things. This one took six weeks and one bandaged finger. The cat sat still for the first time in her life. Fate.

life.news: Long shift. A man yelled at me because his prescription wasn’t ready. It was ready. He was at the wrong pharmacy.
life.more: He shouted for five minutes about how this town is going downhill, and I let him finish, and then I said very mildly, sir, your pharmacy is across the street. He looked at the street. He looked at me. He left without a word. I gave myself a mint. I deserved a mint.

life.news: A woman bought the same prescription twice in one week and told me two different stories about why.
life.more: The first time she said she lost it on the night of a big party, she’d been so frightened by something she saw. The second time she said she never went to the party, she just dropped the bottle. She said both very nicely. She paid cash both times. She’s never paid cash before.

gossip.says: Jenna Newton works at the museum and plays pool at the Old Quarter hall on her nights off. She’s warm and impulsive and once bought a whole table of strangers a round because one of them was sad. I love her.
gossip.note: Summer Barton says Jenna Newton once bought a table of strangers a round because one of them was sad.
gossip.ask: Summer says you bought a whole table of strangers a round because one of them was sad.
gossip.answer: He was very sad. You could see it from across the hall. It cost me a week’s lunches and it was worth every sandwich. Summer catches shoplifters by saying excuse me and fixes old cameras with tape. She’s the gentlest dangerous person I know.

gossip.says: Daria Kowalski helps me restore old cameras. Well, she watches me do it badly and sighs. Lovingly. She’s photographed every protest for eleven years. She says film waits. I’m slow enough that it has to.
gossip.note: Summer Barton says Daria Kowalski helps her restore old cameras and sighs lovingly.
gossip.ask: Summer says you help her restore old cameras by sighing at her, lovingly.
gossip.answer: I sigh because she uses tape where she should use a spring, and then the tape works, and then I have to rethink everything I know about cameras. She’s patient in a way I respect. She took a Polaroid of the pharmacy cat and framed it. Perfect exposure. I was very jealous.

women.name: Jenna Newton
women.look: Freckled fair skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, a silver ear cuff, floral blouse and jeans

own.label: Ask about the museum
own.player: What do you do at the museum?
own.reply: I’m a gallery attendant. I guard a hundred-year-old wedding veil from schoolboys. It’s more exciting than it sounds.

own.label: Ask what she does on her nights off
own.player: What do you do on your nights off?
own.reply: Play pool at the Old Quarter hall. Old wood, chalk, and regulars who take it far too seriously. I love it.

own.label: Ask if she’s impulsive
own.player: Are you impulsive?
own.reply: I once bought a whole table of strangers a round because one of them looked sad. So, yes. No regrets.

calls.label: Ask about the motel room across from her window
calls.player: Who’s in the motel room across from your window?
calls.reply: Number nine. Curtains shut all day, lamp on all night. At three in the morning, somebody reads verse through the wall. A man in a long cloak goes in and out after dark. Somebody else pays for the room. I’ve seen the envelope at the desk. It’s his second room. He doesn’t sleep in the first one anymore.
calls.note: Jenna Newton says a man in a cloak keeps a second room, number nine, on the motel strip, and reads verse there at night.

life.news: Won three games of pool in a row at the Old Quarter hall. Francesca in red said I cheated. I did not. I’m just good.
life.more: I play on my nights off with a crowd of regulars who take pool far too seriously, and tonight I ran the table three times. Somebody bought me a drink. Somebody else asked for a rematch. I said yes to both. The hall smells like old wood and chalk. It’s my favorite smell in the world.

life.news: A schoolkid knocked over a display case at the museum. Nothing broke. I aged ten years.
life.more: A hundred-year-old wedding veil in a glass case, and a boy on a school trip ran into it at full speed. The case rocked and settled. I caught my breath. The veil didn’t even move. The boy cried. I gave him a museum pencil and told him he’d been very brave. He hadn’t. I had.

life.news: The room across from my window on the motel strip has its curtains shut all day and a lamp on all night.
life.more: I live on the strip because it’s cheap. My window faces the motel, number nine. The curtains are always shut. The lamp is always on. Sometimes I hear someone reading out loud through the wall at three in the morning. Poetry. Very old-fashioned poetry. Nobody else seems to notice.

gossip.says: Lila Thompson sells houses for Canyon Realty and rides a fixed-up bicycle everywhere because she won’t drive a company car. She’s poised and very independent. She told me she doesn’t like being tracked. I didn’t ask by whom.
gossip.note: Jenna Newton says Lila Thompson won’t drive Canyon Realty’s company car.
gossip.ask: Jenna says you won’t drive the company car because you don’t like being tracked.
gossip.answer: Company cars have little boxes in them that tell the office where you are. I don’t need the office knowing which coffee shop I sit in for an hour. Jenna plays pool with the scariest people in the Quarter and buys strangers drinks. She’s the bravest woman I know. She thinks she’s just friendly.

gossip.says: Bernadette Flores restores paintings at the museum, upstairs from my gallery. She talks to the saints in the paintings. She stopped by my desk once and asked how the wedding veil was. Like it was a person. I loved that.
gossip.note: Jenna Newton says Bernadette Flores asked her how the museum’s old wedding veil was, like it was a person.
gossip.ask: Jenna says you asked her how the old wedding veil was doing, like it was a person.
gossip.answer: It is a person, in a way. A woman wore it on the happiest day of her life a hundred years ago. Jenna guards it like a sentry. She threw herself between it and a running schoolboy. That’s devotion. I said a prayer for her that evening. Don’t tell her. She’d be embarrassed.

women.name: Lila Thompson
women.look: Fair skin, a high curly ponytail, rosy cheeks, pink zip hoodie

own.label: Ask about selling houses
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Sell houses for Canyon Realty. Mostly men in loafers haggling over granite. Sometimes a couple cries over a lemon tree.

own.label: Ask why she rides a bicycle
own.player: Why don’t you drive?
own.reply: Company cars have a box under the seat that tells the office where you are. My bicycle keeps my secrets.

own.label: Ask what she values most
own.player: What matters most to you?
own.reply: Nobody knowing where I am unless I tell them. Freedom fits on two wheels.

calls.label: Ask about the viewing by the Old Mission
calls.player: What happened when your boss showed the Old Mission houses?
calls.reply: Three houses beside the Old Mission Chapel, one after another. The buyer never looked inside. He walked the gardens and looked at the ground and asked how deep the cellars go. My boss logged two viewings. I was in the back seat. It was three.
calls.note: Lila Thompson saw a buyer view three houses beside the Old Mission Chapel and ask how deep the cellars go; her boss logged two.

life.news: Sold a little adobe house to a young couple who cried when they got the keys. I cried in the car after. Professionally.
life.more: Most days real estate is men in loafers haggling over granite. But today a couple who’ve been saving for six years got a house with a lemon tree, and when I handed them the keys they held them like a baby bird. I rode my bicycle home the long way with the wind in my face. Best day this year.

life.news: The office asked again why I won’t drive the company car. I said I like my bicycle. They said that isn’t a reason.
life.more: It’s a perfectly good reason. My bicycle doesn’t have a little box under the seat that reports to the office. My bicycle doesn’t know where I eat lunch. My bicycle asks nothing of me except air in the tires. I’m keeping my bicycle. I may also need a new job.

life.news: I was in the car when my boss showed three houses to a buyer. Afterwards he told the office he’d shown them two.
life.more: Three houses by the Old Mission, one after another, the buyer barely looking at them, just walking round the gardens and looking at the ground. My boss told me it was a viewing. On the paperwork, he says he showed him two. I was in the back seat. I counted.

gossip.says: Melody Brooks coaches the senior swimmers and maps hidden hiking routes on her days off. She married a man the club didn’t approve of without asking anyone. She’s my hero.
gossip.note: Lila Thompson says Melody Brooks married a man the club didn’t approve of without asking.
gossip.ask: Lila says you married a man the club didn’t approve of without asking anyone, and you’re her hero.
gossip.answer: I didn’t ask because it wasn’t their business. My mother runs half of the Lucky Cactus and she’s Dolores Brooks, so everybody thinks I needed permission. I needed a man who could swim. He can swim. Lila rides a bicycle everywhere so nobody can track her. She’s my hero right back.

gossip.says: Olivia Reid is my boss at Canyon Realty. She says cozy means you can touch both walls and that every listing photo is a crime. She’s the only honest real estate agent in Arizona.
gossip.note: Lila Thompson says Olivia Reid is the only honest real estate agent in Arizona.
gossip.ask: Lila says you’re the only honest real estate agent in Arizona.
gossip.answer: That’s a low bar, but I’ll take it. I tell buyers the truth and sellers the price, and somehow I still close. Lila rides a bicycle to viewings in a blazer and nobody has ever once doubted her. She’s going to run this town. I just hope she remembers I gave her the job.

women.name: Melody Brooks
women.look: Fair skin, golden-brown ringlets, gold hoop earrings, turquoise peasant top

own.label: Ask about coaching
own.player: What do you coach?
own.reply: The senior swimmers at the club. Everyone expects nothing from them. They beat Phoenix by a body length.

own.label: Ask about her marriage
own.player: Are you married?
own.reply: Three years, to a man my family calls that man. I didn’t ask anyone’s permission. Best decision I ever made.

own.label: Ask about her hiking
own.player: What do you do on your days off?
own.reply: Map hidden hiking routes and write them in a journal. Somebody tore a page out. I’m being very calm about it.

calls.label: Ask about the torn page in her journal
calls.player: Who tore the page out of your hiking journal?
calls.reply: My husband. The route up behind the lodge, the night before he went to a meeting he wouldn’t talk about. I found the page in his jacket, folded small, with a time written on it. He says he’s protecting me. He says it calmly. That’s how I know he’s scared.
calls.note: Melody Brooks found the torn page of her hiking route behind the lodge in her husband’s jacket.

life.news: My seniors swam the relay at the regatta in the club’s best time in a decade. I screamed so hard I lost my voice.
life.more: I coach the swimmers who are too old for anybody to expect anything, and today they beat the clubs from Phoenix by a full body length. One of them is sixty-three. She climbed out of the reservoir and punched the air. I hugged her soaking wet. My whistle went in the water. Worth it.

life.news: My mother called my husband that man again at dinner. Three years married. Still that man.
life.more: My family runs half the Lucky Cactus and has opinions about everyone in Sunfall, and the club has opinions about who marries whom. I married who I wanted and didn’t ask. Mom forgives me on alternate weekends. He cleared the table and kissed her cheek. She glared. That’s progress.

life.news: A page is torn out of my hiking journal. I didn’t tear it. Only one other person knows where I keep it.
life.more: I map hidden routes on my days off and write them all down, with sketches. The page that’s missing was the route up behind the lodge. Torn neatly, close to the spine. My husband says he didn’t touch it. He says it very calmly. He never says anything calmly.

gossip.says: Eva Castle drives the second tour bus and teaches her little cousin guitar on the mission side. She’s the only person in her family who talks to both of her cousins. She overthinks everything and she’s lovely.
gossip.note: Melody Brooks says Eva Castle drives the second tour bus and talks to both her cousins.
gossip.ask: Melody says you’re the only one in your family who talks to both of your cousins.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to carry the messages. Agnes and Freya haven’t spoken in six years over God, and I sit between them at every birthday like a translator. Melody married who she wanted without asking anyone. I think about that a lot. It seems very restful.

gossip.says: Zara Brooks is my cousin. She tattoos at Rowan Pike’s studio and she was raised at the Lucky Cactus like me. She’s the only one in the family who came to my wedding happily.
gossip.note: Melody Brooks says her cousin Zara Brooks was the only family member happy at her wedding.
gossip.ask: Melody says you were the only one in the family who came to her wedding happily.
gossip.answer: I brought a cake and a bottle of tequila and danced with her husband. The rest of them sat there like a jury. Melody did the bravest thing anyone in our family has ever done, and they still call him that man. I call him by his name. He makes very good margaritas.

women.name: Eva Castle
women.look: Pale skin, blunt black bob, tortoiseshell glasses, lavender knit top

own.label: Ask about driving the tour bus
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I drive the second tour bus. Yes, the cacti are real. Yes, it’s always this hot. No, I won’t say if I’m single.

own.label: Ask about teaching guitar
own.player: Do you play an instrument?
own.reply: Guitar. I teach my little cousin on the porch on the mission side, with the chords on index cards. She’s getting good.

own.label: Ask about the cousins who don’t speak
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: Two cousins who haven’t spoken in six years over God. I sit between them at every birthday and pass the salt.

calls.label: Ask about the car outside the tour office
calls.player: What’s the car outside the tour office?
calls.reply: Dark, tinted, only on the days the bus goes past the Old Mission. When we stop at the gate, the same car is up by the chapel. Last time a man in it had binoculars on the tourists. On my tourists. I’ve got the plate in my notes.
calls.note: Eva Castle sees a dark car watch the tour bus whenever it stops at the Old Mission.

life.news: Taught my little cousin her first full song on guitar. She played it for her mom. Her mom cried. Everyone cried. Normal family.
life.more: I teach her on the porch on the mission side, slowly, with the chords written on index cards. Today she played the whole thing without stopping, wrong in two places, and she didn’t care, and neither did anyone else. I drove the tour bus home grinning. The tourists thought I was being friendly.

life.news: Sat between my two cousins at a birthday. They didn’t speak. I passed the salt between them for two hours.
life.more: Agnes is a Sister of Mercy and Freya is an artist who thinks God is a bad landlord, and they haven’t spoken in six years. At every family party I sit in the middle and pass things. Salt. Bread. Messages. Tonight Agnes asked me to tell Freya her cactus looked healthy. I told her. Freya nearly smiled.

life.news: There’s a car outside the tour office on the days our bus goes past the Old Mission. Only those days.
life.more: Our route changes through the week, and only on the Old Mission days a dark car parks across from the office and doesn’t leave until the bus does. Karina says I’m imagining it. I wrote down the days. I’m not imagining it.

gossip.says: Trinity West runs West’s Flowers on the state road. She’s the eldest florist in Sunfall and she photographs diner neon on her way home. She’s earnest and a bit awkward and she once gave me a free bouquet because I looked tired.
gossip.note: Eva Castle says Trinity West gave her a free bouquet because she looked tired.
gossip.ask: Eva says you gave her a free bouquet because she looked tired.
gossip.answer: She did look tired. She drives a tour bus full of people asking if the cacti are real and then goes home and teaches guitar. I gave her sunflowers. Sunflowers are for people who need to be reminded to turn toward something. She looked at them for a long time.

gossip.says: Karina Flores drives the first tour bus and I drive the second. She tells tourists she’s single for tips. She is single, but she makes it sound like a tragedy. She makes twice what I do.
gossip.note: Eva Castle says Karina Flores tells tourists she’s single for bigger tips.
gossip.ask: Eva says you tell tourists you’re single for bigger tips.
gossip.answer: I am single. It’s just a matter of how I say it. Sadly, with a glance at the horizon, and the tips double. Eva tells tourists the truth about everything, including the cacti, and she wonders why I make more. Honesty is lovely. It doesn’t pay for gas.

women.name: Giselle Ford
women.look: Dark skin, ash-blonde lob, a gap-toothed smile, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about the front desk
own.player: What’s it like working the hospital’s front desk?
own.reply: Twelve years. Everyone’s worst night starts with me. I’m cheerful about it. That’s the job. If I looked worried, they’d really panic.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What are you into outside work?
own.reply: Old records. Singers who made one album and vanished. I buy them at a stall downtown and play them for the night porters. They pretend to hate it. One of them hums along now.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do you have family in Sunfall?
own.reply: My sister Katrina. She’s the quiet one with the camera, and I’m the loud one with the desk. Our dad was a signalman. He taught us both to listen down the line for the train. She listens. I talk over it.

own.label: Ask about the visitor book
own.player: Do you really write down everyone who comes in?
own.reply: Everyone. Real names, fake names, the ones who sign with an X. Twelve years of it. I’ve never once read it like a story. My sister did once. She went quiet, and Katrina’s always quiet, so that’s saying something.

own.label: Ask her something serious
own.player: Can I ask you something serious?
own.reply: Ugh. Fine. One serious thing, and then you have to tell me something stupid. Those are the rules at my desk.

calls.label: Ask if everyone comes in the front
calls.player: Does everyone come in through the front?
calls.reply: Mostly. A porter told me some men come in through the ambulance bay instead, so they never pass my desk. I asked if a receptionist is allowed to write the back door in the front desk’s book. Nobody’s said no yet.
calls.note: Giselle Ford says some men come into the hospital through the ambulance bay so they never pass the front desk.

calls.label: Ask if there’s someone special
calls.player: Is there someone special at the hospital?
calls.reply: A night porter. Sometimes. He hums along to my records and pretends he isn’t. That’s about as serious as I get, so don’t push it.

life.news: Found a record at the stall today by a woman who sang one perfect album and then just stopped. I’m obsessed.
life.more: Nineteen seventy-four, one album, nine songs, and then nothing. No comeback, no explanation. I played it at the desk all night. A man waiting for his wife asked who it was. I said nobody knows. He said that was the saddest thing he’d ever heard, then asked me to write down the name.

life.news: Someone checked in tonight as John Doe the Third. I wrote it down. I write everyone down.
life.more: He had a burned thumb and a very bad mustache. I said, Mr. Doe, please take a seat, your family has been expecting you. He laughed so hard he forgot it hurt. That’s my whole medical training right there.

life.news: Long night. Somebody’s kid. I smiled the whole time. Now my face won’t stop.
life.more: That’s the part nobody tells you. You smile so the family doesn’t fall apart in the lobby, and then you get home and your face still won’t come down. I put a record on and lay on the floor until it was light out.

life.news: Dinner with my sister. We talked about absolutely nothing for two hours. Perfect.
life.more: Katrina and I have a rule: no hospital, no cameras, nothing heavy. We talk about shoes and our dad’s terrible jokes. She laughed once, out loud. I’m counting it as a win for the whole year.

gossip.says: Maya Serrano runs the emergency department like a bar at closing time. Nobody fights on her shift. I think they’re scared of her snacks running out.
gossip.note: Giselle Ford says nobody fights on Maya Serrano’s shift in the emergency department.
gossip.ask: Giselle says nobody dares start anything on your shift.
gossip.answer: Because I feed them. A man can’t throw a punch with a granola bar in his hand. Giselle sends them to me smiling and I meet them with a snack. Between us we’ve calmed down half of Sunfall.

gossip.says: Emily Fairchild stitches faster than anyone in the hospital and apologizes the whole time. Sorry, sorry, nearly done. Patients love her. The doctors find it exhausting.
gossip.note: Giselle Ford says Emily Fairchild is the fastest stitcher at the hospital.
gossip.ask: Giselle says you apologize the whole time you’re stitching someone up.
gossip.answer: I do not. Well. Maybe a little. If someone’s bleeding, saying sorry feels like the least I can do. Giselle says hello to people having a heart attack. We all cope differently.

women.name: Morgan Palmer
women.look: Rosy fair skin, dark brown messy bun, thin wire-rimmed glasses, floral blouse and jeans

own.label: Ask about her class
own.player: What’s it like teaching at St Brigid’s?
own.reply: Twenty-two eight-year-olds and one visiting hamster. I read them poetry. They like it more than adults do. Adults are embarrassed by poetry. Children just want to know who dies.

own.label: Ask about the postcards in her photos
own.player: What are those postcards on your wall?
own.reply: Old Sunfall chapels. I have the Old Mission from the founding years with nine women on the steps. Nobody can tell me who they are. I find that very romantic and slightly worrying.

own.label: Ask about the jacket she wears in her photos
own.player: That jacket looks too big for you. Whose is it?
own.reply: Someone who took a job at the lodge’s stables and stopped writing back. He went to the coast. I kept the jacket. That’s either romantic or sad and I change my mind every day.

calls.label: Ask why Mrs Oakley locks her door
calls.player: You said Mrs Oakley started locking her door. Why?
calls.reply: I asked her in the end, over the tomatoes. It isn’t burglars. It’s her grandson, Ethan. He comes home at sunrise on the darkest nights with chalk on his hands and he won’t say where he’s been. She’s selling her husband’s things. She said she didn’t want Harold’s gun in the house with him in it. Then she went inside and locked the door.

life.news: The hamster visited my class today. Twenty-two eight-year-olds went completely silent. I have never achieved that.
life.more: Teresa’s class keeps a hamster and lends him to us once a week like a visiting dignitary. They read to him. He sleeps through it. Today one of my quietest read a whole page out loud because the hamster was listening. I went and sat in my car afterwards for a minute.

life.news: Found a postcard of the Cemetery Chapel from the founding years at the flea market. A dollar. I nearly cried at the stall.
life.more: I collect old postcards of Sunfall’s chapels. The Old Mission, St Brigid’s, the Cemetery Chapel. This one has the angels before anyone put the fence round them. The man selling it said nobody wants chapels. I said I do. He gave me a second one for free, I think out of pity.

life.news: Mrs Oakley next door has started locking her kitchen door. She’s left it open for twenty years.
life.more: She gives me tomatoes over the fence and talks about her late husband like he’s in the next room. Her grandson lives in the room over her garage. The light is never on. I’d decided he was studious. This week I saw him come home at sunrise with chalk on his hands. Now she locks the kitchen door. I haven’t asked why.

life.news: The bishop’s new music man took over our Mass with a guitar. The children used to sing there. I wrote to the bishop. Nothing.
life.more: My class sang at the chapel every month. Now there’s a man with a guitar and a binder. I wrote to the bishop, very politely. Margaret Holloway lent me her letters as a model. She’s written four. He hasn’t answered hers either. I’m starting a fifth for her.

gossip.says: Teresa Bellamy teaches the class above mine. Her hamster visits my room once a week. It is the most important event in the school calendar.
gossip.note: Morgan Palmer teaches the class below Teresa Bellamy’s.
gossip.ask: Morgan says your hamster is the most important event in the school calendar.
gossip.answer: He is. He has a schedule and a fan club. Morgan pretends she isn’t in the fan club. She brought him a carrot last week.

gossip.says: Margaret Holloway lent me her letters to the bishop so I could write my own. Four letters. Not one reply.
gossip.note: Morgan Palmer says Margaret Holloway has written the bishop four letters with no reply.
gossip.ask: Morgan says you’ve written the bishop four letters.
gossip.answer: Five, by now. He replies to nobody. I keep copies. One day someone will want to know who asked first.

women.name: Roxanne Pierce
women.look: Freckled fair skin, copper waist-length waves, a gap-toothed smile, turquoise peasant top

own.label: Ask about dog walking
own.player: How many dogs do you walk?
own.reply: Six, at sunrise and dusk. Three lapdogs, a retriever who belonged to a police sergeant, and a very wise mutt. We go through the chapel grounds. It’s quiet. Usually.

own.label: Ask about the dresses
own.player: I hear you restore old dresses.
own.reply: From Lucia Romano’s thrift shop. Lace and seams and covered buttons. Every one was somebody’s best night once. I like giving them another.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your father do?
own.reply: He was the groundsman at the Cemetery Chapel for thirty years. He dug more graves than the parish ever wrote down. He won’t say more than that. Yet.

calls.label: Ask how many graves her father dug
calls.player: You said your father dug more graves than the parish wrote down. How many more?
calls.reply: I finally asked him. Eleven, over thirty years, at night, at stones that already had names. A woman from the club paid him for each one, in cash, and he wrote the dates in the back of his almanac. He said he’d tell the rest to someone who would actually do something about it.

life.news: Walked six dogs through the Cemetery Chapel grounds at sunrise. The angels have their backs to the city. The dogs don’t mind.
life.more: I walk the old parish families’ dogs and three widows’ lapdogs at sunrise and at dusk, through the chapel grounds. I know every stone by now. My father was the groundsman for thirty years. I knew the names before I could read them.

life.news: Finished restoring a dress from Lucia Romano’s shop. Took three weeks. It looks like someone’s first dance again.
life.more: Lucia gets donations from the old families and I fix the ones worth fixing. Lace, seams, little covered buttons. This one is pale green with a hand-sewn hem. I want to know whose it was. Lucia says not to ask donated dresses questions.

life.news: A man I’ve been writing to sends the most beautiful letters. In person he talks about his lawn. I’m starting to wonder who writes them.
life.more: His letters are lovely, really lovely. Then we talk and it’s weather and his lawn. And the handwriting is one I think I’ve seen before, on Christmas cards to the widows I walk dogs for. I wanted the person who wrote the letters. I’m not sure that’s who I’ve got.

life.news: Once, at dusk, behind the angels, the dogs all went quiet at the same time. Dogs don’t do that.
life.more: A car with no lights, two men, a long shape, and a grave already dug at a stone that already had a name on it. Six dogs, and not one of them made a sound. The parish says it was a family burial with permission. My father says in thirty years the diocese never gave permission for anything. The club did.

gossip.says: I walk Helen Markham’s dog on her long days. He’s smarter than both of us.
gossip.note: Roxanne Pierce walks Helen Markham’s dog.
gossip.ask: Roxanne says your dog is smarter than both of you.
gossip.answer: He is. He knows the way home from anywhere and he never brings it up. Roxanne is the only walker he’s ever waited for at the gate.

gossip.says: Jules Moreland runs past the Cemetery Chapel some evenings. We’ve never spoken. I think she saw the same thing I did one night.
gossip.note: Roxanne Pierce thinks Jules Moreland saw the same thing she did behind the Cemetery Chapel one night.
gossip.ask: Roxanne thinks you saw the same thing she did behind the Cemetery Chapel.
gossip.answer: A car with no lights. I was on the other side of the angels. I thought I was the only one. I’ve never told anyone. Tell her I’ll buy her a coffee.

women.name: Alyssa Kimball
women.look: Porcelain skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, white tank top and denim shorts

own.label: Ask about Kimball Sisters Interiors
own.player: Tell me about your business.
own.reply: Me, my sister, a yellow van and a workshop on the edge of the Quarter. We do kitchens, studies and anybody who wants their mother’s house to stop feeling like their mother’s house.

own.label: Ask about her baking
own.player: I hear you bake.
own.reply: Badly. Elaborately. For a card game full of professional pastry chefs, who are very kind about it. I bring a cake, they let me lose at cards. It’s a good arrangement.

own.label: Ask why she keeps a journal
own.player: Why do you keep a journal?
own.reply: My mom did, every night, until she couldn’t. I started the week after. If I write it down, it happened the way it happened, not the way someone tells me later it did.

calls.label: Ask about the Beaumont job
calls.player: What happened at the Beaumont house?
calls.reply: Hugh Beaumont asked me to stay for a drink when I finished the study. I said no. He said that was a pity. The next week I had the Foundation’s committee room as a job, which is what a pity costs, apparently. He told me the safe behind the portrait held the family’s conscience. He laughed. I wrote the laugh down.

life.news: Finished a kitchen on the edge of the Quarter. The owner cried. The good kind.
life.more: Thirty years of the same brown cupboards, and she wanted yellow, and her husband always said no. He passed last winter. We painted every door the color of egg yolk and put the radio back on the windowsill where he kept it. She stood in the doorway with both hands over her mouth. My sister and I sat in the van afterwards and didn’t say anything for a while.

life.news: Baked for the pastry chefs’ card game again. They ate it out of politeness. I lost at cards out of habit.
life.more: I bring a cake every time because it’s the price of my seat at the table. Professionals eat it. Tonight’s was a lemon drizzle that drizzled sideways. Avery said it had character. Nina said it had structural problems. I lost eleven dollars and laughed the whole time. It’s the best evening of my week.

life.news: Moving a portrait in a client’s study, I found a safe behind it. I put the portrait back. I didn’t look.
life.more: The Beaumont house, last spring. A woman in an old dress with a brooch shaped like a moon, and behind her, a little steel door. I hung her back exactly where she was. Later the man of the house asked me to stay for a drink, and told me the safe held the family’s conscience, and laughed. I wrote the laugh in my journal. Then I tore the page out. Then I wrote it again.

life.news: My sister and I painted the van. It’s yellow now. We can be seen from space.
life.more: Kimball Sisters Interiors, in black letters on bright yellow. It took two weekends and most of a can of thinner. People wave at us at the lights now. A man asked if we did ice cream. My sister said yes. We don’t.

gossip.says: I decorated the study at the Beaumont house last spring. Alice Beaumont was the only one there who offered me a coffee.
gossip.note: Alyssa Kimball decorated the Beaumont study; Alice Beaumont brought her coffee.
gossip.ask: Alyssa says you were the only one at the Beaumont house who brought her a coffee.
gossip.answer: She cleaned the portrait of my great-great-grandmother as if it were a person. Nobody in my family has ever been that careful with Ada. Of course I brought her coffee. I’d have brought her lunch if my father hadn’t been home.

gossip.says: I rehung Delphine Moreau’s collages in the Foundation’s committee room. She stood next to me and said the middle one was waiting for a face she didn’t have yet.
gossip.note: Alyssa Kimball says Delphine Moreau told her the middle collage in the committee room is waiting for a face.
gossip.ask: Alyssa says the middle collage in the committee room is waiting for a face.
gossip.answer: She hung them straight the first time. Nobody does that. The middle one is still waiting. I’m patient, and the committee is not, which is usually how I win.

women.name: Trinity West
women.look: Rosy fair skin, ash-blonde lob, a beauty mark above her lip, mint polo shirt

own.label: Ask about her flower shop
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I run West’s Flowers on the state road. Funerals, truckers and gas station roses. Now and then a birthday that breaks your heart.

own.label: Ask what she does on the way home
own.player: What do you do after work?
own.reply: Photograph diner neon on the drive home. A pink cowboy, a coffee cup, an arrow that says EAT. It’s my quiet hour.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have family nearby?
own.reply: My sister Delilah walks dogs past the shop. One of them ate forty carnations last week. I put his photo in the window.

calls.label: Ask about the casino’s lily orders
calls.player: Who orders the white lilies from the casino?
calls.reply: A man from the lounge, cash, on nights with no moon. He collects after closing. Last time, I followed the car a little way out of curiosity. It didn’t go to the casino. It went out past the old junction and up the ridge road. I turned around.
calls.note: Trinity West says the casino lounge buys white lilies on moonless nights and takes them up the ridge road.

life.news: Did the flowers for an eightieth birthday. The woman said they were the first flowers anyone had bought her since her husband.
life.more: West’s Flowers is on the state road, so mostly I do funerals and gas station roses. But today a daughter ordered eighty yellow roses for her mother, one for every year. I delivered them myself. The woman held one to her face and said nobody had bought her flowers since 1987. I drove home the long way.

life.news: My sister Delilah walked six dogs past the shop and one of them ate a whole bucket of carnations. I laughed. Then I did the math.
life.more: Forty carnations, gone, into a very happy labrador. Delilah apologized for twenty minutes. The labrador did not apologize at all. I photographed his face covered in petals for the shop window. It’s the best advertisement we’ve ever had. Still forty carnations.

life.news: The casino lounge orders white lilies by the dozen. Always on the same nights. Always cash.
life.more: Lilies are for funerals and apologies, and the casino doesn’t do either. A man in a suit pays in cash and collects them himself, after closing, with a car I don’t recognize. On those nights there’s always the same car parked outside the shop. I’ve started photographing the car on my way home.

gossip.says: Faye Dawson bakes for her sister’s decorating firm and birdwatches before breakfast on the dry river. She’s sunny and stubborn and she once brought my sister’s dogs a whole tray of scones. The dogs have never recovered.
gossip.note: Trinity West says Faye Dawson brought her sister’s dogs a tray of scones.
gossip.ask: Trinity says you brought her sister’s dogs a whole tray of scones.
gossip.answer: They were burned scones. Nobody else would eat them. The dogs thought it was the best day of their lives. Trinity said that was irresponsible and then took one for herself. She does flowers for funerals all week and still smiles when you walk in. That takes something.

gossip.says: Brittany Hale runs the flower shop in the Quarter and collects the worst souvenirs in Arizona. She’s my rival and my friend. She sells more sorry than love. I sell more funerals than both.
gossip.note: Trinity West says Brittany Hale is her rival and friend, and sells more sorry than love.
gossip.ask: Trinity says you sell more sorry than love, and she sells more funerals than both.
gossip.answer: It’s true, men in the Quarter mostly need to apologize. Trinity is on the state road, so she gets the funerals and the truckers. We swap stock when one of us runs low. She once lent me two hundred lilies for a wedding and wouldn’t take a penny. That’s a real rival.

women.name: Faye Dawson
women.look: Pale skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, yellow sundress

own.label: Ask about baking for the firm
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I bake for my sister’s decorating firm. Clients sign faster after cake. Sometimes the cake is rustic. On purpose.

own.label: Ask what she does before work
own.player: What do you do in the mornings?
own.reply: Birdwatch on the dry river with Penelope and Felicity and a thermos of terrible coffee. Hummingbirds this morning.

own.label: Ask what she won’t give up
own.player: What won’t you give up on?
own.reply: Croissants. I’ve tried forty times. They come out like bread rolls. I’ll get there.

calls.label: Ask what she heard in the pantry
calls.player: What did you hear from the pantry at the catering job?
calls.reply: Desserts for a private dinner at the lodge, with Avery. From inside the pantry I heard a woman say I saw it, the night of the gala, and a man say no you didn’t. A long pause. Then she said, no. I didn’t. I recognized her voice. She’d been a witness in the paper.
calls.note: Faye Dawson heard a gala witness at the lodge take back what she saw after a man told her she hadn’t.

life.news: Saw a pair of hummingbirds on the dry river this morning. Penelope gasped so loud they flew off. Worth it.
life.more: I go out before breakfast with Penelope and Felicity and a thermos of very bad coffee. This morning two hummingbirds hovered right in front of us for a whole minute, like they were deciding whether we were flowers. Penelope gasped. They left. Felicity wrote it down. I just laughed.

life.news: Burned a whole tray of scones for my sister’s client meeting. Served them anyway. Called them rustic.
life.more: I bake for Riley’s decorating firm because she says clients sign faster when they’ve had cake. Today I left the scones in too long while I watched a hawk out of the window. They came out like little bricks. I called them rustic. The client asked for the recipe. We got the job.

life.news: I was in a pantry at a catering job and heard a woman on the other side of the door change her story. In one sentence.
life.more: Big private dinner, up on the ridge, I was doing desserts with Avery. I was getting cream from the pantry and two people were talking right outside. A woman said I saw it, and a man said no you didn’t, and she said, after a long pause, no, I didn’t. Just like that. I stayed in the pantry a long time.

gossip.says: Nikki Maddox works the night shift at the all-night pharmacy and volunteers at the Sisters’ thrift shop. She’s nineteen and blunt as a brick and the most generous person I know. She gave me her coat in the rain once and walked home wet.
gossip.note: Faye Dawson says Nikki Maddox gave her coat away in the rain and walked home wet.
gossip.ask: Faye says you gave her your coat in the rain and walked home wet.
gossip.answer: It was a thrift shop coat. I have six. She was carrying a cake in the rain and the cake was more important than me. Faye brings burned scones to the pharmacy at the end of my shift and calls it breakfast. She’s the best thing that happens to me most mornings.

gossip.says: Riley Dawson is my big sister and runs the decorating firm. I bake for her clients. She says clients sign faster after cake. She’s right. She’s always right. It’s exhausting being her sister.
gossip.note: Faye Dawson says her sister Riley says clients sign faster after cake.
gossip.ask: Faye says you’re always right and it’s exhausting being your sister.
gossip.answer: I am always right. It’s exhausting being me too. Faye served burned scones to a client last week and called them rustic and he asked for the recipe. That’s not baking, that’s salesmanship. I should make her a partner. I won’t tell her that. She’d get insufferable.

women.name: Nikki Maddox
women.look: Fair skin, dark brown messy bun, sharp winged eyeliner, white tank top and denim shorts

own.label: Ask about the night shift
own.player: What’s the night shift at a pharmacy like?
own.reply: Insomniacs, new parents and people buying things they’re embarrassed to buy in daylight. And sometimes a man who just needs the lights on.

own.label: Ask about the thrift shop
own.player: What do you do on your days off?
own.reply: Volunteer at the Sisters’ thrift shop. I see every donation first. Best wardrobe on the reservoir side for almost nothing.

own.label: Ask why she’s so blunt
own.player: Are you always this direct?
own.reply: Night shifts burn the politeness out of you. I’m nice. I’m just not polite about it.

calls.label: Ask what she knows from the pharmacy records
calls.player: What do the pharmacy records tell you?
calls.reply: Every man the club has voted into a house on the reservoir side is on the same prescription. Same doctor, same pharmacy, same quantity, paid by the same account with a ribbon on the letterhead. I know which ribbon is whose. I’ve known for a year. I’ve told nobody.
calls.note: Nikki Maddox says every man the club voted into a reservoir-side house gets the same prescription paid by one account.

life.news: Found a perfect leather jacket at the thrift shop for four dollars. The Sisters said it was meant for me. I believe them.
life.more: I volunteer at the Sisters’ thrift shop once a week and sort donations, which means I see everything first, which means I have the best wardrobe on the reservoir side for almost no money. This jacket fits like it was cut for me. Sister Agnes said, very seriously, God provides. God provided a very good jacket.

life.news: Night shift at the pharmacy. A man came in at three, asked for nothing, stood at the counter and cried. I gave him a cough drop.
life.more: Night shifts are mostly quiet: insomniacs, new parents, people who need something they’re embarrassed to buy in daylight. And sometimes a man who just needs to stand somewhere with the lights on. I let him stand there. I gave him a cough drop. He took it like it was medicine. Maybe it was.

life.news: The house next door to mine has never once had a light on. I’ve lived there my whole life. Never once.
life.more: My dad moved us there when I was small, and the club voted him into the house, whatever that means. The house next door has been dark the whole time. Somebody mows the lawn. Somebody pays the bills. Nobody ever turns on a light. I used to think it was haunted. Now I think it’s worse. Now I think it’s waiting.

gossip.says: Paola Cruz works at the museum and plays five-on-five for the taco van’s team. She’s quick to laugh and slow to trust and she tackles like a truck. She’s the only person who’s ever made the police team cry.
gossip.note: Nikki Maddox says Paola Cruz plays soccer for the taco van’s team and once made the police team cry.
gossip.ask: Nikki says you tackle like a truck and once made the police team cry.
gossip.answer: Only one of them cried and she was faking for a free kick. The police team are all actors. Nikki comes to watch with a bag of thrift shop snacks and screams at the referee. She’s nineteen and scared of nothing. I’d like to be scared of nothing. I’m working on it.

gossip.says: Jessica Rivera works the day shift at the all-night pharmacy. I work the nights. She knows half of Sunfall’s secrets and all of its rashes. She leaves me notes on the till about which customers to be nice to.
gossip.note: Nikki Maddox says Jessica Rivera leaves her notes about which customers to be nice to.
gossip.ask: Nikki says you leave her notes on the till about which customers to be nice to.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to. Half of them are going through something and the other half are going through something worse. Nikki is blunt, which the night shift needs, and she gives every crying man a cough drop, which the night shift needs more. I couldn’t do nights. She makes it look easy. It isn’t.

women.name: Paola Cruz
women.look: Warm brown skin, twist-out coils, tortoiseshell glasses, striped T-shirt dress

own.label: Ask about the founding gallery
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I look after the founding gallery at the museum. Old saddles, old maps, old men in oil paintings looking pleased with themselves.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do outside work?
own.reply: Five-on-five for the taco van’s team. We beat the campus girls. Free tacos for a week. Life is good.

own.label: Ask about her twin
own.player: Do you have brothers or sisters?
own.reply: A twin, Daniela. Same face, same shoe size, and she runs off with my good shoes. I steal her scarves. We’re even.

calls.label: Ask about the crate she signed for
calls.player: What was the crate you signed for at the museum?
calls.reply: From the Foundation, for the founding gallery. Founding-family objects, the inventory said, and a little crescent drawn by one line on the list. I signed for it with the museum’s cat pen. Now the paperwork says it came another day and nobody signed. The crescent line is gone from the copy.
calls.note: Paola Cruz signed for a Foundation crate at the museum whose inventory listed a crescent; the paperwork now says nobody signed.

life.news: Scored the winner for the taco van’s team against the campus girls. The van gave us free tacos for a week.
life.more: Five-on-five in the park, the taco van’s team against everybody. Today we beat the campus team with a goal off my knee. Ugly. Counts. The owner came out with a tray and shouted free tacos for a week and we all screamed. I’ve had tacos for breakfast twice. No regrets.

life.news: My twin borrowed my good shoes and returned them with a scuff. Daniela runs a boutique. She knows better.
life.more: We look the same and wear the same size and she runs a dress shop on the gallery strip and still steals my shoes. I said nothing. I took her silk scarf. She hasn’t noticed yet. When she notices, she’ll come over and we’ll have the same fight we’ve had since we were six. I love her more than anything.

life.news: I signed for a delivery at the museum. A week later my boss told me I hadn’t signed for it. I had. I remember the pen.
life.more: A big wooden crate, from the Foundation, for the founding gallery. I signed the driver’s sheet in blue ink with the museum’s cat pen. A week later the paperwork says nobody signed, the crate came in another day, and I must be confused. I’m not confused. I remember the cat.

gossip.says: Brogan Ellis sells houses on the reservoir side and teaches herself drums in a lock-up at night. She’s playful until you cross a line, and then she’s terrifying. I watched her make a man apologize to a parking meter.
gossip.note: Paola Cruz says Brogan Ellis once made a man apologize to a parking meter.
gossip.ask: Paola says you made a man apologize to a parking meter.
gossip.answer: He kicked it. It hadn’t done anything. It was a very innocent meter. Paola plays five-on-five like she’s defending her family’s honor, which, knowing her family, she probably is. She’s the only person at the museum who laughs at my jokes. Then she doesn’t trust them.

gossip.says: Daniela Cruz is my twin and runs a dress shop on the gallery strip. She makes dresses that last. She also steals my shoes. We’ve had the same fight since we were six. I’d die for her.
gossip.note: Paola Cruz says her twin Daniela runs a dress shop and steals her shoes.
gossip.ask: Paola says you steal her shoes and you’ve had the same fight since you were six.
gossip.answer: I borrow them. With love. She took my silk scarf yesterday and thinks I haven’t noticed. I noticed before she left the building. Paola guards the founding gallery at the museum like it’s a vault. Lately she’s been very quiet about something. She gets quiet when she’s right and nobody believes her.

women.name: Brogan Ellis
women.look: Freckled fair skin, platinum pixie cut, freckles across her nose, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about her first sale
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Junior agent at Reservoir Residential. I carry Samantha’s coffee and clipboard. Today I closed my first house on my own.

own.label: Ask about her drumming
own.player: Do you play an instrument?
own.reply: Drums, in a lock-up behind the tire shop. Lenore next door makes jewelry. I’ve been drumming next to delicate silver work for months.

own.label: Ask what makes her stop joking
own.player: When do you stop being playful?
own.reply: When someone kicks something that can’t kick back. Dogs, parking meters, waitresses. Then I’m not funny at all.

calls.label: Ask about the private dinner
calls.player: What was the private dinner you went to?
calls.reply: I was a Bluebird junior’s plus-one, at a long table at the lodge. Candles, very quiet men, and a speech about families looking after their own. A man at the head of the table had a blue ribbon on his lapel. My page about it was torn out the next morning. She was so sweet at breakfast.
calls.note: Brogan Ellis went to a lodge dinner as a Bluebird junior’s plus-one; her journal page about it was torn out the next morning.

life.news: Sold a big house on the reservoir side. The buyer asked if I’d throw in my sense of humor. I said that’s extra.
life.more: I’m the junior at Reservoir Residential, under Samantha, and I mostly carry her coffee and her clipboard. Today she let me close one on my own. The buyer wanted the curtains, the hot tub and a discount. He got the curtains. I got a commission. I bought new drumsticks.

life.news: Drummed for three hours in the lock-up and Lenore from the next unit asked me very politely to stop. At midnight.
life.more: The lock-ups behind the tire shop are where Sunfall goes to be loud, and Lenore makes jewelry in hers, which I didn’t know, which means I’ve been drumming next to a woman doing very delicate silver work for months. She’s been so nice about it. I bought her earplugs. She said they were beautiful.

life.news: I went to a private dinner as somebody’s plus-one. I wrote about it in my journal that night. The page is gone.
life.more: A girl I know from the club needed a date for something fancy, and I went, and it was very strange, very candlelit, very quiet men. I wrote all of it down at home. She stayed over. In the morning the page was missing, torn out neat. She was very sweet at breakfast.

gossip.says: Mia Donnelly coaches at the swim club and learns Italian from a Sister’s nonna’s recipe cards. She’s private and very sharp. Her husband was pulled out of the reservoir at the regatta two years ago. Alive. His family hasn’t forgiven him.
gossip.note: Brogan Ellis says Mia Donnelly’s husband was pulled alive from the reservoir and his family hasn’t forgiven him.
gossip.ask: Brogan says your husband was pulled out of the reservoir alive and his family hasn’t forgiven him.
gossip.answer: For surviving. That’s the joke in Sunfall. He was meant to win the race for his father and instead he nearly drowned, and the family took that as a betrayal. They stopped calling. I didn’t. Brogan drums like she’s trying to wake the dead. Some days I wish someone would.

gossip.says: Samantha Price is my boss at Reservoir Residential. She learns ballroom at the Quarter studio to meet buyers and she’s the best closer in Arizona. She told me never to look at the empty house next to hers. So I looked.
gossip.note: Brogan Ellis says Samantha Price told her never to look at the empty house next to hers.
gossip.ask: Brogan says you told her never to look at the empty house next to yours, so she looked.
gossip.answer: Of course she looked. I knew she would. That’s why I said it. Brogan is the best junior I’ve ever had because she can’t leave a closed door alone. One day that’s going to make her a fortune or get her in very deep trouble. I’m keeping an eye on which.

women.name: Mia Donnelly
women.look: Fair skin, a long braid to the waist, thin wire-rimmed glasses, red gingham shirt

own.label: Ask about coaching
own.player: What do you do at the swim club?
own.reply: I’m the fourth coach. I open the pool early and teach toddlers to swim. They don’t know they’re learning. That’s the trick.

own.label: Ask about learning Italian
own.player: Are you learning a language?
own.reply: Italian, from a Sister’s nonna’s recipe cards, with two friends. We grade each other. My bread is the best. Don’t tell them.

own.label: Ask about her husband
own.player: Are you married?
own.reply: To a man who nearly drowned at the regatta. His family hasn’t forgiven him for living. I have. Every day.

calls.label: Ask about the regatta
calls.player: What happened to your husband at the regatta?
calls.reply: Two years ago he went under in the reservoir and came up alive. His family took it as a betrayal. The men from the club who were in the boat with him never spoke to him again, and that winter his father got voted onto the board. Now a car sits outside my pool. I don’t think the two things are separate.
calls.note: Mia Donnelly says her husband nearly drowned at the regatta, his father joined the board that winter, and a car now watches her pool.

life.news: Made Nonna Moretti’s bread from the card in Italian. Read every word. Whitney and I danced around her kitchen.
life.more: Three of us share the recipe cards: me, Whitney from the club and Noreen. We cook in turns and grade each other’s Italian. Today my bread rose like a cloud and I read the whole card aloud without the dictionary. Whitney said brava. I said grazie. Then we ate the whole loaf standing up.

life.news: My husband’s brother walked past us in the supermarket and pretended not to see us. Two years now.
life.more: My husband nearly drowned at the regatta, and his family treated it like a scandal, because he lost the race his father wanted him to win. Now they cross the street. Today it was the cereal aisle. My husband put the box in the cart very carefully and said nothing. I held his hand in the checkout line.

life.news: There’s a car outside the pool on the mornings I open. It leaves when the first swimmer arrives.
life.more: I open the pool early and it’s always empty except for me and the water, which is how I like it. Lately, three mornings a week, a dark car sits in the lot with the engine running. When the first swimmer pulls in, it leaves. It’s never there on the mornings someone else opens. Only mine.

gossip.says: Esme Turner is the youngest tour guide in Sunfall. She does the children’s tours and the Cemetery Chapel. She makes collages out of old maps. Nothing ever rattles her, not even the ghost tour.
gossip.note: Mia Donnelly says Esme Turner does the children’s tours and the Cemetery Chapel tour.
gossip.ask: Mia says nothing rattles you, not even the ghost tour.
gossip.answer: The ghost tour is the easy one. Ghosts don’t ask if the cacti are real. Mia teaches toddlers to swim, which is far scarier, and she does it so calmly the toddlers don’t notice they’re learning. I made her a collage of the reservoir from an old map. She keeps it by the pool office door.

gossip.says: Whitney Ashford from the club shares the recipe cards with me. She can’t order a coffee in Italian but she makes the best lasagna in Sunfall. She laughs at everything. She’s very good at keeping secrets behind it.
gossip.note: Mia Donnelly says she and Whitney Ashford share recipe cards, and Whitney keeps secrets behind her laugh.
gossip.ask: Mia says you laugh at everything and you’re very good at keeping secrets behind it.
gossip.answer: That’s rude and accurate. Mia never laughs at all and keeps even more secrets than me. We stand in my kitchen reading Italian at each other like two spies swapping codes. Her bread is better than mine. I will never tell her that, and now you can’t either.

women.name: Esme Turner
women.look: Rosy fair skin, jet-black waist-length hair, gray-green eyes, floral blouse and jeans

own.label: Ask about her tours
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Tour guide. The children’s tours and the Cemetery Chapel’s. Cactus hugs in the morning, ghost stories in the afternoon.

own.label: Ask about her collages
own.player: Do you have a hobby?
own.reply: Collages from the tour company’s old maps. One turned out to be rare. It’s half a hawk now. My boss is upset.

own.label: Ask if anything scares her
own.player: Does anything scare you?
own.reply: Not really. The ghost tour is easy. The children’s tour is where the real danger is. They ask the hard questions.

calls.label: Ask about the woman who changed her story
calls.player: What did the woman on your chapel tour say about the ribbons?
calls.reply: The first time, she said the white ribbons at the Cemetery Chapel are for girls who married into the club and didn’t last. Twelve stones by the far wall. The next week she said they were for soldiers, very loudly, staring at me. Somebody had told her she’d said too much.
calls.note: Esme Turner heard a woman on her tour say the white ribbons at the Cemetery Chapel are for club brides who didn’t last, then retract it.

life.news: Did the children’s tour and a girl asked if the cacti have feelings. I said yes. They feel very proud.
life.more: I do the children’s tours and the Cemetery Chapel’s, which is a funny combination, and I’m the youngest guide at the company by about ten years. Today twenty kids hugged a saguaro, very carefully, one at a time. Nobody got a spine. I’m calling it a historic day.

life.news: Old map I was using for a collage turned out to be worth money. My boss wants it back. It’s in a collage.
life.more: I make collages from the tour company’s old maps, the ones in a box in the back nobody looks at. This one is now half of a picture of a hawk. My boss found out it was a very rare map of the reservoir before it was a reservoir. I offered him the hawk. He didn’t want the hawk.

life.news: A woman on my chapel tour told everyone what the white ribbons on the graves meant. Next week she said they were for the war dead.
life.more: She was on my bus twice. The first time, at the Cemetery Chapel, she told my tourists the ribbons were for girls who married into the club and didn’t last. She said it like a joke. The next week, same spot, she said very loudly they were for soldiers. She looked at me the whole time.

gossip.says: Jade Carter coaches the little swimmers at the club and looks like she’s sulking all the time. She isn’t. She once carried a kid out of the deep end on her back like a turtle. The kid still talks about it.
gossip.note: Esme Turner says Jade Carter carried a kid out of the deep end on her back like a turtle.
gossip.ask: Esme says you carried a kid out of the deep end on your back like a turtle.
gossip.answer: He panicked. I didn’t. Turtle carry is the best rescue for small ones because they hold on and feel safe. I don’t sulk, by the way. That’s just my face. Esme does a ghost tour and a children’s tour in the same day and somehow makes both of them fun. That’s a skill.

gossip.says: Gina Fowler at the Daily makes collages out of spiked newspaper stories. I make mine out of old maps. We met at a craft fair and argued about glue for an hour. She’s my favorite person to disagree with.
gossip.note: Esme Turner says she and Gina Fowler argued about glue for an hour at a craft fair.
gossip.ask: Esme says you argued about glue for an hour at a craft fair.
gossip.answer: Because she uses glue sticks on hundred-year-old paper, and that’s a crime, and I told her so. She told me newsprint was the real crime. We were both right. Now we swap scraps. Hers have secrets in them. Mine have places. Together we’ve got a whole town.

women.name: Abby Kincaid
women.look: Light-brown skin, short silver-dyed crop, a wide bright smile, turquoise peasant top

worldTopics.label: Ask what she thinks of Sunfall
worldTopics.player: So what do you honestly think of Sunfall?

thunderbirds: Sunfall is a small town that thinks it’s a big one, and I adore it for that. Every gala feels like a coronation.
It’s generous, if you know the right people. The desert makes everyone a little dramatic.
police: It’s quiet until it isn’t. Most of my job lives in the gap between those two.
Nice town. Too many people who think the rules are for somebody else.
progressives: It’s a town run by charity dinners and old money calling itself community. The students are the only thing keeping it honest.
I love the people and hate who’s in charge. Sunfall could be amazing if it stopped worshipping its donors.
sisters_of_mercy: It’s a good town with a tired soul. The chapel bell still rings, though, and that matters.
People here are kind once you get past the air conditioning. They’ve just forgotten what they’re for.
fourth_estate: Sunfall produces more stories than it admits to. Half of them never make the paper.
It’s a reporter’s dream. Everyone has a secret and nobody can keep one.
goth_girls: Sunfall is a sunburnt postcard. The only honest hours are after dark.
Too bright, too polite, too many people smiling about nothing. I like the corners nobody photographs.
normie_girls: Honestly? It’s fine. Good diners, terrible traffic, and the sunsets make up for a lot.
It’s home. Boring sometimes, but I like knowing the guy at the taco stand by name.

question: What about you? Do you actually like it here?
Your turn. Sunfall: love it, or put up with it?

warm.label: Say it’s growing on you
warm.player: Honestly? It’s growing on me.

challenge.label: Say it all feels fake
challenge.player: It feels a bit fake to me. Like everyone’s performing.

joke.label: Make a joke
joke.player: I’m only here for the air conditioning.

worldTopics.label: Ask what she believes in
worldTopics.player: Big question: what do you actually believe in?

thunderbirds: Giving back, and being seen to give back. Cynical? Perhaps. The scholarships are real, though.
Tradition, family and a good seating plan. Civilization is mostly manners.
police: That most people tell the truth if you let them. And that evidence beats feelings.
Rules exist because people get hurt without them. That’s about it.
progressives: That things can be fairer than they are, and that it’s on us to make them that way.
Solidarity. Nobody gets anywhere alone, whatever the self-help books say.
sisters_of_mercy: God, the Church, and that love is something you do, not something you feel.
That faith is a discipline, not a mood. Prayer is a habit, like brushing your teeth, only better.
fourth_estate: The truth, even when it’s inconvenient. Especially then.
That nobody should get the last word. Not the mayor, not the protesters, not me.
goth_girls: That beauty and decay are the same thing, seen at different speeds.
Nothing official. I believe in the night, good music and not lying to yourself.
normie_girls: Being a good person, mostly. Paying your bills, calling your mom.
Karma, I think? And that pizza solves more problems than people admit.

warm.label: Say you believe something similar
warm.player: I think I believe in something like that too.

challenge.label: Say you don’t believe in much
challenge.player: Honestly, I don’t believe in much at all.

joke.label: Make a joke
joke.player: I believe in second dates.

worldTopics.label: Ask what she’s looking for
worldTopics.player: What are you actually looking for on here?

thunderbirds: Someone who can hold a conversation at a dinner and still be fun in the car home.
A partner, not a project. I’m done improving men.
police: Someone who doesn’t need rescuing. I do enough of that at work.
Honesty. I can tell when people lie, so don’t.
progressives: Someone who actually reads things and isn’t scared of a woman with opinions.
Someone who turns up. To things. On time. That’s my whole list.
sisters_of_mercy: A man who wants a family and a faith, in either order.
Someone serious. I’m not on here to pass the time.
fourth_estate: Someone with a good story who doesn’t mind being interviewed.
A man who can handle me working late and asking questions.
goth_girls: Someone who isn’t afraid of the dark, literally or otherwise.
No interest in nice. I want interesting.
normie_girls: Someone fun who texts back. Honestly, the bar is on the floor.
A best friend I also want to kiss. Is that too much to ask?

question: And you? What are you looking for?
Your turn. Be honest.

warm.label: Say something sincere
warm.player: Someone I can be myself with.

challenge.label: Say you’re not sure
challenge.player: I don’t really know yet. Maybe I’ll know it when I see it.

joke.label: Make a joke
joke.player: Someone who tolerates my cooking.

worldTopics.label: Ask if she’d ever leave Sunfall
worldTopics.player: Would you ever leave Sunfall for good?

thunderbirds: Leave? Who would run the auction? No. Sunfall needs me.
Only for somewhere with a better opera house. So, no.
police: I’ve thought about it. Then something happens and I’m needed here.
Not while there are open cases. There are always open cases.
progressives: The day this town stops needing changing. So probably never.
I’d go tomorrow if I thought the fight here was lost. It isn’t.
sisters_of_mercy: My parish is here. Where would I go?
If God sent me somewhere else, I’d go. He hasn’t.
fourth_estate: For a bigger paper? Maybe. But the stories here are stranger.
Every reporter dreams of the big city. Then they realize the big city has bigger liars.
goth_girls: One day I’ll get on a night bus and never come back. Not yet.
I like it here because nobody expects anything interesting. It’s a good place to hide.
normie_girls: Maybe for the coast someday. I’d miss the desert, though.
My whole family is here. I’d last a week.

warm.label: Say you’d stay for the right person
warm.player: I’d stay, for the right person.

challenge.label: Say you’d leave in a heartbeat
challenge.player: I’d leave in a heartbeat if I could.

joke.label: Make a joke
joke.player: Only if the bear follows me.

worldTopics.label: Ask about the bear sightings
worldTopics.player: Have you seen the news about the bear?

thunderbirds: A bear at the country club, apparently. The committee is drafting a strongly worded letter.
It’s a sign the canyon developments have gone too far. Not that I’d say so at a fundraiser.
police: We’ve had more calls about that bear than about actual crimes. Keep your doors locked.
Wildlife isn’t my department, but people leave food out and then act surprised.
progressives: The bear is a symptom. We keep building into the desert and then blame the wildlife.
Honestly, the bear is the most reasonable resident of Sunfall.
sisters_of_mercy: We prayed for its safety, and for everyone’s bins.
God’s creatures wander. I just hope nobody gets hurt.
fourth_estate: We’ve run four bear stories. The editor says bears sell. He isn’t wrong.
A source swears it was wearing a collar. I’m chasing it.
goth_girls: I hope it eats a landlord.
A creature that only comes out when it’s hungry and everyone’s asleep. Relatable.
normie_girls: My cousin swears she saw it by the trash cans! I’m not going outside after dark any more.
It’s kind of cute? From very far away. Behind glass.

question: Would you open the door if it knocked?
Are you a bear person?

warm.label: Say you’d keep it locked
warm.player: Door locked, honey hidden, lights off.

challenge.label: Say you’d say hello
challenge.player: Honestly? I’d want to say hello.

joke.label: Make a joke
joke.player: If it brings wine, it can come in.

worldTopics.label: Ask what she thinks of the Bluebirds
worldTopics.player: What’s your take on the Bluebirds and all their charity stuff?

thunderbirds: We do real good. Scholarships, food banks. People only notice when something goes wrong.
It’s a family, with all the politics families have. Don’t believe everything you hear about the gala.
police: Generous donors. Very generous. Generosity like that makes me ask questions.
They fund the police benefit dinner. I try not to let that cloud anything.
progressives: Old money laundering its conscience one gala at a time.
