beats.note: Noelle Sanderson sent you her photographs of the pages from the gala envelope: forty thousand to the Halcyon Ridge Trust on gala night and twenty-five thousand the next day, signed off A.P.

beats.label: Tell her a radio researcher asks about the junction
beats.player: There’s a woman at the radio station, Odette Price, asking questions about the junction.
lines: Odette Price. She got a letter telling her to stop asking. I got the same paper, different words.

If she wants Paul, she can have him. Paul Sanderson, highway engineer, who said the ridge road survey was false and the quarry was hollowing the canyon. Dead at the junction a week later. Weather, on a dry night.

choices.label: Tell her you’ll pass it to Odette
choices.player: I’ll tell Odette. She’ll put his name on the air.
reply: Then say it properly. Paul. Not the engineer. Paul.

news.title: ON THE LATE SHOW: THE ENGINEER WHO SAID THE RIDGE WAS HOLLOW
news.summary: Local radio named the highway engineer who died at the old junction.
news.body: The late request show on local radio last night named Paul Sanderson, a highway engineer who died at the old junction on the interstate in a crash recorded as weather. Before his death he told colleagues that the survey of the ridge road was false. Listeners rang in for two hours. One caller said only: there were no skid marks.

choices.label: Tell her to keep him to herself
choices.player: Keep him to yourself. He’s yours.
reply: He is. He was. Thank you. Nobody has said that about a man the club took.

lines: Hendry’s had the chain. I put it on myself. Paul’s bicycle goes.

I’m riding it to the junction with the lilies. I’m on the phone with you, the earpiece in. Talk to me. The weigh station is just ahead and there’s a light on in the office. There has never been a light on in that office.

choices.label: Tell her to turn around
choices.player: Turn around, Noelle. Ride home.
reply: I’m leaving the lilies at the sign.
Turning. I’m going home on Paul’s bicycle, and it’s working, and I’m crying, and I can steer.

choices.label: Tell her to see who’s in the office
choices.player: Get closer. See who’s in there.
reply: A man at the desk. Gray suit. He’s looking at a map of the canyon with a lamp. He hasn’t seen me.
He’s seen me.

news.title: WIDOW’S BICYCLE FOUND AT OLD JUNCTION
news.summary: A red bicycle and a bunch of white lilies were found by the boarded weigh station.
news.body: A red bicycle was found lying beside the old weigh station on the interstate, with a bunch of white lilies tied to its handlebars. It belongs to Noelle Sanderson, 38, a Blue Ribbon Foundation administrator, whose husband died at the same junction. Police say she may have gone away for a few days. The weigh station’s office was locked and dark.

choices.label: Tell her you’re calling the police
choices.player: Stay back. I’m calling the police.
reply: Which ones? Never mind. I’ll stay by the sign. The light just went off.
Somebody drove away without headlights. A gray car. I got the first three letters of the plate. I’m going home.
choices.note: Noelle Sanderson saw a light in the weigh station office at the junction and a gray car drive away from it without headlights.

endings.graves: The chart went to the detective
endings.sister: The chart went to his sister

lines: Rosa and I found it. The shop for the café. Main Street, a window that gets the morning, a counter somebody loved.
The landlord is a company with a made-up name and no address. The lease is beautiful and cheap. Should a nurse sign a lease with a company that has no address?

choices.label: Tell her to sign it
choices.player: Sign it. You’ve waited long enough.
reply: Signing. Rosa is crying into a croissant. We open the day after tomorrow.

fates.line: We opened. The first customer was a man in a gray suit who said the coffee was very good and asked my name, and then my sister’s name, and wrote neither down. He tipped fifty.

choices.label: Ask who’s behind the company
choices.player: Find out who’s behind the company first.
reply: I asked the agent. She said a trust on the ridge. Then she said she shouldn’t have said that.
No lease, then. Rosa will bake in our mom’s kitchen another year. I hate you a tiny bit.
choices.note: Maya Serrano says the landlord company with no address on Main Street belongs to a trust on the ridge.

beats.label: Ask what she’ll do with Caleb Marsh’s chart
beats.player: You still have Caleb Marsh’s chart, under the other name. What will you do with it?
lines: It says the burns were from a garden-center accelerant. The doctor wrote that. It’s the fire at the Professor’s house, written up as gardening.
I can give it to the detective on the case, Eleanor Graves. Or to his sister. Or I can do what nurses do, which is nothing, very carefully.

choices.label: Tell her to take it to Detective Graves
choices.player: Take it to Detective Graves.
reply: That makes me a witness. I’ve never been a witness. I’ve been the person who holds the witness’s hand.
Okay. Tomorrow, before my shift.
choices.note: Maya Serrano is taking Caleb Marsh’s chart, burns from an accelerant, to Detective Graves.

choices.label: Tell her to give it to Adeline Marsh
choices.player: Give it to his sister, Adeline Marsh.
reply: The woman in the beautiful gloves who collected him. She tipped the orderly a hundred dollars.
Okay. I’ll ring her. I’ll be very kind about it, the way you’re kind to a woman about to be very unkind back.

choices.label: Tell her to ask the student group about him
choices.player: Ask the students he sits with. They’ll know what he did.
reply: The ones at the back of his seminar. Okay. One of them has a nice voice on the phone. I’ll ring her.

news.title: NURSE’S CAR BURNS IN HOSPITAL PARKING LOT
news.summary: Nobody was hurt. Fire investigators found an accelerant.
news.body: A car belonging to an emergency department nurse burned out in the hospital parking lot during the night shift. Nobody was hurt. A fire investigator said an accelerant of the kind sold in garden centers had been used. The nurse, Maya Serrano, said she had left a packet of cookies on the seat.

fates.line: My car’s gone. Burned in the lot. They left the chart alone because it was in my locker, not the car. I’ve stopped ringing people. I’ve started being very quiet.

choices.label: Tell her nurses don’t tell
choices.player: Nurses don’t tell. Keep it in your locker.
reply: That’s what my mom would say. That’s what my mom did for thirty years, and she sleeps fine.
I don’t, but okay.

lines: Hard shift. Cookies in the car. The car next to mine had a man in it doing the exact same thing. Same brand.
He works up at the lodge. He told me what’s under the stables because I’m a nurse and nurses don’t tell. A cold room. A chain on the door. Somebody they feed.
Hard shift. Cookies in the car. The man in the next car works up at the lodge.

He told me about a stall at the end of the stables with a chain on the door, and the cold room under it, and somebody they feed. A vet’s assistant’s dad heard knocking in that stall years ago. It’s the same place, isn’t it.

beats.note: Maya Serrano says a lodge worker told her there is a cold room under the lodge’s stables, chained, where somebody is kept and fed.

choices.label: Tell her to tell somebody
choices.player: You have to tell somebody about that.
reply: I just did.
You’re somebody. Now you know too. That’s how it works with nurses: we share it out so nobody has to carry the whole thing.

choices.label: Tell her to forget she heard it
choices.player: Forget you heard it.
reply: I’ve been forgetting things in that parking lot for six years. This one won’t go.

lines: A man came into the department tonight with a dog bite on his forearm and asked for me by name. Not the nurse. Maya.

It was the man from the next car in the parking lot. He let me clean it and said, very kindly, that I should forget about the stables. Then he bought a packet of cookies from the machine and left it on my chair.

choices.label: Tell her to put him on the night ward’s list
choices.player: Put him on the list. The men from the ridge.
reply: He’s on it. Name, bite, the lodge’s dog. The list is in Veda Thorn’s mom’s locker, behind her good shoes.
I ate his cookies. I’m not wasting cookies on a principle.
choices.note: Maya Serrano added the lodge man with the dog bite to the night ward’s list of men from the ridge.

choices.label: Tell her to swap onto day shifts for a while
choices.player: Swap onto days for a while.
reply: Days. Sunburned tourists and cactus spines. Okay.
I left his cookies on the chair. Let somebody braver eat them.

endings.slice: Two forks in the back booth

beats.label: Ask what the men in the back booth ordered
beats.player: Those two men in the back booth. What did they order?
lines: Coffee, black, and one slice of the cherry, two forks. Nobody shares the cherry. That’s how I knew they weren’t friends.
The one who paid read the check twice and tipped exactly fifteen percent, which is what men tip when they want you to remember nothing.

choices.label: Ask if she saw a name on his card
choices.player: Did you see a name on his card?
reply: I read everything. Marchbanks. L. Marchbanks. He saw me read it.
He smiled. That’s the part I keep thinking about. He smiled like I’d passed something.
choices.note: Madison Pike read the name on the card that paid in the back booth: L. Marchbanks. He saw her read it.

choices.label: Ask who used the second fork
choices.player: Who used the second fork?
reply: Nobody. That’s the other thing. They ordered two forks and only one ate.
The treasurer from the paper just watched the other one eat my cherry pie like it was a report.

lines: Big news at the Cactus. The Foundation wants to buy us a new sign. Neon, a cactus with a horseshoe, it would light up the whole road.

All we have to do is let the club use the back booth for its smaller breakfasts. Dolores’s booth. The Brooks sisters are split right down the middle, and they want to know what I think, because I’m not family. What would Dolores have said?

choices.label: Tell her Dolores would say the booth isn’t for sale
choices.player: Dolores would say the booth isn’t for sale. Not for a sign. Not for anything.
reply: I said it. Exactly that. Then I kicked the jukebox and it played her song.
We’re keeping the old sign. Half the C is out. It says ACTUS. I love it more than anything.

choices.label: Tell her a sign is a sign
choices.player: Take the sign. The diner needs it.
reply: The sign goes up on the first of the season. The booth gets a little brass plate.
Members only. Nobody asked what Dolores would say after all.

fates.line: The club had its first breakfast in the back booth. They asked for me by name. Not Madison. My mom’s name. Pike. They know the strip. They know my dad.

choices.label: Ask what she thinks Dolores would say
choices.player: What do you think she’d say?
reply: She’d say: the booth is for people who need to sit down. That’s what she said every time somebody tried to reserve it.
Okay. I knew that. I just needed somebody to ask me first.

lines: Beatrice from the Daily came in again and ordered nothing and listened. She asked if I’d ever heard the name Marchbanks.
I haven’t told anybody but you. Should I tell her?

choices.label: Tell her to tell the reporter
choices.player: Tell her. Say it out loud.
reply: I told her. She wrote it on a napkin and then ate the napkin. I’m not even joking. She said it was safer.
choices.note: Madison Pike told Beatrice Hale of the Daily that the man who paid in the back booth was L. Marchbanks.

die.line: A man in a gray suit at your door, smiling as if you’d passed something. He knew your name. He’d read it somewhere.

choices.label: Tell her to keep it to herself
choices.player: Keep it to yourself.
reply: Okay. I’ll pour her coffee and talk about the weather.
I hate the weather. There isn’t any.

lines: Zara came in tonight. Dolores’s niece. First time in four years. I didn’t say anything, I just brought the slice I save for her every night.
She’s sitting in the back booth. Dolores’s booth. Nobody sits there. She’s staring at the pie like it’s going to say something.

choices.label: Tell her to sit down with Zara
choices.player: Sit down with her. In the booth.
reply: I sat. In Dolores’s booth. My legs were shaking like I’d broken a law.
We worked out Dolores told us both the same thing, years apart: the men who sit in this booth decide who doesn’t come back. Then we ate the pie with two forks and both used them.
choices.note: Dolores Brooks told both Madison Pike and her niece Zara that the men who sit in the back booth decide who doesn’t come back.

choices.label: Tell her to let Zara eat in peace
choices.player: Let her eat in peace.
reply: I kicked the jukebox on my way past. It played Dolores’s song. Zara laughed with her mouth full.
She left a twenty under the plate and a note: same time tomorrow.

endings.dawn: The man in the dinner jacket

lines: The video of me saving that little boy went round again today. Celeste Van Doren’s grandson. His mom filmed it for her followers and never said thank you. A hundred thousand views of my face.
Under it, ten thousand people saying what a brave mom. I’m about to type something.

choices.label: Tell her to type you’re welcome
choices.player: Type: you’re welcome.
reply: Typed. Posted. Four thousand likes in an hour. Somebody made it a sticker.
The club manager wants to see me tomorrow. I think I’m in trouble. I feel amazing.

choices.label: Tell her to let it go
choices.player: Let it go. You know what you did.
reply: I do. I pulled him out by the back of his little swim shirt. He held onto my ear.
Okay. Letting it go. Mostly.

beats.label: Ask whose phone she thinks it is
beats.player: Whose phone do you think you fished out of the pool?
lines: The lock screen is a blue dress on a hanger, next to a notebook. A woman who photographs her dress and her notebook is going to work, not to a party.
The organizer in the paper wore blue that night. I’m not saying anything. I’m a lifeguard. I just notice who’s struggling.

choices.label: Tell her to keep an eye on it
choices.player: Keep an eye on it. Nobody else is.
reply: I check the plant room every morning. Same sandwich bag, same corner. The battery’s dying. So am I, a bit, every time I look.

choices.label: Tell her to hand it in to the police
choices.player: Hand it in to the police.
reply: The police already had an evidence bag from that night. A friend of my mom’s says the SIM card went missing out of it.
So no. The phone stays with the people who drown for a living. Lifeguards, I mean.
choices.note: Erin Doyle won’t hand the phone from the pool to the police: she has heard a SIM card went missing from their evidence bag from that night.

lines: The club manager called me in about my comment. Very nice chair. He had a form for me to sign about the pool.
It says I did not find anything in the deep end on the morning after the party. Anything at all. I fished a phone out of it with my own net.
The club manager called me in. Very nice chair. He had a form for me to sign about the pool.
It says I did not find anything in the deep end on the morning after the party. Anything at all. I fished a phone out of it with my own net.

choices.label: Ask what happens if she doesn’t sign
choices.player: What happens if you don’t sign?
reply: He didn’t say. He just pushed the pen a little closer. My mom cleans his office.
So. Do I sign?

choices.label: Tell her to sign it and keep her job
choices.player: Sign it. Keep your job.
reply: Signed. The pen was very heavy for a pen.

choices.label: Tell her not to sign
choices.player: Don’t sign it.
reply: I put the pen down and said I’d have to think about it. Nobody has ever said that to him in his life. I could see it.

choices.label: Tell her to sign it and keep her job
choices.player: Sign it. Keep your job.
reply: Signed. It took one second. The pen was very heavy for a pen.
I’m staff, not a member. I keep forgetting what that means and they keep reminding me.

choices.label: Tell her not to sign
choices.player: Don’t sign it.
reply: I put the pen down. I said I’d have to think about it. Nobody has ever said that to him in his life, I could see it.

lines: Sacked. Clear my locker by tonight.
Thing is, the lost property box is in the plant room, and the plant room has a key, and I copied it at Hendry’s three weeks ago because I was sick of waiting for somebody’s dad to open it for me.

choices.label: Tell her to take the phone tonight
choices.player: Go in tonight and take the phone.
reply: It’s in a sandwich bag in my jacket. Elena’s phone, if you believe the lock screen. Still locked.
And tucked in the case, behind the phone: half a ticket to the party, torn. Somebody wrote on it in pencil.
choices.note: Erin Doyle took the phone from the club’s lost property: tucked in its case, half a torn ticket to the gala with pencil on it.

choices.label: Tell her to leave it where it is
choices.player: Leave it. Just clear your locker and go.
reply: Okay. I’m keeping the key, though. A girl should have a key to something.

lines: I still swim at dawn. I climb the fence now.
There was a man in the deep end this morning, face down, in a dinner jacket. I pulled him out. He’s alive, coughing on the tiles. He says he jumped. He’s one of the husbands. The voted-in kind.

choices.label: Tell her to call an ambulance and the police
choices.player: Call an ambulance. And the police.
reply: Calling. He grabbed my wrist and said not the police, please, they know my wife.
I called them anyway. That’s my job. Save first, ask later.

news.title: CLUB MEMBER PULLED FROM POOL AT DAWN
news.summary: A sacked lifeguard saved a Bluebird Club member found face down in the deep end.
news.body: A member of the Bluebird Club was pulled alive from the club pool at dawn by a lifeguard who had been dismissed the week before. He was taken to hospital. The club described it as a swimming accident. He was wearing evening dress. His wife, a member of the club’s committee, said he had been under strain.

choices.label: Tell her to ask him why
choices.player: Ask him why he jumped.
reply: I asked. He said, because the ones who don’t jump fall.
Then he asked me not to tell his wife I saved him. Not that he jumped. That I saved him.
choices.note: A voted-in Bluebird husband pulled from the club pool told Erin Doyle he jumped, because the ones who don’t jump fall.

choices.label: Tell her to get out of there
choices.player: Get out of there before anyone sees you.
reply: I’m over the fence. He’s sitting by the pool in his wet jacket, staring at the water.
I’ll read the paper tomorrow and see if he’s in it.

news.title: BLUEBIRD HUSBAND DIES IN FALL
news.summary: A member of the Bluebird Club has died after a fall at his home.
news.body: A member of the Bluebird Club died after a fall at his home on the reservoir side, two days after an accident at the club pool. The club has sent a wreath tied with blue ribbon. He was voted in four years ago.

endings.markham: The box went to Helen Markham
endings.dev: Dev walked away from the back row

beats.label: Ask if she’ll ever open the box on shelf nine
beats.player: Will you ever open the box on shelf nine?
lines: Every day I decide not to. Kelsey says it’s an old filing error. Kelsey is my boss and she’s been kind to me since my first morning.
But nobody dusts a filing error every week.
It’s gone. Kelsey carried it upstairs to Sergeant Markham herself and came back down with her coat on. Suspended.
She left me her records and a cactus in a coffee mug. I didn’t even know she liked cacti. I think she bought it for me.
They found Kelsey in the reservoir. They say there’s nothing suspicious. The box is still on shelf nine.
Nobody dusts it now. I keep looking at it.

choices.label: Tell her to open it
choices.player: Open it. You’ve waited long enough.
reply: Okay. After the others go home. Stay on with me. I’ll tell you what’s inside.

choices.label: Tell her to leave it shut
choices.player: Leave it shut. It isn’t yours.
reply: That’s what I tell myself. It sounds better in your voice.
Shelf nine stays shut.

choices.label: Ask how she’s doing without Kelsey
choices.player: How are you doing without her?
reply: I’m the archive now. Twenty years old, in charge of the worst days in Sunfall.
I labeled every box today. Even the ones that were already labeled. Sergeant Markham came down and said good work. I cried in the cold room.

lines: I opened it. A brown envelope of wages nobody collected, made out to Dale Pruett. A sign-out sheet for the party evidence with a sergeant’s name on it: Lowry. And a note in another hand saying who told him to sign the bag out.
Kelsey kept this. Kelsey knew. I don’t know what to do with my hands.
beats.note: Imani Harper opened the box on shelf nine: Dale Pruett’s uncollected wages, a sign-out sheet with Sergeant Lowry’s name, and a note saying who told Dale to sign the evidence out.

choices.label: Tell her to take it to Sergeant Markham
choices.player: Take it upstairs to Sergeant Markham. Tonight.
reply: Helen Markham. Okay. The light’s on in her office. It always is.
I’m taking the stairs. The lift goes past the custody suite and I don’t want anyone to see my face.

fates.line: Sergeant Markham read everything twice. Then she asked whether I wanted to be a police officer. I said I wanted to be an archivist. She said that’s the same thing done properly.

choices.label: Tell her to put it back exactly as it was
choices.player: Put it all back exactly as it was.
reply: Exactly as it was. Same dust. I even put the dust back. I’m a very good archivist.
I won’t sleep. That’s fine. Nobody here sleeps.

lines: Dev comes back from his meetings pale. Every time. He’s Nadia’s brother and the gentlest man I’ve ever dated and he comes home and washes his hands for a long time.
He sits at the back of those lectures with the people who never vote. Do you know what those meetings are?

choices.label: Tell her what the back row is planning
choices.player: They’re planning something against the Professor. Something with fire.
reply: Fire. Okay.
I told him I knew. I didn’t say how. He sat on the kitchen floor and said he never wanted to go back. He’s not going back.
choices.note: Imani Harper says her boyfriend Dev Okafor has walked away from the students at the back of Professor Vale’s lectures.

choices.label: Tell her you don’t know
choices.player: I don’t know what they are.
reply: Okay. I’ll keep watching his hands. That’s what an archivist does. Watch, and write down.

lines: My mom rang. She found your number in my phone. She wanted to know if you’re the reason I won’t come home.
I told her you’re not. I told her the reason is a box. She asked what kind of box and I couldn’t explain. Should I go home?

choices.label: Tell her to go home
choices.player: Go home, Imani. You’ve done enough here.
reply: I booked it. One bag, thirty-two cacti in a box with holes in it.
Thank you. I needed somebody here to say it, not her.

choices.label: Tell her Sunfall needs her
choices.player: Stay. Sunfall needs somebody who labels things properly.
reply: It does. Nobody else here even knows what properly means.
I’ll tell her soon. I always say soon.

endings.ranch: She made it to the ranch

lines: A lawyer’s letter came to the co-op. Thick paper. The charity that saved us gave us a loan, not a gift, secured on the building, and they can call it in with seven days’ notice.
Forty students. If I tell them, half of them are in their cars by tomorrow. If I don’t, they’re in their cars in seven days anyway.
A lawyer’s letter came to the co-op. The charity that saved us gave us a loan secured on the building, and they can call it in with seven days’ notice.
Rosa Gutierrez says it’s the same trust whose car sits outside her building watching the meetings. So they own our roof and they watch our friends. Forty students. What do I tell them?

choices.label: Tell her to tell the co-op tonight
choices.player: Tell them tonight. All of it.
reply: House meeting in the kitchen. I’m going to stand on the counter, it’s the only way anyone hears me.

choices.label: Tell her to find the money first
choices.player: Find the money first. Then tell them.
reply: Find it where? We have a jar. The jar has a button in it.
Okay. I’ll try. Seven days.

lines: Forty students in one kitchen. I stood on the counter. Nobody left.
Jennifer Tate stood on a chair and said we pay it ourselves, a dollar at a time, gig by gig, and then everybody was shouting yes, and a goth DJ offered three free nights. We might actually do it.

news.title: STUDENTS RAISE THEIR OWN ROOF
news.summary: The housing co-op has paid off a loan from a charity with no office.
news.body: Forty members of the student housing co-operative have paid off a loan secured on their building, raised through three benefit nights in the Old Quarter, a bake sale and what organizer Inez Morales called a jar with a button in it. The lender, a trust with an address on the ridge, did not reply to questions.

beats.label: Ask who gave the co-op its big drum
beats.player: Jennifer Tate’s big protest drum. Who gave the co-op that?
lines: A man in a charity lanyard, the same week the money came. I signed for it. The lanyard said Blue Ribbon and I didn’t think twice, because I was signing for a free drum.
I’m thinking about it now. Who gives a protest a drum?

choices.label: Tell her somebody wants the protests loud
choices.player: Somebody wants your protests loud. Loud gets noticed.
reply: And noticed gets blamed.
Oh, that’s horrible. That’s exactly what I’d do if I were them.
choices.note: Inez Morales signed for a protest drum given to the co-op by a man in a Blue Ribbon lanyard, the week the loan came.

choices.label: Tell her a free drum is a free drum
choices.player: A free drum is a free drum.
reply: Spoken like a man who doesn’t live underneath one.

lines: Day five. The jar has forty-one dollars and the button. I’ve rung every grant in the state. One of them asked if we’d considered the Blue Ribbon Foundation.
Two days. What do I do?

choices.label: Tell her to ask Sable Marlow for a benefit night
choices.player: Ask Sable Marlow at the Cellar Door for a benefit night.
reply: Sable said yes before I finished the sentence. Three bands, a DJ, and she’s working the door herself.
We paid it. Every cent, in small bills that smell of the Cellar Door. I’m framing the button.

choices.label: Tell her to tell them now
choices.player: Tell them now. They deserve two days.
reply: Kitchen. Counter. Forty faces.
Nobody shouted at me. Jennifer Tate said we’d have been fine with seven days, and she’s right, and I’ll be sorry about that for a long time.

choices.label: Tell her to let the building go
choices.player: Let it go. Find them somewhere else.
reply: Forty students and a list of sofas.
I’ll take the door again, wherever we end up. The organizer sleeps by the door.

news.title: STUDENT CO-OP LOCKED OUT
news.summary: Forty students were given notice by a lender on the ridge.
news.body: Forty members of the student housing co-operative were locked out of their warehouse building after a lender called in a loan secured on it. The lender, a trust registered at an address on Halcyon Ridge, has applied to redevelop the canal side. Students were seen sleeping in cars on the faculty lot.

lines: Something weird on my press. Somebody printed a poster on it overnight and cleaned up after. Badly. There’s a plate drying in the rack.
Black, very elegant, a little moon with a bite out of it. My boyfriend has a key. My boyfriend has started wearing a pendant.

choices.label: Tell her to destroy the plate
choices.player: Break the plate.
reply: Snapped it over my knee. I’m keeping the pieces in a coffee can, because I’m my father’s daughter and I keep evidence of grudges.
choices.note: Inez Morales found a plate for an elegant poster with a bitten moon, printed on her press overnight; her boyfriend wears a pendant.

choices.label: Tell her to ask him about it
choices.player: Ask him. Straight out.
reply: I asked. He said it’s for a party on the night with no moon and it’s none of my business. Then he said I wouldn’t understand.
I understand perfectly. I’ve changed the locks on the press.
choices.note: Inez Morales’s boyfriend printed a poster on her press for a party on the night with no moon.

lines: My sister rang from the ranch. Old Mr. Whitlock collapsed and there’s a developer’s man at the gate. Isabel needs me.
I’m driving the canyon road now. Earpiece in. Talk to me. There’s a gray car behind me with its lights off. It’s been behind me since the junction.

choices.label: Tell her to put her foot down
choices.player: Put your foot down. Lose him.
reply: Going. The Civic does not want to go. Third bend coming up.
He’s right behind me.

news.title: STUDENT ORGANIZER DIES ON CANYON ROAD
news.summary: Inez Morales, 22, crashed at the third bend.
news.body: Inez Morales, 22, who ran the student housing co-operative, died when her car left the canyon road at the third bend overnight. A trucker who stopped said there was a second car that did not. The sheriff’s office said the road was dry. Her sister Isabel, a horse trainer at the Whitlock ranch, has asked for any witnesses to call.

choices.label: Tell her to pull over and let it pass
choices.player: Pull over. Let it pass.
reply: Pulling over. He’s slowing down. He’s next to me. He’s looking in.
He drove on. He waved. I’m shaking so hard the earpiece fell out. I’m going on. Slowly.

choices.label: Tell her to take the fire road
choices.player: Take the old fire road. He won’t know it.
reply: The fire road. Dad taught us that road with the lights off, for coyotes.
Lost him. I’m at the ranch gate. Isabel is running down the drive in her socks.

endings.saved: The Old Quarter saved the Cellar Door

beats.label: Ask who sits at the back of her goth nights
beats.player: Who sits at the back on your goth nights?
lines: A man in a good suit who never drinks and never dances and tips the bar staff in fifties. He watches the room like he owns shares in it.
He doesn’t look at the bands. He looks at the girls with the pendants.

choices.label: Ask if she knows who he is
choices.player: Do you know who he is?
reply: I know his card. Events director, the Bluebird Club. The casino’s bank holds my loan, and the casino’s board sits at his club. So I pour him a soda water and smile.

choices.label: Tell her to throw him out
choices.player: Throw him out.
reply: I’m a goalkeeper. I stand in the way of things. But that one owns the goal.

lines: That deleted photo from the borrowed camera. I got it back off the card. A girl handing an envelope to the man in the good suit, at the back of my own room.
And somebody else has the same frame. Tova Lindqvist at the Night Wire. Her photographer used the same card before he left it with me. Neither of us has done anything with it.

choices.label: Tell her to put her copy with Tova’s and print it
choices.player: Put your copy with Tova’s. Two copies of one frame is a story.
reply: Tova said the exact same thing, in worse language. It goes in the Night Wire tomorrow.
I’m going to have a very bad week. Good.

news.title: THE DELETED FRAME
news.summary: A photo erased from a goth night shows a club director taking an envelope.
news.body: A photograph deleted from a camera at the Cellar Door, and restored separately by the venue and by this paper, shows a young woman in sunglasses handing an envelope to the Bluebird Club’s events director at the back of a goth night. The club said its director attends many cultural events. The young woman has left town.

fates.line: The casino’s bank rang. They want the whole loan back in thirty days. Or I sell the Cellar Door to the chain. Funny timing.

choices.label: Tell her to keep it hidden
choices.player: Keep it. Hidden. You’ve got a loan to think about.
reply: Sensible. I hate sensible. Fine. It’s in my glove bag with the goalkeeper gloves, where nobody would go.

choices.label: Tell her to show it to the man himself
choices.player: Show it to him. See what he does.
reply: Standing in the way of things. My favorite.
He’s here tonight. I’m walking over with my phone.

fates.line: He looked at it for a long time and said I have a very good eye. Then he said the Cellar Door must be very hard to insure.

news.title: FIRE AT THE CELLAR DOOR
news.summary: The Old Quarter venue burned overnight. Nobody was inside.
news.body: The Cellar Door, the music venue in the Old Quarter, was gutted by fire overnight. Nobody was inside. Its owner, Sable Marlow, a goalkeeper in the women’s five-on-five league, could not be reached. Investigators said it was too early to say how it started.

lines: Thirty days to find the whole loan, or the chain gets my dad’s bar back. I’ve been sitting on the stage in the dark.
What do I do?

choices.label: Tell her to ask the Old Quarter for help
choices.player: Ask the Old Quarter. Every band you ever gave a night to.
reply: That band from the storm. Their label. Alice. The tattooists. Everybody who ever played acoustic in the dark in my room.
One night. Every act in the Quarter. Okay. Okay, I’m making a poster.

news.title: THE OLD QUARTER PACKS THE CELLAR DOOR
news.summary: Every act in the Quarter played one night to save the venue.
news.body: Every band, DJ and singer in the Old Quarter played the Cellar Door in a single night to pay off the venue’s loan, ahead of a deadline set by the casino’s bank. The line went round the block twice. The owner, Sable Marlow, worked the door herself in her goalkeeper gloves and let nobody in a suit through.

choices.label: Tell her to sell it to the chain
choices.player: Sell it. Start again somewhere they can’t reach.
reply: Twice in one family. Okay.
I’ll hand them the keys myself and I won’t cry until I’m in the car. Antony would’ve fought. I’m not Antony.

beats.label: Ask about the girls with the pendants
beats.player: The girls with the pendants he watches. Who are they?
lines: Five or six of them now. Same little moon on a chain. They used to dance. Now they stand at the edge of the floor and watch the door, like they’re waiting to be collected.

choices.label: Tell her Lenore Vale made those pendants
choices.player: Lenore Vale made those pendants. Her mark is on every one.
reply: Lenore from the lock-ups. She’s been in here three nights running, counting. I thought she was cruising.
She was taking a census. I’m going to buy her a drink and ask for the list.
choices.note: Sable Marlow is going to ask Lenore Vale for her list of who wears the thirteen pendants at the Cellar Door.

choices.label: Tell her to keep an eye on them
choices.player: Keep an eye on them.
reply: I’m a goalkeeper. I keep an eye on everything that comes at me.
I’ve put the bar’s best bouncer on the door and told him nobody leaves with the man in the suit.

lines: My sister came round. Estelle. She stood in front of the sunset painting I framed for her club and looked at it for a whole minute without blinking.
I hid the original brief for that social club symbol behind the backing of that painting, with the envelope the cash came in. I never told her that.

choices.label: Ask why she hid it there
choices.player: Why hide it there?
reply: Because the envelope has the Foundation’s watermark on the flap. The cash for a secret club symbol came in charity stationery.
And because Estelle is the only person who comes to my apartment.
choices.note: Hana Park has the envelope the cash for the circle’s symbol came in: it carries the Blue Ribbon Foundation’s watermark.

choices.label: Ask if her sister knows about the commission
choices.player: Does your sister know about the commission?
reply: I never told her. She never asked. Estelle asks about everything.
Oh. Oh no.

beats.label: Ask how she paid for art school
beats.player: How did you pay off art school?
lines: Estelle paid it. Her savings, she said. She sells insurance. I never once did the sums on how much insurance you’d have to sell.
You’re asking because you already did the sums.

choices.label: Tell her the money came from the same people
choices.player: I think the money came from the same people who paid you for the symbol.
reply: The same envelope, probably. Watermark and all.
I’m going to ask her. Not today. Tomorrow. Today I’m going to lie on the floor and listen to the waltz through the ceiling.

choices.label: Tell her it doesn’t matter who paid
choices.player: It doesn’t matter who paid. You did the work.
reply: It matters. But thank you for saying the other thing.

lines: A print shop sent me a proof to check. An anniversary invitation in my font, my symbol at the top, nine women in a circle and a line underneath: welcome into the family.
The date on it: {night}. I designed none of this except the bits they stole. I can pull the job. One phone call.
beats.note: Hana Park was sent the proof of an anniversary invitation with the circle’s symbol, nine women and the line welcome into the family.

choices.label: Tell her to pull the job
choices.player: Pull it. Make the call.
reply: Pulled. I told them the file was corrupt. It is, in every sense.
Somebody is going to have to hand-write a lot of invitations now. I hope their hand cramps.

choices.label: Tell her to let it print
choices.player: Let it print. Keep a proof.
reply: One proof in the frame behind the sunset, with the brief and the envelope. My little museum of being used.

lines: I asked Estelle. She didn’t deny it. She said: you think art school pays for itself?
Then she said the club looks after its own, and I’m her own, and I should be grateful and quiet. And then she asked where the sunset painting was.

choices.label: Tell her to move the painting tonight
choices.player: Move the painting tonight. Somewhere she doesn’t know.
reply: Naomi downstairs has a closet nobody opens. The sunset is in it, wrapped in my winter coat.
My sister just texted me a heart. She’s never sent me a heart.

choices.label: Tell her to give her sister the painting
choices.player: Give her the painting. She’s your sister.
reply: She is.
She took it under her arm and kissed my head. I watched her car turn the corner. I think I just handed the club my only proof, and I don’t even mind as much as I should.

lines: Two men came to the pantry today with a clipboard. From the diocese, they said. They counted cupboards.
They asked me whether every cabinet in the storeroom is in use. I said I would have to check, and they said they would come back.

choices.label: Ask what she’ll tell them
choices.player: What will you tell them when they come back?
reply: The truth. That the cabinet in the storeroom is unused.
Nobody uses it. It is only full.

choices.label: Tell her to tell Margaret
choices.player: Tell Margaret about the men with the clipboard.
reply: Margaret already knows. Her hand went to that cabinet when I said diocese.
Then Evelyn touched her collar. They didn’t look at each other. They never do when it matters.

lines: The men with the clipboard came back. I stood in the storeroom doorway with a box of tins.
One of them put his hand on the locked cabinet and asked me what is in it.

choices.label: Tell her to say it’s unused
choices.player: Tell him it’s unused.
reply: I said it is unused. He said, then you won’t mind opening it. I said I don’t have the key, which is also true.
He wrote something down and left. Margaret made me tea, which she has never done. I think I did right.

choices.label: Tell her to send for Margaret
choices.player: Send for Margaret. Let her answer him.
reply: Margaret came down the stairs like the weather. She told him the Sisters have kept that cabinet since before his bishop was born and he could write that down.
He wrote it down.

choices.label: Tell her to say nothing at all
choices.player: Say nothing. Keep stacking tins.
reply: I stacked tins. He waited. I stacked more tins. Silence is very hard to argue with when there are beans in it.
He left. He’ll be back.

lines: I noticed something and I don’t know who to tell, so I am telling you, which is foolish.
Lucia carries meals up to the flat over the Sisters’ charity shop every evening. Two trays. Nobody lives up there. One tray comes back empty.
beats.note: Eliza Montoya says Lucia Romano carries two trays every evening up to the empty flat over the Sisters’ charity shop, and one comes back empty.

choices.label: Tell her to keep it to herself
choices.player: Keep that to yourself. Whoever it is, they’re safe with the Sisters.
reply: That is what I hoped you would say.
I put an extra cake in the bowl tonight. The collapsed kind. It came back empty too.

choices.label: Tell her to ask Lucia
choices.player: Ask Lucia who it’s for.
reply: I asked. Lucia said, for the poor, and looked at me in a way that meant: you are grown now, do not make me lie to you.
So I won’t.

beats.label: Ask if the man who cried came back
beats.player: The man in the suit who cried in the storeroom. Did he ever come back?
lines: He came back. Another check. Then he asked whether the Sisters pray for the dead whose names they don’t know.
I said we pray for everyone. He said: not everyone. Then he asked me to pray for a caretaker, and he left before I could ask which.

choices.label: Ask which caretaker
choices.player: Which caretaker?
reply: There was only ever one. Aurelio, who looked after our bell tower. He stopped coming for his wages one winter. Margaret said he went home to his family.
He had no family. I’ve only just thought of that.
choices.note: Eliza Montoya says the man who cried in the pantry asked the Sisters to pray for a caretaker: Aurelio, who looked after St Brigid’s bell tower and stopped collecting his wages one winter.

choices.label: Tell her to pray for him, then
choices.player: Then pray for him.
reply: I already did. I lit a candle for a man I never asked about.
I should have asked. That’s the sin, I think. Not asking.

lines: Someone left an iron key at the pantry door this morning, wrapped in black velvet, with a note with no name: for the people who pray at the Old Mission.
Margaret held it a long time. Then she unlocked the cabinet, put it inside, and locked it again. I have never seen her hands shake before.
My father’s watch started. I fixed the balance wheel at the bench. He wound it and cried and pretended it was the dust.

Then he said the casino let him go the week he saw a crate in one of his delivery vans with the Foundation’s ribbon stamped on it. He has never said that to anyone. I don’t know why he said it to me, and I don’t know why I’m saying it to you.
beats.note: Eliza Montoya’s father says the casino let him go the week he saw a crate stamped with the Foundation’s ribbon in one of his delivery vans.

lines: Is the stripe a choice? Please tell me it’s a choice.
My friend thinks you shaved a racing stripe on purpose. I told her nobody would do that on purpose.
It looks like someone started mowing your head and gave up halfway.
Wear a hat. Wear two hats.
Hair doesn’t grow back there, you know. That’s just skin now. Shiny skin.
Every photo, my eyes go straight to the top of your head. Like a runway.
Your face looks like a map of a country nobody visits.
Is that sunburn, or did something happen to you? Something happened to you.
Pink, then white, then pink again. Your face has stripes, like a flag.
My friend asked if you were in a fire. I said worse. A nail salon.
Does it still peel? It looks like it peels.
I keep zooming in on your skin, and I keep wishing I hadn’t.
Your teeth lit up my whole screen. I had to turn the brightness down.
Do they glow in the dark? Be honest. They glow in the dark.
You’re missing one, right? Front left. I can see the gap from here.
Those aren’t teeth. Those are bathroom tiles.
Please don’t smile in your next picture. Please.
My cat saw your photo and hissed. It was the teeth.
Is one of your legs longer than the other? You’re leaning in every photo.
My friend saw you at the grocery store. She says you walk in a slow circle.
You’re tilted. In every picture. Like a shelf somebody hung wrong.
Do you need a cane? You look like you need a cane.
How do you even stand in line? Do you just go around and around?
Those legs were supposed to make you taller, right? Now you’re just crooked.

names: the left side of your face
lines: Which eye am I supposed to look at?
Your face looks like it slid off to the left and stopped halfway.
One of your eyes is lower than the other. I’m not being mean. It just is.
It looks like someone put your face back on in the dark.
My mom saw your photo over my shoulder and crossed herself.
Your nose points at the door and your eyes point at the window.

open: Okay, I matched just to ask. What happened to {botch}?
Hi. Sorry. I have to say it before anything else. What happened to {botch}?
My friends and I matched you as a group. We have one question, and it’s about {botch}.
I swiped right because I thought the photo was a filter. It’s not a filter, is it.
Hey. Before we talk. Is that permanent? It looks permanent.
jab: Sorry, I’m still thinking about {botch}.
I keep scrolling back up to look at {botch}.
My mom saw your photo and asked if you were okay.
No offense, but I can’t really focus on what you’re saying.
That’s honestly the least weird thing about you right now.
I showed my roommate. She screamed a little.
I keep picturing introducing you to my friends, and then I stop.
It’s hard to be normal about this. Sorry.
I tried to describe {botch} to my sister. She thought I was exaggerating. I wasn’t.
Okay, I looked again. Still there.
Is it rude if I keep my camera off forever?
I’m being nice, but my face isn’t.
Every time you text I see {botch} in my head. Every time.
I’m rooting for you. From a distance.

open: Mother would ask what happened to {botch}. So I am asking for her.
Good evening. I matched you by accident, and then I saw {botch}, and now I simply have to know.
Daddy has a surgeon. Daddy’s surgeon would not touch {botch}. I asked.
I don’t usually message first. I am making an exception for {botch}.
Darling. What on earth did you do to yourself?
jab: Mother says a man is his face. Hers is very good.
I couldn’t take you to the club like that. They have rules. Unwritten ones, but rules.
We hide our mistakes in Sunfall. You’re wearing yours.
I’m afraid it was all anyone at brunch could talk about.
One simply doesn’t recover from {botch}. One relocates.
I’m being polite. You can tell because I haven’t laughed.
The Bluebirds have a word for men like you now. It isn’t a nice word.
Do keep the camera further away in your pictures, darling.
Darling, {botch} is the sort of thing one discusses with lawyers.
I’ve been to three charity dinners this week. None of them were for {botch}, sadly.
The tennis pro asked after you. I said you were indisposed. Permanently.
Father would have you escorted off the grounds. Kindly, but firmly.
One doesn’t say it. One simply looks away.
I’ve seen better work on a hedge.

open: I’m a reporter, so I’ll just ask. What happened to {botch}?
There has to be a story behind {botch}. Tell me there’s a story.
On the record or off the record: was it a cheap clinic?
Hi. Our photo desk saw your picture. They want to run it next to a piece about cheap surgeons.
I matched for research. I’m writing about men who got botched. You’re the lead.
jab: Sorry, I’m taking notes.
Good quote. Nobody will hear it over {botch}.
I’ve covered car wrecks I could look at for longer.
Every story needs a picture. Yours would sell papers.
Can I ask who did it? Readers will want a name.
My editor says there’s no follow-up to {botch}. It’s the whole story.
I’ve already got the headline. You won’t like it.
I can’t print what I’m thinking. Not in a family paper.
Off the record, {botch} is the worst thing I’ve seen this year.
Sorry, I was fact-checking {botch}. It checks out.
If you ever want to tell your side, call the newsroom. They’ll want photos.
Our photographer asked for your angle. I said there isn’t one.
You’d make a great cautionary feature.
I keep drafting a reply and deleting the adjectives.

open: I want to say this kindly. What happened to {botch}?
Bodies are bodies and I don’t judge. But wow. {Botch}.
I matched because I feel strongly about predatory clinics. Was it a predatory clinic?
Hi. I’m really trying not to center your appearance. It’s hard.
I support everyone’s right to change their body. I just didn’t know it could go like this.
jab: This is a beauty standards problem. It’s also a you problem.
I’m not judging. My face is, a little.
We should be fighting the system that sold you this. You should also wear a hat.
I’m trying to make eye contact with your photo. It’s hard.
Honestly? This is what capitalism does to people.
There’s no shame in it. There’s just no coming back from it.
I can hold space for this. I can’t hold your hand.
I need a minute before I can be normal about {botch}.
I want to be supportive about {botch}. I’m working on it.
Your body, your choice. Your face, though.
I’m unlearning my reaction to {botch}. Slowly.
This is not a moral failing. It is a visual one.
I signed a petition about cheap clinics because of you.
Let’s talk about anything except {botch}. I’ll go first.

open: Finally. Someone on here who looks like he crawled out of a crypt.
I collect strange things. You’re the strangest thing on this app.
Are you cursed? You look cursed. I mean that as a compliment, a little.
Did you sell your face to something in the desert? Because it kept the receipt.
jab: Even I have limits. You’re standing on them.
I’d put your picture on my wall. Not you. Your picture.
Morbid isn’t the same as romantic. You’re morbid.
The girls at the Rialto think you’re a costume.
There’s dark, and then there’s {botch}.
I love ruins. I don’t date them.
You’re like a haunted house. Fun to look at. Nobody moves in.
My tarot cards turned up the Tower three times tonight. I think they meant you.
I’ve seen gargoyles with better luck.
Carve {botch} on a tombstone and it would look great. On you, less so.
Even the bats are concerned.
I wrote a poem about {botch}. It doesn’t rhyme. Nothing does anymore.
Beautiful decay is a phrase. You’re just the decay.
Midnight is kind to most faces. Not yours.

open: Sunfall Police. I’m off duty, but I have to ask: was {botch} an assault?
We had a report about a cheap clinic over the border. Was that you?
Hi. Just so you know, I’ve seen worse at crime scenes. Not much worse.
Before anything else: is anyone pressing charges for {botch}? Somebody should.
I matched you to see if you’re a witness. You look like a witness.
jab: Sorry. I keep looking at {botch} like it’s evidence.
If you ever go missing, at least the description will be easy.
I’ve put men in lineups who looked better.
In my professional opinion, that isn’t going to heal.
We have a sketch artist. Even she couldn’t make that look good.
Copy that. Still thinking about {botch}.
My partner saw your picture and asked if we should open a file.
That face is a permanent record.
Noted {botch} for the file. Distinguishing features: all of them.
If someone did that to you on purpose, I’d arrest them.
You’d never get away with anything. Witnesses would remember.
I’ve seen wanted posters with friendlier faces.
Off duty, I’m allowed to wince. So I am.
Ten-four. Still processing {botch}.

open: God bless you. I mean it. What happened to {botch}?
I will pray for you. I have already started.
The Lord made you once. Somebody else tried again, and here we are.
Hello. I am not supposed to stare. I am staring. Forgive me.
Sister Agnes saw your picture and lit a candle.
jab: Vanity is a sin. So is laughing, so I am not laughing.
God forgives everything. Your face, He may take longer over.
I will keep you in my prayers. That is all I can keep you in.
Some crosses we carry. Yours shows.
Mercy is for the soul. The body has to fend for itself.
Perhaps it was meant as a lesson. It worked on me.
Father says it is what is inside that counts. Father has not seen {botch}.
I am sorry. I truly am. But no.
I said a rosary for {botch}. I may need another.
Pride goes before a fall. So, it seems, does {botch}.
Sister Agatha saw your picture and crossed herself.
I am trying to see your soul. Something keeps getting in the way: {botch}.
Charity is patient. I am working on patience.
We are told not to stare. I am failing.

open: Oh my God. Oh my God. What happened to {botch}?
Okay, the whole house is looking at your profile right now. Like, the whole house.
Hi! Sorry! Was it a dare? Did someone dare you to do that?
I literally screamed. Not in a good way.
Babe. No. Babe. What did you do?
jab: Sorry, Stacey just walked past my phone and said ew. Like, out loud.
We have a rule. No botches. It’s in the bylaws.
I’m literally so sorry. I literally can’t.
Everyone in this house is a ten. You’re, like, a question mark.
Can you not like any of my pictures? People will see.
The vibes are so off right now.
Honestly, you’re trending in our group chat. Not in a good way.
I showed the girls {botch}. Brynn had to sit down.
Brynn wants to know if {botch} is, like, contagious.
I can’t be seen texting you during rush week.
We did a vote. It was unanimous. Sorry.
Stacey said your picture is giving horror movie.
Okay, but like, who did that to you?
I had to mute you so my feed stays cute.

witty-sceptic.bad: Not as bad as it looks? It looks exactly as bad as it looks. That’s how looking works.
witty-sceptic.past: See past it? I’d need a periscope.
witty-sceptic.fix: Fixed. Sure. And I’m getting my money back from the lottery.
witty-sceptic.date: One date. With {botch}. I have a reputation, and it isn’t for charity.
witty-sceptic.back: No. There’s no coming back. There’s only going forward, slowly, in a hat.

principled-plainspoken.bad: I’m going to be straight with you, because nobody else will. It’s worse than it looks.
principled-plainspoken.past: I try to see past things. I tried with {botch}. I couldn’t.
principled-plainspoken.fix: Nobody fixes that. Whoever says they can is after your money again.
principled-plainspoken.date: No. I won’t lead you on. That would be crueler.
principled-plainspoken.back: No. You did something you can’t undo. I’m sorry. That’s the truth.

tomboy-writer.bad: I write horror on the side. I couldn’t have made up {botch}.
tomboy-writer.past: I see past a lot. Scars, tattoos, a guy who collects swords. Not this.
tomboy-writer.fix: In a story, this is where the hero gets fixed. In Sunfall, he doesn’t.
tomboy-writer.date: I’d go out with you for the material. Then I’d feel bad. So no.
tomboy-writer.back: It’s the end of the chapter. There isn’t a next one.

meddling-matchmaker.bad: I set people up all the time. I went through my whole list. There’s nobody for {botch}.
meddling-matchmaker.past: I asked around. Nobody can see past it. I asked a lot of people.
meddling-matchmaker.fix: Honey, I’ve seen men try. It doesn’t get fixed. It gets a nickname.
meddling-matchmaker.date: I wouldn’t set you up with my worst enemy, and she deserves it.
meddling-matchmaker.back: There’s no coming back. I checked with everyone. Everyone said no.

dreamy-chatterbox.bad: Oh, it’s bad, it’s so bad, I keep zooming in and out and in again and it doesn’t get better.
dreamy-chatterbox.past: I tried to imagine you without it, like squinting, and I squinted so hard I got a headache.
dreamy-chatterbox.fix: Fixed? Like, fixed fixed? I looked it up. It’s not a thing.
dreamy-chatterbox.date: A date? With people watching? Everybody would watch. Everybody.
dreamy-chatterbox.back: I don’t think so. Things don’t go back. They just go.

all-in-romantic.bad: I wanted to fall for you. I really did. I can’t get past {botch}.
all-in-romantic.past: Love is supposed to see past everything. I guess I’m not in love.
all-in-romantic.fix: If a fix existed, somebody would have married it.
all-in-romantic.date: I give everyone a chance. I gave you one when I matched. Then I saw it properly.
all-in-romantic.back: There’s no happy ending for this one. I cried a little, actually.

reserved-sensible.bad: It is about as bad as it looks. Possibly worse in person.
reserved-sensible.past: I try to be reasonable. Reasonably, no.
reserved-sensible.fix: Surgery doesn’t usually work in reverse. I’d save your money.
reserved-sensible.date: I don’t think that would be sensible for either of us.
reserved-sensible.back: I don’t believe there is. I’m sorry to be the one who says it.

wild-heart.bad: I’ve done some crazy things. Never anything that permanent.
wild-heart.past: I see past everything. Rules, curfews, my dad. I can’t see past {botch}.
wild-heart.fix: There’s no fixing that, wild boy. That’s you now.
wild-heart.date: I’d ride on the back of anybody’s motorcycle. Not yours.
wild-heart.back: No. You went too far and you can’t come back. Even I know that.

charming-schemer.bad: Oh, it’s much worse than it looks, sweetheart. And it looks dreadful.
charming-schemer.past: I see past things when there’s something in it for me. There’s nothing in this for me.
charming-schemer.fix: Darling, the only fix for that is a new town and a new name.
charming-schemer.date: Be seen with you? I have plans. You are not part of them.
charming-schemer.back: There’s no way back. Even I couldn’t talk my way out of {botch}.

unflappable-mastermind.past: I’ve worked it out from every angle. There’s no angle where it looks fine.
unflappable-mastermind.fix: I ran the numbers on a fix. There aren’t any numbers.
unflappable-mastermind.date: A date would be a strategic error. Mine.
unflappable-mastermind.back: Game over. I don’t say that lightly.

organised-brave.bad: I’ll be brave and say it. It’s bad.
organised-brave.past: I made a list of what I could see past. You weren’t on it.
organised-brave.fix: I’ve organized a lot of things. Nobody organizes that back.
organised-brave.back: No. Better you hear it now, from someone who means well.

velvet-mystery.bad: Mm. Let’s just say I’ve seen it, and I can’t unsee it.
velvet-mystery.past: Some things are beautiful in the dark. That isn’t one of them.
velvet-mystery.fix: Fixed? No. Some things only get stranger.
velvet-mystery.date: I keep my secrets. You can’t keep yours. It’s on your face.
velvet-mystery.back: No, darling. The door you went through only opens one way.

golden-careless.bad: Oh no. Oh no no no. Yeah, it’s bad.
golden-careless.past: I can’t see past it. It’s literally all I can see.
golden-careless.fix: Fixed? Like with makeup? I don’t think makeup goes that far.
golden-careless.date: My friends would never let me live it down. Never. Like, at my wedding.
golden-careless.back: I don’t think there is? I think that’s just you now. Sorry!

cool-sporty.past: I see past bad calls. That’s a career-ending injury.
cool-sporty.fix: Some injuries heal. That one retired you.
cool-sporty.back: No comeback from that. Not this season. Not any season.

restless-heartbreaker.bad: I’ve broken a lot of hearts. I’ve never seen one look like {botch}.
restless-heartbreaker.past: I don’t see past anything. I just move on. Moving on.
restless-heartbreaker.fix: Nobody comes back from that. I’d know. Men try to come back from me all the time.
restless-heartbreaker.date: One date. Then you’d want two. And I’d have to look at you both times.
restless-heartbreaker.back: No. And I’m not even being mean this time.

thrill-seeker.bad: I’ve jumped out of a plane. Looking at {botch} was scarier.
thrill-seeker.past: I love a risk. You’re not a risk. You’re a sure thing, and the thing is no.
thrill-seeker.fix: There’s no undo button. I’ve looked for one on a lot of things.
thrill-seeker.date: I’d rather skydive without a parachute. That’s how much I mean no.
thrill-seeker.back: No. That ride only goes one way.

earnest-heart.bad: I don’t want to hurt you. But yes. It’s really bad.
earnest-heart.past: I tried. I honestly tried. I looked at your picture for a whole minute.
earnest-heart.fix: I really hope so. I just don’t think it’s true. I’m so sorry.
earnest-heart.date: I can’t. I’d spend the whole time being sad for you, and that isn’t a date.
earnest-heart.back: I don’t think there is. I wish there was. I really do.

curious-contrarian.bad: Everyone says it’s bad. For once I agree with everyone.
curious-contrarian.past: I usually argue the other side. There isn’t another side to {botch}.
curious-contrarian.fix: I looked into it. Nothing reverses that.
curious-contrarian.date: I’d go out with you just to be different. That’s how bad it is: I won’t.
curious-contrarian.back: No. And believe me, I wanted to disagree.

spellbinding-storyteller.bad: There’s an old Sunfall story about a man who wanted a new face. You’re that story now.
spellbinding-storyteller.past: In the old stories, the curse breaks when someone looks past it. Nobody ever does.
spellbinding-storyteller.fix: It doesn’t get fixed in any version I know. The ending is always the same.
spellbinding-storyteller.date: I’ll tell people about you for years. I won’t go out with you.
spellbinding-storyteller.back: No. That’s how the story ends. Nobody comes back.

dignified-outsider.bad: I know what it is to be looked at. This is something else.
dignified-outsider.past: I see past most things. People don’t see past mine. I can’t see past yours.
dignified-outsider.fix: I won’t lie to you. It isn’t going to be fixed.
dignified-outsider.date: I keep to myself. I’ll keep to myself.
dignified-outsider.back: No. Learn to live with it. That’s all any of us do.

girl-sleuth.bad: I investigated. It’s exactly as bad as the evidence suggests.
girl-sleuth.past: I notice everything. That’s the problem. I can’t stop noticing {botch}.
girl-sleuth.fix: I looked into who did it. Nobody can undo it. Case closed.
girl-sleuth.date: I solve mysteries. You’re not a mystery. Everyone can see what happened.
girl-sleuth.back: No. I followed every lead. It’s permanent.

chaotic-sweetheart.bad: Oh my God, okay, it’s really bad, I’m sorry, I laughed, I’m a terrible person.
chaotic-sweetheart.past: I tried! I put my hand over half the screen. Then the other half. Nope.
chaotic-sweetheart.date: I love you as a person. As a concept. From far away.
chaotic-sweetheart.back: No. But I’ll send you memes. Supportive ones.

glamorous-rival.bad: It’s a catastrophe, darling. A fashion catastrophe and a medical one.
glamorous-rival.past: I don’t see past things. I see everything, in good light, and judge it.
glamorous-rival.fix: No amount of money fixes that. I would know. I have a lot of money.
glamorous-rival.date: Be photographed next to you? I’d rather die.
glamorous-rival.back: None. You’ll be the cautionary tale at every party I go to this year.

shy-gentle.bad: I don’t want to say. But it is. It is really bad.
shy-gentle.past: I’m sorry. I tried. I really did.
shy-gentle.fix: I don’t think it can be. I’m sorry. I don’t like saying that.
shy-gentle.date: I don’t think I could. I’d be too nervous to look at you. Or too sad.
shy-gentle.back: I don’t think so. Please don’t be upset with me.

practical-princess.fix: I priced it out for you. It doesn’t come back at any price.
practical-princess.date: A date is an investment. You’re a write-off.
practical-princess.back: No. Cut your losses. That’s what I’d tell anyone.

devout-quiet.bad: I won’t lie. Lying is a sin. It is very bad.
devout-quiet.past: I pray to see the good in everyone. I am still praying.
devout-quiet.fix: Only God could fix that, and I think He is cross with you.
devout-quiet.back: No. Some things are not undone in this life.

steadfast-second-chance.bad: I believe in second chances. That face used them all up.
steadfast-second-chance.past: I’ve looked past a lot in my life. A divorce, a fire, a man who sold my car. Not this.
steadfast-second-chance.fix: I wanted to tell you it gets better. It doesn’t.
steadfast-second-chance.date: I give second chances. You had yours. It’s on your face.
steadfast-second-chance.back: No. And I’m the one who always says yes to second chances.

sorority.bad: Babe, it’s worse. It’s so much worse in the light.
sorority.past: I can see past, like, a bad haircut. Not a bad face.
sorority.fix: Fixed? Babe. Our house mom says you can’t un-ring a bell.
sorority.date: If anyone saw me with you, I’d have to transfer schools.

jobs.line: I’m a nurse. I’ve seen men come back from car wrecks. Nobody comes back from that.
I work in a pharmacy. We don’t sell anything for that. Nobody does.
I look at faces up close all day for work. I’ve never wanted to look away from one this fast.
I work at a vet’s. We have a word for when something can’t be fixed. We don’t use it on people.
I photograph crime scenes. I’d still look away from yours.
I keep things in boxes for a living. If you were evidence, you’d go in the bottom one.
I’ve stood at accident scenes for hours. I couldn’t stand next to you for five minutes.
I take pictures for a living. There’s no light that helps you.
I write things down for a living. Some things I’m glad I can’t un-write. You’re one of them.
I work in radio. Thank God you’d only be heard.
I grade work all day. This would fail.
I work with art. Some pieces you look at and think, somebody meant this. Nobody meant you.
I work at a music venue. I’ve seen every kind of face in the front row. Never one like yours.
I dig through record bins all night. Some are so scratched nobody will ever play them again. You’re one of those.
I make jewelry. I can fix a broken clasp. I can’t fix anything on you.
I’m a florist. Even the dead flowers look better than that, and we still sell those sometimes.
If something came out of my oven like that, it would go straight in the trash.
I’ve served every face in Sunfall. I’d ask a coworker to take your table.
I sell houses. Some of them you can’t fix. You knock them down.
I decorate rooms. Some rooms you can’t save. You just close the door.
I coach people. Some injuries end careers. That one ended yours.
I raise money for good causes. Even I couldn’t raise money for {botch}.
I run numbers for a living. Your numbers are bad.
I campaign for things that can still be saved. You’re not on the list.
I tattoo people. I could cover a scar. I can’t cover that.
I work a front desk. If you walked in, I’d say we were closed.
I give tours. People would pay to see you. That isn’t a compliment.
I walk dogs. The dogs would bark at you. The calm ones.
I research things for a living. There is nothing in any book about coming back from that.
I write about places to go. I’d tell my readers to avoid you.
I plan events. I’d seat you behind a pillar.
I act. Even with stage makeup, we couldn’t do that to someone.
I’m a student. I’d write a paper about you. I’d never go on a date with you.

SORORITY-01.back: I have a beauty mark everyone loves. You have {botch}. Nobody will ever love that. Not me, not anyone.
jab: I’m Stacey. I decide who gets near this house. You don’t. Not now, not ever.

SORORITY-02.back: I get dimples when I smile. I can’t make them happen looking at you. Nobody can.
jab: In fashion we say you can’t fix a bad cut. I didn’t think it applied to faces.

SORORITY-03.back: I’m six feet tall and I still look down on you. Everyone will, forever.
jab: Legs are kind of my thing. Yours are a tragedy.

SORORITY-04.back: People think my freckles are cute. Nobody will ever think anything on you is cute again.
jab: I study nutrition. There’s no diet for {botch}.

SORORITY-05.back: As chapter president I’m making it official: you’re banned from the house. For life.
jab: I have two different colored eyes and people call it striking. On you, everything is striking. Like a car.

SORORITY-06.back: My hoops are bigger than my patience for this, and my patience is gone. Forever.
jab: I screenshotted your profile on my rhinestone phone. It’s the ugliest thing that’s ever been on it.

SORORITY-07.back: I have a gap in my teeth and it’s cute. That’s the difference between a flaw and a botch. You can’t come back from a botch.
jab: I study psychology. I mostly want to know why you thought this was a good idea.

SORORITY-08.back: I do marketing. I couldn’t sell you. Not on sale, not for free, not ever.
jab: I took my glasses off to look at your picture. It helped.

SORORITY-09.back: I study economics. You’re what we call a sunk cost. You don’t get it back.
jab: I raised one eyebrow at your picture and it hasn’t come down.

SORORITY-10.back: I cut all my hair off once and everybody called me brave. Nobody is ever calling you brave. Nobody is calling you at all.
jab: I study art history. Even the ugliest paintings in my textbook had someone who loved them.

SORORITY-11.back: Back home, when a horse came out like that, there was no fixing it. There was just a long, quiet walk.
jab: I never take my hat off. Get one, and never take it off either.

SORORITY-12.back: I’m Miss Sunfall. In pageants one flaw and you’re out. You’re not out. You were never in.
jab: I have cheekbones you could cut glass on. You have {botch}.

SORORITY-13.back: I have a scar too. Mine’s from a stunt and it’s hot. Yours is from a coupon, and it’s forever.
jab: A scar tells a story. Yours tells a joke.

SORORITY-14.back: I’m the ice queen of the house, and even I feel bad for you. A little. Not enough to ever say yes.
jab: Ballet is all lines. You don’t have a single one going the right way.

SORORITY-15.back: In musical theater we have a word for this. A tragedy. There’s no second act.
jab: You heard my laugh, right? The whole house heard it. That was about you.

SORORITY-16.back: Sisterhood chair here. The sisters voted. It was unanimous. Never.
jab: My smirk is lopsided on purpose. Yours is a whole face.

MATCH-003.back: I like things nobody else likes. Records nobody buys. Chapels nobody prays in. Not you, though. Nobody comes back from that.
jab: I would have taken you somewhere dark and beautiful. Now you’d frighten the bats.

MATCH-020.back: I can fix a bad squat. I can fix a bad back. I can’t fix that, and nobody else can either.
jab: I spot guys at the gym all day. I couldn’t spot you. I couldn’t look.

MATCH-028.back: I cast faces for a living. Yours is cast now. Nobody is ever casting you again.
jab: My client asked about you again. I said you’d retired. It was kinder.

MATCH-042.back: I chair the Bluebird gala. I would seat you in the kitchen, behind the ice machine, for the rest of your life.
jab: Mother has asked me never to mention you at dinner again.

MATCH-010.back: I give money to lost causes. You are the first one I won’t give a cent to.
jab: I have a foundation for nearly everything. Not for {botch}.

MATCH-043.back: I could raise money for almost anything in this town. Nobody would pay to bring you back.
jab: I’m planning a gala. You’re not invited. Sorry, darling.

MATCH-052.back: I fight for lost causes, but I pick ones that can still win. You can’t.
jab: We’re marching downtown on the weekend. Please don’t come. You’d be the only thing in the photos.

MATCH-053.back: I looked it up properly, because that’s my job. There’s no study where anyone comes back from that.
jab: I’m a research assistant. You’d be a fascinating paper. A terrible boyfriend.

MATCH-049.back: I go undercover for a living. You never can again. Everyone will know that face, forever.
jab: I’ve had worse looking suspects. Not many.

MATCH-192.back: I make jewelry out of broken things. Even I don’t use what’s left of you.
jab: I melted down a bad ring last night. I thought of you.

MATCH-163.back: On the radio nobody can see you. Try radio. Nothing else is ever going to work for you.
jab: We did a whole segment on botched surgery. I didn’t say your name. I wanted to.

MATCH-041.back: We’re doing a horror play next month and the director asked if you were free. I said no. For you. That’s the only role left.
jab: I can do a lot with stage makeup. Not that.

MATCH-024.back: Animals come in from the cheap clinic over the border too. They never come back right either.
jab: We have a cone for dogs who won’t stop looking at their stitches. You need one for the whole town.

MATCH-054.back: I’m writing my thesis on bodies and power. You’re a footnote now. Forever.
jab: My seminar group saw your photo. We had a whole discussion.

MATCH-168.back: I’m a photography assistant. I know how to light anything. I can’t light that. Nobody can.
jab: My boss saw your picture and asked if it was for the before-and-after campaign. Just the before.

MATCH-115.back: I keep evidence in boxes for the court. If you were evidence, I’d label you closed. For good.
jab: I see a lot of photos of what people do to each other. You did it to yourself.

open: It’s not as bad as it looks.
then: Give me one date. Just one.
Is there really no coming back?

end: Nobody in Sunfall is going to date you. Not me. Not anyone. Not ever.
Every girl on this app has seen it by now. It’s over for you here.
There’s no version of this where a woman says yes. I’m sorry.
You can keep messaging. Every one of us is going to say the same thing.
It isn’t a phase and it isn’t a bad week. It’s the rest of your life.
You could save a hundred people and marry none of them. Not looking like that.
refuse: Go out with you? Like that? No. Never. Nobody will.
I would rather stay single forever. I mean that literally.
Ask every woman on this app. You’ll get the same answer from all of us.
Not with {botch}. Not with anybody watching. Not with nobody watching.
A date means being seen with you. I can’t be seen with you.
No. That isn’t going to change, so please stop asking.
botched.ruined: There is no coming back from this. No woman in Sunfall will say yes to you now, whatever you do. The game cannot be won like this.
botched.told: Every woman in Sunfall will say the same. Nobody will date you, marry you or take you anywhere like this. The game cannot be won.
botched.questNo: You did it, and the paper says so. But nobody in Sunfall wants to be seen with that face. No win like this.
